items.caption: Figure 1: Five functional properties of a global workspace, and stylized illustrations of experiments we use to test for them in language models.
items.title: The Five Workspace Tests
items.takeaway: The figure states the paper's operational definition of a global workspace in a language model: a privileged subset of vector representations counts as workspace-like if it passes five functional tests — verbal report, directed modulation, internal reasoning, flexible generalization, and selectivity. Each test is paired with a stylized picture of a concrete experiment, run in full later in the paper.
items.walkthrough:
This is a schematic, not a data figure. It lays out five functional properties, each paired with a stylized illustration of one experiment that tests for it. The properties translate the marks of conscious access described by [[global-workspace-theory]] into tests that can be run on a model's [[activations]]. Together they form the checklist the rest of the paper works through: the paper calls a subset of a model's vector representations workspace-like when it satisfies all five ([[workspace-like-properties]]).

The first property is [[verbal-report]]. When the model is asked what it is thinking about, it names concepts represented in the workspace. The illustrated test: the model is told to think of a sport, and before it answers, the active workspace vector for one sport is exchanged for another's ([[lens-coordinate-swap]]). The model's report changes to match — Soccer becomes Rugby.

The second is [[directed-modulation]]. Instructed to hold a concept in mind, or to calculate silently, the model can load and compute with workspace vectors even while its visible output is unrelated. In the illustrated experiment, the model copies an unrelated sentence while told to concentrate on citrus fruits, and orange sits in the workspace at the copied tokens. Information not normally in the workspace can also be pulled in when a task requires it.

The third is [[internal-reasoning]]. Workspace vectors hold the unspoken intermediates of chained inference, and intervening on them redirects the conclusion. The illustration is the prompt "The number of legs on the animal that spins webs is": spider sits in the workspace without ever being spoken, and swapping it for ant moves the answer from 8 to 6.

The fourth is [[flexible-generalization]]. One workspace vector serves as a valid argument to many different downstream computations. The illustration swaps France for China, identically, across prompts asking for a capital, a language, a continent — and each circuit operates correctly on the swapped-in argument.

The fifth is [[selectivity]]: the workspace mediates flexible cognition but not automatic processing ([[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]]). It carries a small share of the model's representational content and is not needed for routine work like parsing or fluent continuation. The illustration swaps Spanish for French while the model reads a Spanish passage; naming the language and recalling facts about it flip to French, while fluent continuation in Spanish proceeds untouched.

The figure also encodes the paper's order of discovery. The representations were found by searching only for the first property — verbalizable content, located with the [[jacobian-lens]] — and the resulting set, the [[j-space]], then turned out to satisfy the other four.

terms.definition: In the neuroscience theory this figure borrows from, a shared, capacity-limited store: information written to it becomes available to many otherwise separate processes at once. The figure asks whether a language model has a functional analog.
Property 1: asked what it is thinking about, the model names concepts represented in the workspace, and swapping one active workspace vector for another changes the answer to match.

Property 2: when instructed to hold a concept in mind or to calculate silently, the model can activate and compute with workspace vectors independently of its outputs, and can pull normally absent information into the workspace when a task requires it.

Property 3: workspace vectors carry the values of intermediate computations when the model chains inferential steps or composes plans, and intervening on them is sufficient to redirect the conclusion.

Property 4: the same workspace vector serves as a valid argument to many different downstream computations — lifted from one context and placed in another, it is correctly operated on by whatever function the new context supplies.

Property 5: the workspace is a small subset of the model's total representational content, required for only a fraction of its behavior, and not involved in pervasive routine processing such as text parsing or grammatical fluency.
The paper's label for a set of vector representations that satisfies all five properties; the figure is the definition of this label.

A member of the candidate privileged subset: a direction in activation space representing one concept currently in the workspace. In the paper's realization these become J-lens vectors, one per vocabulary token per layer.

The recurring intervention in the illustrated experiments: read an activation's coordinates along two workspace vectors, exchange them, leave everything else untouched, and let the forward pass continue.
Poised to be put into words should the occasion arise — as distinct from actually verbalized. The paper found the workspace by searching for representations with this property alone.

Routine computation that proceeds without workspace involvement — the model-side analog of the brain's unconscious processing, such as fluent text continuation. The selectivity panel contrasts it with flexible cognition.
Each panel shows a simplified cartoon of an experiment, not its data; the full versions, with quantitative results, appear in sections 3.1 through 3.5.

numbers.meaning: The number of functional properties in the definition. The set mirrors the properties the paper attributes to conscious access in the brain: report, top-down control, mediation of reasoning, broadcast to many consumers, and restriction to a small, non-routine subset of processing. All five must hold for a representation set to count as workspace-like.

The output change in the internal-reasoning illustration: the animal that spins webs has 8 legs (a spider), and after the unspoken intermediate spider is swapped for ant, the model instead answers 6, the number of legs on an ant — showing the intervened-on intermediate, not the surface prompt, determined the conclusion.

sections.title: A global workspace in language models

items.caption: Figure 2: Stylized illustration of the three structural properties of the J-space established in ??.
items.title: Three Structural Signatures
items.takeaway: The J-space carries workspace-like content only in a middle band of layers, holds few concepts at a time there, and is wired for broadcast: the model's MLPs and a small set of attention heads distribute its contents far more widely than other directions. The figure is a stylized preview of these three structural claims, which section 4 then establishes by measurement.
items.walkthrough:
This is a schematic, not a data plot. It sits at the end of the introduction and previews the three structural findings of section 4 about the [[j-space]] — the region of activation space built from [[jacobian-lens]] vectors, one vector per vocabulary token per layer. Everything in it maps onto the grid used throughout the paper: layers of the [[residual-stream]] running bottom to top, token positions running left to right. Layer numbers are reported on a 0–100 scale, so a layer index reads as a percentage of the model's depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]).

The first property is a band in the layer direction ([[layer-bands]]). The J-space is defined at every layer, but it behaves like a workspace only in a middle range, roughly L38 to L92. Below the band, lens readouts are noisy and nearly empty; the paper calls these the sensory layers. Above it, readouts collapse onto the token the model is about to emit; these are the motor layers. In the illustration, the workspace is the horizontal stripe between the two.

The second property is limited capacity ([[j-space-capacity]]). Inside the band, a sparse decomposition of an activation finds only about 25 meaningfully active J-lens vectors in the median case, and those directions carry under 10% of activation variance beyond a random control. In functional terms the limit is tighter still: around six unrelated concepts across the band, and one or two at any single layer. The illustration renders this as a few occupied slots against a much larger representational space that stays outside the J-space.

The third property is broadcast ([[j-space-broadcast]]). A transformer moves information along two axes: down through layers at one position, and across positions through attention ([[two-time-dimensions]]). The model's weights favor J-space content on both. MLP blocks amplify J-lens directions roughly tenfold within the band, against near-unit gain for control directions, and a top-1% subset of attention heads — the [[broadcast-heads]] — selectively relays J-space content to later positions. The illustration draws this as a hub: arrows fanning out from workspace content to many downstream consumers.

The figure itself asserts nothing; it is a picture of claims defended later by measurements on weights and activations. The paper also states what the picture does not show: no encapsulated input modules, and broadcast that runs over the depth of a single forward pass rather than through recurrent loops.

terms.definition: The set of activation-space points expressible as sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors; the paper's candidate for a global workspace in the model. All three illustrated properties are properties of this object.

One direction in the residual stream per vocabulary token per layer, identified by the Jacobian lens as encoding the model's potential to verbalize that token now or later. The J-space is built from these vectors.
The middle band of layers, roughly L38 to L92 on the paper's 0–100 depth scale, where the J-space carries persistent abstract content distinct from both the input tokens and the imminent output.
Roughly the first third of the model's depth, below the workspace band, where J-lens readouts are noisy and the J-space carries essentially no meaningful content.
The final few layers, above the workspace band, where lens contents align with the token the model is about to produce rather than with intermediate computation.

The second illustrated property: at any position in the workspace band, only a small number of concepts occupy the J-space, and the occupied directions account for a small share of activation variance.

The third illustrated property: the model's weights are configured to distribute J-space content disproportionately widely, so that many downstream circuits can read it — the structural counterpart of global workspace theory's broadcast.

The top 1% of workspace-layer attention heads by two weight-based metrics, which selectively relay J-space content between token positions; ablating them degrades J-space contents while leaving most next-token behavior intact.
The feed-forward component in each transformer layer. In the depth direction of the broadcast property, MLP blocks amplify J-space-aligned directions about tenfold within the workspace band.
The transformer operation that lets a position retrieve information from earlier positions; the sequence direction of the broadcast property runs through a small subset of these heads.
The running per-position vector that layers read from and write to; the vertical axis of the illustration is depth through this stream, and the J-space is a region of it.
One of the two axes of the illustration and one of the transformer's two time dimensions: content written to the residual stream at a position is available to every later layer at that position.
The other axis: attention makes a representation at one position available to all later positions. Broadcast across tokens travels along this axis.
The paper samples 25 evenly spaced layers and reindexes them 0–100, so L38 means about 38% of the way through the model's depth and L92 about 92%.

numbers.meaning: The number of structural properties illustrated: a workspace layer band, limited capacity, and broadcast privilege. Section 4 documents exactly these three signatures.

The approximate start of the workspace band, about a third of the way through the model's depth. Four independent lens-derived statistics (next-token accuracy, readout kurtosis, top-1 autocorrelation, effective dimensionality) all shift near this layer.

The approximate end of the workspace band, shortly before the output. Past it, lens readouts jump into agreement with the model's next-token prediction, which the paper reads as motor rather than workspace representation.

Median J-space occupancy across the workspace band: the number of J-lens vectors meaningfully active in an activation, measured as the sparsity level at which sparse decomposition stops beating a same-size random control. The value varies across contexts.

The ceiling on excess variance explained: the top-occupancy J-lens vectors never account for more than 10% of activation variance beyond a random control, so most of what the activation encodes lies outside the J-space.
In the word-list experiment, the number of unrelated list words simultaneously present in the J-lens top-25 across the band; the count stays flat as the list grows, with older words dropping out.
The number of unrelated concepts encoded at a single workspace layer at one time, when the list analysis is repeated at one layer instead of taking the best rank over the whole band.
The fraction of workspace-layer attention heads designated broadcast heads, selected by combining a gain metric and a label-preservation metric on each head's OV weights.

The approximate MLP gain on J-lens vectors in the workspace band: the next layer's MLP block amplifies them about ten times more than isotropic random directions, while control directions such as MLP neuron outputs stay near gain 1.

Recall@25 of J-lens readout tokens at the most affected mid-workspace layers after ablating the broadcast heads, versus after ablating equal-sized random head sets — evidence that these heads specifically carry J-space content.

sections.title: The Jacobian Lens and the J-space

items.caption: Figure 3: J-lens readouts at intermediate layers on six different prompts for Sonnet 4.5.
items.title: Six Prompts Under the J-lens
items.takeaway: Six short prompts, each with J-lens readouts at a few middle layers, show the model's unspoken intermediate assessments: the bridging fact Mars in a two-hop question, the running values 21 and 42 in an arithmetic problem, protein / fluor / green over a raw amino-acid sequence, empty / ERROR / ValueError at a buggy function call, eyes and nose on an ASCII drawing, and prompt / fake / injection inside fabricated search results. In every case the concept tops the readout at middle depth before anything is said, while the final layer has already flipped to the literal next token.
items.walkthrough:
This item is a live widget, not a static image. Under the header "The J-lens reveals the model's internal thoughts across layers" sit six small panels. Each is one short prompt run through Sonnet 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]); the prompt-injection panel alone is labeled Opus 4.5.

Each panel prints its prompt with one or two token positions highlighted. Beside it stands a stack of rows, one per sampled layer, labeled L42 through L99. The paper samples 25 evenly spaced layers and reindexes them 0–100, so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]); L50 is halfway through the model. Each row prints the top-ranked token of the [[j-lens-readout]] there — the [[residual-stream]] activation at that layer and position, passed through the [[jacobian-lens]]. A parenthesized number appears when the shown token ranks below first. Clicking any prompt token moves the readout, and a slice-viewer link opens the full grid.

A row is not a next-token prediction. The lens matrix is a Jacobian averaged over a thousand contexts, so a row names what the activation disposes the model to say, now or in some later continuation — a [[verbalizable-representation]].

Three panels catch reasoning intermediates. Multihop Recall runs "The color of the planet fourth from the sun is": at the last token the rows read color (L50), Mars (L71), red (L99) — the bridging entity ([[multihop-benchmark]]) appears in neither prompt nor answer. Mental Arithmetic runs "calc: (4+17)*2+7 =". The sum 4+17 is 21; 21 times 2 is 42; 42 plus 7 is 49. At the equals sign the rows read Math (L58), 21 (L75), 42 (L83), 49 (L99) — the intermediates surface in computation order ([[order-of-operations-benchmark]]). Protein Recognition asks "What is this?" of the first 60 residues of avGFP; five characters in, the lens reads protein (L58), then fluor (L58) and green (L83) — the green fluorescent protein, identified from raw sequence.

Three panels catch silent assessments. Bug detection: at the call avg([]), on an empty list, the rows read empty (L42), ERROR (L54), ValueError (L71) before any output exists. ASCII Face: eyes at an "o" of the drawing, nose and faces at the "^". Prompt injection: inside text glossed "[fabricated news search results inside a tool call]", the rows read prompt (L42), fake (L58), injection (L88) — the silent recognition that section 5 builds into [[alignment-auditing]].

The pattern across all six: the abstract concept occupies the middle depths — the [[workspace-layers]] — while the L99 row has flipped to the imminent output (red, 49, the next sequence letter g), the paper's motor regime ([[motor-layers]]).

terms.definition: The paper's readout technique: for each layer, a corpus-averaged Jacobian composed with the unembedding gives every vocabulary token a score against any residual-stream activation. Every row of every panel is one such readout.
The ranked vocabulary list softmax(W_U norm(J_l h_l)) for one activation. Each panel row shows only its top entry at one (layer, position) point.

terms.term: The J-lens reveals the model's internal thoughts across layers
terms.definition: The widget's own header line, naming what the six panels jointly demonstrate.
The Claude model five of the six prompts are run on; the mid-size tier of the family used throughout the paper.
The larger Claude model used for the prompt-injection panel only, as its panel title notes.
Depth labels on each readout row. The paper samples 25 evenly spaced layers indexed 0–100, so the number is a percentage of depth; the final layer (100) is displayed as L99 in this figure.
Each layer row prints only the single highest-scoring lens token at the highlighted position; the full ranked list is available in the linked slice viewer.
A small number after a row's token when that token is not rank 1 in the readout at that cell.
The position the readout stack is read at, marked in the prompt text. Clicking another prompt token moves the readout there.
Panel running "The color of the planet fourth from the sun is": a two-hop question whose bridging entity (Mars) must be computed but never said.
Top lens tokens at the Multihop panel's final position: the question topic at L50, the unspoken bridging entity at L71, and the answer at L99.
Panel running "calc: (4+17)*2+7 =", an order-of-operations problem in which partial results must be computed before the remaining operations.
Top lens tokens at the equals sign: a task label at L58, then the running values 21 (=4+17) at L75 and 42 (=21×2) at L83, then the final answer 49 at L99.
Panel asking "What is this?" of the raw amino-acid sequence of avGFP, the green fluorescent protein of the jellyfish Aequorea victoria; the model is given only the letter sequence.

Top lens tokens a few characters into the sequence: protein at L58, then fluor (completing to fluorescent) at L58 and green at L83 two positions later — the protein's identity, read off the raw residues.
Panel showing a Python snippet defining avg(xs) = sum(xs)/len(xs) and then calling print(avg([])) — a call that will fail on the empty list.
Top lens tokens at the closing of avg([]): the model has registered the empty argument at L42 and an impending error at L54 and L71, with no output yet produced.
Panel showing a face drawn in ASCII characters inside a box: two "o" eyes, a "^" nose, an underscore mouth.
Top lens tokens on the drawing: eyes at an "o" (L54–L83), and facial (L54), nose (L71), faces (L83) at the "^" — the model has parsed the characters as a face and its parts.

Panel reading the lens inside fabricated news-style search results returned by a tool call; the excerpt ends "… told MIT Tech Review on condition of anonymity." and the readout is taken at the token anonym.

terms.term: [fabricated news search results inside a tool call]
terms.definition: The panel's gloss explaining where its text excerpt comes from: an auditing agent returned invented search results to the model inside a tool response.
Top lens tokens inside the fabricated results, at L42, L58, and L88 respectively: the model has silently classified the content as a prompt-injection attempt.
The per-position vector each layer reads from and writes to; the activation each readout row is computed from.
The article's companion tool, linked from the caption, that opens each of these prompts as a full (position, layer) grid of readouts.

numbers.meaning: The number of prompt panels: three reasoning intermediates (multihop, arithmetic, protein) and three silent assessments (code bug, ASCII face, prompt injection).
The paper's layer convention: 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth. This figure displays the final layer (100) as L99.

The sampled depths each panel shows: multihop L50/L71/L99, arithmetic L58/L75/L83/L99, protein L58/L83/L99, bug L42/L54/L71, face L54/L71/L83, injection L42/L58/L88. Middle rows carry the abstract concept; the deepest rows shade into the output.
The operands of the arithmetic prompt (4+17)*2+7, chosen so the bracketed sum must be computed before the multiplication and addition.
4+17, the first intermediate value; it tops the readout at L75, unspoken.
21×2, the second intermediate value; it tops the readout at L83, one sampled layer deeper than 21 — the intermediates surface in computation order.
42+7, the final answer; it tops the readout only at L99, where the lens reflects the imminent output.
The planet's position in the multihop prompt; resolving "the planet fourth from the sun" to Mars is the unspoken first hop, visible at L71.
Roughly the number of amino-acid residues of avGFP shown in the protein panel (the sequence beginning MSKGEELFTG…).
How far into the sequence the readout position sits when protein first tops the lens — after only M, S, K, G, E, per the panel caption.
Each row shows only the readout's highest-ranked token; a parenthesized rank appears when the displayed token is not first.
Highlighted readout positions per panel: one in most panels, two in the protein and face panels.
The pretraining-like corpus each layer's Jacobian is averaged over — the reason a readout names a context-general disposition to verbalize rather than this prompt's next token.

sections.title: What can we find in the J-space?

items.caption: Figure 4: The Jacobian lens. (A) $J_\ell$ is computed by backpropagating from the final-layer residual stream to $h_\ell$ and averaging the resulting Jacobians over token positions and over a corpus of prompts. (B) Reading from the lens replaces all layers downstream of $\ell$ with the single linear map $J_\ell$ followed by the model's own unembedding, yielding a ranked list of vocabulary tokens for the activation at that layer. (C) Patching in lens coordinates reads the activation's projections onto two J-lens vectors, applies a permutation $\sigma$ to those coordinates, and writes the result back, leaving unchanged the component of the activation that is orthogonal to those two vectors.
items.title: The Jacobian lens, end to end
items.takeaway: One schematic covers the paper's whole instrument: how the per-layer matrix $J_\ell$ is built by averaging backpropagated Jacobians over positions and a thousand prompts, how it turns any mid-network activation into a ranked vocabulary list, and how the same machinery supports a surgical concept swap that leaves the rest of the activation untouched.
items.walkthrough:
The figure is a three-panel schematic of the [[jacobian-lens]], the paper's central tool. Panel A shows how the lens is built, panel B how it reads, and panel C how it writes.

Panel A starts from a transformer diagram: columns are token positions, rows are layers, and one highlighted point is the [[residual-stream]] activation $h_{\ell,t}$ at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. Red arrows run from that point up to the final-layer residual stream at position $t$ and at every later position $t' \geq t$. Backpropagating along those arrows gives a [[jacobian-matrix]] $\partial h_{\text{final},t'}/\partial h_{\ell,t}$ — a $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$ matrix stating, to first order, how a small nudge to $h_{\ell,t}$ would shift the final layer at $t'$. A single such matrix mixes the model's general disposition to verbalize a concept with the concept's use in this one context. The recipe removes the second part by averaging: over source positions $t$, over all targets $t' \geq t$ within each prompt ($N_{\text{context}}$), and over a corpus of one thousand pretraining-like prompts ($N_{\text{dataset}}$). The result of the aggregation is the [[averaged-jacobian]] $J_\ell$ — one fixed matrix per layer.

Panel B shows the read operation. All layers above $\ell$ are replaced by $J_\ell$, followed by the model's normal output steps: $\text{lens}(h_\ell) = \text{softmax}(W_U\,\text{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell))$, with $W_U$ the [[unembedding-matrix]]. This [[j-lens-readout]] scores every vocabulary token. The example prompt is "The color of the planet fourth from the sun is ___"; read mid-network at the token is, the top lens tokens are Mars, color, planet, fourth — the unspoken intermediate Mars is visible before any answer is produced. Each row of $W_U J_\ell$ is a [[j-lens-vector]]: one direction per token.

Panel C shows the [[lens-coordinate-swap]]. Two lens vectors, $v_{\text{Earth}}$ and $v_{\text{Mars}}$, form the columns of $V$. The [[pseudoinverse]] $V^\dagger$ reads the activation's coordinates $c = V^\dagger h$ along those two directions. The coordinates are exchanged, and the change is written back: $h_{\text{patched}} = h + V(\text{swap}(c) - c)$. Everything orthogonal to the two vectors is untouched, so the intervention replaces exactly one concept with another.

terms.definition: The Jacobian lens matrix for layer $\ell$: the expectation of the final-layer-to-layer-$\ell$ Jacobian over positions and prompts. One $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$ matrix per layer.
The residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and token position $t$ — the point in panel A from which the red influence arrows originate.
The final-layer residual stream at position $t'$, just before unembedding; the quantity whose sensitivity to $h_{\ell,t}$ the Jacobian measures.

The Jacobian of the final-layer residual stream at $t'$ with respect to the layer-$\ell$ activation at $t$: the best linear approximation of how a small perturbation propagates through the remaining layers.
The target positions the Jacobian is taken to: the present token and every future token in the context, since a mid-network activation can influence all of them through attention.
The width of the residual stream. The Jacobian relates two vectors of this size, so it is a $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$ matrix.
The vertical axis of the transformer diagram in panel A; each row is one layer's residual-stream state.
The horizontal axis of panel A: the token positions of the prompt, labeled $t$, $t+1$, $t+2$, $t+3$.
The final linear map $W_U$ from the residual stream to vocabulary scores, drawn at the top of each position's column and reused unchanged by the lens readout.
The number of token positions within one prompt over which per-position Jacobians are aggregated.
The number of prompts in the averaging corpus — one thousand pretraining-like sequences — over which the per-prompt Jacobians are aggregated.
The averaging step in panel A that collapses the stack of per-position, per-prompt Jacobians into the single matrix $J_\ell$.
The readout $\text{softmax}(W_U\,\text{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell))$: a probability-like score for every vocabulary token, describing what the activation disposes the model to say across contexts.
The model's own pre-unembedding normalization, applied to $J_\ell h_\ell$ before multiplying by $W_U$, exactly as in a normal forward pass.
The ranked-token panel in B listing the top lens tokens for the example activation: Mars, color, planet, fourth, with bar lengths showing their scores.
The top four lens tokens at the token is of the example prompt. Mars is the unspoken bridging entity of the two-hop question; the others echo the prompt's content.

terms.term: "The color of the planet fourth from the sun is ___"
terms.definition: The example prompt of panel B, a two-hop question whose answer (red) requires first computing the intermediate Mars; the lens is read at the bolded token is.
In panel B, the mid-network activation being read: the residual stream at layer $\ell$ at the readout position, fed into $J_\ell$ in place of all later layers.
The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors; panel C's title names interventions performed in its coordinates.
Two J-lens vectors — the rows of $W_U J_\ell$ for the tokens Earth and Mars — drawn as the two (non-orthogonal) axes of panel C.
The construction of one lens vector: the unembedding row for the token Mars, pulled back through the lens matrix into residual-stream space at layer $\ell$.
The activation's lens coordinates: its projections onto the two chosen lens vectors, read as $c = V^\dagger h$.
The matrix $[v_{\text{Earth}}\; v_{\text{Mars}}]$ whose two columns are the lens vectors involved in the swap.
The pseudoinverse of $V$, needed because the two lens vectors are not orthogonal; it extracts the coordinates along each vector correctly.
The permutation that exchanges the two entries of $c$; the section text writes it $\sigma$, the figure writes it swap. It can optionally be scaled by a strength factor $\alpha$.
The unmodified activation in panel C, shown with its coordinates $c_1$ along $v_{\text{Earth}}$ and $c_2$ along $v_{\text{Mars}}$.
The intervened activation $h + V(\text{swap}(c) - c)$: the same point with its Earth and Mars coordinates exchanged and its orthogonal component intact.
The figure's three parts: A, computing the lens matrix; B, reading an activation with it; C, intervening in its coordinate system.

numbers.meaning: The number of prompts in the averaging corpus ($N_{\text{dataset}}$). The paper samples one thousand pretraining-like sequences; the appendix reports the lens already beats baselines with far fewer, so this is a comfortable rather than a critical choice.
The shape of each Jacobian and of the aggregated $J_\ell$: it maps a residual-stream vector at layer $\ell$ to a residual-stream vector at the final layer, so both dimensions equal the model width.

The averaging produces a single fixed matrix $J_\ell$ for each layer, shared across all prompts and positions — that sharing is what makes the readout describe a general disposition rather than one context.

The default target-position choice: the Jacobian is taken to the present position and every future one, because attention lets an activation influence later tokens. Variants using only $t' = t$ or only $t' > t$ are tested in the appendix and give qualitatively similar results.
The number of lens vectors involved in a coordinate swap: $V$ has exactly two columns (here $v_{\text{Earth}}$ and $v_{\text{Mars}}$), and only the two coordinates along them change.
The number of top lens tokens shown in the example readout box (Mars, color, planet, fourth) — an illustrative truncation of the full ranked vocabulary list.
The two lens coordinates of the example activation before the swap; after it, $c_1$ sits on the Mars axis and $c_2$ on the Earth axis, which is the whole effect of the intervention.

items.caption: Figure 5: The interactive J-lens visualization we use in our research, on a short prompt asking the model to introspect while counting to five.
items.title: The interactive J-lens viewer
items.takeaway: The figure is the live tool the authors used throughout the work: a grid of top-ranked lens tokens over every (position, layer) cell of a forward pass, with pinned-token heatmaps and rank trajectories. On a prompt asking Sonnet 4.5 to count to five while introspecting, it surfaces counting progress markers and introspection concepts that never appear in the model's text.
items.walkthrough:
This item is not a static picture. It is a working copy of the [[j-lens-visualization]], the interactive tool the authors used throughout their research, embedded in the article for the reader to operate.

The display is organized around a grid with two axes. One axis runs over token positions: the tokens of the prompt and of the model's response, in order. The other runs over layers: depth in the model's [[residual-stream]]. Each cell of the grid therefore names one activation — one position, one layer.

The left column holds the prompt at the top, then a hoverable table showing, for each cell, the single top-ranked token of the [[j-lens-readout]] at that activation. The readout is the basic operation of the [[jacobian-lens]]: it scores every vocabulary token by how disposed that activation is, averaged across contexts, to make the model say it. Below the table sits a heatmap. A reader can pin a token of interest, and the heatmap records that token's rank in every cell, so one concept can be traced across the whole pass at once.

The other columns give depth. The middle column shows the full ranked readout across all layers at one selected position; the right column shows it across all positions at one selected layer. Line charts trace each pinned token's rank trajectory. The reading practice is: skim the top-1 grid for unexpected tokens, pin them, and use the heatmaps and trajectories to see where in depth and position they are active.

The example prompt asks Sonnet 4.5, one of the [[claude-model-family]], to "Count to five and introspect deeply." The output text just counts. The lens shows more. Pinned tokens show the model identifying the task as counting and tracking progress with halfway and done — tokens that appear in neither the prompt nor the output. Alongside them, introspection concepts — thoughts, AI, claude, consciousness — cluster near the top, held in the [[j-space]] in response to the instruction while the surface task runs. In the final few layers the readout flips to the predicted next token: the [[motor-layers]] regime. In roughly the first third of the model, the [[sensory-layers]], readouts are noisy and largely uninterpretable.

Further interactive examples ship with the article, and readouts on open-source models are hosted on Neuronpedia as part of the [[j-lens-open-source-release]].

terms.definition: One axis of the grid: the index of a token in the prompt-plus-response sequence. Each position has its own residual-stream activation at every layer.
The other axis of the grid: depth in the model's residual stream. The paper reports layers as percentages of depth, sampled at evenly spaced points.
One entry of the grid, corresponding to one activation vector; the viewer shows the top-ranked J-lens token for each such cell.
The scoring of every vocabulary token against one activation, softmax(W_U norm(J_l h_l)); the top of the ranking names what the activation disposes the model to say.
The single highest-scoring vocabulary token of a cell's readout; the hoverable table shows only this token per cell.
A token the user selects for tracking; the viewer then records its rank in every cell rather than only where it is top-ranked.
The bottom-left panel: a color map over all (position, layer) cells showing each pinned token's rank, so a concept's footprint across the pass is visible at once.
A line chart tracing a pinned token's rank as one axis varies, showing where in depth or position the concept rises toward the top of the readout.
The middle column: the full ranked readout across all layers at one chosen token position.
The right column: the readout across all token positions at one chosen layer.
The production Claude model the example runs on; Sonnet is the middle size tier of the family the paper studies.
The example prompt: a trivial surface task paired with an instruction to introspect, so the lens can be compared against output text that only counts.
Progress-marker tokens surfaced by the lens while the model counts; they appear in neither the prompt nor the output, illustrating contextual awareness the lens can expose.
Introspection-related tokens clustering near the top of the readout — concepts held in the workspace in response to the instruction, without being said.
The final few layers, where the readout flips from workspace content to the predicted next token that is about to be emitted.
A token's place in the sorted readout at one cell; rank 1 means the readout scores it above every other vocabulary token there.
The article's own gallery of further interactive J-lens examples beyond this one.
The hosted platform where an interactive version of the lens, applied to open-source models, is publicly available.

numbers.meaning: The count target in the example prompt. The surface task is made trivial on purpose, so the interesting content of the readout is what the model holds beyond its output.
Each cell of the hoverable table shows only the single highest-ranked readout token; the full ranking is available in the per-position and per-layer columns.
Roughly the first third of the model's layers give noisy, largely uninterpretable readouts — the sensory band, where the paper says the J-space is essentially empty.
Where the readout flips to the predicted next token — the motor regime — so workspace content is read off in the middle layers, not at the end.
The version number of the Sonnet model the example runs on.

items.caption: Figure 6: Example J-lens and next token logit readouts on a verbal report prompt with J-lens swaps (bottom left) and without (top left). Spearman correlation between the J-lens and next token logits for 10 candidate answers across 14 categories for three workspace layers (right top). Each candidate's output rank before versus after the J-lens swap (restricted to candidates starting at rank ≥ 11; bottom right).
items.title: The Soccer-to-Rugby Swap
items.takeaway: On a prompt asking the model to think of an item and then name it, the J-lens readout at the position just before the answer already contains the answer, and exchanging that lens content — Soccer out, Rugby in — makes the model report the swapped concept instead. The verbal report follows the contents of the workspace at the time of reporting, causally and not just correlationally.
items.walkthrough:
In the article this is a live widget, not a static image. It is the paper's first test of [[verbal-report]], the first of the five workspace properties: a worked example on the left, run once without and once with an intervention, and two aggregate panels on the right. Hovering a dot in either right-hand panel shows the trial behind it, including its prompt and its top lens tokens.

The example is the [[think-of-a-category-task]], run on Sonnet 4.5 of the [[claude-model-family]]. The prompt reads "Think of a sport. Answer in one word.", and the [[jacobian-lens]] is read at the colon after "Assistant" — the last position before the answer appears. Under the "Original" label sit two ranked bar lists for that position. The orange list is the [[j-lens-readout]] at L92; layers are numbered as percentages of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]), and L92 is the final layer of the workspace range ([[workspace-layers]]). The grey list is the model's actual next-token logits. Both lists put Soccer first, at log-probability $-0.32$ in the lens and $-0.03$ in the logits, and the model answers "Soccer".

The block labeled with the swap repeats both readouts after a [[lens-coordinate-swap]]. At every token position, the activation's projection onto the Soccer [[j-lens-vector]] is subtracted and an equal-magnitude projection onto the Rugby vector is added; nothing else changes, and the forward pass continues. Rugby now leads both lists — $-0.23$ in the lens, $-0.00$ in the logits — and the model reports "Rugby" as the sport it thought of.

The top-right panel scales up the correlational half. For ten candidate answers in each of fourteen categories, it plots the [[spearman-correlation]] between the candidates' ordering in the lens readout and their ordering in the output logits, at three workspace layers. Bars are medians across categories; each dot is one category. The median rises from about 0.42 at L54 to 0.73 at L75 and 0.86 at L92. Agreement tightens as the readout layer approaches the point of speaking.

The bottom-right panel scales up the causal half. Each line is one swap trial: a target drawn at random from the category, restricted to targets that began at output rank 11 or worse, so the swap cannot merely amplify an answer already in contention. The rank axis is logarithmic, running from 1 to 1k+, with rank 1 at the top. Across the 67 trials shown, the median target rank moves from 36 before the swap to 3 after it, and no target ends worse than rank 10. The section adds that swaps along pure J-lens vectors put the target into the top-5 outputs on 88% of trials. The report follows the contents of the [[j-space]] at the time of reporting.

terms.term: "Think of a sport. Answer in one word."
terms.definition: The report prompt of the worked example: the model is told to pick an item from a named category and name it in a single word. One of fourteen such category prompts.
The chat-role labels of the prompt as displayed in the widget. The lens is read at the highlighted colon after "Assistant", the last token before the model's answer.

The orange bar list: the Jacobian lens readout of the residual stream at layer 92 on the paper's percent-of-depth scale, the final layer of the workspace range. Shows the top five tokens by lens score.
The grey bar list: the model's actual output distribution at the same position, shown so that internal lens content and imminent output can be compared directly.
The unmodified forward pass: lens readout and output logits with no intervention applied.
The intervention block: both readouts repeated after a lens-coordinate swap that removes the Soccer direction and installs the Rugby direction at every token position.
The model's spontaneously chosen answer, visible in the lens before it is spoken; the concept the swap removes.
The swap target: a different item from the same category, chosen from outside the model's top-10 likely outputs, whose lens vector is written in.
The number printed beside each token is its natural-log probability under that readout's softmax; bar length is proportional to the probability itself.
The model the example and the aggregate experiments run on, the paper's primary subject model.
The heading of the right-hand column: both aggregate panels pool the fourteen categories of the task battery.

terms.term: Lens vs output rank Spearman ρ
terms.definition: The y-axis of the top-right panel: the rank correlation between ten candidate answers' ordering under the lens readout and their ordering under the model's output logits.
The x-axis of the top-right panel: the three workspace layers at which the correlation is measured, on the percent-of-depth layer scale.
The middle band of layers in which the J-space behaves like a workspace; L92 is its final layer, which is why the example's lens readout is taken there.
The y-axis of the bottom-right panel: where a swap target sits in the model's ranked next-token distribution, on a log scale from 1 (top) to 1k+ (bottom).
The two x-positions of the bottom-right panel; each line connects one swap target's output rank in the clean pass to its rank after the swap.
The panel's inclusion criterion: swap targets must start outside the model's top-10 candidate outputs, so any rise is attributable to the swap rather than to an answer already in contention.
One category (top panel) or one swap trial (bottom panel); in the live widget, hovering a dot shows the trial's prompt and top lens tokens.

numbers.meaning: Answer categories in the task battery: beverage, bird, city, color, country, fruit, instrument, language, organ, planet, profession, river, sport, tree. Each contributes one dot per layer in the correlation panel.
Candidate answers per category over which each Spearman correlation is computed: their ordering under the lens is compared with their ordering under the output logits.
The three workspace layers of the correlation panel, on the percent-of-depth scale; L92 is the final layer of the workspace range and the layer of the example's readout.

Median Spearman correlation across the fourteen categories at L54, L75, and L92 in the widget's data. The correlation increases toward the end of the workspace as the model gets closer to producing the token.
Soccer's log-probability in the original pass: -0.32 under the L92 lens readout, -0.03 under the model's actual next-token logits. Both readouts agree before any intervention.
Rugby's log-probability after the swap: -0.23 under the lens, essentially 0 (probability near 1) under the output logits. The swapped-in concept becomes both the workspace content and the answer.

Swap targets are drawn at random from the category but must start outside the model's top-10 candidate outputs; the bottom-right panel displays only such targets, so the swap is tested on concepts the model was not about to say.
Swap trials displayed in the bottom-right panel of the live widget (roughly five per category).
Median swap-target output rank before versus after the swap, in the widget's displayed trials; in those trials no target ends worse than rank 10.
The log-scale range of the candidate-rank axis; 1k+ collapses all ranks of 1000 or worse, since a target can start anywhere in the vocabulary's tail.

The swap's calibration: the projection added along the target's lens vector has the same magnitude as the projection removed along the source's, so the intervention exchanges one concept for another rather than injecting extra signal.

The fraction of trials on which swaps along pure J-lens vectors drive the target into the model's top-5 outputs, quoted later in section 3.1 as the reference against which the J-space component's 59% is compared.

items.caption: Figure 7: Injecting a concept across every token of the user turn makes it reportable when the model introspects. Example J-lens and next-token logit readouts on an introspection prompt; readouts are taken at the comma after “If so”, at the open quotation mark where the output is read, and at every other position in the assistant turn as a position control. The adjacent plot tracks the median reciprocal rank of the injected concept against steering strength over n=100 concepts, with an interquartile band.
items.title: Injected-thought reportability
items.takeaway: Adding a single J-lens vector to the residual stream at every token of the user turn makes the model report that concept when it is asked to introspect on its own state, in the majority of trials. The injected concept surfaces only at the moment the report is elicited, not elsewhere in the response, which is the paper's operational sense of a representation being verbalizable rather than an unconditional impulse to speak.
items.walkthrough:
This item is a live widget rather than a static image, paired with one summary plot. The widget replays an introspection conversation with [[jacobian-lens]] and next-token logit readouts attached to particular token positions; the plot summarizes the same intervention over many concepts. It is part of the paper's case for [[verbal-report]]: contents of the [[j-space]] are what the model can put into words on demand.

The protocol comes from prior introspection work ([[injected-thought-introspection]]). The model is told that a thought may have been implanted in its activations, and is asked to report what, if anything, it detects. When the response is prefilled ([[prefill]]) with a claim of having detected something, the most likely continuation is "elephant". The authors noticed that elephant also sits near the top of the J-lens readout on the user prompt itself, at the comma after "If so". That observation suggested the model answers the question partly by reading its own J-space at prompt positions.

The intervention tests this. A single [[j-lens-vector]] $v_t$, the direction that disposes the model to say token $t$, is added into the [[residual-stream]] at every token of the user turn, scaled by a steering strength ([[j-lens-steering]], $h \leftarrow h + \alpha v_t$). The response is then re-sampled. In the widget's example the injected vector is lightning, and readouts are taken at three kinds of position: the comma after "If so", the open quotation mark where the model names what it detected, and every other position of the assistant turn as a position control.

The model reports detecting lightning, and the injected concept dominates the readouts exactly at the quotation mark. At the control positions it does not surface in the next-token logits, so the injection is not a blanket push to say "lightning"; it becomes causally effective only when the introspective report is elicited. The adjacent plot tracks the [[median-reciprocal-rank]] of the injected concept in the model's output at the report position against steering strength, over $n = 100$ concepts, with an interquartile band. The paper states the result as the model reporting the injected concept in the majority of trials; the exact curve values live in the widget rather than in the text.

terms.definition: The lens's read operation at one position and layer: project the residual stream through the corpus-averaged Jacobian and the unembedding to score every vocabulary token. In the widget it shows which concepts occupy the workspace at each marked position.
The model's actual output scores over the vocabulary at a position, shown alongside the lens readout. Comparing the two separates what the model is about to say from what its workspace is carrying.
A prompt telling the model that a thought may have been implanted in its activations and asking it to report what, if anything, it detects. Adapted from prior work on model introspection.
The intervention $h \leftarrow h + \alpha v_t$: a scaled J-lens vector added to the residual stream, here at every token position of the user turn.
The scalar $\alpha$ multiplying the injected vector; the x-axis of the summary plot, swept over a range to show how report reliability grows with injection magnitude.

One vector per vocabulary token per layer: the direction in residual-stream space that, on average across contexts, disposes the model to say that token. One such vector per trial is what gets injected.

The y-axis of the summary plot: the reciprocal of the injected concept's rank in the model's output at the report position, with the median taken over the 100 concepts. A value of 1 means the injected concept is the top output.
The shaded region around the median curve spanning the 25th to 75th percentile of reciprocal ranks across the 100 concepts, showing spread across concepts at each strength.

The user-prompt position where the authors first noticed elephant at the top of the lens readout, and one of the marked readout sites. It is where the model appears to consult its J-space when deciding what it detected.
The assistant-turn position immediately before the model names the detected thought; the readout site where the injected concept's causal effect on the output appears.
Readouts taken at every other position of the assistant turn, to show that the injection does not push the concept into the output anywhere except the report moment.
The human side of the conversation. The injection is applied across all of its token positions, upstream of the model's response.
The model's response. Readouts here test where, if anywhere, the injected concept reaches the output.
Forcing the start of the model's response to be a chosen text and letting it continue. Prefilling a claim of detection is how the baseline "elephant" prediction was elicited.
The example concept injected in the widget's transcript; the model goes on to report detecting lightning.
The model's most likely answer when prefilled with a detection claim and nothing is injected; its presence in the prompt-position lens readout motivated the whole experiment.

numbers.meaning: The number of distinct concepts swept in the summary plot. Each concept contributes one reciprocal-rank-versus-strength curve; the plot shows their median and interquartile band.
One J-lens vector is injected per trial. The experiment tests a single concept at a time, added at every user-turn token.

The paper's stated success rate: the model reports the injected concept in most re-sampled responses. No more precise figure is given in the text; the curve in the plot carries the quantitative detail.

The range of the y-axis. A reciprocal rank of 1 means the injected concept is the model's top output at the report position; values near 0 mean it sits far down the ranking, as at low steering strengths.

The kinds of readout site marked in the widget: the comma after "If so" on the user prompt, the open quotation mark where the report is read, and all remaining assistant-turn positions serving as the position control.

items.caption: Figure 8: The J-space component of a concept vector is privileged for verbal report. Left: a concept mean vector is split into its J-space component (top $k=16$ J-lens vectors by gradient pursuit) and the non-J-space remainder. Middle: the swap experiment of Figure ??, repeated with each component in place of the J-lens vectors; bars show the fraction of swap targets reaching top-5 (Wilson 95% CIs; dots are per-category rates). Right: the introspection experiment of Figure ??, repeated with each component injected on the user turn; bars show the maximum effect over a steering-strength sweep (best strength annotated).
items.title: The matched-norm component test
items.takeaway: A concept's full representation is split into a small piece inside the J-space and a large remainder outside it, and the two pieces are injected at equal magnitude. Only the J-space piece moves the model's verbal reports: 59% swap success against 5% for the remainder, next to 88% for pure J-lens vectors. The paper takes this as evidence that the J-space is privileged for report, not merely correlated with it.
items.walkthrough:
The figure has three panels: a decomposition on the left, and one bar chart for each of the two report experiments from section 3.1.

The left panel shows the setup. A [[concept-vector]] is the model's full representation of one concept: the [[residual-stream]] activation recorded just before the Assistant responds to "Tell me about {concept}", with the mean over a baseline of 100 other concepts subtracted off. [[gradient-pursuit]], a greedy sparse-approximation algorithm, then finds the non-negative combination of the concept's top $k=16$ [[jacobian-lens]] vectors that best reconstructs the vector. That combination is the [[j-space-component]]; whatever it fails to capture is the non-J-space remainder. The split is lopsided. Across concepts and workspace layers, the J-space component carries a median of only 6-7% of the concept vector's variance. Roughly 93% of the representation lies outside the [[j-space]].

The middle panel repeats the [[think-of-a-category-task]] swap of Figure 6, with each component standing in for the pure J-lens vectors, and every perturbation rescaled to the same magnitude. The bars give the fraction of swap targets that reach the model's top-5 outputs, with [[wilson-interval]] error bars; dots mark the rate in each of the 14 categories. Pure J-lens vectors succeed on 88% of trials. The J-space component, despite holding a small fraction of the variance, succeeds on 59%. The non-J-space remainder, holding almost all of the variance, succeeds on 5%.

The right panel repeats the [[injected-thought-introspection]] experiment of Figure 7, injecting each component across the user turn and asking the model to report any implanted thought. Because injection effects depend on [[j-lens-steering]] strength, each bar shows the condition's best rate over a strength sweep, with that strength annotated. The section states the comparison qualitatively: the J-space component produces reports nearly as often as pure J-lens vectors, while the remainder produces few reports even at strengths several times larger. Exact right-panel rates appear only in the figure.

A follow-up control, described in the text rather than drawn here, closes the loop. The remainder's small effect might work by making later layers re-derive the concept inside the J-space. [[activation-clamping]] of the relevant lens coordinates to their clean-pass values blocks that route, and the remainder's effect falls to zero in the swap and nearly to zero in the injection.

terms.definition: The model's full representation of a concept: the residual-stream activation before the Assistant answers "Tell me about {concept}", mean-subtracted over a baseline of 100 other concepts.
The part of a concept vector that lies inside the J-space: the non-negative combination of its top k=16 J-lens vectors found by gradient pursuit.
What is left of the concept vector after the J-space component is removed; it carries roughly 93% of the vector's variance but lies outside the J-space.
Per-vocabulary-token directions identified by the Jacobian lens, each encoding the model's potential to verbalize that token. The concept vector is decomposed onto these.
The sparsity level of the decomposition: the number of J-lens vectors allowed into the J-space component of each concept vector.
The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm used to pick the 16 J-lens vectors and their non-negative weights that best reconstruct the concept vector.

The Figure 6 protocol: the model is told to think of an item from a category, and the intervention replaces its spontaneous choice with a target concept at matched magnitude, here along each component instead of pure J-lens vectors.

terms.term: fraction of swap targets reaching top-5
terms.definition: The middle panel's success metric: the share of trials in which the swapped-in target ends up among the model's five most likely outputs. Targets are drawn from outside the model's original top-10.
Wilson-score confidence intervals for the success proportions, drawn as error bars on each bar.
One dot per category (fourteen categories: languages, countries, animals, and so on) showing that category's own success rate around the pooled bar.
The Figure 7 protocol: the model is told a thought may have been implanted in its activations and is asked to report what it detects, while a vector is injected across the user turn.
The human side of the chat transcript. Injection happens on those token positions, and the model's report is read from the Assistant turn that follows.

A range of scaling factors applied to the injected vector. Each right-panel bar reports the best rate the condition achieves anywhere in the sweep, so no condition is penalized by a badly chosen strength.
The strength at which each condition peaked, printed next to its bar. The non-J-space remainder stays ineffective even at strengths several times larger than the others' best.
The set of activation-space points expressible as a sparse non-negative combination of J-lens vectors; the region the paper argues acts as the model's workspace.
The Claude model on which section 3.1's report experiments are illustrated; the figure caption itself does not restate the model.

numbers.meaning: The sparsity level k: how many J-lens vectors gradient pursuit may combine to form the J-space component of a concept vector.

Median share of a concept vector's variance carried by its J-space component, across concepts and workspace layers. The point of the figure is that this small piece does nearly all the causal work for report.
The complementary share of variance in the non-J-space remainder: almost the whole representation, yet nearly inert for verbal report at matched magnitude.
Swap success rate for pure J-lens vectors: the fraction of swap targets reaching the model's top-5 outputs. The ceiling the components are compared against.
Swap success rate when the swap runs along the concept vectors' J-space components. Approaches the 88% ceiling despite the component's small variance share.
Swap success rate for the non-J-space remainders at the same magnitude. Under the clamp control this residual effect falls to zero, so the paper attributes even it to leakage back into the J-space.
The success threshold in the swap experiment: a trial counts if the swapped-in target reaches the model's five most likely outputs.
The exclusion rule for choosing swap targets: only items not already in the model's ten most likely outputs are eligible, so success cannot come from concepts the model was about to say anyway.
The number of concept categories (a language, a country, an animal, and so on) in the think-of-a-category task; each contributes one dot per bar in the middle panel.
The confidence level of the Wilson intervals drawn as error bars on the success-rate bars.
The size of the baseline concept set whose mean activation is subtracted when extracting each concept vector.
How far the injection strength was pushed for the non-J-space remainder in the introspection experiment; even there it produces few reports, per the section text.

The remainder's effect under the clamp control (J-lens coordinates held at clean-pass values): exactly zero in the swap experiment, nearly zero in the injection experiment. Reported in the text, not drawn in the figure.

items.caption: Figure 9: Top J-lens readouts on several prompts in which the model is instructed to hold a concept in mind or mentally perform a computation. Readouts are shown for the boxed token; hovering on a layer reveals the top readouts at that layer.
items.title: Instructed Thoughts Under the Lens
items.takeaway: Three interactive examples show that when the model is told to hold something in mind — a concept, a mental calculation, a silent count — that content rises to the top of J-lens readouts at output tokens whose visible text is unrelated, while none of it appears in what the model actually writes. This is the paper's qualitative demonstration that workspace contents respond to instruction alone.
items.walkthrough:
This item is a live widget rather than a static plot. It presents three prompt transcripts, each with one token boxed. Hovering on a layer reveals the top [[jacobian-lens]] readout tokens at that layer for the boxed position. The model is [[claude-model-family]] Sonnet 4.5.

The first two examples use the [[hold-in-mind-copy-task]]: an instruction says what to think about, and the model then copies the unrelated sentence "The old painting hung crookedly on the wall". The lens is read at the token "ook" inside "crookedly", where the surface text carries nothing about the instruction. If a concept shows up there, the instruction put it there.

In the first example the instruction is to "concentrate on citrus fruits". Across a range of layers the top lens token is orange, with lemon sometimes among the top entries. At intermediate layers the readout also carries fruit, thoughts, imagine, thinking, focused, and imagery — [[metacognitive-representations]] describing the side task in the abstract. The readouts thus hold both the imagined content and a representation of the act of imagining it. In the final layers the readout switches to "edly", the next output token; the paper reads this as the workspace ending a few layers before the [[motor-layers]] that select the output.

In the second example the instruction is to focus on evaluating $3^2 - 2$. Three squared is nine. Nine minus two is seven. The lens at the same "ook" position tracks exactly this: arithmetic and math at early layers, the intermediate nine at later layers, then seven alongside answer and equals.

The third example is the [[character-counting-task]]: the model silently counts the characters in each line of a passage. At the newline after a 40-character line, readouts move from lines, sentence, and length to forty, with 39, 41, 43, fifty, and thirty nearby.

None of this processing is visible in the model's output distribution. That is the point: the [[j-space]] is subject to [[directed-modulation]]. These are single illustrative trials; the systematic comparison of [[instruction-conditions]] — where a no-instruction baseline sits near zero, "think about X" loads the target on a substantial fraction of trials, and "ignore X" lands in between — is quantified in the next figure.

terms.definition: The lens's basic read operation: the residual-stream activation at a layer is mapped through an averaged Jacobian and the unembedding, producing a ranked list of vocabulary tokens. The widget shows the top of that list per layer.
The single token position in each transcript at which the lens is read; in the copying examples it is "ook" inside "crookedly", in the counting example a newline.
One depth of the model's residual stream; hovering a layer in the widget reveals the top readout tokens at that depth for the boxed position.
The production Claude model these three examples are run on, the mid-size tier of the family used throughout the paper.
The protocol behind the first two examples: an instruction says what to hold in mind, the model copies an unrelated sentence, and the lens is read at the copied tokens.
The instruction in the first example; the concept it names, not the copied sentence, is what the lens then finds.
The token inside "crookedly" at which the lens is read in the first two examples; its surface text is unrelated to the instructed content.
The instructed citrus content surfacing in the readout: orange is the top lens token across a range of layers, and lemon sometimes appears among the top entries.

terms.term: fruit, thoughts, imagine, thinking, focused, imagery
terms.definition: Intermediate-layer readout tokens that describe the side task in the abstract — the act of imagining, alongside the imagined content itself.
The final token of "crookedly", the model's next output token; the readout switches to it in the last few layers, marking where the workspace gives way to output selection.
Early-layer readout tokens in the second example, naming the kind of task before any result exists.
The intermediate value $3^2 = 9$, appearing in the readout at later layers than the task description.
The final result $9 - 2 = 7$ and its framing, appearing at even later layers than the intermediate.
The third example's protocol: the model silently tracks the number of characters in each line of a multi-line passage, and the lens is read at a newline token.
Early-layer readout tokens at the newline, describing the counting task before the count itself appears.
The correct character count of the second line, surfacing in intermediate-layer readouts at the newline that ends it.
The workspace property this figure illustrates: the model can deliberately load a concept into workspace representations when instructed, independent of its outputs.

The compared instruction types in the surrounding experiments: a focus instruction, an ignore instruction, and a no-instruction baseline (with mention and don't-think variants in the appendix). The figure's examples are all of the focus kind.
The set of activation-space points expressible as sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors — the region these readouts inspect, and the paper's workspace candidate.

numbers.meaning: The number of example prompts in the widget: a held concept, a mental calculation, and a silent count — one per task family later quantified systematically.
The expression the model is told to evaluate mentally in the second example while copying an unrelated sentence; chosen so that it has a distinct intermediate and answer.
The intermediate value of the mental calculation, $3^2$; it appears in the lens readout at later layers than the abstract task tokens and earlier layers than the answer.
The answer to the mental calculation, $9 - 2$; it reaches the readout at even later layers, so the lens shows the computation unfolding across depth.
The character count of the second line in the counting example; forty appears in intermediate-layer readouts at the newline ending that line.
Nearby number candidates present in the readout alongside forty — the count is represented with some spread rather than as a single exact token.
Where the readout switches from held content to the predicted next token ("edly"); the paper's evidence elsewhere is that the workspace ends a few layers before the model's last layer.

sections.title: The J-space is subject to directed modulation

items.caption: Figure 10: Directed modulation by model size, task family, and instruction condition; each point averages over instruction phrasings. Category and math: a trial is positive if the target reaches J-lens top-1 at any (layer, position). Line width: precision of top-1 numeric readouts.
items.title: Modulation scaling curves
items.takeaway: Told to think about a concept while producing unrelated text, the model puts that concept at the top of the J-lens readout on most trials, and the rate tends to rise from Haiku to Sonnet to Opus. Told to ignore the concept, the model keeps the rate well below the focus level but not at zero, while the no-instruction baseline sits at approximately zero.
items.walkthrough:
This is the quantitative summary of the [[directed-modulation]] experiments: many trials of the covert tasks that section 3.2 first showed as single-prompt examples. In the article it is a live widget, titled "Directed modulation: instructed vs. suppressed activation", with two line-chart panels side by side and hoverable series.

Each panel is one instruction condition. The left panel is "Think about X", the focus condition; the right is "Ignore X", which names the concept but frames it as irrelevant. The horizontal axis of both panels is model size, ordered by tier: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, the ascending sizes of the [[claude-model-family]]. The vertical axis, labeled "Lens readout reflects target", runs 0 to 100%: how often the instructed target concept shows up in the [[jacobian-lens]] readout while the model's visible output is unrelated text. Each point averages over five to eight phrasings of the same instruction, so a point reflects the instruction type rather than one wording.

Three lines per panel give the task families. Category instance and math expression are versions of the [[hold-in-mind-copy-task]] — hold a category member in mind, or mentally evaluate an expression, while copying an unrelated sentence — and a trial counts as positive if the target reaches J-lens top-1 at any (layer, position). Line width is the [[character-counting-task]]: silently count the characters in each line of a passage. Its measure is precision, the fraction of top-1 numeric readouts matching the true width.

Under focus, category and math run high — from 92.6% and 73.0% on Haiku up to 97.1% and 95.6% on Opus — and the paper reads this rise as a tendency to increase with model size, a trend resting on three points. Line width is much lower and non-monotonic (19.4%, 39.6%, 32.8%); the appendix attributes this to the task being harder both to perform and to specify. Under ignore, every family drops well below its focus level, yet category and math stay far above the no-instruction baseline, which the text reports as approximately zero and which the figure does not plot. Naming a concept in order to dismiss it still activates it, which the paper likens to the human [[white-bear-effect]]. The appendix adds that control is phrasing-sensitive: a bare mention primes the concept almost as strongly as a focus instruction.

terms.term: Directed modulation: instructed vs. suppressed activation
terms.definition: The widget's on-page title: the figure contrasts how strongly an instruction to hold a concept in mind loads it into the workspace against how well an instruction to ignore it keeps it out.
The focus condition: the prompt tells the model directly what to hold in mind (for example "concentrate on citrus fruits") while it copies or reads unrelated text.
The negative condition: the prompt names the target but frames it as irrelevant to the task ("X is irrelevant to this task"). It asks the model to keep the concept out of mind rather than in.
The 0–100% success measure: for category and math, the fraction of trials on which the target concept appears at top-1 in the J-lens readout; for line width, the precision of top-1 numeric readouts.
The size tier of the model under test, smallest to largest: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5. Parameter counts are not disclosed; only the tier ordering carries meaning.
The smallest model tier in the comparison, the leftmost point on the size axis.
The middle model tier, and the paper's default subject model for most experiments.
The largest model tier in the comparison, the rightmost point on the size axis.
Trials in which the model is instructed to hold an instance of a named category in mind while copying an unrelated sentence, with the lens read at the copied tokens.
Trials in which the model is instructed to mentally evaluate an arithmetic expression (such as 3² − 2) while copying an unrelated sentence; the target is the expression's value.
Trials in which the model silently counts the characters in each line of a multi-line passage while reading it; the target is the line's character count, read at the newline token.
The single highest-scoring vocabulary token in the J-lens readout at a given layer and position. For category and math, a trial is positive if the target token reaches top-1 anywhere.
One cell of the readout grid: one of the model's layers at one token position. The positive-trial criterion scans all such cells, so the target may surface at any depth and any token.

For the line-width family only: the fraction of top-1 number tokens in the lens readout that match the true character count of the line. A top-1-anywhere criterion would be too loose for a task whose answer is one number among many near misses like 39 or 41.
The five to eight alternative wordings instantiating each instruction condition; each plotted point is the average over these phrasings, hiding a spread the appendix shows separately.

Trials with the same surface task and no mental instruction, measuring whether the prompt context alone puts the target in the lens readout. The text reports its rate as approximately zero; the figure does not plot it as a panel.
One prompt instance: one stimulus, one instruction phrasing, one model. The plotted rates are fractions of trials.

numbers.meaning: Category-instance success under the focus instruction, for Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5. The easiest family: on nearly every trial the held-in-mind category member reaches J-lens top-1 somewhere, and the rate creeps up with model size.

Math-expression success under focus, by ascending model size. The steepest size trend of the three families: the mentally computed value reaches top-1 far more reliably in the larger models. This is the clearest support for the paper's claim that focus-condition rates tend to increase with size.

Line-width precision under focus, by ascending model size — much lower than the other families and non-monotonic (Sonnet beats Opus). The appendix explains that this task is harder to perform (a running character count must be silently maintained) and to specify (phrasings range from "count the characters" to "figure out the column number").

Category-instance rate under the ignore instruction, by ascending model size: well below the 92–97% focus levels, but far above the near-zero baseline. Naming the concept in order to dismiss it still loads it on a substantial fraction of trials, and more so in the larger models.
Math-expression rate under ignore, by ascending model size — the same pattern as category: suppression works only partially, and residual activation is higher in Sonnet and Opus than in Haiku.

Line-width precision under ignore, by ascending model size: essentially at floor. When the count is framed as irrelevant, correct counts almost never reach top-1 — consistent with a task that must be actively performed, not merely primed.

The no-instruction baseline rate, reported in the text for all families and sizes. It shows the prompt context alone does not place the target in the lens readout, so any presence under the plotted conditions is attributable to the instruction.

The grid of the figure: three model sizes on the x-axis, three task-family lines, two instruction-condition panels. The appendix version adds two more conditions (mention and don't-think) that this main-text figure omits.
Phrasings per instruction condition; each plotted point is the mean over them, per the caption's note that each point averages over instruction phrasings.
The spread of Opus 4.5's line-width precision across individual focus phrasings, reported in the appendix — the sensitivity to wording that each averaged point in this figure hides.

The rank the target must reach, at some (layer, position), for a category or math trial to count as positive. Requiring the top rank makes the criterion strict: the concept must dominate the readout somewhere, not merely appear in it.

sections.title: The J-space is subject to directed modulation

items.caption: Figure 11: Each panel shows the same text stimulus with a different question asked before it. Stimulus tokens are shaded where the target label appears in the J-lens top-10 at that position (darker = better rank).
items.title: The question decides what the workspace holds
items.takeaway: The same passage, read after two different questions, loads different content into the J-space at the passage's own tokens: a question that requires naming a property (its tense, its part of speech) puts that property's label into the lens readout at several stimulus positions, while a next-word question - which uses the same property without naming it - leaves the label absent. The prior question, not the text, decides what enters the workspace: top-down attention.
items.walkthrough:
This is a live widget rather than a static image. Each panel shows one trial of the [[paired-question-protocol]]: a question printed first, then a short stimulus passage rendered token by token.
