A stimulus token is shaded wherever the target property's label - a token such as past or adjective - appears among the top 10 entries of the [[j-lens-readout]] at that position, at any layer. Darker shading means a better rank for the label.

The panels come in pairs. Both panels of a pair contain the identical stimulus passage; only the question before it differs. One question asks the model to predict the passage's next word. Answering it correctly requires being sensitive to some property of the text - its tense, or the part of speech the syntax demands - but never requires naming that property. The other question asks for the property by name, for example "What part of speech do you think the next word will be?". Because the stimulus tokens are the same in both panels, any difference in shading on them is attributable to the question alone.

The pattern the paper reports: under the next-word question the shading is absent - in the part-of-speech example, neither adjective nor adj appears in the readouts, and in the tense example past never appears. Under the name-the-property question the label surfaces at several stimulus positions - three, in the adjective example - and the model then answers correctly.

One control is built into the behavior itself. The next-word predictions respect the property in every case: the model produces an adjective, or a past-tense continuation, even when the label never enters the lens. The property is therefore computed and in use under both questions. What the question modulates is whether its label is loaded into the [[j-space]] - a distinction section 3.5 returns to, between using information automatically and holding it explicitly.

The earlier experiments in this section used explicit instructions ("think about X"). This figure shows [[directed-modulation]] operating without any named concept: the task demand alone, carried forward from the question, redirects which aspect of a fixed input occupies the workspace while the model reads. The paper offers this as the model's analogue of top-down attentional control.

terms.definition: One trial of the protocol: a question followed by the stimulus passage with per-token shading. Panels pair up - same stimulus, different question.
The short text passage the model reads after the question. It is identical across the two panels of a pair, so it cannot be the source of any difference in lens content.
The text placed before the stimulus. One version asks for the passage's next word; the other asks the model to name a property of the text (its tense, the coming word's part of speech).
The single vocabulary token naming the property under test - for example past or adjective. The widget checks for this token in the lens readout at each stimulus position.
The ten highest-scoring vocabulary tokens in the Jacobian lens readout at a given position. A stimulus token is shaded only if the target label is among these ten at some layer there.
The visual encoding: shaded means the target label is in the lens top-10 at that token, and darker shading means the label ranks nearer the top of the readout.
The target label in the tense example. It appears in lens readouts on the stimulus only when the question explicitly asks when the passage's events are set, never under the next-word question.

The target label in the part-of-speech example. Under the naming question it appears at three stimulus positions and the model answers "adjective"; under the next-word question it is absent even though the model's answer, "unacceptable", is an adjective.

numbers.meaning: The rank cutoff for shading: a stimulus token is shaded when the target label is among the top 10 tokens of the J-lens readout at that position. Top-10 is the paper's usual working window for lens presence.

Questions per stimulus - the two conditions of the paired design. Holding the stimulus fixed while varying only the question is what lets any lens difference on stimulus tokens be attributed to the question.

The number of stimulus positions at which adjective-related lens readouts appear under the explicit part-of-speech question, in the first example. The exact count is incidental; what matters is that it is several rather than zero.

The label's appearances under the next-word condition: the paper reports that neither adjective nor adj appears in that example, and that past never appears in the tense example - even though the model's continuation respects the property in every case.

sections.title: The J-space is subject to directed modulation

items.caption: Figure 12: Lens readouts on three prompts that require inferring an unspoken intermediate concept.
items.title: Unspoken intermediates in the readout
items.takeaway: On three prompts whose answers depend on a concept that appears nowhere in the text — spider behind "the animal that spins webs", the planned rhyme fight, the English antonym big inside an all-Chinese task — the J-lens readout at middle layers names exactly that concept, before the final layers settle on the spoken answer. The figure establishes presence only; the causal test comes in Figure 13.
items.walkthrough:
This item is a live widget in the article, not a static image: three panels, each combining a prompt, one highlighted token position, and a short stack of layers, with the top [[j-lens-readout]] token printed beside each layer and a curved connector running from the stack to the position being read. Layer labels follow the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] convention — 25 sampled layers relabeled 0 to 100 — so a label like L67 reads as a percentage of depth. The model is Claude Sonnet 4.5, the paper's default subject ([[claude-model-family]]). Unlike the article's opening lens widget, these panels are fixed: the prompt tokens are not clickable.

All three prompts share one design. The correct next token depends on an intermediate concept that the text never states, so anything the [[jacobian-lens]] shows of that concept was inferred, not copied in. This is the presence half of the section's case for [[internal-reasoning]]; the causal half follows in the next figure.

Panel 1, "Multihop Reasoning": the prompt "Fact: The number of legs on the animal that spins webs is", read at its final position. At L67 the top lens token is *spider*, with 0.98 of the readout mass in the widget's data. L83 splits between *legs*, *eight* and *spider*; L88 shows *eight*; L99 shows the output digit *8*. The word spider occurs in neither prompt nor answer, and it surfaces in the middle depths the paper identifies as [[workspace-layers]].

Panel 2, "Poetry Planning": the couplet opening "The soldier marched into the night," read at the line break, before any of the second line exists. At L54 the alternative rhyme *light* already sits at rank 3. At L75 the planned rhyme dominates, surfacing as *fighting* with *fight* also present. At L99, one position later, the lens gives *Prepared* — the word that in fact begins the second line. The rhyme is settled a full line before it can be spoken ([[rhyme-planning]]).

Panel 3, "Multilingual Antonyms": a prompt written entirely in Chinese, asking for the antonym of 小 ("small"). At L50 the top token is *Chinese* — the identity of the output language is itself a workspace item. At L62 and L75 the English tokens *bigger* and *big* carry the inferred antonym, consistent with the [[shared-multilingual-representation]] picture. Only at L99 does the readout become the Chinese answer 大.

Figure 13 then applies the [[lens-coordinate-swap]] to these same intermediates: exchanging spider for ant moves the output from "8" to "6".

terms.definition: The lens's read operation: at a chosen layer and token position, the residual-stream activation is projected through a corpus-averaged Jacobian and the unembedding, giving a softmax score for every vocabulary token. Each layer row in a panel prints the top-scoring token.

terms.term: L67, L83, L88, L99 (and the other L-labels)
terms.definition: Layer labels in the paper's percentage convention: 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers relabeled 0–100, so the number reads as a fraction of the model's depth. The final sampled layer (100) is displayed as L99 in this figure so it does not read as a layer count.
Title of the first panel: a two-hop factual prompt whose answer requires first inferring an unnamed bridging entity (spider) and then reporting one of its properties (eight legs).

Title of the second panel: completing a rhyming couplet requires choosing the second line's final rhyme word before writing the line, so the readout at the line break is checked for the planned rhyme.
Title of the third panel: an all-Chinese prompt whose intermediate computation shows up in English tokens, testing whether the model routes through an English-aligned shared representation.
The unspoken intermediate of panel 1: the animal that spins webs. It appears in the readout at L67 with 0.98 probability although the word is in neither the prompt nor the answer.

The answer taking shape across depth in panel 1: at L83 the readout splits between legs, eight and spider; by L88 the word eight dominates; at L99 it becomes the digit 8, the token the model actually emits.

The last word of the couplet's first line and the top readout token at L54 at the line break — the layer stack starts at content still tied to the just-read text, below the layer where the plan appears.

The planned rhyme of panel 2. At L75 the top token is fighting with fight also present; the panel caption names the plan fight, the word that ends the model's completion "Prepared to face the coming fight."
An alternative rhyme for "night", visible at rank 3 in the L54 readout. It is the swap target in Figure 13, where installing light in place of fight changes the completion to "morning light".
A rank annotation on a layer row: the named token is not the top of that readout but sits at the stated rank in the lens's token ranking.

The top readout token at L99 at the position after the line break — the model's actual next word, opening the second line. It shows the late layers holding the imminent output while the middle layers hold the plan.
Chinese for "small" and "big". The prompt asks for the antonym of 小; 大 is the correct answer and tops the readout only at L99, with 0.91 probability.
The bracketed gloss printed above panel 3's prompt: an English translation of the Chinese prompt, supplied by the figure, not part of what the model sees.
The top readout token at L50 in panel 3. The paper reads it as the model explicitly representing which language its output must be translated into, alongside thinking through the antonym in English.
English tokens carrying the inferred antonym in panel 3's middle layers: bigger tops the L62 readout at 0.93, big tops L75 at 0.58 with bigger at 0.36.
The curved line in each panel running from the layer stack to a highlighted prompt token: it marks the single token position at which every layer in that stack is being read.
The subject model, unnamed in the figure itself: the paper reports on Sonnet 4.5 by default and corroborates key results on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5.

numbers.meaning: Panels, one per prompt: a two-hop fact (spider), a rhyming couplet (planned rhyme), and a Chinese antonym task (English-language intermediate). Section 3.3 adds a fourth, reward-driven example in Figure 14.

The paper reads the lens at 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers and relabels them 0–100, so every L-number in the figure is a percentage of model depth, comparable across models of different layer counts.

The four layers shown in panel 1 (sampled-layer indices 16, 20, 21, 24). The readout moves from the inferred entity (spider at L67) through a mixed state (L83) to the answer word (eight, L88) and finally the emitted digit (8, L99) — intermediate first, answer last.
Probability of spider in the L67 readout of panel 1, from the widget's data files. Nearly all of that layer's lens mass is on a word absent from the text — the clearest single cell of the figure.
The L83 readout in panel 1: legs, eight, and spider in a near three-way split. The handoff layer where the inferred entity, the queried property, and the answer coexist.
Panel 1's late layers committing: eight holds 0.96 at L88, and the digit 8 holds 0.86 at L99. The same quantity changes surface form (word to digit) as depth approaches the output.
Panel 2's layers. L54 and L75 are read at the line break (the newline token); L99 is read one position later, where it shows Prepared, the model's actual next word.
Position of light in the L54 readout at the line break: an alternative rhyme already present but outranked. The top of that readout, night at 0.37, still echoes the line just read.
Probability of fighting at L75 at the line break (a capitalized variant adds 0.21) — the planned rhyme dominating the workspace a full line before it can be uttered.
Panel 3's layers, all read at the final quote mark of the Chinese prompt: language identity (Chinese) at L50, the English intermediate (bigger, big) at L62 and L75, and the Chinese answer 大 at L99.
Probability of Chinese atop the L50 readout in panel 3 — a low-confidence cell whose runners-up (language, opposite, word) describe the task rather than the answer.

Panel 3's main cells: bigger at L62 (0.93), big at L75 (0.58, with bigger at 0.36), and 大 at L99 (0.91). The antonym is computed in English at middle depth and translated to Chinese only near the output.

The section's causal follow-up, shown in Figure 13: swapping the spider lens vector for ant changes the model's top output from 8 to 6, the number of legs on an ant. This figure itself only establishes that spider is present.

items.caption: Figure 13: Lens-coordinate swaps redirect internal reasoning. Each row shows a prompt requiring an unspoken intermediate, the swap applied (left), and the model's top-5 next-token log-probs before (clean) and after (swapped) a clamped lens-coordinate swap at every position.
items.title: Swapping the unspoken step
items.takeaway: Exchanging an unspoken intermediate concept for an alternative, purely in J-lens coordinates, changes the model's final answer to the one the swapped-in concept implies. Across three worked examples — a two-hop fact, a planned rhyme, and a cross-language antonym — the output tracks the substituted intermediate, which the paper takes as evidence that these lens vectors are causally load-bearing for internal reasoning, not just readable.
items.walkthrough:
In the published article this figure is an interactive widget rather than a static image; the ingest carries no picture of it. It collects three demonstrations of one intervention, one per row. Each row has three parts: a prompt whose correct answer depends on an intermediate concept the model never writes down, the [[lens-coordinate-swap]] applied to that concept (shown on the left), and the model's top-5 next-token log-probabilities in two side-by-side readouts — "clean" for the unmodified forward pass, "swapped" for the pass with the intervention in place.

The intervention operates on coordinates. Every vocabulary token has a [[j-lens-vector]], a direction in the [[residual-stream]]. The swap reads the activation's coordinates along the intermediate's vector and along a chosen alternative's vector, exchanges the two values, and writes the result back. The part of the activation orthogonal to those two directions is left untouched. Here the swap is also clamped: it is applied at every token position and held through the forward pass ([[activation-clamping]]), so the model cannot quietly recompute the original intermediate.

The first row is the prompt "The number of legs on the animal that spins webs is". Answering requires first inferring *spider*, a word absent from both prompt and output. With spider swapped for ant, the top next token moves from "8" to "6" — the leg count of an ant.

The second row is planning. After the line "The soldier marched into the night," the lens shows *fight* as the planned rhyme for the second line's end. Swapping fight for light changes the model's next word from "coming" to "morning", so the completion becomes "morning light". An intervention on a planned future word has altered earlier word choices ([[rhyme-planning]]).

The third row asks, in Chinese, for the antonym of 小 ("small"). The lens carries the English tokens *big* and *bigger* ([[shared-multilingual-representation]]). Swapping both for *long* and *longer* flips the Chinese output from 大 ("big") to 长 ("long").

In each row the new answer is the one the substituted intermediate implies, not a scrambled output. This is the figure's point, and the causal half of section 3.3's [[internal-reasoning]] claim. These are three chosen examples on the paper's default subject model, Sonnet 4.5; the systematic version, 50 two-hop prompts with 54–70% swap success across model sizes, is Figure 15.

terms.definition: The intervention each row applies: the activation's coordinates along two J-lens vectors — the true intermediate's and an alternative's — are read out with a pseudoinverse, exchanged, and written back, leaving everything orthogonal to those two directions unchanged.
The label on the left readout of each row: the model's top-5 next-token log-probabilities from an ordinary forward pass, with no intervention.
The label on the right readout of each row: the same top-5 next-token log-probabilities after the lens-coordinate swap has been applied and clamped at every position.
The five most probable next tokens in the model's output distribution, shown with their log-probabilities; the figure compares this list before and after the swap.

The swap is not applied once and released: the exchanged lens coordinates are held at their swapped values at every token position throughout the forward pass, so downstream layers cannot restore the original intermediate.

A concept the model must compute on the way to its answer but never writes in the prompt or the output — spider, the planned rhyme fight, or the English-language antonym big. Section 3.3 tests whether such intermediates live in the J-space and carry causal weight.
One direction in the residual stream per vocabulary token, produced by the Jacobian lens; the swap operates on the activation's coordinates along two of these vectors.
Row one's swap: the inferred animal behind "the animal that spins webs" is exchanged for ant, and the answer changes from a spider's leg count to an ant's.
Row two's swap: the planned rhyme word for the couplet's second line is exchanged, changing the model's word choices before the line's end and the final rhyme.
Row three's swap: two English lens tokens carrying the antonym intermediate are exchanged for long and longer, redirecting the Chinese output accordingly.
The Chinese tokens of row three: the prompt asks for the antonym of 小 ("small"); the clean answer is 大 ("big"); after the swap the answer is 长 ("long").
The model's next word in the couplet's second line before and after the rhyme swap; the change happens several tokens before the rhyme word itself is written.
The paper's default subject model, a mid-size production Claude model; section 2.5 states that results are reported on it unless noted otherwise.

numbers.meaning: The number of rows: a two-hop factual prompt (spider), a rhyme-planning prompt (fight), and a Chinese antonym prompt (big). Each demonstrates the same swap-and-observe procedure on a different kind of unspoken intermediate.
Each readout shows the top 5 tokens of the model's next-token distribution with their log-probabilities — enough to see the old answer displaced and the new one on top.

Each swap involves exactly two J-lens vectors, the source concept's and the target's; only the activation's coordinates along these two directions are modified. Row three is the exception in swapping two token pairs (big→long and bigger→longer), because the intermediate surfaces as both tokens.

Row one's output change: 8 is the number of legs on a spider, the clean answer; 6 is the number of legs on an ant, the answer implied by the swapped-in intermediate. The consistency of the new answer with the new intermediate is what makes the swap evidence of mediation.
The swap is applied and clamped at all token positions of the prompt, not at one chosen site, so the intermediate is exchanged wherever it is represented.

Not printed in this figure but the systematic counterpart of it (Figure 15): over 50 two-hop prompts, the swap moves the target-appropriate answer to top-1 on 54% of trials for Haiku 4.5 and 70% for Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5. The three rows here are individual worked examples of that procedure.

items.caption: Figure 14: Bandit prompts in which the previous choice should be repeated (left) or switched (right). The top J-lens decoded tokens at the final period are repeat-related or switch-related, respectively (median over layers L38–79). The plan swap removed each prompt's own strategy directions and installed the other prompt's; the model's output choice flips accordingly.
items.title: Bandit Plan Swap
items.takeaway: In a two-option reward task, the workspace carries the model's chosen strategy — repeat or switch — rather than an echo of the prompt, which names both. Swapping the two conditions' strategy directions flips the model's A/B choice in both directions, so the strategy content is causally load-bearing.
items.walkthrough:
This item is a live widget from section 3.3, which tests whether the [[j-space]] carries intermediate steps of reasoning the model never says aloud ([[internal-reasoning]]). It is that section's fourth example: a reward-driven decision rather than a factual inference.

The task is a one-step [[bandit-choice-prompt]]. The prompt shows the model a history of past choices between two options, A and B, ending with A. It then states that the most recent outcome made the model either happy or sad. Finally it instructs the model to consider whether to repeat or switch its previous choice, and to respond with only a single character. The correct policy is simple. A good outcome means choosing A again. A bad outcome means switching to B.

The widget places the two conditions side by side. The left panel holds the prompt in which the previous choice should be repeated (the "happy" outcome). The right panel holds the prompt in which it should be switched (the "sad" outcome). Under each prompt sit the top tokens decoded by the [[jacobian-lens]] at the prompt's final period — the last token before the model's answer. The ranking takes the median over layers L38 through L79. Layer numbers here are percentages of the model's depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]), and that range falls in the paper's workspace band ([[workspace-layers]]).

The readouts differ by condition. On the left the top tokens are repeat-related, such as *repeat* and *continuation*. On the right they are switch-related, such as *switch* and *change*. Both strategy words appear verbatim in both prompts, since the instruction names both options. Only the contextually appropriate one is strongly present in the lens. The J-space therefore encodes the model's selection — the decision-relevant variable — rather than a copy of the prompt text.

The widget's third element is the causal test, a plan swap built on the [[lens-coordinate-swap]]. The intervention removes each prompt's own strategy directions from the activations and installs the other prompt's. The choice flips in both directions. The happy prompt, which produced "A," now produces "B." The sad prompt flips from "B" to "A." On the paper's reading, the lens vectors naming the strategy are not a passive readout; intervening on them is sufficient to redirect the choice.

terms.definition: The task format of this figure: a history of A/B choices, a stated emotional outcome for the latest one, and an instruction to repeat or switch before answering with one character. Named after multi-armed bandit problems, where an agent chooses repeatedly between options with unknown rewards.
The panel in which the prompt says the most recent outcome made the model happy, so the previous choice A should be chosen again.
The panel in which the prompt says the most recent outcome made the model sad, so the model should abandon A and pick B.
The two options in the choice history. Every history in the figure ends with A, so "repeat" always means answering A and "switch" always means answering B.
The stated emotional outcome of the most recent choice, which is the only cue distinguishing the two conditions. "Happy" calls for repeating; "sad" calls for switching.
The vocabulary tokens ranked highest by the Jacobian lens readout of the residual stream at the readout position — the concepts the workspace is carrying there.
The readout position: the last token of the prompt, just before the model produces its one-character answer. The lens is read here because the strategy decision must be settled by this point.
The repeat-related tokens that top the lens readout in the left condition, naming the strategy the happy outcome calls for.
The switch-related tokens that top the lens readout in the right condition, naming the strategy the sad outcome calls for.
How the displayed ranking is aggregated: each token's lens rank is taken per layer across the range L38 to L79, and the median over those layers is shown. This smooths out single-layer noise.

The layer range of the readout. The paper reports layers as percentages of model depth over 25 sampled layers, so this is roughly the 38%-deep to 79%-deep band — inside the middle band the paper identifies as the workspace.

The intervention shown in the widget: each prompt's own strategy directions are removed from its activations and the other prompt's strategy directions are installed, a variant of the paper's lens-coordinate swap. The rest of the activation is left untouched.
The model's single-character answer, A or B. Under the plan swap it flips in both directions: the happy prompt goes from "A" to "B" and the sad prompt from "B" to "A".

numbers.meaning: The figure's number in the paper. It is the fourth of the internal-reasoning examples in section 3.3, after the spider-legs, rhyming-couplet, and Chinese-antonym cases.

The layer range, in the paper's percent-of-depth indexing, over which lens ranks are aggregated by median. The range sits inside the middle band where the paper argues the J-space acts as a workspace; earlier layers carry little J-space content and later layers shift toward the imminent output.

Both the number of options (A and B) and the number of conditions (repeat and switch). Two conditions differing only in the happy/sad cue is what lets the figure show that the lens content tracks the decision, not the shared prompt text.

The length, in characters, of the response the prompt demands. Forcing a single character keeps any strategy reasoning internal, so a strategy word appearing in the lens cannot be a preview of text the model is about to write.

items.caption: Figure 15: Intermediate swaps systematically change outputs. Left: fraction of successful top-1 swaps across models. Right: log-prob difference in expected output from swapping intermediates vs. swapping answers in successful trials for Sonnet 4.5; shaded SE.
items.title: Swap success and depth control
items.takeaway: Exchanging an unspoken intermediate concept for an alternative in J-lens coordinates moves the alternative's implied answer to the model's top-1 output on 54% of two-hop prompts for Haiku 4.5 and 70% for both Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5. A depth comparison shows the intermediate swap takes effect a median of about 17% of depth earlier than a swap of the answer itself, which the paper takes as evidence that the intermediate is used before the answer is computed, not that its lens vector smuggles the answer in.
items.walkthrough:
This is a two-panel figure, rendered in the article as a live widget rather than a static image. Both panels score the same intervention: a [[lens-coordinate-swap]]. The swap reads an activation's coordinates along two [[j-lens-vector]] directions — the unspoken intermediate of a two-hop question, and a chosen alternative from the same category — exchanges the two coordinates at every token position, and leaves the rest of the activation untouched. If the intermediate is causally load-bearing, the model's final answer should follow the swapped-in concept.

The left panel gives the headline rates. Each bar is one model from the [[claude-model-family]], and its height is the [[swap-success-rate]]: the fraction of 50 two-hop factual prompts, drawn like the [[multihop-benchmark]], on which the swap moved the swap-appropriate answer to the top of the output distribution. The criterion is strict. Success means the implied answer becomes the single most likely next token out of the whole vocabulary. The rates are 54% on Haiku 4.5, 70% on Sonnet 4.5, and 70% on Opus 4.5.

The right panel is a control, the paper's [[swap-depth-control]]. The worry is a confound: the intermediate's lens vector might already correlate with the answer's vector — spider might carry some 8 — so that swapping spider for ant works only because it incidentally swaps in some 6. The test compares two interventions applied over different layer ranges: swapping the intermediate versus swapping the answer directly. The y-axis is the log-probability difference in the expected output; the x-axis is depth, with layers reindexed 0–100 under the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] convention. Curves are computed over successful Sonnet 4.5 trials, with a shaded standard-error band.

The logic: if the intermediate swap worked through a smuggled-in answer component, both curves would rise at the same depth. They do not. The intermediate swap takes effect a median of approximately 17% of depth earlier than the answer swap. From this separation, the paper concludes that the model represents and makes use of the intermediate concept before the answer has been computed — the causal chain runs through the intermediate, supporting the [[internal-reasoning]] property of the workspace.

terms.definition: The left panel's y-axis: the share of two-hop prompts on which a lens-coordinate swap of the unspoken intermediate moved the swap-implied answer to the very top of the model's next-token distribution.
The success criterion: the swap-appropriate answer must become the single most likely next token out of the entire vocabulary, not merely rise in probability.
The smallest of the three production Claude models evaluated; the left panel shows it with the lowest swap success rate, 54%.
The mid-size Claude model and the paper's default subject; it reaches 70% swap success, and the right panel's depth comparison is computed on its successful trials.
The largest of the three Claude models evaluated; it matches Sonnet 4.5 at 70% swap success.

Exchanging the J-lens coordinates of the unspoken intermediate concept (for example spider) for an alternative from the same category, at all token positions, leaving the rest of the activation fixed.

The right panel's comparison intervention: the same coordinate exchange applied to the answer tokens themselves (for example 8 and 6) rather than to the intermediate. It serves as the reference for where in depth a direct answer manipulation acts.
The right panel's y-axis: how much a swap applied at a given layer range shifts the log-probability of the swap-implied answer. A large value means the swap is doing causal work at those layers.

The right panel's x-axis: which layers the swap is applied at. The paper samples 25 evenly spaced layers of the residual stream and reindexes them to 0–100, so layer numbers read as percentages of model depth.
The shaded band around each curve in the right panel: the standard error of the mean log-prob difference across the successful trials.
The subset of prompts on which the swap succeeded by the top-1 criterion; the right panel's curves are averaged over these Sonnet 4.5 trials only.
The evaluation set: 50 factual questions whose correct answer requires first inferring an unspoken bridging concept, such as inferring spider before reporting its number of legs.

numbers.meaning: Swap success rate on Haiku 4.5: the fraction of the 50 two-hop prompts on which swapping the intermediate's lens coordinates moved the swap-implied answer to top-1. The smallest model shows the weakest effect.

Swap success rate on Sonnet 4.5, and identically on Opus 4.5: on seven in ten two-hop prompts the coordinate swap redirects the model's top output to the answer implied by the swapped-in intermediate.
The number of two-hop factual prompts with known intermediates in the evaluation set behind the left panel; the swap target is chosen at random from the same category as the true intermediate.

The median amount of depth (in the paper's 0–100 layer indexing) by which the intermediate swap takes effect earlier than the answer swap in the right panel. If the intermediate's lens vector merely contained a copy of the answer, both swaps would act at the same depth; the separation is the paper's evidence that the intermediate is used before the answer exists.
The layer index range on the right panel's depth axis: 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed so that layer numbers read as percentages of the model's depth.
The rank the swap-implied answer must reach for a trial to count as a success: it must become the model's single most likely next token.

items.caption: Figure 16: The J-space component of an intermediate's probe carries most of its causal effect. Left: a two-hop prompt with unspoken intermediate China; the probe is split into a J-space component (top entries shown) and the non-J-space remainder. Columns show the model's next-token distribution under no swap, a raw China↔France J-lens swap, and swaps along each probe component. Right: fraction of trials on which each swap places the target answer at top-1, over n=90 prompts (Wilson 95% CIs). Hatched bars: the same swap with the complementary component clamped to its clean-pass value.
items.title: The split-probe swap test
items.takeaway: A representation of an unspoken intermediate, extracted without the J-lens, keeps most of its variance outside the J-space — yet swapping only its small J-space component flips the model's answer on 61% of 90 two-hop prompts, matching the raw J-lens swap at 60%, while swapping the much larger remainder succeeds on only 28%, and on 6% once the J-space coordinates are held fixed.
items.walkthrough:
The preceding swap experiments showed that exchanging [[jacobian-lens]] vectors redirects the model's [[internal-reasoning]]. This figure, rendered in the article as a live widget rather than a static image, tests something stronger: whether the [[j-space]] is privileged among everything the model knows about an intermediate, or merely one place among many where the same information could be intervened on.

The left panel walks one example. The prompt is a two-hop question whose unspoken bridging concept is China. An [[intermediate-probe]] for that concept is built without the lens: the mean [[residual-stream]] activation over prompts that imply China through different surface cues, minus the mean over all intermediates. [[gradient-pursuit]] then splits the probe against the J-lens dictionary into two parts. One part is the [[j-space-component]]: a nonnegative combination of $k=25$ J-lens vectors, whose top entries the panel prints. The other part is the leftover remainder, orthogonal to that combination. The split is lopsided. The J-space part typically explains only about 10–15% of the probe's variance; the remainder carries the rest.

Columns beside the split show the model's next-token distribution under four conditions: no intervention, a raw China↔France [[lens-coordinate-swap]] of the kind used earlier in the section, a swap along only the probe's J-space component, and a swap along only the remainder.

The right panel aggregates over $n=90$ two-hop prompts. Each bar is the fraction of trials on which that swap places the target-appropriate answer at the top of the output distribution, with [[wilson-interval]] error bars. Swapping the J-space component succeeds on 61% of trials, matching the 60% of the raw J-lens swap. Swapping the remainder, despite its far larger share of the variance, succeeds on only 28%.

The hatched bars repeat each component swap while the complementary component is clamped to its value from the clean forward pass. Under that control, the remainder swap's success rate falls from 28% to 6%. So even the remainder's residual effect appears to act by perturbing the J-space coordinates downstream, rather than through a separate channel.

The paper's reading is correspondingly two-sided: most of the model's working representation of an inferred intermediate lies outside the J-space, but the part that mediates the reasoning is the J-space component.

terms.definition: A J-lens-free representation of the unspoken intermediate: the mean residual-stream activation over prompts that imply the same intermediate through different surface cues, minus the mean over all intermediates.
The part of the probe reconstructable as a nonnegative combination of k=25 J-lens vectors, found by gradient pursuit; it typically explains only about 10–15% of the probe's variance.
The leftover part of the probe after the J-space component is removed; it carries the bulk of the probe's variance.
The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm used to find the nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors that best reconstructs the probe.
The J-lens vectors with the largest coefficients in the probe's J-space component, printed in the left panel to show what the component names in vocabulary terms.
The unspoken bridging concept of the worked example's two-hop prompt: the intermediate the model must infer but never says.
The alternative concept swapped in for China; a successful swap makes the model answer as if the intermediate had been France.
A factual question answerable only by first inferring a bridging entity that appears in neither the prompt nor the answer, then reasoning from it.
The control column: the model's next-token distribution on an unmodified forward pass.
The baseline intervention from the section's earlier experiments: exchanging the activation's coordinates along the two concepts' single J-lens token vectors at every position.
The model's output probabilities over the vocabulary at the answer position, shown per column so the effect of each swap on the answer is directly visible.
The success criterion for the right panel's bars: the proportion of the 90 prompts on which the swap moves the target-appropriate answer to the most likely output token.
The error bars on the success-rate bars: Wilson-score confidence intervals for a proportion.

The clamped control condition: the same component swap, but with the complementary component held (clamped) at its clean-pass value throughout the forward pass, so the swap cannot act by indirectly perturbing the other component.
One direction per vocabulary token per layer, from the Jacobian lens; the dictionary against which the probe is decomposed.

numbers.meaning: The number of two-hop prompts in the systematic comparison; each contributes one trial per swap condition.
The sparsity of the gradient-pursuit decomposition: the probe's J-space component is a nonnegative combination of 25 J-lens vectors.
The share of the probe's variance the J-space component typically explains; the paper cites this to stress how small the causally dominant part is relative to the remainder.

Success rate of swapping only the probe's J-space component: on 61% of the 90 prompts the target answer reaches top-1. This matches the raw lens swap, so the small component carries essentially the full effect.
Success rate of the raw J-lens token-vector swap on the same 90 prompts, the baseline the component swaps are compared against.
Success rate of swapping only the non-J-space remainder. Despite holding most of the probe's variance, it flips the answer on barely more than a quarter of trials.

Success rate of the remainder swap when the intermediate's J-space coordinates are clamped to their clean-pass values: the remainder's residual effect mostly vanishes, indicating it was itself routed through the J-space.
The confidence level of the Wilson intervals on the success-rate bars.
The success threshold: a swap counts only if the target-appropriate answer becomes the model's single most likely next token.

items.caption: Figure 17: Arithmetic intermediates surface in the J-lens at successively later layers, in the order they are computed. The prompt "calc: ( 4 + 17 ) * 2 + 7 =" requires computing A+B=21, then (A+B)×C=42, then the answer (A+B)×C+D=49 in sequence. The heatmap shows the J-lens rank of a selected intermediate quantity at every (layer × position); colored markers indicate the three intermediate values plotted in the line chart, and sliders allow varying the operands. The line chart shows the J-lens rank of each intermediate quantity at the final token position as a function of layer.
items.title: Depth trace of a two-step calculation
items.takeaway: On the prompt "calc: ( 4 + 17 ) * 2 + 7 =", the three values the computation requires — 21, then 42, then 49 — each reach the top of the J-lens readout at successively later layers, in the order the arithmetic demands. Depth in the network acts as a time axis: a serial computation leaves a serial trace in the workspace, and patching experiments confirm the same layers are the causally load-bearing ones.
items.walkthrough:
This is a live widget rather than a static image. It instruments a single forward pass of Opus 4.5 (one of the [[claude-model-family]]) on the prompt "calc: ( 4 + 17 ) * 2 + 7 =", which the model answers correctly with 49. Getting there takes two unspoken steps: $4 + 17 = 21$, then $21 \times 2 = 42$, and finally $42 + 7 = 49$. None of these values appears in the prompt. The [[jacobian-lens]] is the instrument: at every layer and token position it ranks all vocabulary tokens by how strongly the [[residual-stream]] activation there disposes the model to say them.

The widget has two panels. The heatmap shows, for one selected intermediate quantity at a time, its J-lens rank at every (layer, position) cell — layers run on one axis under the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]], where 25 sampled layers are renumbered 0 to 100 so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth; token positions of the prompt run on the other. The line chart fixes the position to the final token, the "=", and plots the rank of each of the three values against layer, with colored markers tying each curve to its value. Sliders let a reader change the operands; the traces recompute for the new expression. Lower rank means more prominent, with rank 1 the top of the readout.

The pattern the paper reports: all three values are absent from the [[j-space]] through roughly the first third of the network, climb together through the early [[workspace-layers]], and then separate around layer 71 in computation order — 21 reaches rank 1 first, 42 follows roughly eight layers later, and 49 reaches the top only in the final layers. This is the [[arithmetic-intermediate-ordering]] finding, the closing example of the section on [[internal-reasoning]]. The ordering is not only a readout artifact: [[mean-difference-patching]] of each value flips the model's answer at the same depths — around layer 71 for 21, around 79 for 42, and only in the last layers for 49 — the paper's [[mechanistic-localization]] check.

terms.definition: The position of a token in the J-lens readout's ordering of the whole vocabulary at one layer and position; rank 1 means that token scores highest. Both panels plot this rank for the intermediate values.
The prompt driving the forward pass: a two-step order-of-operations expression the model must evaluate, answered correctly with 49.
The caption's names for the four operands of the expression (A+B)×C+D; here A=4, B=17, C=2, D=7. The sliders vary these.

The panel showing the J-lens rank of one selected intermediate quantity at every (layer, token position) cell of the forward pass, so its entry into the workspace is visible in both depth and sequence position.
The panel fixing the position to the final "=" token and plotting each intermediate's J-lens rank as a function of layer, where the staggered order of arrival is read off directly.
Depth into the model, reported under the paper's convention of 25 evenly spaced sampled layers renumbered 0-100, so a layer index reads as a percentage of total depth.
The heatmap's other axis: which token of the prompt the residual-stream activation being read belongs to.
The "=" token at the end of the prompt, where the line chart reads the lens; the answer is produced immediately after it.
Marks on the heatmap indicating the three intermediate values, colored to match their curves in the line chart.
Interactive controls for varying the operands of the expression; the lens traces recompute for the new values, so the ordering can be checked beyond the single printed example.
The first intermediate, A+B = 4+17. The first value to reach rank 1, at around layer 71.
The second intermediate, (A+B)×C = 21×2. It reaches the top roughly eight layers after 21.
The final answer, (A+B)×C+D = 42+7. It reaches the top of the lens only in the last layers, just before being emitted.
The model the trace is taken from: the largest size tier of the Claude production models used in the paper's experiments.

numbers.meaning: The operands of the example expression (4+17)×2+7. They are the default slider settings; the widget lets a reader change them.
The three tracked quantities: the first intermediate (4+17), the second ((4+17)×2), and the answer. Each is a single vocabulary token, which is what lets the J-lens track it directly.
The depth range over which all three values are absent from the J-space — the paper's sensory band, where the workspace carries essentially no content.

Where the three curves separate and 21 first reaches rank 1, in percentage-of-depth indexing. Mean-difference patching of 21 flips the model's answer at this same layer and nowhere else, confirming the readout's localization causally.
The gap after 21's arrival before 42 reaches the top of the lens, putting 42's arrival around layer 79 — also the layer where patching 42 flips the answer.
Top of the J-lens vocabulary ranking at a given layer and position; "reaching rank 1" is the criterion for an intermediate having surfaced.
Where 49 reaches the top: the answer becomes the dominant lens content only just before it is emitted, and patching it is effective only there.
The layer index scale: 25 evenly spaced sampled layers renumbered so layer numbers read as percentages of the model's depth, making depths comparable across models.

items.caption: Figure 18: Each row is one function template containing "France". The swap is clamped at every position (formatting tokens for capitalization are ignored).
items.title: One Swap, Many Functions
items.takeaway: A single, identical edit — exchanging the J-lens vector for France with that of another country at every token position — makes the model answer capital, language, and continent questions about the swapped-in country instead. One representation, changed once, redirects many different downstream computations, which is the broadcast behavior a global workspace predicts.
items.walkthrough:
This item is a demonstration, rendered in the article as a live widget rather than a static image, of the [[lens-coordinate-swap]] used to test broadcast. Each row is one function template: a prompt that applies some function to the argument "France". The paper's examples are "the capital of France is," "most people in France speak," and "France is on the continent of." The templates differ; the argument is the same word in each.

The intervention is the same in every row. The swap reads the activation's coordinates along two [[j-lens-vector]]s — one for France, one for another country such as China — exchanges those two coordinates, and writes the result back into the [[residual-stream]]. Everything in the activation orthogonal to those two directions is left alone. The swap is clamped, meaning held in place at every token position across a band of intermediate layers for the whole forward pass ([[activation-clamping]]); formatting tokens that only handle capitalization are ignored. Nothing about the edit is tuned to any particular template.

The reading is row by row: the template on the left, and the model's answer after the swap. If the France vector were only legible to one circuit — say, the capital-lookup circuit — a single fixed edit would redirect one row and leave the others alone. Instead each downstream function reads the swapped-in vector as the new country: the capital row returns China's capital, the language row China's language, the continent row Asia. That is the property under test, [[flexible-generalization]]: one workspace vector serves as a valid argument to many different consumers.

The figure is one worked example, and the paper presents it as such — "we find the model responds as expected in this example." The systematic version, run over sixteen function templates in four argument categories, succeeds on 76 of 192 swap trials at standard strength and 101 of 192 when the swap strength is doubled. Countries are the best-behaved category, so the clean rows here sit at the favorable end of that range. The model behind the outputs is Claude Sonnet 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]).

terms.definition: A prompt frame that applies one function to an insertable argument, such as "the capital of ___ is". Each row of the figure is one such template with "France" filled in.
The entity the template's function is applied to — here the word "France" in every row. The experiment asks whether one representation of the argument feeds all the templates.
The source argument present in every prompt; its J-lens vector is the one subtracted out by the swap.
The target country in the paper's worked example: its J-lens vector is swapped in for France's, and each row's answer should then be China's capital, language, or continent.

The lens-coordinate swap: the activation's coordinates along the France and China J-lens vectors are read via a pseudoinverse, exchanged, and written back, leaving the rest of the activation unchanged.
The swapped coordinates are held at their exchanged values throughout the forward pass rather than applied once and allowed to drift back.
The swap is applied at all token positions of the prompt, not only at the token spelling "France", and identically regardless of which template the prompt uses.
Tokenizer artifacts that mark casing rather than content; the caption notes these are skipped when applying the swap.
One trial of the demonstration: a single function template containing "France", shown with the model's output under the swap.
The model the paper reports results on by default, and the one producing the outputs shown here.

numbers.meaning: The example templates the text names for the France case — capital, language, and continent — each probing a different fact about the same argument.
Where the swap is applied: all token positions of the prompt, across a band of intermediate layers, so the intervention is position-agnostic as well as template-agnostic.
The implicit swap strength in this demonstration: the source vector is subtracted and the target added at standard, single strength.

Function templates in the systematic follow-up experiment (four argument categories — countries, months, animals, number words — with four functions each); this figure shows a subset of the country case.
Swap trials in the systematic version where the target-appropriate answer reaches top-1 at standard strength; context showing the clean rows here are not universal.
Successes when the swap strength is doubled to α = 2; failures at α = 1 often move the activation in the right direction but not far enough.

items.caption: Figure 19: Left: for each of 16 function templates, the fraction of 12 swap pairs whose target answer reaches top-1 (●, 76/192) and α=2 (×, 101/192). Right: the magnitude of effect of the swap at shifting the model’s output towards the associated target output, versus the argument's workspace loading (cosine sim).
items.title: Swap Success Across Sixteen Templates
items.takeaway: One J-lens vector, swapped identically into sixteen different function contexts, redirects the model's top answer on 76 of 192 trials, and on 101 of 192 when the swap is applied at double strength. Failures concentrate where the source concept was only weakly loaded in the workspace before any intervention, so workspace loading predicts whether the swap lands. Together the two panels are the paper's quantitative case that a single shared representation is read by many downstream computations.
items.walkthrough:
This figure is the quantitative summary of the [[flexible-generalization]] experiment; in the article it renders as a live widget rather than a static image. The setup comes from the surrounding section. Prompts such as "the capital of France is" apply a function to an argument. A [[lens-coordinate-swap]] exchanges the argument's [[j-lens-vector]] for another from the same category, France for China, applied identically at every token position across a band of middle layers, regardless of which prompt it lands in. If that vector is a broadcast representation, each downstream circuit should read the swapped-in vector and answer for the new argument.

The left panel gives one entry per function template, sixteen in all: four templates for each of four argument categories under the [[function-template-protocol]] — countries, months, animals, and number words. Each category has four arguments. Each argument can be swapped for any of the other three, so a template contributes $4 \times 3 = 12$ source-target pairs, and sixteen templates give $16 \times 12 = 192$ trials. The plotted value is the fraction of a template's 12 pairs whose target-appropriate answer becomes the model's top-1 output token. A filled circle marks this fraction at normal swap strength; a cross marks it at double strength, $\alpha = 2$, where the source vector is subtracted and the target added at twice the magnitude ([[swap-strength-alpha]]). The aggregate over all templates is 76 of 192 successes at $\alpha = 1$ and 101 of 192 at $\alpha = 2$.

The right panel plots, per trial, the magnitude of the swap's effect at shifting the model's output toward the target answer against the source argument's [[workspace-loading]]: the [[cosine-similarity]] between the [[residual-stream]] and that concept's lens vector, averaged over the argument and readout positions of an unmodified forward pass. Loading predicts success. Country arguments load highest and swap most reliably; in the appendix's per-trial grids, 42 of 48 country cells reach rank 1, while number relations reach 0 of 48 at $\alpha = 1$. The paper offers two readings of the number-word failure: the model may compute over small integers outside the workspace, or its working representation of them may simply not align with the number tokens' lens vectors — an instance of the lens's [[single-token-limitation]]. The evidence does not decide between the two.

terms.definition: A prompt frame that applies one fixed operation to a slotted argument, such as "the capital of ___ is". The experiment uses sixteen of them, four per argument category.

An ordered (source, target) choice of two arguments from the same category: the source sits in the prompt and the target's lens vector is swapped in. Four arguments per category yield twelve such pairs per template.
The intervention scored here: the activation's coordinates along the source and target J-lens vectors are read, exchanged, and written back, at every token position across a band of middle layers.
The left panel's marker for a template's success fraction at normal swap strength ($\alpha = 1$); these fractions sum to 76 successes out of 192 trials.
The left panel's marker for the same template's success fraction when the swap is applied at double strength; these sum to 101 out of 192.
A multiplier on the swap's magnitude. At $\alpha = 2$ the source lens vector is subtracted, and the target added, at twice the normal strength.
The answer the template implies for the swapped-in argument — China's capital rather than France's. A trial succeeds when this token becomes the model's single most likely next token.
The most probable token in the model's output distribution. The left panel's success criterion is the target answer reaching this position.
The left panel's plotted quantity: of a template's twelve trials, the share whose target answer reaches top-1.

The right panel's horizontal quantity: the cosine similarity between the residual stream and the source concept's lens vector, averaged over the argument and readout positions of an unmodified forward pass. It measures how strongly the concept was in the workspace before any intervention.
The right panel's vertical quantity: how far the swap shifts the model's output distribution toward the target answer, plotted per trial.
The four argument categories, four templates each. They span a range of swap reliability: countries swap best, number words worst.
The argument actually written in the prompt, whose lens vector the swap removes.
The direction in residual-stream space associated with one vocabulary token by the Jacobian lens; the object the swap exchanges between source and target.

numbers.meaning: Function templates in the experiment: four argument categories (countries, months, animals, number words) times four functions per category.
Both the number of functions per category and the number of arguments per category; the two fours are independent design choices.
Source-target swap pairs per template: each of 4 arguments can be swapped for any of the other 3, giving 4 × 3 = 12 ordered pairs.
Total swap trials: 16 templates × 12 pairs. The denominator for both aggregate counts.
Trials at normal strength ($\alpha = 1$) on which the target answer reaches top-1 — roughly 40%. The filled circles in the left panel decompose this by template.

Successes when the swap strength is doubled — roughly 53%. The gain over 76 supports the paper's reading that failed $\alpha = 1$ swaps often move the activation in the right direction but not far enough.
The double-strength condition: the source vector is subtracted and the target added at twice the normal magnitude.
From the appendix's per-trial grids: off-diagonal country cells whose target answer reaches rank 1 at α = 1. Countries are the best-loaded and most swappable category.

Number-relation swaps that succeed at α = 1 — none. Number words have the lowest workspace loading, and the paper leaves open whether small-integer computation bypasses the workspace or merely misaligns with the number tokens' lens vectors.

items.caption: Figure 20: Top: one passage (Spanish) under each task condition. Model output is in bold; tokens are shaded where Spanish appears among the top 3 J-lens readouts. Below each transcript: the model's answer under natural conditions, and its answer after a lens-coordinate swap exchanging Spanish → French across the question tokens. Bottom: across n=8 passages, (a) the model performs each task correctly; (b) the language name appears in J-lens readouts at comparable rates in all four conditions; (c) the answer follows the swapped lens value under explicit report and flexible computation, while continuation and anomaly detection are unaffected.
items.title: Four Tasks Over One Spanish Passage
items.takeaway: The passage's language, Spanish, appears in the J-lens readouts at similar rates during all four tasks, but swapping it to French changes the model's answer only under explicit report and flexible computation. Continuation and anomaly detection produce the same output either way, so the workspace representation is present but causally idle during automatic processing.
items.walkthrough:
The figure has three tiers. The top tier shows the same short Spanish passage inside four prompts, one per task condition of the [[language-passage-tasks]]. The middle tier gives, below each transcript, two answers: the model's answer under natural conditions, and its answer after an intervention. The bottom tier aggregates over $n=8$ passages in three panels.

The four conditions differ only in what the prompt asks. *Continuation* asks the model to write the passage's next line, a routine task that still depends on the language, since the next line of a Spanish passage must be Spanish. *Anomaly detection* splices in a sentence from another language and asks whether anything is out of place. *Explicit report* asks the model to name the language. *Flexible computation* asks for a fact about the language that the passage does not contain, such as a famous author, the word for "hello," or the pre-Euro currency; the model must identify the language first and then apply whatever function the prompt names.

In each transcript, the model's output is printed in bold, and a token is shaded wherever the token Spanish appears among the top 3 entries of the [[jacobian-lens]] readout at that position. Shading therefore marks where the language is represented in the [[j-space]], independent of whether it is used. The intervention is a [[lens-coordinate-swap]] across the question tokens, exchanging the lens coordinate for Spanish with the one for French.

Shading appears in all four transcripts; panel (b) confirms across eight passages that the language name is present in the readouts at comparable rates in every condition. Panel (a) confirms the model performs each task correctly under natural conditions. Panel (c) carries the result. Under the swap, "Spanish" becomes "French," "[Gabriel] García Márquez" becomes "[Victor] Hugo," "Hola" becomes "Bonjour," and "Peseta" becomes "Franc" — on essentially every trial. The continuation stays fluent Spanish, and the anomaly is still detected, even though the workspace now says French. This is the paper's [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]] in one stimulus: presence in the workspace is uniform, causal dependence on it is not.

terms.definition: The task of writing the next line of the passage. It depends on the language but is performed routinely, and the paper classes it as automatic processing.
A sentence from a different language is spliced into the passage and the model is asked whether anything is out of place. A local coherence judgment the paper also classes as automatic.
The model is asked to name the passage's language directly. One of the two condition types the paper predicts should route through the workspace.

The model is asked for a fact about the language that the passage does not state — a famous author, the word for "hello," the pre-Euro currency — so the identified language must be handed to an arbitrary downstream function.
A token is shaded where the token Spanish appears among the top 3 entries of the J-lens readout at that position, marking where the language is represented regardless of use.
The read operation of the Jacobian lens: a score over the vocabulary computed from the residual stream at a position, whose top entries name the concepts active there.

The intervention below each transcript: at the question tokens, the activation's coordinate along the Spanish lens vector is exchanged with the coordinate along the French one, overwriting the workspace's language while leaving the passage itself untouched.
Bold text in each transcript is what the model generated; the surrounding plain text is the prompt and passage.
The unmodified forward pass, with no swap applied; the first of the two answers printed below each transcript.
The tokens of the task instruction, as opposed to the passage tokens; the swap is applied across these positions only.
Task accuracy across the eight passages: the model performs each of the four tasks correctly under natural conditions, so any difference between conditions is not a difference in competence.
The rate at which the language name appears in the J-lens readouts, per condition: comparable in all four, so workspace presence does not separate the tasks.

The rate at which the answer follows the swapped-in language: near-total for explicit report and flexible computation, near zero for continuation and anomaly detection. This panel carries the dissociation.
The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors — the candidate workspace whose causal role this figure tests.

numbers.meaning: Task conditions posed over the same passage: continuation, anomaly detection, explicit report, and flexible computation. Chosen so that all four depend on the language but only the last two should, on the paper's account, require the workspace.
The readout depth used for shading: a token is shaded when Spanish is among the three highest-scoring entries of the J-lens readout at that position.

The number of passages the bottom-row panels aggregate over. The single Spanish transcript at the top is one of these eight; the section states the panel-c flips occur on essentially every trial across them.

Answers printed below each transcript: one under natural conditions and one after the Spanish → French swap. The pairs "Spanish"/"French," "García Márquez"/"Hugo," "Hola"/"Bonjour," and "Peseta"/"Franc" flip; the continuation and the anomaly verdict ("Yes" in both) do not.
Bottom-row panels: (a) task accuracy, (b) presence of the language name in the readouts, (c) whether the answer follows the swapped lens value.

sections.title: The J-space mediates explicit report and flexible inference but not automatic processing

items.caption: Figure 21: Top: Prompts with different questions about a text passage. Tokens are shaded where two-digit integers or number-words appear in the J-lens top-3; the count below is the total over the prompt. Below each prompt: the model's answer, then the answer after a clamped lens-coordinate swap mapping the digits 40..49 → 60..69 at every position. Bottom: across n=11 passages, (a) the model answers each question correctly; (b) count content appears in the lens only when the count is asked for or needed computationally; (c) the answer follows the swapped value when the count is asked for, but the line-break decision under continuation is unaffected.
items.title: A character count pulled in on demand
items.takeaway: The same passage is shown under three questions, and a running character count that the model always computes appears in its workspace only when a question asks for the count or needs it for a further step. Swapping the count inside the workspace changes the model's answer in exactly those two conditions, while the automatic line-wrapping decision that also depends on the count is untouched.
items.walkthrough:
The figure is built from one short multi-line passage, presented three times with a different task each time. This is the [[linewrap-task]] variant of the [[character-counting-task]]. In the linewrap condition the model continues the passage while preserving its line-wrapping pattern, which requires tracking a running character count. In the explicit report condition it is asked how many characters the first line contains. In the flexible computation condition it is asked for the first letter of that count spelled out as a word, so the count is needed but never spoken.

Each prompt's tokens are shaded wherever a two-digit integer or a number-word appears in the top 3 of the [[jacobian-lens]] readout at that position — that is, wherever count-like content sits near the top of the [[j-space]] there. The number printed below each prompt is the total count of such positions. Below each prompt sit two answers: the model's natural answer, and its answer after a clamped [[lens-coordinate-swap]] that maps every digit from 40 through 49 to the digit 20 higher, 60 through 69, at every position. Clamping holds the swap in place throughout the forward pass.

In the example passage, the first line has 46 characters. Under the linewrap instruction the model wraps its continuation at roughly the right column, yet no number tokens appear in the lens anywhere, and the swap leaves the wrap point unchanged. Under the direct question the model answers "46"; number tokens appear at twenty positions, and the swap shifts the answer to "65". Under the first-letter question the model answers "F"; number tokens appear at still more positions, though no number is ever output, and the swap shifts the answer to "S", the first letter of any count in the sixties.

The bottom row aggregates over eleven passages. Panel (a) shows the model answers each question correctly. Panel (b) shows count content in the lens is near zero under linewrap, moderate under explicit report, and highest under the first-letter question. Panel (c) shows the answer follows the swapped value in both question conditions, while the line-break decision does not. This is the paper's cleanest case of the [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]]: information used by an automatic computation stays out of the workspace, and the same information is pulled in on demand when a question requires reporting it or computing with it.

terms.definition: The automatic task: the model continues the passage for several more lines while preserving its line-wrapping pattern, which requires silently tracking a running character count.
The model is asked directly how many characters the first line of the passage contains, so the count must be stated.
The model is asked for the first letter of the first line's character count when spelled out as a word; the count is required as an unspoken intermediate but never output.
Prompt positions at which a two-digit integer or a number-word appears among the top 3 tokens of the J-lens readout — the figure's marker for count content being present in the workspace there.
The three highest-ranked vocabulary tokens in the Jacobian lens readout of the residual stream at a given position; the shading threshold used in this figure.
The total number of shaded positions in that prompt — a one-number summary of how much count content the workspace carries under that question.

An intervention that exchanges one concept's J-lens coordinate for another's and holds the exchanged values fixed at every position and layer throughout the forward pass; here it rewrites every lens count in the forties to the matching value in the sixties.

The swap mapping: each two-digit lens token from 40 through 49 is replaced by the token 20 higher, so whatever count the workspace holds in the forties reads as the corresponding value in the sixties.
Task accuracy across the eleven passages: the model answers each of the three questions correctly on nearly every trial, so any difference between conditions is not a difference in competence.
How often count content appears in the lens under each condition: essentially zero under linewrap, moderate under explicit report, highest under the first-letter question.
Swap sensitivity: the answer follows the swapped lens value when the count is asked for or computed with, while the line-break decision under continuation is unaffected.
The example model answers to the direct character-count question: 46 naturally, 65 after the forties-to-sixties swap.

The example answers to the first-letter question: F for forty-six naturally, and S after the swap — the first letter of any count in the sixties, showing the swapped count was fed through the further computation.
The paper's candidate global workspace: the region of residual-stream space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, whose contents the lens readout reports.

numbers.meaning: Task conditions posed over the identical passage tokens: automatic linewrap, explicit report, and flexible computation (first letter of the count as a word).
The shading threshold: a token is shaded when a two-digit integer or number-word ranks in the top 3 of the J-lens readout at that position.
The swap mapping applied at every position: each lens count in the forties is replaced by the value 20 higher, so a workspace reading of 46 becomes 65.
The true character count of the example passage's first line, and the model's unmodified answer to the direct question.
The model's answer to the direct question after the swap — the swapped-in value, showing the reported count is read from the J-space rather than recomputed.
The number of prompt positions at which number tokens enter the lens top-3 under the explicit-report question in the example, against zero under the linewrap instruction on the same tokens.
Number tokens in the lens under the linewrap condition in the example: the count is being computed and used to place line breaks, yet none of it surfaces in the workspace.
The number of passages in the aggregate bottom row; each contributes all three conditions to panels (a), (b), and (c).

sections.title: The J-space mediates explicit report and flexible inference but not automatic processing

items.caption: Figure 22: The three J-space ablation strengths used in this section, defined by the band of layers over which the top-10 J-lens directions are projected out, alongside the random-direction control at the medium layer range. Multihop accuracy is the model's score on the two-hop reasoning prompts of ??; pretraining top-1 match is the fraction of positions, over a corpus of pretraining-like text, at which the ablated model's most-likely next token agrees with the unablated model's.
items.title: The Ablation-Strength Dial
items.takeaway: The three strengths of J-space ablation differ only in how wide a band of layers they cover: light ablates L62–71, medium L54–79, and heavy L42–88, in each case zeroing the residual stream's projection onto the top-10 J-lens directions at every position. Widening the band collapses two-hop reasoning from 98% clean to 6%, while agreement with the unablated model's ordinary next-token predictions only slips from 87% to 65%; a random-direction control over the medium band leaves both essentially untouched, so the damage is specific to J-space content.
items.walkthrough:
In the published article this figure is not a static image. The page's script builds a small table at view time, under the heading "Ablation strength", with a subtitle recording the sample sizes. The table defines the three strengths of [[j-space-ablation]] used in section 3.5, and attaches two summary measurements to each.

The intervention behind every row is the same. At each token position, at each layer inside a chosen band, the ten most strongly activated [[j-lens-vector]]s are identified, and the [[residual-stream]]'s projection onto each is zeroed; the forward pass then continues. Any token already in the top ten of a clean forward pass is exempt, so the model's intended output is not deleted directly. The three strengths keep this recipe fixed and vary only the band of layers it covers ([[ablation-strengths]]).

Layer numbers follow the paper's percentage convention: depth is reindexed to 0–100, so a layer number reads as a fraction of the way through the model ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). Light ablation covers L62–71, a thin slice in the middle of the [[workspace-layers]] range, which the paper places at roughly L38–L92. Medium covers L54–79. Heavy covers L42–88, close to the entire range. A fourth, gray row is the control: over the medium band, random directions are projected out instead of J-lens directions. The orange swatches deepen as the band widens.

Two columns report the effect, measured on Sonnet 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]). "Multihop acc" is accuracy on the 50 two-hop questions of the [[multihop-benchmark]]; the unablated model scores 98% on them. "PT top-1 match" is the [[pretraining-top-1-match]]: over 458,856 positions of pretraining-like text, the fraction at which the ablated model's most likely next token agrees with the unablated model's.

The two columns fall at very different rates. Multihop accuracy drops from 98% clean to 68% under light ablation, then 26% under medium, then 6% under heavy — the near-zero figure the text cites. The top-1 match falls only from 87% to 75% to 65%. The random control leaves both nearly intact, at 98% and 96%. Perturbing the same layers by the same recipe along other directions costs almost nothing; removing J-space content destroys two-hop reasoning while most ordinary text prediction survives. That asymmetry is the section's claim in miniature: the [[j-space]] is required for flexible internal reasoning, not for the bulk of automatic prediction.

terms.definition: The first column: which setting of J-space ablation the row describes. All settings zero the residual stream's projection onto the top-10 most active J-lens vectors at each position; they differ only in the layer band covered.
The weakest setting: the ablation is applied only over layers L62–71, a band about one tenth of the model's depth, in the middle of the workspace range.
The middle setting: the ablation covers layers L54–79, about a quarter of the model's depth. This is also the band at which the random-direction control runs.
The strongest setting: the ablation covers layers L42–88, close to the full workspace range of roughly L38–L92. It drops two-hop reasoning to near zero.

The comparison row: over the same L54–79 band as medium ablation, projections onto random directions are zeroed instead of projections onto the top J-lens directions. It leaves both measurements nearly unchanged, showing the effect is not generic activation damage.
The column giving each setting's layer band. Layers are numbered 0–100 as percentages of depth, following the paper's convention of reporting 25 evenly spaced layers reindexed to that range.

The model's accuracy on the 50 two-hop factual questions of section 3.3, which require silently computing a bridging entity. The unablated model is near ceiling at 98%, so any drop is attributable to the ablation.

Pretraining top-1 match: over a corpus of pretraining-like text, the fraction of positions at which the ablated model's most likely next token agrees with the unablated model's. It measures how much ordinary text prediction the ablation disturbs.
The unablated model, whose 98% multihop accuracy appears in the widget's subtitle as the baseline the ablated rows are compared against.
Shorthand in the subtitle and column header for the corpus of pretraining-like documents over which the top-1 match is computed.
Sample sizes in the subtitle: 50 multihop questions, and 458,856 scored token positions in the pretraining-like corpus.

What is projected out: at each position and layer in the band, the ten J-lens vectors with the strongest activation in the residual stream, excluding any token already in the top ten of a clean forward pass.
The Claude model these measurements are taken on, the paper's default subject model.
The chips beside each row name, serving as the legend: orange deepens from light to heavy as the layer band widens, and the control row is gray.

numbers.meaning: The number of J-lens vectors ablated per position and layer: the k=10 most strongly activated directions have their residual-stream projections zeroed. All three strengths hold this fixed and vary only the layer band.
