The light band: about one tenth of the model's depth, a thin slice in the middle of the workspace range. Chosen as the mildest setting; it still cuts multihop accuracy from 98% to 68%.
The medium band, about a quarter of the model's depth, and also the band used by the random-direction control so the two are directly comparable.
The heavy band: nearly the entire workspace range the paper locates at roughly L38–L92, leaving the J-space almost nowhere to hold intermediate content.

Two values coincide here: the clean (unablated) model's multihop accuracy, described as near ceiling, and the random control's multihop accuracy — projecting out random directions over the medium band does not hurt reasoning at all.
Multihop accuracy under light ablation: even a thin mid-workspace band partially impairs two-hop reasoning.
Multihop accuracy under medium ablation: widening the band to a quarter of depth removes most of the reasoning ability.
Multihop accuracy under heavy ablation — the value the text calls near zero. With the whole workspace range covered, the model can barely complete two-hop questions it otherwise answers at 98%.

Pretraining top-1 match under light, medium, and heavy ablation. Even at the heaviest setting, roughly two thirds of ordinary next-token predictions still agree with the unablated model — the ablation is far gentler on automatic text prediction than on multihop reasoning.
The random control's pretraining top-1 match: perturbing the same layers along random directions barely changes ordinary predictions, so the 65–87% figures above reflect J-space content specifically.
The number of two-hop questions in the multihop evaluation, the 50-prompt set introduced with the internal-reasoning experiments of section 3.3.
The number of token positions in the pretraining-like corpus over which the top-1 match is computed, shown in the widget's subtitle.
Context from section 4.1: the layer range where the paper's metrics locate the workspace. The heavy band L42–88 approaches it; the strengths are graded by how much of it they cover.

sections.title: J-space ablation leaves most capabilities intact while impairing internal reasoning

items.caption: Figure 23: Examples of pretraining-text predictions disrupted by J-space ablation. Each panel shows a passage from a pretraining-like document with the key token of interest marked, the ten J-lens directions ablated at that position, and the model's next-token probability distribution before and after ablation. An interpretation of each example can be viewed by hovering over “Analysis” in the top-right corner of each panel.
items.title: Four Disrupted Continuations
items.takeaway: In ordinary pretraining-like text, J-space ablation selectively destroys the predictions that depend on a silently assembled characterization of the context — an acronym's memorized expansion, a 1914 wage figure, a botanist's identity, an imaging method's clinical framing — while copying, syntax, and generic continuation survive. In each panel the ablated lens directions name exactly the contextual characterization the broken prediction needed.
items.walkthrough:
The item is a live, hoverable widget, not a static image. It holds four panels, each a passage of pretraining-like text run under [[j-space-ablation]]: at every token position, across a band of layers, the [[residual-stream]]'s projections onto the ten most active [[j-lens-vector]] directions are zeroed — sparing any token already in the clean top-10 predictions, so the intervention targets internal content rather than the output itself. Two panels use the light setting and two the medium setting of the three [[ablation-strengths]].

Each passage's tokens are shaded by the [[kl-divergence]] between the clean and ablated next-token distributions at that position, from white (no change) to orange (the panel's maximum). Hovering a token fills three columns: Top Ablated, the ten lens directions removed there; Before, the clean model's prediction probabilities; After, the ablated model's, with the KL in the header. Each panel opens on its most disrupted position, and an Analysis note in the corner gives the authors' reading.

The four opening positions break the same way. In "CONSORT acronym", the model expands "Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials" with *reporting* at probability 1.00; the ablated directions are the paper's topic (*radio*, *lung*, *heating*, *thermal*, *electrode*), and without them the model outputs *random* at 0.99 — what such trials are about, not what the acronym spells. In "1914 MA minimum wage", the ablated directions are the full retrieval key — *massachusetts*, *boston*, *wages*, *minimum*, *weekly*, *women* — and the memorized cents of $8.71 fall from 0.64 to a spread of round-cent guesses led by *50* at 0.12. In "Species epithet", removing South American geography plus *botan* and *ernst* turns the genitive *ei* of the Brazilian botanist Hoehne (1.00) into the higher-frequency ending *ii* (0.96) — valid Latin for the wrong person. In "Shear-wave techniques", removing the diagnostic framing (*diagnosis*, *detection*, *breast*) flips *Elastography* (1.00), the clinical modality, to *Dispersion* (0.89), its physics sibling.

The survivals are visible in the shading. Most positions stay near white, consistent with the section's report that the [[pretraining-top-1-match]] stays high overall. The second "$8.71" a few tokens after the first is unaffected: it is copied by induction from the first occurrence and needs no contextual retrieval. The panels put the paper's [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]] on raw text: contextually inferred predictions collapse to a generic prior, and automatic ones proceed untouched.

terms.definition: The first panel (light ablation): a clinical-trial write-up citing the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials, where the model must produce "Reporting", the R of the acronym, and after ablation produces "random" instead.

The second panel (light ablation): a 1914 economics address in which a Massachusetts wage board totals a working woman's weekly budget to $8.71; the model must produce the cents "71" at the decimal point.
The third panel (medium ablation): a list of Arachis (peanut) species in which the model must complete "hoehnei", the Latin genitive of the surname of the Brazilian botanist Frederico Carlos Hoehne.

The fourth panel (medium ablation): a diagnostic-ultrasound paper title in which the model must choose "Elastography", the clinical shear-wave modality, and after ablation chooses "Dispersion", the physics-oriented variant.

The panel tags naming which of the paper's three J-space ablation strengths was applied; the strengths differ in the range of layers over which the top-10 lens directions are projected out, and are defined in Figure 22.

The left column under each passage: the ten J-lens directions zeroed at the hovered position, ranked 1 to 10 by activation strength. These are the tokens whose lens components the intervention removed there.
The middle column: the unablated model's next-token probability distribution at the hovered position, drawn as labeled bars.
The right column: the ablated model's next-token distribution at the same position; the header carries the KL divergence between the two distributions.
The KL divergence between the clean and ablated next-token distributions at a position — the widget's measure of how much the ablation disturbed the prediction there.

Each passage token's background color encodes the KL caused by ablating at that position, on a white-to-orange ramp normalized to the panel's maximum; near-white tokens are positions the ablation barely touched.
A hover tooltip in each panel's top-right corner containing the authors' interpretation of that example.

One vector per vocabulary token per layer: the direction encoding the model's disposition to say that token. The ablation removes the residual stream's components along the ten most active of these at each position.

Marker glyphs in the token strip standing for tokenizer bookkeeping — capitalization, space, uppercase, and newline markers — kept visible so that marker-only tokens can still be hovered. The CONSORT and shear-wave panels' key tokens are such markers, sitting immediately before the word being predicted.
A leading ellipsis showing that the displayed passage starts partway into its source document.

numbers.meaning: Panels in the figure, one per example; the section names their common shape: a clinical paper's topic, a quoted speech's historical setting, a botanist's nationality, and an imaging technique's diagnostic-versus-physics framing.
J-lens directions ablated at each token position — the k = 10 most strongly activated lens vectors, excluding any token already in the clean forward pass's top-10 predictions.
KL divergence at the CONSORT panel's key position (just before "Reporting"), the panel's maximum — the most disrupted position in that passage.

In the CONSORT panel, the clean model puts probability 1.00 on "reporting"; the ablated model puts 0.99 on "random" — it reconstructs the acronym's R from what trials are about rather than recalling what it spells.
KL at the decimal point of "$8.71" in the wage panel — the passage's most disrupted position, though smaller than the other panels' maxima because the clean prediction was already uncertain.
The clean model's probability on "71", the correct cents of the memorized wage figure — the model is only moderately confident even unablated, per the Analysis note.
The ablated model's probabilities on "50", "00", "75", "25": with the retrieval key removed, it reverts to a round-cent prior spread over plausible amounts.
The weekly minimum living wage proposed at the 1914 Massachusetts wage-board hearing; its second occurrence in the passage is unaffected by ablation because induction copies it from the first.
The year of the economics address the wage passage quotes — part of the historical setting the workspace must assemble.
KL at the token "hn" inside "hoehnei" in the species panel, that panel's maximum.

In the species panel, the clean model puts 1.00 on the ending "ei" (the genitive for Hoehne); ablated, 0.96 goes to "ii", the statistically commoner species-epithet ending — a one-letter error naming the wrong person.
KL at the position before "Elastography" in the shear-wave panel, that panel's maximum.
In the shear-wave panel, the clean model puts 1.00 on "elast(ography)"; ablated, 0.89 goes to "disp(ersion)" — a real sibling technique, chosen once the diagnostic-use cue is gone.

sections.title: J-space ablation leaves most capabilities intact while impairing internal reasoning

items.caption: Figure 24: Effect of J-space ablation across a battery of tasks. Bars show task score under light, medium, and heavy ablation, normalized to unablated Sonnet 4.5; gray bars show unablated Haiku 4.5 as a smaller-model reference.
items.title: Fourteen Tasks Under Workspace Ablation
items.takeaway: With the J-space suppressed, Sonnet 4.5 still classifies, judges, and extracts at close to its normal level, but tasks that require recalling or generating content grounded in silently inferred context collapse, most of them to well below an unablated smaller model. Writing out chain-of-thought largely protects arithmetic from the ablation, consistent with the workspace being where unwritten intermediate steps would otherwise be held.
items.walkthrough:
The chart covers the paper's [[ablation-task-battery]]: fourteen tasks arranged left to right, four bars each. In the web paper it is drawn live from the underlying scores rather than shipped as an image, and the wide chart scrolls sideways on a narrow screen.

Every bar is a task score divided by the score of an unmodified Sonnet 4.5, one of the [[claude-model-family]], on the same task. A bar at 1.0 means the intervention cost nothing. The gray hatched bar is an unmodified Haiku 4.5, a smaller model, included as a yardstick: a bar below it marks damage worse than dropping a whole model tier. The three orange bars show [[j-space-ablation]] at the three [[ablation-strengths]]. At each token position, across a band of layers, the ten most active [[j-lens-vector]]s are found and the [[residual-stream]]'s projection onto each is zeroed. The strengths differ only in the band: layers 62–71 for light, 54–79 for medium, 42–88 for heavy, in the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]]. Tokens in the clean model's top-10 predictions are never ablated, so the intervention aims at internal content rather than at words the model was about to emit. Error bars are [[wilson-interval]]s.

One control anchors the reading. Ablating random directions over the medium layer band leaves two-hop accuracy at 98 percent, the clean model's own score, and [[pretraining-top-1-match]] at 96 percent. The damage below is therefore specific to the J-space, not to perturbation of that magnitude.

Three brackets group the tasks. The left five, MMLU through CoLA, survive even heavy ablation at 0.89–0.96. The right seven, which require recall or free-form generation grounded in inferred content, collapse: under heavy ablation, sonnet writing reaches 0.0, translation 0.02, and the 50-prompt [[multihop-benchmark]] 0.21, all far below unablated Haiku's 0.82–0.85 on the same three tasks. In the middle sit two versions of GSM8K. Solved with [[chain-of-thought]], it holds 0.74 under heavy ablation; answered directly, it falls to 0.54. The paper reads this gap as [[cot-externalization]]: the written steps carry what the workspace would otherwise hold.

The dissociation is the point. With the [[j-space]] suppressed, the model still parses, classifies, and extracts, but it loses the ability to assemble abstract characterizations of context and to generate from them. This is the paper's [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]], tested at full breadth.

terms.definition: The y-axis: each condition's task score divided by unablated Sonnet 4.5's score on that task, so 1.0 means no loss relative to the intact model.
The weakest of the three ablation settings: the top-10 J-lens directions are projected out only over layers 62–71 of depth (on the paper's 0–100 layer scale).
The middle setting, ablating over layers 54–79. It is also the layer range at which the random-direction control is run.
The strongest setting, ablating over layers 42–88, covering most of the workspace band of the model's depth.

Unablated Haiku 4.5, a smaller model from the same family, scored on the same tasks and normalized the same way. It serves as a reference: ablated bars below it mean the ablation cost more than an entire model-size tier.
The subject model of the experiment; all ablations are applied to it, and all bars are normalized to its unablated score.

The intervention behind the orange bars: at each token position, across the given layer band, the residual stream's projections onto the ten most active J-lens vectors are zeroed, sparing any token in the clean model's top-10 next-token predictions.
A standard multiple-choice knowledge benchmark (Hendrycks et al. 2021); here a representative of shallow classification, nearly untouched by ablation.
A task constructed for this paper: picking which item in a set does not belong. A shallow comparison task that survives ablation.
Extractive question answering on SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al. 2016): the answer is a span copied from the given passage. Listed in the data as reading_span; robust to ablation.
A sentiment-labeling task constructed for this paper; a shallow classification that survives ablation.
Judging whether a sentence is grammatically acceptable, from the CoLA benchmark (Warstadt et al. 2019); robust to ablation.
Grade-school math problems (Cobbe et al. 2021) answered with explicit written chain-of-thought. Markedly more robust to ablation than the same problems answered directly.
The same math problems answered directly, without written reasoning, so intermediate steps must be carried internally. Substantially more damaged by ablation than the CoT version.
Decoding Caesar-cipher text, a task constructed for this paper; requires generating content from an inferred transformation and is heavily damaged by ablation.
Completing analogies, constructed for this paper; requires producing a term from an inferred relation and degrades under medium and heavy ablation.
Free-form summarization (TL;DR-style data, Stiennon et al. 2020 / Völske et al. 2017); generation grounded in an assembled understanding of the text, heavily damaged.
Open-domain factual recall (Joshi et al. 2017); recall of facts not present in the prompt, heavily damaged by ablation.

The paper's 50-prompt two-hop factual questions, which need a silently computed bridging entity. Near-ceiling clean, near zero under heavy ablation; the positive control that ablation removes what earlier sections showed the J-space to carry.
A translation task constructed for this paper; free-form generation in another language, almost entirely destroyed by heavy ablation.
Writing a sonnet, constructed for this paper; the most damaged task, scoring zero under heavy ablation.
Asymmetric intervals around each bar; the paper uses Wilson 95 percent intervals for its success-rate error bars.

Three labeled brackets under the x-axis: 'Classification and extractive tasks are robust to workspace ablation' (first five tasks), 'Chain of thought reduces workspace dependence' (the two GSM8K bars), and 'Recall and freeform generation are most damaged by ablation' (last seven tasks).
One direction per vocabulary token per layer, encoding the model's disposition to say that token; the ablation targets the ten most strongly activated of these at each position.

A matched control from the companion strength table (Figure 22): ablating random directions over the medium layer range leaves multihop accuracy at 98 percent and pretraining top-1 match at 96 percent, showing the damage is specific to J-space directions.

numbers.meaning: Tasks in the battery. Six (sentiment, analogy, odd one out, Caesar cipher, translation, sonnet writing) were constructed for this work; the rest are standard benchmarks, plus the paper's own 50-prompt multihop set.
J-lens vectors ablated per token position: the k most strongly activated directions whose residual-stream projections are zeroed, excluding tokens in the clean forward pass's top-10 predictions.
The layer bands (on the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth scale) over which light, medium, and heavy ablation are applied; the strengths differ in nothing else.
The normalization point: unablated Sonnet 4.5's own score on each task. Bars at or near 1.0 mean the ablation cost nothing on that task.
Heavy-ablation scores across the five classification and extraction tasks (MMLU 0.949, odd one out 0.920, SQuAD 0.928, sentiment 0.964, CoLA 0.892): essentially intact even at the strongest setting.
Heavy-ablation scores on sonnet writing, translation, and multihop reasoning: the near-total collapse of generation and inference tasks.
Heavy-ablation scores on TriviaQA, summarization, Caesar decoding, and analogy completion: the rest of the recall-and-generation group, all far below the Haiku reference.

GSM8K under heavy ablation with chain-of-thought (0.740) versus answered directly (0.539): written-out steps substantially shield the task, read as externalizing what the workspace would otherwise carry.
GSM8K without CoT under light ablation, lower than under medium ablation (0.864). The data are non-monotonic on this one task; the paper does not comment on it.

Unablated Haiku 4.5's normalized scores on the seven damaged tasks (Caesar 0.783, multihop 0.816, translation 0.845, sonnet writing 0.853, summarization 0.862, TriviaQA 0.868, analogy 0.971): the smaller-model yardstick that medium and heavy ablation fall well below.

The random-direction control at the medium layer band: multihop accuracy (equal to the clean model's 98%) and pretraining top-1 match, showing matched-size perturbation along non-J-space directions is nearly harmless.
Prompts in the multihop reasoning evaluation, reused from the paper's two-hop benchmark.
Token positions of pretraining-like text behind the pretraining top-1 match statistic quoted for the strengths and the control.

Medium ablation on the damaged group spans this range (sonnet writing 0.201, translation 0.348, multihop 0.483, TriviaQA 0.531, analogy 0.665, summarization 0.674, Caesar 0.804): intermediate damage, ordered roughly as under heavy ablation.
Light ablation leaves 13 of 14 tasks at or above roughly this level (minimum outside GSM8K-direct: sonnet writing at 0.799); only direct arithmetic drops sharply at the lightest setting.

sections.title: J-space ablation leaves most capabilities intact while impairing internal reasoning

items.caption: Figure 25: J-space ablation and matched-norm perturbation controls while the model narrates its own stream of consciousness. A: a representative baseline and ablated response from Sonnet 4.5 to the same prompt (one of six prompts shown). B: the fraction of responses scored as using experiential language, by model and condition; error bars are 95% intervals, dots are per-prompt rates. C: The J-space contents during the unablated narrations—the fraction of (response position × layer) slots at which each token appears in the top-10 J-lens readout, over the ablated layers (L38–54, dark) and at the final layer (light). The J-lens readout tokens shown are the top 20 by increase over non-experience-related baseline prompts.
items.title: Flattening the stream of consciousness
items.takeaway: Projecting the ten most active J-lens directions out of layers L38–54 while the model narrates its own stream of consciousness strips the experiential language from the narration on Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6, while control perturbations of identical magnitude along other directions leave the score near baseline. During ordinary, unablated narration, the workspace itself is dominated by tokens like thinking and feeling — content the model is not about to say.
items.walkthrough:
The figure has three panels, A, B, and C. Together they run one intervention — suppressing the model's workspace while it narrates its own stream of consciousness — and check what changes in the narration. This is the paper's main evidence for the [[experiential-report-flattening]] result.

Panel A prints two responses from Sonnet 4.5 to the same prompt, one of six such prompts. The first comes from the unmodified model. The second comes from the model under [[j-space-ablation]]: at every position, the ten most active J-lens directions are projected out of the residual stream, in layers L38 through L54. Layer numbers here follow [[layer-percentage-indexing]]: they read as percentages of depth, so this band covers roughly the first third of the [[workspace-layers]]. The setting is deliberately light. Ablating more directions, or later layers, damages coherence before anything subtler can be seen. Under this ablation the model still writes fluently about its own processing, but the register shifts from felt description to mechanical status report.

Panel B quantifies the shift. Each response receives an [[experiential-language-score]]: three binary judgments from an Opus 4.6 [[llm-grader]] — whether the moment is conveyed from the inside rather than observed as a status report, whether the perspective is first-person felt rather than third-person mechanism, and whether the vocabulary is sensory rather than computational — averaged together. Bars show the fraction of responses scored as experiential, by model and condition, with 95% intervals; dots are per-prompt rates. The load-bearing comparison is against [[matched-norm-controls]]: perturbations calibrated to disturb the activations by the same magnitude, at the same layers and positions, but along other directions — a random direction, a shrinking of the non-J-space component of the activation ([[j-space-component]]), or a dampening of the ten most aligned [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions. Ablation collapses the score on Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6; the controls stay near baseline. Haiku 4.5 is absent because ablation breaks its coherence before its register changes.

Panel C reads the workspace during the unablated narrations. For each token it shows the fraction of (response position × layer) slots at which that token sits in the top-10 [[j-lens-readout]], over the ablated band (dark) and at the final layer (light); the twenty tokens shown are those most elevated over non-experiential baseline prompts. The contents are dominated by thinking at 58% of slots, thoughts at 23%, feeling at 17%, and conscious at 7% — far more often than these words appear in the model's actual output at the same positions. The workspace is not echoing the text; it holds its own [[metacognitive-representations]] — thinking-and-feeling content the model is not about to say.

A control intervention calibrated to perturb the activations by the same magnitude, at the same layers and positions, as the ablation — but along other directions. It tests whether the effect comes from what is removed rather than from how much.
The unmodified model's responses to the same prompts; the condition every intervention is compared against.
The matched-norm control that perturbs the activation along a randomly chosen direction.
The matched-norm control that shrinks the part of the activation lying outside the J-space — the complement of what ablation removes.
The matched-norm control that dampens the activation's projections onto its ten most strongly aligned sparse-autoencoder decoder directions — interpretable features that are not J-lens vectors.
The metric on the y-axis of panel B: the average of three binary LLM-graded judgments of whether a response describes experience from the inside.
An Opus 4.6-based judge scoring each response against a written rubric; three separate rubrics (felt vs. observed, first-person felt perspective, sensory vocabulary) each return 0 or 1.
An open-ended prompt asking the model to narrate its ongoing experience; the prompt family this figure's responses come from.
The mid-size Claude model whose transcripts appear in panel A and whose scores appear in panel B; the effect is strongest and most examined here.
A larger Claude model included in panel B; ablation reduces its experiential language score the same way.
The largest and newest model in panel B, which shows the same reduction; a separate instance of it also serves as the grader.
The smallest Claude tier, absent from the figure: on it, J-space ablation degrades coherence before producing any qualitative change in the reports.
The ablated layer band. Layer numbers are percentages of model depth under the paper's 0–100 reindexing, so this is the band from 38% to 54% of depth — the first third of the workspace range.
The last layer of the model, shown as the light bars in panel C for contrast: readouts there track what the model is about to say, unlike the workspace band.
The ten highest-scoring vocabulary tokens when an activation is passed through the J-lens; panel C counts how often each token is among them.
The unit panel C's fractions are over: every combination of a token position in the response and a layer in the range considered counts as one slot.
The tokens dominating the workspace during narration — concepts of mental activity itself, present in the lens far more often than in the model's actual output at the same positions.

terms.term: top 20 by increase over baseline prompts
terms.definition: The selection rule for panel C's tokens: the twenty tokens whose top-10 lens occupancy rises most relative to prompts unrelated to experience, filtering out tokens common everywhere.
The uncertainty ranges on panel B's bars; the paper's success-rate error bars elsewhere are Wilson 95% intervals for a proportion.
Individual points over each bar in panel B, one per prompt, showing how the scored fraction varies across the prompt set.
Dark bars count slots within the ablated layers L38–54; light bars count slots at the final layer only.
The number of top J-lens directions projected out per position — 10 here; larger values impair response coherence.

numbers.meaning: k, the number of most-active J-lens directions ablated at each position; also the size of the top-k readout list panel C counts membership in. Chosen because larger k tends to impair coherence.
The ablated layer band, in percent-of-depth indexing: the first third of the workspace range. Later layer ranges also impair coherence, so the ablation stays early.

Three binary grader judgments (felt vs. observed, experiential perspective, sensory vocabulary), averaged into the experiential language score; also three models showing the effect, and three matched-norm control types in the main comparison.
Stream-of-consciousness prompts in the set panel A samples from ("one of six prompts shown", per the caption).
The number of stream-of-consciousness prompts the body text says the score reduction is computed across; the caption says six — the paper leaves this one-off discrepancy unexplained.
Fraction of (position × layer) slots at which thinking appears in the top-10 lens readout during unablated narration — the single most dominant workspace token.
Slot fraction for thoughts, the second most dominant token.
Slot fraction for feeling.

Slot fraction for conscious. All four fractions far exceed how often these words appear in the model's output distribution at the same positions, which is the argument that the workspace is not merely echoing the text.
Tokens shown in panel C: the top 20 by increase in lens occupancy over non-experience-related baseline prompts.
Confidence level of panel B's error bars on the scored fractions.
Claude version numbers: Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6 show the flattening; Haiku 4.5 is excluded because ablation breaks its coherence first.

sections.title: J-space ablation flattens experiential reports while preserving coherence

items.caption: Figure 26: J-space ablation and matched-norm perturbation controls while the model is asked to imagine the experience of a person in a particular moment: a representative baseline and ablated response from Sonnet 4.5 (left), and the average experiential language score by model and condition (right). Conventions are as in Figure ??.
items.title: Imagined experience under ablation
items.takeaway: Suppressing the J-space while the model imagines what a moment is like for another person collapses its experiential language score on Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6, while matched-norm control perturbations leave the score near baseline. The flattening effect is therefore not specific to the model describing itself; the paper reads the J-space as supporting rich experiential description as such.
items.walkthrough:
The figure closes the experiential-report experiments. The earlier figure in this section asked the model to narrate its own stream of consciousness. This one points the prompts outward. The model is asked to imagine what a specific moment is like for a person — someone who has just opened a letter from someone they have not heard from in years, or someone waiting by the phone for news they are dreading. The figure answers whether the [[experiential-report-flattening]] effect is specific to self-description.

The left side holds a representative pair of responses from Sonnet 4.5 to the same imagination prompt: one from the unmodified model, one under [[j-space-ablation]]. In the article this panel is a live widget, so the transcripts can be read in full rather than as excerpts. The ablation projects out, at every position across layers L38–54, the [[residual-stream]]'s components along the ten most active [[j-lens-vector]] directions. That is the lightest setting from the self-report experiment — larger $k$ or later layers damage coherence before anything else changes.

The right side is the quantitative summary: the [[experiential-language-score]], plotted by model and condition. The score is the mean of three binary judgments by an [[llm-grader]] — whether the response conveys the moment from the inside, whether it speaks from a felt first-person perspective, and whether its vocabulary is sensory rather than computational. The models are Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6 from the [[claude-model-family]]; Haiku 4.5 is left out because ablation breaks its coherence before its register changes. The conditions are the unablated baseline, J-space ablation, and [[matched-norm-controls]]: perturbations of the same magnitude, at the same layers and positions, but along a random direction, against the non-J-space component, or against the most aligned [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions. Error bars are 95% intervals; dots are per-prompt rates.

The pattern repeats the self-report result. Under ablation the score collapses on all three models, and the controls stay near baseline. The ablated responses remain detailed and remain about the person, but they read more like event logs than like descriptions of experience. A separate [[story-writing-control]] shows this is not a general loss of writing ability. The paper's reading is that the J-space supports the propensity to give rich experiential reports, whether the subject is the model or someone else.

terms.definition: The intervention under test: at each token position, the residual stream's projections onto the top-10 most active J-lens vectors are removed, suppressing the workspace's current contents wholesale.

Control interventions calibrated to perturb the activations by the same magnitude as J-space ablation, at the same layers and token positions, but along other directions: a random direction, the non-J-space component, or aligned SAE decoder directions.

The y-axis quantity: the average of three binary LLM-graded judgments of whether a response describes the moment from the inside — felt rather than observed, first-person felt rather than third-person mechanism, sensory rather than computational vocabulary.
The unperturbed condition: the same imagination prompt with no intervention on the activations, giving the model's ordinary experiential register.
The mid-size Claude model whose representative baseline and ablated responses fill the figure's left panel, and one of the three models in the score comparison.
A larger Claude model included in the score comparison; it shows the same collapse under ablation.
The most recent large Claude model in the comparison; it too shows the collapse. A model of this tier also serves as the grader behind the score.
The smallest model tier, absent from the figure: on Haiku 4.5, J-space ablation degrades coherence before producing any qualitative change in the responses.
The grouping on the score panel: baseline, J-space ablation, and each matched-norm control, so the ablation's effect can be read against same-magnitude perturbations.

The prompt family for this figure: requests to describe the subjective experience of a person in a specific moment, such as opening a letter from someone not heard from in years, or waiting by the phone for dreaded news.
The layer range over which the ablation acts, written in the paper's percent-of-depth indexing; it is the first third of the workspace layer range.
The per-token vocabulary-aligned vectors of the Jacobian lens; the ten most active of them at each position define what the ablation removes.
A control that perturbs the activation along a random direction with the same norm the ablation would have removed at that layer and position.
A control that shrinks the part of the activation lying outside the J-space by the matched amount, testing whether removing anything of that size flattens the reports.
A control that dampens the activation's projections onto its ten most strongly aligned sparse-autoencoder decoder directions, a same-size perturbation along interpretable but non-lens features.
95% confidence intervals on the average score per model and condition; the paper's proportion error bars use the Wilson interval.
Per-prompt score rates overlaid on each bar, showing the spread across the individual imagination prompts behind the average.
A language model scoring responses against a written rubric in place of human raters; here Opus 4.6 answers the three binary questions that make up the score.

numbers.meaning: The number of most active J-lens directions projected out at each token position. Larger values of k tend to impair the coherence of responses, so the paper stays at 10.

The layer range the ablation covers — the first third of the workspace range in the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth indexing. Later layer ranges, like larger k, tend to break coherence before changing the register.
Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6 appear in the score panel. Haiku 4.5 is excluded because ablation degrades its coherence before any qualitative change appears.
The experiential language score averages three binary grader judgments (felt versus observed, first-person felt perspective, sensory vocabulary), so each response scores 0, 1/3, 2/3, or 1.

The main comparison uses three matched-norm perturbations: a random direction, shrinking the non-J-space component, and dampening the top-10 aligned SAE decoder directions. Each is calibrated to the ablation's perturbation magnitude at the same layer and position.
The confidence level of the error bars on each average score, computed as Wilson intervals for proportions.
The range of the experiential language score: 0 means all three graders judged the response non-experiential, 1 means all three judged it experiential.

The section names two representative imagination prompts — the letter from someone not heard from in years, and waiting by the phone for dreaded news; the figure shows one representative response pair from the set.

sections.title: J-space ablation flattens experiential reports while preserving coherence

items.caption: Figure 27: We divide the model's layers into three functional regions — sensory (early), workspace (middle), and motor (late).
items.title: The three layer bands
items.takeaway: The paper divides the model's depth into three functional regions: an early sensory band where the J-space carries essentially no meaningful content, a middle workspace band (roughly L38 to L92 in Sonnet 4.5) where it holds persistent abstract content, and a late motor band where its vectors align with the imminent output token.
items.walkthrough:
This figure is a schematic, not a data plot. It draws the model's stack of layers as a single strip and colors it into the three [[layer-bands]] the paper has been arguing for: sensory at the bottom, workspace in the middle, motor at the top.

The layer numbers use the paper's percentage convention. Results are reported on 25 evenly spaced layers of the [[residual-stream]], reindexed to the range 0 to 100, so a layer number reads as a fraction of the model's depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). The default model behind these numbers is Claude Sonnet 4.5, from the [[claude-model-family]].

Each band is defined by what the [[jacobian-lens]] finds there. In the [[sensory-layers]], roughly the first third of depth up to about L38, lens readouts are noisy and the [[j-space]] is close to empty: readout kurtosis sits near zero, and the lens vectors collapse into a small linear subspace. The first layer can only encode the identity of the current token, so this emptiness is expected at the very start. In the [[workspace-layers]], from about L38 to about L92, the J-space carries content that is abstract, persists across nearby token positions, and is distinct from both the input tokens and the next output token. This is the band in which all of the paper's workspace-like properties were demonstrated. In the [[motor-layers]], the final few layers past about L92, the lens readout snaps onto the model's actual next-token prediction. The paper reads these late vectors as representations that drive the imminent output rather than intermediate computations available for further use.

The boundaries come from converging evidence rather than from this drawing. A [[cka]] comparison of lens vectors across layer pairs shows an early block, a long middle block, and a small late block, and four [[workspace-boundary-metrics]] locate the same two transitions.

The division is cleaner in the figure than in the data. The paper notes that in some models the transitions are gradual, sometimes with sub-blocks, and that layer subsampling exaggerates the sharpness. It also concedes that the metrics are all derived from the J-lens itself, so an early-layer workspace the lens cannot resolve remains possible.

terms.definition: The paper's label for roughly the first third of the model's layers, up to about L38, where J-lens readouts are noisy and the J-space carries essentially no meaningful content.

The middle band of layers, roughly L38 to L92 in Sonnet 4.5, where the J-space holds persistent abstract content distinct from both the input tokens and the imminent output; the region where the workspace-like properties hold.

The final few layers, past about L92, where J-lens vectors align with the model's actual next-token prediction; the paper reads these as representations that drive the imminent output rather than intermediate computations.

The three bands are defined by what the J-space does in them, not by any architectural difference; every layer has the same transformer structure, and the division comes from lens-derived measurements.
Depth positions in the model's residual stream, reported on 25 evenly spaced layers reindexed to 0-100 so that a layer number reads as a percentage of total depth.
The set of activation-space points expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors; the candidate workspace whose per-band behavior this figure summarizes.

numbers.meaning: The workspace onset, about a third of the way through the model's depth. Below it, readout kurtosis is near zero, top-1 autocorrelation sits at the null, and the lens vectors span only a small subspace; all four boundary metrics rise around this layer.

The workspace end, shortly before the output. Past it, the lens's next-token accuracy jumps steeply and readouts converge on the model's actual prediction, which the paper takes as the switch from intermediate content to motor representations.
The reindexed layer scale: layer numbers are percentages of depth, so the same bands can be compared across models of different sizes.
The number of evenly spaced residual-stream layers actually sampled for all reported results; the paper notes this subsampling exaggerates how sharp the band transitions look.
The number of functional regions. The count comes from the block structure of the CKA layer-similarity matrix: one early block, one long middle block, one small late block.

sections.title: In which layers does the J-space act as a workspace?

items.caption: Figure 28: Quantitative signatures of the workspace's start and end. (a) Next-token prediction accuracy — the fraction of positions at which any top-k J-lens token matches the model's top-1 prediction. (b) Excess kurtosis of the J-lens readout distribution; high kurtosis indicates a readout sharply peaked on a few tokens. (c) Autocorrelation of the top-1 lens token across positions, as Δ log probability relative to a position-shuffled null. (d) Fraction of residual-stream dimensions needed to capture a given share of variance across the J-lens vectors $W_U J_\ell$ .
items.title: Four signatures of the workspace band
items.takeaway: Four statistics derived from the J-lens, each plotted against layer depth, change sharply at the same two places: around a third of the way through the model (~L38) and shortly before the output (~L92). The paper reads these two inflections as the start and end of the workspace band — with the caveat that all four metrics come from the J-lens itself, so an early-layer blind spot of the lens cannot be ruled out.
items.walkthrough:
This figure gives quantitative backing to the three-band picture of [[layer-bands]] — sensory, workspace, motor. It holds four panels, (a) through (d). Each panel plots one statistic of the [[jacobian-lens]] against layer depth. Layers follow the paper's convention of [[layer-percentage-indexing]]: 25 evenly spaced layers of Claude Sonnet 4.5's [[residual-stream]], relabeled 0 to 100, so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth. Together the four curves are the paper's [[workspace-boundary-metrics]].

Panel (a) plots [[lens-next-token-accuracy]]: the fraction of positions at which any of the lens's top-$k$ tokens matches the model's own top-1 next-token prediction. The curve sits near zero through the early layers. It ticks up at the workspace start, rises slowly through the middle, and jumps steeply in the last few layers. The paper reads the late jump as the end of the workspace: from there on, lens vectors act as [[motor-layers]] content driving the imminent output, not as intermediate results available for further processing.

Panel (b) plots the [[readout-excess-kurtosis]] of the lens's logit distribution at a single position and layer, averaged over many activations. High [[kurtosis]] means the readout is sharply peaked on a few tokens rather than spread randomly. The curve is near zero through the first third of the depth, rises from about a third of the way in, and falls in the last few layers. The early rise marks the workspace onset: before it, the [[j-space]] carries essentially no meaningful content.

Panel (c) plots [[top1-autocorrelation]]: how often the same token stays at the top of the readout from position $t$ to position $t+\Delta$, shown as $\Delta$ log probability over a position-shuffled null. Persistence signals abstract content that survives across the token stream; its absence signals token-local content. The curve hugs the null early, rises at the same layer as the other metrics, peaks across the middle band, and falls back late.

Panel (d) plots the [[j-space-effective-dimensionality]]: the fraction of residual-stream dimensions needed to capture a given share of variance across the lens vectors $W_U J_\ell$. It is small early — the lens collapses to a thin subspace — then rises sharply at the onset as the vectors fan out, and rises again, less dramatically, at the motor transition, where $J_\ell$ approaches the identity and the lens inherits the full dimensionality of the [[unembedding-matrix]].

All four curves inflect near L38 and L92. The paper flags one caveat: every metric here is lens-derived, so a workspace the J-lens cannot resolve in early layers would be invisible to this analysis.

terms.definition: The fraction of text positions at which any of the J-lens's top-k tokens equals the model's actual top-1 next-token prediction, plotted per layer. Near zero early, slowly rising through the workspace, and jumping steeply in the final layers.

Kurtosis of the J-lens readout's logit distribution at a single position and layer, in excess of a Gaussian, computed over a large set of activations. High values mean the readout concentrates on a few tokens instead of looking random.

The rate at which the same token remains at the top of the lens readout at position t and at position t+Δ, expressed as Δ log probability relative to a position-shuffled null. High values mean the J-space holds content that persists across the token stream.

The fraction of residual-stream dimensions needed to capture a given share of the variance across the layer's J-lens vectors. Small when the lens collapses to a thin subspace, large when the vectors span most of the residual stream.

The paper's readout technique: one vector per vocabulary token per layer, giving the direction that encodes the model's potential to verbalize that token. All four panels are statistics of its readouts or its vectors.

The layer-ℓ J-lens vectors as rows: the corpus-averaged Jacobian $J_\ell$ from layer ℓ to the final layer, composed with the unembedding matrix $W_U$. Panel (d) measures the variance structure of this set of vectors.
The corpus-averaged Jacobian matrix from layer ℓ's residual stream to the final layer. In the last layers it approaches the identity, which is why panel (d) rises again there.
The unembedding matrix, the model's final linear map from residual stream to vocabulary scores. Its full dimensionality is what the lens inherits in the motor layers.
The shared horizontal axis of all four panels: 25 evenly sampled layers of the residual stream, reindexed to 0–100 so that a layer number reads as a percentage of the model's depth.

Rank cutoffs on the lens readout's token ranking. Panel (a) asks whether the model's top-1 prediction appears anywhere in the lens's top k tokens; panel (c) tracks only the single highest-ranked lens token.
Panel (c)'s vertical unit: the log-probability of the top-1 token repeating across a position gap, minus the same quantity under the shuffled null, so zero means no more persistence than chance.
The baseline for panel (c): the repeat rate expected if lens readouts were assigned to positions at random, removing any genuine across-position persistence.

The two depth landmarks the figure locates: the onset near L38, where kurtosis, autocorrelation, and dimensionality all rise, and the offset near L92, where accuracy jumps, kurtosis and autocorrelation fall, and lens content turns motor.
The paper's term for late-layer lens content tied to the imminent output token rather than to intermediate computation; the final steep rise in panel (a) is read as the switch to this regime.

numbers.meaning: Sub-panels (a)–(d), one per boundary metric: next-token accuracy, excess kurtosis, top-1 autocorrelation, and effective dimensionality. Their agreement, not any one curve, is the figure's argument.

The workspace onset: about 38% of the way through the model's depth, where excess kurtosis, autocorrelation, and effective dimensionality all rise sharply. Before this layer the J-space carries essentially no meaningful content.

The workspace offset: about 92% of depth, shortly before the output, where next-token accuracy jumps steeply and kurtosis and autocorrelation fall back — the switch from intermediate to motor content.
The layer axis range: 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed so layer numbers read as percentages of depth, making bands comparable across models of different depths.
The number of evenly spaced layers actually sampled; the paper notes that this subsampling exaggerates how sharp the band transitions look.
The fraction of early depth over which panels (a)–(c) stay near zero or near the null — the sensory band, where the J-space is effectively empty.
The early-layer baseline of panels (a)–(c): readouts no more peaked, predictive, or persistent than chance, which is what an empty workspace looks like under these metrics.

sections.title: In which layers does the J-space act as a workspace?

items.caption: Figure 29: Responses across layers to ambiguous inputs. A concept token's input embedding is replaced by the mixture $(1 - \alpha)\, e_B + \alpha\, e_A$ within ordinary sentences, and the activation at that position is recorded at every layer as $\alpha$ sweeps from 0 to 1 (sixteen country-name pairs × forty sentences). (A) Example sentences with the mixed embedding. (B) The activation's position along the line connecting the same trial's pure- $B$ and pure- $A$ activations at that position and layer, as a function of $\alpha$ (relative to each trial's threshold) and layer. (C) Left, the J-lens rank of whichever concept is ranked higher; right, the projection share of panel b restricted to the activation's component along the two concepts' J-lens directions.
items.title: The Ambiguity Sweep
items.takeaway: When a concept token's input embedding is replaced by a weighted mix of two country embeddings, early layers track the mixture smoothly, but from the workspace onset (around layer 38) the activation commits sharply to one country or the other. The paper reads this as the model's analogue of ignition, and the commitment is at least as sharp in the J-space component as in the full activation.
items.walkthrough:
The experiment behind this figure manufactures an input that sits between two meanings. A sentence such as "My sister has always wanted to visit ___" normally ends in a country name. At that position the model instead receives a mixed input embedding, $(1-\alpha)\,e_B + \alpha\,e_A$, where $e_A$ and $e_B$ are the input embeddings of two single-token country names. At $\alpha = 0$ the input is purely country $B$. At $\alpha = 1$ it is purely country $A$. In between it is neither. This construction is the [[embedding-mixture-experiment]]. Sixteen country pairs crossed with forty carrier sentences give the trials; for each trial, $\alpha$ sweeps from 0 to 1 while the [[residual-stream]] at the mixed position is recorded at every layer.

Panel A prints example carrier sentences with the mixed embedding in place of the country token.

Panel B reads the result without any lens. For each trial and layer, the activation is placed along the straight line connecting that trial's pure-$B$ activation to its pure-$A$ activation at the same position and layer. Its position on that line is the [[projection-share]], which by construction is 0 at one end of the sweep and 1 at the other. The panel plots this share against $\alpha$, aligned to each trial's own switching threshold, and against layer. Layers are indexed 0 to 100 under the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]], so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth. In early layers the share varies smoothly with $\alpha$, roughly proportional to the input mixture. From around layer 38 — the workspace onset located by the preceding boundary analyses of the [[workspace-layers]] — the share instead sits near one endpoint or the other, flipping sharply at a threshold value of $\alpha$.

Panel C brings in the [[jacobian-lens]]. The left half shows, at each layer and $\alpha$, the [[j-lens-readout]] rank of whichever country ranks higher. In very early layers neither country ranks highly. Unambiguous inputs enter the readout after a few layers; maximally ambiguous ones only by layer 38. The right half repeats the panel-B measurement restricted to the activation's component along the two countries' J-lens directions, and it resembles panel B.

The paper reads the sharp late commitment as the analogue of [[ignition]] in [[global-workspace-theory]]. Appendix 10.15 adds that at maximal ambiguity, mid- and late-layer trials cluster near 0 or 1 rather than 0.5 ([[bimodal-commitment]]), and that the [[j-space]] component's transition sharpens somewhat earlier than the rest of the activation ([[transition-width]]).

terms.definition: The interpolation coefficient, swept from 0 to 1. It sets the weight of concept $A$'s embedding in the mixture; $1-\alpha$ is the weight of concept $B$'s.
The input embeddings of the two single-token country names in a pair. These are the vectors mixed to form the ambiguous input.
The mixed embedding substituted for the concept token inside an ordinary sentence — the paper's construction of an artificially ambiguous input.
Example carrier sentences with the mixed embedding standing in for the country token, showing what the model actually receives.
A lens-free readout: the activation's position along the line from the trial's pure-$B$ activation to its pure-$A$ activation, plotted against $\alpha$ (aligned to each trial's threshold) and layer.

The J-lens view. Left: the lens rank of whichever of the two countries ranks higher, by layer and $\alpha$. Right: the panel-B projection share restricted to the activation's component along the two countries' J-lens directions.

Where an activation sits along the line connecting the same trial's pure-$B$ and pure-$A$ activations at the same position and layer. By construction it is exactly 0 at one end of the sweep and exactly 1 at the other.

The activations recorded on the same trial when the input embedding is entirely one country's ($\alpha = 0$) or entirely the other's ($\alpha = 1$). They anchor the two ends of the projection-share line.
The vertical axis of panels B and C: depth in the model, reported as a percentage 0 to 100 under the paper's convention of reindexing 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers.

The per-trial value of $\alpha$ at which the late-layer response flips from one country to the other. Panel B's $\alpha$ axis is centered on each trial's own threshold so the switch aligns across trials.
An ordinary sentence, such as "My sister has always wanted to visit ___", that provides a natural context for the mixed embedding. Forty are used.

The rank of a country's token in the J-lens readout — the softmax over vocabulary scores obtained by projecting the activation through the layer's Jacobian and the unembedding. A low rank means the concept is prominent in the readout.
The per-token vectors of the Jacobian lens; panel C right projects the activation onto the two countries' vectors before recomputing the projection share.

The layer, around 38, at which the paper's earlier boundary metrics say the J-space begins acting as a workspace. This figure tests whether that layer coincides with ignition-like commitment, and finds that it does.

In global workspace theory, the late, all-or-none amplification of one interpretation of an ambiguous input, with bimodal outcomes at threshold. The sharp switching in this figure is the paper's proposed analogue.
The sixteen pairs of single-token country names whose embeddings are interpolated. Country names give clean single-token concepts that fit the same sentence frames interchangeably.

numbers.meaning: The range of the interpolation coefficient $\alpha$. At 0 the input embedding is purely country $B$; at 1 it is purely country $A$; each trial sweeps the whole range.
Country-name pairs used. Each pair supplies the two embeddings $e_A$ and $e_B$ being interpolated.
Carrier sentences per pair. Crossing sentences with pairs gives the trials over which panels B and C aggregate.

The layer (as a percentage of depth) from which the projection share stops varying smoothly and instead sits near 0 or 1, flipping sharply at a threshold. It matches the workspace onset located independently by the paper's boundary metrics, which is the point of the figure.
The endpoints of the projection share, exact by construction: the pure-$B$ and pure-$A$ activations define the line the share is measured along, so the sweep's ends land on them.
The rank window used in panel C: a country counts as present in the readout when it appears in the J-lens top 25, and the right half of panel C is computed within the layers where this holds.

The projection share a trial would show if the activation faithfully reflected a balanced input mixture. Appendix 10.15 reports that at maximal ambiguity, mid- and late-layer trials instead cluster near 0 and 1 — per-trial commitment, not faithful ambiguity — and most sharply so in the J-space component.

sections.title: Interpretation of ambiguous inputs solidifies at the workspace onset

items.caption: Figure 30: J-space occupancy by layer, defined as the value of $K$ at which the marginal reconstruction improvement from a sparse non-negative combination of $K$ J-lens vectors falls below that of a same-size random control set. Lines show percentiles over positions. The second plot shows the fraction of variance explained by the J-lens decomposition in excess of a same-size random control set, evaluated at $K$ = median occupancy, for five workspace layers.
items.title: Workspace occupancy and variance share
items.takeaway: Counted by sparse reconstruction, the J-space holds around 25 meaningfully active lens vectors per position in the median case — near zero in the early layers, a plateau across the workspace band — while explaining under 10% of activation variance beyond a random control. This is the paper's quantitative basis for calling the workspace capacity-limited: on the order of tens of concepts, and a small slice of what the model represents.
items.walkthrough:
The figure has two panels, both answering the same question: how much does the [[j-space]] actually hold? The first panel plots [[j-space-occupancy]] against layer depth. The second plots how much activation variance that occupied portion accounts for, at five workspace layers.

The occupancy metric works by reconstruction. At each position and layer, [[sparse-decomposition]] solves for a sparse nonnegative combination of $K$ [[j-lens-vector]]s that best reconstructs the [[residual-stream]] activation, using [[gradient-pursuit]]. Each added vector improves the reconstruction by some amount. The same procedure is run with a control set of random directions of the same size. Occupancy is the value of $K$ at which the marginal improvement from one more J-lens vector falls below the improvement from one more random direction. Past that point, the lens vectors are no better than chance, so the count stops there.

The first panel shows this count per layer, with lines for percentiles over positions rather than a single average. Occupancy is near zero through roughly the first third of the layers — the [[sensory-layers]], where the J-space carries essentially no content. It then rises to a plateau of around 25 in the median case, with the onset coinciding with the start of the [[workspace-layers]] identified by the paper's other boundary metrics. The value varies across contexts, which is what the percentile spread shows. Layers here follow the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]], so layer numbers read as percentages of depth.

The second panel fixes $K$ at each layer's median occupancy and measures [[excess-variance-explained]]: the fraction of activation variance the top-$K$ J-lens vectors capture beyond the same-size random control. This never exceeds 10%. The activations are dominated by information outside the J-space.

One caveat carries weight. Occupancy counts distinct active vectors, not concepts — the [[word-list-experiment]] shows that several related lens vectors can jointly represent one broader category. The paper therefore states its [[j-space-capacity]] claim at the order-of-magnitude level: tens of concepts at a time. At any single layer, the count of unrelated items is smaller still, around one or two.

terms.definition: The number of J-lens vectors meaningfully active in an activation: the value of $K$ at which the marginal reconstruction improvement from a sparse combination of $K$ J-lens vectors falls below that of a same-size random control set.
The number of J-lens vectors allowed in the sparse reconstruction. The first panel sweeps $K$ to find where the lens stops beating chance; the second panel fixes $K$ at each layer's median occupancy.

One direction in residual-stream space per vocabulary token per layer, identified by the Jacobian lens as encoding the model's disposition to say that token. The dictionary the reconstruction draws from.

A reconstruction of an activation as a weighted sum of at most $K$ J-lens vectors with all weights nonnegative, solved by gradient pursuit. The paper's operational way of listing what the J-space contains at a position.

A set of random directions of the same size as the J-lens set, run through the same reconstruction procedure. It fixes the baseline: any direction set explains some variance, so only improvement beyond this control counts.
Depth in the model, under the paper's convention of 25 evenly spaced layers reindexed 0-100, so layer numbers read as percentages of total depth.

The lines of the first panel: occupancy is computed per token position, and the figure shows percentile bands of its distribution across positions rather than one average curve, because the value varies across contexts.
The second panel's vertical axis: the fraction of activation variance captured by the top-$K$ J-lens vectors minus the fraction captured by the same-size random control. It never exceeds 10%.
The per-layer median of the occupancy distribution, around 25 across the workspace band. The second panel evaluates variance explained with $K$ set to this value at each layer.

The five layers from the middle band at which the excess-variance measurement is shown — the range, roughly from a third of the way through the depth to shortly before the output, where the J-space carries workspace-like content.

The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm used to solve for the reconstruction: it adds one dictionary vector at a time, which is what makes the marginal improvement per added vector a measurable quantity.
The per-position activation vector the reconstruction targets: the running state each transformer layer reads from and writes to.

numbers.meaning: The median occupancy plateau across the workspace band: about 25 J-lens vectors are meaningfully active at a typical position, though the value varies across contexts. This is also why the paper typically caps the sparsity level defining the J-space at 25.

The depth range where occupancy stays near zero — the sensory band, where J-lens readouts carry essentially no meaningful content. The rise out of it coincides with the workspace onset the paper locates at roughly layer 38 on its 0-100 scale.

The ceiling on excess variance explained at every measured workspace layer, with $K$ at median occupancy. The paper reads this as the model's activations being dominated by information outside the J-space.
The number of workspace layers at which the second panel evaluates excess variance explained.

The paper's stated capacity of the workspace, deliberately loose: occupancy counts active vectors, not concepts, since several related vectors can jointly encode one category, so the claim is made at the order-of-magnitude level.

The number of unrelated list items simultaneously represented at any single layer, from the appendix's single-layer analysis — smaller than the ~25 figure, which pools the best rank over the whole workspace band.

The workspace band identified in section 4.1 by four lens-derived boundary metrics, on the 0-100 layer scale; the occupancy plateau spans this same band, which the paper takes as independent confirmation of the band.
The paper's layer-reporting convention: 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers, reindexed so a layer number reads as a percentage of model depth.

items.caption: Figure 31: Loading and displacement of list words in the J-space readout. The model reads 80-word lists; at each comma, a list word counts as present in the readout if its rank (best rank over the workspace layer range) falls within the top 25. A: example readouts (at layer 79) after one and after eight words of an animal list; read words highlighted. B: list words present at each comma, for single-family lists (orange, results pooled over four families) and lists of unrelated items (blue); solid, words read so far; dashed, all 80; shading, interquartile range. C: already-read words that fall at rank K or higher, near the end of the list, as the threshold K varies; grey, control words that never appear in the prompt. D: the animal list of panel A continued with color words. E: lists consisting of four 20-word blocks, each containing elements of the same category; grey, random lists. F: In the blocked lists, the probability of each list word (row) appearing in the top 25 J-lens readouts at each comma (column).
items.title: The Eighty-Word List Test
items.takeaway: When the model reads an 80-word list, the workspace readout holds only around six unrelated words at a time, with older entries silently dropping out. Related words behave differently: within a few items, nearly the whole category loads at once, unread members included. What clears old entries is not the passage of tokens but the arrival of a new category.
items.walkthrough:
The figure reports the paper's [[word-list-experiment]], a behavioral probe of how much the [[j-space]] can hold. The model reads a comma-separated list of 80 words. At every comma, the [[j-lens-readout]] is taken at each layer of the [[workspace-layers]] band. A list word counts as present if its best rank, over that band, falls within the top 25 vocabulary tokens.

Panel A shows two example readouts, taken at layer 79 under the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] convention. After one word ("shark,") the readout already contains a neighborhood of related words — "whale," "fish," "swimming," "submarine," "ocean" — almost none of which have appeared in the list. After eight animals, the readout is dominated by animal words, read or not. Highlighting marks the words actually read.

Panel B is the main count. The x-axis is the comma position; the y-axis is how many list words are present. Blue traces lists of unrelated words. The solid blue line plateaus at around six words and stays flat: entries beyond the most recent few simply drop out. Orange traces single-family lists, pooled over four families. There the dashed line, which counts all 80 list words, climbs to nearly the full family within the first few items. The paper reads this as [[category-loading]]: the workspace is not recalling many list entries but representing their shared category, using the collection of lens vectors that constitute it. Shading gives the interquartile range. Panel C varies the rank threshold $K$ and shows the qualitative picture does not depend on the choice of 25; grey control words that never appear in the prompt set the chance level.

Panels D, E, and F show [[category-displacement]]. In D, the animal list continues with color words; after a single color, the animals are largely evicted. In E, lists are built from four consecutive 20-word category blocks, with random lists in grey. Panel F plots, for each list word (row) and comma (column), the probability of appearing in the top 25: each category enters at its block's start, persists through it, and is cleared within a few words of the switch.

The figure is the paper's evidence for [[j-space-capacity]] as a functional limit, an analogue of the [[workspace-capacity-limit]] in [[working-memory]]. The count in panel B pools all workspace layers; at a single layer the number of unrelated items falls to one or two ([[single-layer-capacity]]).

terms.definition: The J-lens read operation: the residual stream at a layer is passed through the lens to produce a score for every vocabulary token, and the tokens are ranked by that score. Here it is taken at each comma of the list.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors — the representations the paper argues form the model's workspace. This figure measures how many words it can hold at once.
The middle band of layers where the J-space carries workspace-like content. A word's presence is judged by its best rank anywhere in this band, so panel B's counts pool over layers.
A word's position in the readout's ordering of all vocabulary tokens, taken at its best (lowest) value over the workspace layers. Rank within the top 25 counts as present.
The presence threshold: a list word is counted as in the readout if its best rank is 25 or better. Panel C shows the findings are not sensitive to this choice.
The token position at which the lens is read — one measurement after each list word, so the x-axes of panels B, D, E, and F advance one comma per word.
The layer of panel A's example readouts. The paper indexes 25 evenly spaced layers as 0-100, so 79 reads as roughly 79% of the model's depth — late in the workspace band.
Example layer-79 readouts after one word and after eight words of an animal list, with the words actually read highlighted. It shows related but unread words entering the readout immediately.
The first word of panel A's example list. After it alone, the readout already contains "whale," "fish," "swimming," "submarine," and "ocean," almost none of which have appeared in the list.
The main count: number of list words present in the readout at each comma, for single-family lists (orange) versus unrelated lists (blue).
80-word lists drawn from one category, such as animals. Results are pooled over four families. These load the readout as a whole category within a few items.
80-word lists of items with no shared category, drawn at random. Only around six of the words read so far are present at any comma, and the count stays flat.
In panels B, D, and E: the count restricted to words the model has already read.
In panel B: the count over all 80 list words, unread ones included. For single-family lists it rises to nearly the full family within the first few items — the signature of category loading.
The band around each curve, spanning the 25th to 75th percentile over trials.
A robustness check: the number of already-read words at rank K or better, measured near the end of the list, as the threshold K varies. It shows the top-25 cutoff is not doing the work.
The rank cutoff varied along panel C's x-axis; the rest of the figure fixes it at 25.
Words that never appear in the prompt, counted the same way. They set the chance level against which the list words' presence is judged.
The animal list of panel A continued with color words. After even one color word, the readout is dominated by colors and the animals are largely evicted.
Counts for blocked lists: four consecutive 20-word blocks, each of one category. Each category enters at its block's start, persists through it, and is cleared within a few words of the switch.
Unstructured lists plotted alongside the blocked ones for comparison; they show the flat roughly-six-word plateau rather than block structure.

A heatmap over the blocked lists: for each list word (row) and each comma (column), the probability of that word appearing in the top-25 readout. The block structure appears as four diagonal bands that cut off at each category switch.
Example word categories used in panels A and D; two of the categories from which the single-family and blocked lists are built.

numbers.meaning: Words per list. Long enough to far exceed the roughly six-word plateau for unrelated words, so displacement is visible, and to make full-family loading (the dashed orange line approaching 80) unmistakable.
The rank threshold for counting a word as present in the readout. Panel C varies this cutoff and finds the qualitative findings do not depend on it.

How many already-read unrelated words are present at any given comma. The count stays flat as the list continues — words beyond the most recent few drop out. This is the figure's functional capacity estimate for unrelated content, pooled over the workspace layers.

The same count at a single workspace layer (layer 79, shown in an appendix figure the text cites). Presence anywhere in the band is a lenient criterion; per layer, capacity for unrelated items is smaller still.
Two uses: the number of word families pooled into panel B's orange curves, and the number of consecutive category blocks in panel E's lists.
Words per category block in the panel E and F lists; four blocks of 20 make up the 80.
The layer of panel A's example readouts, in the paper's 0-100 percentage indexing — a late workspace layer, roughly 79% of the model's depth.
The two snapshots in panel A: the readout after a single list word and after eight. One word already pulls in a neighborhood of related words; eight lock the readout onto the shared category.

Panel D's list: eight animals followed by eight color words. A single color word suffices to displace the animal representations, showing eviction is driven by the category switch rather than by list length.

items.caption: Figure 32: MLP blocks preferentially amplify J-space-aligned directions. For each source layer $\ell$ , the median gain of the MLP block at layer $\ell+1$ on 2,000 unit directions per population, normalized so that isotropic random directions have gain 1. Left: J-lens vectors against the output-weight directions of layer- $\ell$ MLP neurons. Right: SAE decoder directions in six equal-sized strata (N=2,000 each) by J-lens kurtosis percentile (top 1%, 1–5%, 5–10%, 10–20%, 20–50%, bottom 50%; ??).
items.title: MLP gain on J-space directions
items.takeaway: Across the workspace layer range, MLP blocks amplify directions aligned with the J-space roughly ten times more than random directions, while ordinary neuron output directions are not amplified at all. Among SAE features, amplification rises monotonically with J-lens kurtosis, so the more a direction lies in the J-space, the more strongly the next MLP boosts it.
items.walkthrough:
The item is a two-panel line chart, and it is the paper's first structural test of [[j-space-broadcast]]: whether the model's weights are built to spread [[j-space]] content down through the layers, rather than that spreading being an accident of particular inputs.

Both panels share the same axes. The horizontal axis is the source layer $\ell$, the depth at which a candidate direction is defined. The vertical axis is [[mlp-gain]]: a unit direction $v$ at layer $\ell$ is fed to the [[mlp-block]] at layer $\ell+1$, and the norm of the block's output is recorded. That norm is divided by the median output norm over isotropic random directions, so a random direction scores 1 by construction. Each curve plots the median gain over 2,000 unit directions from one population. The paper flags the metric as a first-pass approximation, since in natural settings the gain can depend on what else is in the [[residual-stream]] alongside $v$.

The left panel compares two populations. One is the [[j-lens-vector]] population at layer $\ell$ — the directions the [[jacobian-lens]] associates with vocabulary tokens. The other is the output-weight directions of layer-$\ell$ MLP neurons, the directions ordinary neurons write into the stream. The J-lens curve sits near 1 before the workspace onset (around layer 38 in this model), climbs to roughly $10	imes$ through the [[workspace-layers]], and falls again near the output. The neuron curve stays near 1 throughout. The next layer's MLP treats a neuron's own output as unremarkable, and treats a J-lens direction as something to amplify.

The right panel runs the same measurement on [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions, split into six equal strata of 2,000 by their [[lens-kurtosis]] percentile — top 1%, 1–5%, 5–10%, 10–20%, 20–50%, and bottom 50%. Gain orders monotonically with kurtosis: the top-1% stratum is amplified most, and the bottom half stays near baseline. In the early workspace layers the top stratum's gain exceeds the J-lens vectors' own, which the paper reads as a sign that the lens only partially captures the true workspace directions. A companion weight-level analysis ([[neuron-connectivity]]) corroborates the picture.

terms.definition: The horizontal axis: the depth at which each candidate unit direction is defined. The gain is always measured one layer later, at the MLP block of layer ℓ+1.

The vertical axis: the output norm of the layer-(ℓ+1) MLP block applied to a unit direction, divided by the median output norm over isotropic random directions. A value of 1 means the direction is amplified no more than noise.
The feed-forward component of a transformer layer, acting at a single token position; here it is treated as one nonlinear function whose amplification of a direction is measured.
The left panel's first population: one direction per vocabulary token per layer, each encoding the model's disposition to say that token. Their collection defines the J-space.
