terms.definition: The y-axis of every panel: the fraction of known intermediate concepts that appear among the top $k$ tokens of a lens's readout, at any layer of the model. It is a recovery rate, not an accuracy on the model's own output.
The x-axis: how many of the lens's highest-scoring vocabulary tokens are inspected at each layer. Larger $k$ is a looser test, so every curve is non-decreasing in $k$.

The number in parentheses after each legend entry: the area under that method's pass@k curve when plotted against $\log k$, normalised so a method that always ranks the intermediate first would score 1. Here it is not the area under an ROC curve.
The legend title in each panel. It labels the three lines by method and gives each method's normalised AUC for that panel's distribution.

The paper's own method, drawn in black. For each vocabulary token it holds a residual-stream direction — obtained from a corpus-averaged Jacobian from layer $\ell$ to the final layer — that disposes the model to say that token.

The earlier baseline, drawn in red: apply the model's unembedding matrix directly to the intermediate residual stream. In the paper's formulation this is the J-lens with the Jacobian replaced by the identity.

The other baseline, drawn in blue: per-layer affine maps trained so that the decoded distribution matches the model's own next-token distribution. The paper argues that objective is correlational rather than causal.

The known single-token word that the model must compute for a given prompt, chosen so that it is neither present in the input nor identical to the predicted output. Recovering it is what pass@k scores.

The panel for two-hop factual questions whose surface tokens have no direct association with the answer, so a bridging entity must be computed — for example Mars, before answering that the fourth planet's colour is red.

The panel for prompts written entirely in a non-English language, testing whether the model routes through English-aligned representations. Four intermediates are sought per item: the language, the relation, and the English equivalents of the input and output words.
The panel for rhyming couplets, where the lens is read at the newline between the two lines and the target is the second line's final word — a word the model has planned but not yet written.
The panel for arithmetic expressions such as (2 + 3) × 4. Two intermediates are sought per item, the partial result and the pending operation, with single-token synonyms accepted.

The panel for short passages that depict a concept through behavioural cues without naming it. The lens is read at the closing period, and no single token is the trigger — the concept must be assembled from accumulated context.
The panel for sentences ending on a common misspelling. The target is the correctly spelled word, read at the final fragment of the misspelled token, where the model is not about to say that word.
The rule under which recovery is scored: an intermediate counts as recovered if it reaches the top $k$ at any depth of the network, so each method is credited with its best layer.

The $k$ highest-scoring entries of a lens's distribution over the tokenizer vocabulary at one position and layer. The intermediates are all chosen to be single-token words so that they can appear in such a list.

numbers.meaning: The number of panels, one per prompt distribution in the benchmark suite. Each distribution is a different way for a model to be forced to compute a concept it does not say.
The seven values of $k$ at which pass@k is measured, marked by dots on each curve. They are spaced roughly evenly on a log scale, which is also the scale the AUC integrates over.
The y-axis range of every panel, gridded at 0.2. It is a fraction of intermediates recovered, so 1.0 means every known intermediate was found within the top $k$ at some layer.
The AUC a method would score if it always placed the intermediate at rank 1 for every item. The normalisation is defined against this ceiling, which makes AUC values comparable across panels.

Multihop AUC for the Jacobian, logit and tuned lenses. The paper calls the J-lens margin over the logit lens modest here; two-hop bridging entities are the case earlier work had already shown the logit lens can decode.
Multilingual AUC for the three lenses. A gap of 0.18 between the J-lens and the logit lens — one of the four distributions where the paper describes the margin as substantial.

Poetry AUC for the three lenses. The tuned lens's 0.18 is its second-worst score; the paper attributes it to the readout position being a newline, whose next token carries no information about the planned rhyme.
Order-of-operations AUC for the three lenses. 0.89 is the J-lens's highest score in the figure — partial arithmetic results are recovered at or near rank 1 for most items.
Association AUC for the three lenses. The J-lens and logit lens are within 0.03 of each other, the narrowest gap in the figure, while the tuned lens's 0.11 is the lowest value anywhere in it.
Typo AUC for the three lenses. The 0.31 gap between the J-lens and the logit lens is the widest in the figure.

The range of the J-lens's pass@1 across the six panels — about 0.36 on association, 0.42 multilingual, 0.46 poetry, 0.55 multihop, 0.56 order_ops, 0.57 typo. Roughly half the intermediates are already the single top-ranked token at some layer.

The J-lens's pass@100 on five of the six panels; poetry and order_ops reach 1.00 by $k=50$, multihop and typo sit near 0.98, multilingual 0.91 and association 0.90. Almost every intermediate appears somewhere in the top 100.

The tuned lens's pass@1 across the panels — near zero on association, about 0.02 on poetry, 0.06 typo, 0.24 multihop, 0.25 multilingual, 0.37 order_ops. It rarely ranks an unspoken intermediate first.
The tuned lens's pass@100 on association, its lowest endpoint. Even with a hundred tokens inspected at every layer, it misses the implied concept on roughly two thirds of items.

The approximate range of $k$ over which the blue tuned-lens curve crosses above the red logit-lens curve on multihop, order_ops and typo. Its deficit on those three is in ranking rather than in the concept being absent.

Item counts for multihop, multilingual, poetry, order_ops, association and typo respectively, from the section text rather than the figure. The multilingual and order_ops sets look for several intermediates per item, so the pass@k denominator counts intermediates, not prompts.

items.caption: Figure 53: KL divergence induced on the model's output distribution by ablating each lens's intermediate direction at all positions (except in the poetry case, where we exclude the target position).
items.title: Output damage from ablating each lens's direction
items.takeaway: Zeroing the residual-stream component along a lens's vector for the intermediate concept moves the model's output distribution further when that vector comes from the Jacobian lens than when it comes from the logit lens or the tuned lens, on all three prompt distributions shown. On the multihop set the J-lens ablation induces roughly twice the KL divergence of the other two. The paper reads this as evidence that the J-lens direction is the one the model actually computes with, not merely the one that displays the concept.
items.walkthrough:
A grouped bar chart. The x-axis carries three prompt distributions from the paper's [[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]]: the [[multihop-benchmark]], the [[multilingual-benchmark]] and the [[poetry-benchmark]]. Within each group stand three bars, one per lens, keyed by the legend titled "Lens Type": black for the [[jacobian-lens]], red for the [[logit-lens]], blue for the [[tuned-lens]]. Bar height is the mean [[kl-divergence]] induced on the model's output distribution, averaged over the items in that benchmark.

The intervention behind a single bar runs as follows. Every lens assigns each vocabulary token a direction in the [[residual-stream]] — for the J-lens this is the [[j-lens-vector]]. Each benchmark item has a known intermediate concept the model must compute but never sees and never says, such as Mars in "the color of the planet fourth from the Sun is". The lens's vector for that intermediate token is taken, and the residual stream's component along it is projected to zero. The KL divergence between the resulting output distribution and the undisturbed one is recorded. This is the paper's [[ablation-kl-effect]]. A larger value means the erased direction mattered more to the answer.

The caption states that the projection is applied at all positions, with the poetry items excluded at the target position — the place where the rhyme word itself is produced. The body text of the same section instead describes ablating at the readout position; the caption is the more specific statement for this chart.

Reading the heights, the black bar is the tallest in every group. Multihop shows the widest gap: about $2.12$ for the J-lens against about $0.93$ and $0.88$, the "roughly twice" the text reports. Multilingual gives $0.91$, $0.67$ and $0.48$. Poetry gives $0.59$, $0.23$ and $0.34$, and there the tuned lens edges above the logit lens.

The error bars carry the qualification. On multihop and multilingual the black interval clears both others. On poetry it overlaps the tuned-lens interval, so the ordering within that group is not separated by this measure. The figure also does not label what the bars represent, and it covers three of the six distributions. The companion evidence is the [[swap-success-rate]], reported separately.

terms.definition: The vertical axis: the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the model's next-token distribution after the ablation and its distribution without the ablation, averaged over the items of one benchmark. Larger means the ablation disturbed the output more.
The legend key: which of the three interpretability methods supplied the direction that was ablated. Colour, not position, identifies the lens.
The paper's own method, which assigns each vocabulary token the residual-stream direction that disposes the model toward saying that token. Its bar is the black one in each group.
An earlier method that decodes an intermediate residual-stream state by applying the model's final unembedding to it directly. Its token direction is simply the corresponding unembedding row.

A method that trains a per-layer affine map so that the decoded distribution matches the model's own final output distribution. Its objective is agreement with the output rather than exposure of intermediates.
The benchmark of two-hop factual questions where the model must compute a bridging entity, for example computing Mars before answering "red". Fifty items.
The benchmark of prompts written entirely in a non-English language, testing whether the model routes through English-aligned representations. Fifty-four items, each with four intermediates.
The benchmark of rhyming couplets where the intermediate is the final word of the second line, sought at the newline between the lines. Fifty-two items.

The lens's vector for the token naming the item's known intermediate concept — the thing ablated in this experiment. Each lens supplies a different vector for the same token, which is what the chart compares.
The intervention that removes the residual stream's component along a chosen direction while leaving the rest of the activation untouched. Here it is applied to the intermediate direction.
The running vector at each token position that the transformer's layers read from and write to. It is the space in which every lens vector lives and in which the ablation is performed.
In the poetry items, the position at which the rhyme word is produced. The caption says ablation is applied at all positions except this one for poetry.
The vertical whiskers on each bar, marking the spread around the mean across items. The figure does not state what they represent.
The paper's name for the quantity plotted: the causal metric measuring how much the output moves when a lens's intermediate direction is removed.
The second causal metric in the same comparison, reported in the next figure rather than here: how often exchanging one intermediate for another flips the model's top-1 output.

numbers.meaning: The range of the y-axis. It is set by the tallest bar, the multihop J-lens value near 2.12; every other bar sits below 1.0.

Multihop, Jacobian lens: the mean KL divergence from ablating the J-lens direction for the bridging entity. The largest effect in the figure, and the basis for the text's claim of roughly twice the other lenses.
Multihop, logit lens. Ablating the unembedding direction for the same intermediate token moves the output less than half as far as the J-lens direction does.
Multihop, tuned lens. Close to the logit-lens value, and likewise far below the J-lens bar.
Multilingual, Jacobian lens. The J-lens again leads its group, though the whole group sits much lower than multihop.
Multilingual, logit lens. Second in its group, above the tuned lens.
Multilingual, tuned lens. The smallest of the three in this group, and the tightest error bar in the figure.
Poetry, Jacobian lens. The leading bar of the group, but with a wide error bar.
Poetry, logit lens. The smallest bar in the whole figure. The poetry readout sits at a newline, a position where next-token-aligned directions carry little of the planned rhyme.
Poetry, tuned lens. The one place in the figure where the tuned lens exceeds the logit lens.
The J-lens interval clears both others with a gap, so the ordering in this group is not explained by item-to-item spread.
All three intervals are disjoint, giving the cleanest three-way separation in the figure.
The J-lens interval overlaps the tuned-lens interval, so the J-lens advantage over the tuned lens is not separated here. It does clear the logit-lens interval.
The paper's summary of the multihop gap. The arithmetic: 2.12 divided by 0.93 is about 2.3, and 2.12 divided by 0.88 is about 2.4, so "roughly twice" is a conservative statement of the ratio.
The number of items in the multihop, multilingual and poetry benchmarks respectively, over which each bar's mean is taken. The counts come from the section text, not from the figure.
The chart covers three of the six prompt distributions the section builds. Order of operations, typo and association are not plotted here.

items.caption: Figure 54: Fraction of items whose top-1 output flips to the implied answer under a lens coordinate swap, across three model scales.
items.title: Swap success across three model scales
items.takeaway: Exchanging one concept for another along J-lens directions flips the model's top-1 answer to the implied one far more often than the same exchange along logit-lens or tuned-lens directions, and the ordering holds on all three model sizes tested. This is a causal check rather than a readout check: it tests whether the lens found a direction the model actually computes with, not merely one that displays the right word.
items.walkthrough:
The chart is a grouped bar chart with nine bars. Three groups sit along the horizontal axis, one per model: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5, which are ascending size tiers in the [[claude-model-family|Claude family]]. Within each group the three bars are the three techniques being compared: the paper's [[jacobian-lens|Jacobian lens]] in black, the [[logit-lens]] in red, and the [[tuned-lens]] in blue. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 1 and carries a single quantity, the swap success fraction. Black whiskers on each bar are error bars.

The quantity being plotted comes from an intervention rather than a readout. Each lens assigns every vocabulary token a direction in the residual stream. The [[lens-coordinate-swap]] takes a source token $s$ and a target token $t$, forms $V = [v_s\; v_t]$ from their two lens vectors, reads the activation's coordinates along them as $c = V^\dagger h$ using the [[pseudoinverse]], and writes back $h + V(\sigma(c) - c)$, where $\sigma$ exchanges the two entries. The part of the activation orthogonal to those two directions is left alone. Here the exchange is applied at full strength, $\alpha = 1$.

A trial counts as a success only when the model's top-1 output token flips to the answer implied by the swapped-in concept. A probability shift that does not reach the top of the distribution counts as a failure.

This figure is one of the paper's two causal comparisons, alongside the [[ablation-kl-effect|ablation KL measure]] of Figure 53. Both exist because a lens that surfaces the right word in its readout has not thereby shown that the model computes with that direction.

The black bars are highest in every group: 0.54 for Haiku, 0.70 for Sonnet, 0.70 for Opus. The corresponding logit-lens bars are 0.34, 0.48 and 0.40, and the tuned-lens bars 0.16, 0.42 and 0.26. The weakest J-lens result, 0.54 on Haiku, still exceeds the strongest non-J result anywhere in the chart, 0.48.

Two things the figure does not establish deserve saying. Success does not rise monotonically with model size, since Opus matches rather than beats Sonnet on the J-lens and falls below it on the other two. And at Sonnet the logit and tuned intervals overlap, so the chart separates the J-lens from the pair but not that pair from each other.

terms.definition: The y-axis quantity: the share of swap trials in which the model's top-1 output token becomes the answer implied by the concept swapped in. It is a strict pass/fail per trial, so partial movement of the output distribution scores nothing.

The intervention behind every bar. It reads an activation's coordinates along two lens vectors, exchanges those two coordinates, and writes the result back, leaving the rest of the activation untouched.
The legend title. It labels the three colored bars within each model group, each bar being one method for assigning a residual-stream direction to a vocabulary token.

The black bar, and the paper's own technique. For each vocabulary token it identifies the direction encoding the model's potential to verbalize that token, derived from an averaged Jacobian rather than from an output-matching objective.
The red bar. An earlier technique that decodes intermediate residual-stream states by applying the model's final unembedding matrix directly, so a token's direction is simply its unembedding row.

The blue bar. A technique that trains a per-layer affine map so that decoding an intermediate state reproduces the model's own next-token distribution; the paper argues this objective is correlational rather than causal.
The smallest of the three models on the x axis. The main-body swap experiments of the paper are run on this model.
The mid-size model on the x axis, one tier above Haiku in the same release generation.
The largest model on the x axis. Its presence is what lets the caption speak of three model scales.

The black whiskers on each bar, marking uncertainty in a proportion estimated from a finite number of trials. The paper's companion swap figures use 95% Wilson intervals, and the widths here are consistent with that, though this caption does not name the interval.
The single highest-probability token in the model's output distribution at the answer position. The success criterion asks whether this token, not merely its probability, changes.
The answer that follows from the concept swapped in rather than the one swapped out. If the intermediate is changed from Mars to Neptune, the implied answer is the color of Neptune.
One prompt from the appendix's benchmarks of known intermediate concepts, at which the lens is applied and a swap attempted. The fraction plotted is over these items.

A concept the model must compute internally that is neither present in the prompt nor identical to the answer, such as the bridging entity in a two-hop question. The swap exchanges one of these for another.

The other causal measure the appendix reports, shown in the neighboring figure: the KL divergence induced on the model's output by projecting out a lens's intermediate direction. It is named here only to place this figure as the second of a pair.

numbers.meaning: The y-axis range, with gridlines every 0.2. It is a fraction of trials, so 1.0 would mean every swap flipped the top-1 output to the implied answer and 0.0 that none did.
J-lens swap success on Haiku 4.5, the lowest of the three black bars. It is still above every red and blue bar in the chart.
Logit-lens swap success on Haiku 4.5, about six tenths of the J-lens value on the same model.
Tuned-lens swap success on Haiku 4.5, the lowest bar anywhere in the figure. Roughly one swap in six flips the output.
J-lens swap success on both Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5, the joint highest bars. The two are equal to the plotted precision, so the figure shows no gain from Sonnet to Opus on this measure.
Logit-lens swap success on Sonnet 4.5. It is the highest non-J-lens bar in the figure, and still below the weakest J-lens bar, 0.54.
Tuned-lens swap success on Sonnet 4.5. This is the one place where the tuned lens comes close to the logit lens, their intervals overlapping.
Logit-lens swap success on Opus 4.5, lower than the same lens on the smaller Sonnet. Success on this measure does not rise monotonically with model size.
Tuned-lens swap success on Opus 4.5, again below its Sonnet value.

The half-widths of the error bars, read off the plot. For a proportion near 0.5 a 95% interval of this width corresponds to a couple of hundred trials per bar; the caption does not state the trial count, so this is an inference from the width rather than a figure the paper gives.

The strength of the swap used for this comparison, stated in the surrounding text: the source coordinate is removed and the target coordinate written in at full size, with no doubling. The main body elsewhere reports a double-strength variant at alpha = 2, which is not used here.
The number of models compared, giving the three groups on the x axis, and also the number of lenses, giving the three bars per group. Nine bars in total.

The item counts of the appendix's six prompt distributions - multihop, multilingual, order of operations, poetry, typo and association - which are the pool of prompts with known intermediates that these comparisons draw on. The caption does not say which of the six supply the swap pairs plotted here.

The rough factor by which ablating a J-lens direction exceeds ablating a logit- or tuned-lens direction in output KL divergence, reported in the text for the companion figure. It is quoted here only to show that the two causal measures agree in direction.

items.caption: Figure 55: Per-layer agreement between each lens and the model's true next-token distribution, measured using KL divergence, entropy, and top-1 accuracy.
items.title: Next-token agreement by lens and layer
items.takeaway: Measured against the model's own next-token distribution, the tuned lens is the best match at every depth and the J-lens is the worst, carrying higher KL divergence than even the uncorrected logit lens through most of the network. The paper treats that ranking as a feature rather than a defect: the J-lens is not fitted to anticipate the output, and the comparisons that precede this one found that the directions which best anticipate the output are not the ones that best expose, or causally drive, the computation producing it.
items.walkthrough:
This is the third and last of the quantitative comparisons in the paper's [[lens-evaluation]] suite, and the only one on which the [[jacobian-lens]] finishes behind the alternatives. The section is explicit about why it is reported: it is the metric the [[tuned-lens]] was trained on.

The horizontal axis is depth, under the paper's convention of [[layer-percentage-indexing]]. Twenty-five evenly spaced layers of Claude Sonnet 4.5's [[residual-stream]] are relabeled 0 to 100, so that a layer number reads as a percentage of the way through the model. Three measures are plotted against that axis, and each carries one curve per lens: the J-lens, the [[logit-lens]], and the tuned lens.

All three measures compare against one fixed target. That target is the model's actual output distribution over the vocabulary at the position in question — the distribution produced by [[next-token-prediction]] at the end of the full forward pass. A lens readout is a distribution over the same [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], computed at an intermediate layer; for the J-lens it is $\text{softmax}(W_U\,\text{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell))$, the [[j-lens-readout]]. The question at each depth is how close the intermediate readout already is to the final answer.

The first measure is [[kl-divergence]] between the two distributions. It is zero when they match and grows as the lens puts probability mass where the model does not. The second is entropy: how spread out each lens's readout is at that layer. The third is top-1 accuracy: the fraction of positions at which the lens's highest-scoring token is also the model's highest-scoring token.

The tuned lens is the best predictor of the model's output at every depth. The paper attributes this to construction rather than to insight, since matching the output distribution is precisely the objective its per-layer affine maps were fitted to. The J-lens is the worst, with higher KL than the uncorrected logit lens through most of the network.

The section reports that ordering in terms of KL. It names entropy and top-1 accuracy as measures without stating how the three lenses rank on them.

The paper's reading of the result is that anticipating the output and exposing the computation are different things, and that this figure measures the first.

terms.definition: The quantity the figure reports: how closely a lens's readout at a given depth matches the model's own final output distribution. Higher agreement means the intermediate readout already looks like the answer.
The reference every curve is scored against: the probability distribution over the vocabulary that the full model actually produces at that position, after all layers.
One of the three measures. It is zero when the lens readout and the model's output distribution coincide, and grows as the lens places mass on tokens the model does not. Lower is closer agreement.

One of the three measures: how spread out a lens's readout distribution is at each layer. A peaked readout has low entropy, a diffuse one high entropy. The section names this measure but does not report which lens ranks where on it.
One of the three measures: the fraction of positions at which the lens's single highest-scoring token equals the model's own highest-scoring next token. Higher is closer agreement.
The shared horizontal axis, running 0 to 100. It indexes 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed so the number reads as a percentage of the model's depth.

The paper's own readout method, drawn in black in the companion figures of this section. It assigns each vocabulary token a direction at each layer via the corpus-averaged Jacobian to the final layer. On this figure it is the worst match to the output.

The earlier method that applies the unembedding matrix directly to an intermediate residual stream, equivalent to setting $J_\ell = I$. Drawn in red in this section's figures. Here it sits between the tuned lens and the J-lens.

A method that fits a per-layer affine map — a linear transform plus a bias — trained to match the model's output distribution. Drawn in blue in this section's figures. It is the best match here by construction.
The legend heading used across this section's comparison figures, listing the three curves: Jacobian Lens, Logit Lens, Tuned Lens.

The distribution over vocabulary tokens that a lens produces from a single residual-stream activation at one layer and position. For the J-lens it is $\text{softmax}(W_U\,\text{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell))$.
The corpus-averaged Jacobian from layer $\ell$'s residual stream to the final layer, the matrix that distinguishes the J-lens from the logit lens. It approaches the identity in the last layers.
The unembedding matrix: the model's final linear map from residual stream to scores over the vocabulary. All three lenses end by applying it.
The residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and the position being read — the input each lens decodes into a vocabulary distribution.

The paper's phrasing for the logit lens taken as-is, without the Jacobian correction the J-lens applies. Naming it that way sharpens the result: the correction makes agreement with the output worse, not better.
The default model for results in the paper, and the one these per-layer curves are computed on. Key results elsewhere are corroborated on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5.
The fixed token set the model's tokenizer produces. Both the lens readouts and the model's output are distributions over this same set, which is what makes them comparable.

numbers.meaning: The curves in each measure: the J-lens, the logit lens, and the tuned lens. The whole point of the figure is their ordering on a metric the tuned lens was trained for.
KL divergence, entropy, and top-1 accuracy, all computed per layer against the same reference distribution. The section reports the lens ordering only for KL.
The depth range after reindexing, so a layer number is a percentage of the model's depth. This makes the same axis usable across models of different layer counts.

The number of evenly spaced residual-stream layers actually sampled and plotted. Everything between them is interpolation, and the paper notes elsewhere that this subsampling makes transitions look sharper than they are.

The floor of the KL panel, reached only when a lens readout exactly equals the model's output distribution. Curves are expected to fall toward it in the final layers, where all three lenses converge on the next-token prediction.
The range of the accuracy measure: 0 when the lens never picks the model's top token, 1 when it always does. Near the output, all three lenses approach the upper end.

The range of the entropy measure: 0 for a readout concentrated on a single token, $\log$ of the vocabulary size for a uniform one. The model's own output entropy sets the scale a lens is being compared against.

The workspace band's start and end as located elsewhere in the paper. This figure is not reported as marking them, but they are the depths at which the paper expects lens content to shift from empty, to intermediate, to output-driving.

Context from the comparison immediately before this one, not from this figure: ablating J-lens directions induced about twice the output KL of ablating logit- or tuned-lens directions on the multihop task. It is the counterweight the paper places against losing here.

items.caption: Figure 56: Pairwise agreement between the logit, tuned, and Jacobian lenses by layer. Left: mean cosine between corresponding lens vectors. Middle: symmetric KL between readout distributions. Right: top-1 agreement. The shaded band marks the workspace layers.
items.title: Where the three lenses agree, layer by layer
items.takeaway: Comparing the logit, tuned, and Jacobian lenses against each other rather than against an external target, the three agreement measures pick out four ranges of depth whose boundaries line up with the workspace band identified independently in section 4.1. Direction agreement and readout agreement come apart in the early workspace: the J-lens and logit lens vectors swing into rough alignment while their actual readouts still disagree.
items.walkthrough:
Three panels compare the lenses against one another rather than against any outside standard. Three lenses are in play: the [[logit-lens]], the [[tuned-lens]], and the paper's own [[jacobian-lens]]. Each panel therefore carries three curves, one for each unordered pair of lenses.

The horizontal axis of every panel is depth, in the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] convention. Twenty-five evenly spaced layers are reindexed to 0-100, so a layer number reads as a percentage of the way through the network. The default model is Claude Sonnet 4.5. A shaded band marks the workspace layers, roughly L38 to L92, which is the middle of the three [[layer-bands]].

The panels measure three different kinds of agreement. Left is the mean [[cosine-similarity]] between the two methods' vectors for the same vocabulary token, averaged over the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. That asks whether the two lenses point a given token in aligned directions in [[residual-stream]] space. Middle is the symmetric [[kl-divergence]] between the two lenses' readout distributions. Right is top-1 agreement, the rate at which the two lenses rank the same token first. Both readout measures are averaged over a held-out set of pretraining-style text.

The paper reads four layer ranges off these curves.

Before the workspace, at layers 0-33, no pair agrees on readouts: top-1 agreement is near zero and symmetric KL is high. The logit-tuned cosine is nonetheless around 0.9. The tuned lens is an affine map, and cosine sees only its linear part; stripping out the learned bias collapses the logit-tuned KL to near zero here. The paper reads this as the tuned lens's early advantage coming from the bias alone, which means it is ignoring the input. J-lens vectors are close to orthogonal to both, a consequence of their being confined to a low-rank subspace at these depths.

Through the early workspace, about L38 to L58, the J-logit cosine climbs from near zero to around 0.7 over some twenty layers. Their KL stays near its peak and top-1 agreement stays low. The directions align before the readouts do.

Through the late workspace, about L62 to L92, the J-logit KL falls monotonically and their top-1 agreement is the first pairing to rise appreciably above zero. The tuned lens stays the outlier on both readout measures.

Past the workspace, all three collapse together: cosine approaches one, KL drops to zero, top-1 rises to one. Every lens has converged on [[next-token-prediction]].

terms.definition: The earlier readout method that decodes an intermediate residual-stream state by applying the model's final unembedding matrix directly. One of the three lenses compared here.

A readout method that trains a per-layer affine map so the decoded distribution matches the model's own next-token distribution. It is the only one of the three trained on an output-matching objective.
The paper's own lens, built from a corpus-averaged Jacobian from layer L to the final layer, giving one vector per vocabulary token per layer. Written J-lens in the panel legends.
The quantity plotted: each curve is one unordered pair of lenses, so the three curves are logit-tuned, logit-J, and tuned-J. No curve compares a lens against the model itself.
Depth in the network, running left to right across all three panels. Reported on the paper's 0-100 reindexing rather than as raw layer counts.

The cosine similarity between the two lenses' vectors for the same vocabulary token, averaged over the whole vocabulary. It measures whether the two methods point a token in the same direction in activation space, ignoring scale.
The direction in residual-stream space that a lens assigns to one vocabulary token at one layer. The left panel compares these directions token by token.

The KL divergence between the two lenses' readout distributions, symmetrized so neither lens is treated as the reference. Large values mean the two lenses report different things about the same activation.
The probability distribution over the vocabulary that a lens produces from an activation. The middle and right panels compare these distributions; the left panel does not.
The fraction of positions at which two lenses put the same token in first place. It is the coarsest of the three measures, and the least forgiving.
The marked span of workspace layers, roughly L38 to L92, carried over from the layer-band analysis of section 4.1. It is an annotation on the plot, not something the agreement measures produce.
The middle band of depth where the paper argues the J-space carries persistent abstract content, distinct from the input tokens and from the imminent output.
Layers 0-33, before the shaded band. The paper reports that none of the three lenses produces meaningful readouts here.
Roughly L38 to L58. The range where the J-lens starts recovering intermediate concepts that the logit lens still misses.
Roughly L62 to L92. The range where the logit lens starts surfacing useful intermediates too and its readouts converge toward the J-lens's.
The final few layers past the workspace, where lens vectors drive the imminent output rather than carrying intermediates. All three lenses agree here.
The running per-position vector that transformer layers read from and write to. It is the space in which the left panel's cosines are computed.
The tokenizer's fixed token set. The left panel's cosine is averaged over it, one token at a time.
The text the middle and right panels are averaged over: ordinary pretraining-like sequences, not the six intermediate-concept benchmarks used elsewhere in the appendix.
A linear transform plus a bias term, which is the form of the tuned lens. The distinction matters here because cosine similarity sees only the linear part and is blind to the bias.
The constant vector the tuned lens adds after its linear transform. The paper reports that in early layers this term alone carries the divergence between the tuned and logit lenses.
The small linear subspace the J-lens vectors collapse into in early layers, measured separately in Figure 28d. It explains why the J-lens is near-orthogonal to the two full-rank lenses there.
The model these curves are computed on, the paper's default throughout. This figure does not repeat the measurement across model scales.
The model's output distribution over the following token. It is what all three lenses converge on in the final layers, which is why the panels collapse there.

numbers.meaning: The number of lenses compared: logit, tuned, and Jacobian. It fixes the rest of the layout.
One per unordered pair of three lenses: logit-tuned, logit-J, tuned-J. Three items give exactly three pairs.
Mean cosine on the left, symmetric KL in the middle, top-1 agreement on the right. Each answers a different question about the same pair of lenses at the same layer.
The number of evenly spaced residual-stream layers the paper reports on. Every layer-wise plot in the paper, this one included, is sampled at these 25 depths.
The range the 25 layers are reindexed onto, so an x-axis value reads as a percentage of network depth rather than an absolute layer count.
The pre-workspace range the paper reads off these curves. Through it, top-1 agreement is near zero and symmetric KL is high for every pairing.

The logit-tuned mean cosine through the pre-workspace layers. It is high because the tuned lens's linear transform is effectively the identity there, so only its bias separates it from the logit lens.
Top-1 agreement for every pairing before the workspace. The paper takes this as consistent with none of the three producing meaningful readouts at these depths.

The symmetric KL between logit and tuned readouts in early layers once the tuned lens's learned bias is removed. This is a separate measurement reported in the text, not a curve on the plot, and it is what supports the claim that the bias carries the whole difference.
The workspace onset layer, where the shaded band begins. It is the same boundary the four independent metrics of section 4.1 converge on.
The early workspace range. Here the J-lens starts recovering intermediates while the logit lens largely does not.
The J-logit mean cosine reached by the end of the early workspace, up from near zero at the start of the band. The vectors are pointing in broadly similar directions by this depth.
The span over which that J-logit cosine climbs from near zero to about 0.7. On the 0-100 indexing this is a fifth of the network's depth.
The late workspace range, where the J-logit symmetric KL falls monotonically and their top-1 agreement is the first pairing to rise appreciably above zero.
The workspace offset layer, where the shaded band ends. Past it the layers are read as motor layers driving the output.
Cosine similarities approach one for every pairing past the workspace. All three lenses are pointing each token in the same direction there.
Symmetric KL drops to zero past the workspace. The readout distributions themselves have become the same, not just the directions.
Top-1 agreement rises to one past the workspace. Every lens is surfacing the model's next-token prediction, so there is nothing left to disagree about.

The number of layer ranges the paper picks out of these curves: pre-workspace, early workspace, late workspace, and motor. The paper's point is that these boundaries line up with the workspace boundaries found independently in section 4.1.

items.caption: Figure 57: Sonnet 4.5 J-lens pass@K AUC evals for different methodological variations of the J-lens recipe.
items.title: Recipe ablations for intermediate recovery
items.takeaway: Five ways of building the J-lens matrix are graded on the same six intermediate-recovery benchmarks, under both mean and median aggregation across prompts. Four of the five recipes land close together, so the lens's readout quality is not very sensitive to these design choices; the exception is restricting the Jacobian to the current token, which is clearly the weakest recipe under mean aggregation.
items.walkthrough:
Two heatmaps sit side by side, reporting the same measurement under two different ways of averaging. Both grade variants of the [[jacobian-lens]] on how well the lens surfaces a concept the model had to compute internally but never wrote out.

Rows are five recipes for building the lens matrix $J_\ell$. Columns are the six prompt distributions of the [[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]] — [[multihop-benchmark|multihop]], [[multilingual-benchmark|multilingual]], [[poetry-benchmark|poetry]], [[order-of-operations-benchmark|order_ops]], [[association-benchmark|association]] and [[typo-benchmark|typo]] — plus an `avg` column set off by a white gutter, which is the mean of the six cells to its left.

Each cell is a normalized [[pass-at-k-auc|pass@k AUC]]: pass@k measured across a range of $k$, integrated against $\log k$, and scaled so that a lens ranking the target intermediate first every time would score 1. Higher is better. The viridis bar runs from about 0.54 to 0.89, dark purple low and yellow high.

The panels differ only in [[jacobian-aggregation]]. The left takes the per-element mean of the per-prompt Jacobians; the right takes the per-element median.

In the mean panel the penultimate-layer recipe leads at 0.79, ahead of the default at 0.76, freeze-qk at 0.75, future-only at 0.73 and current-token-only at 0.65. Its margin comes almost entirely from two columns: multilingual, 0.71 against 0.66, and typo, 0.83 against 0.76.

The current-token-only row is the one clear loser. Restricting the Jacobian to $t' = t$, one of the [[target-position-variants]], sends multilingual to 0.54 and typo to 0.55 — the two darkest cells in the figure. Both are readout positions where the intermediate is not the next token, so a lens confined to the present position has little to work with.

The freeze-qk row, the [[frozen-qk-variant]], tracks the default within about 0.02 in every column.

The median panel compresses the spread. Four rows fall between 0.74 and 0.76, and current-token-only recovers to 0.71.

Two places cut against the ordering. Future-only takes the best multihop cell in both panels, 0.86 and 0.82. And on association every recipe lands between 0.65 and 0.69, so that column separates nothing.

The paper reads the figure as showing the methods are "fairly consistent," with penultimate under mean aggregation a small improvement.

terms.definition: The model these ablations were run on; the mid-size tier of the Claude family and the model used for most of the paper's lens comparisons.

The Jacobian lens: for each layer, an averaged Jacobian $J_\ell$ from the residual stream at that layer to the target layer, composed with the unembedding to give a vocabulary readout of an activation. Every row of this figure is one way of computing that matrix.
The title's name for the experiment: holding the evaluation fixed and varying one construction choice of the lens at a time, to see how much each choice matters.

The metric filling every cell. An intermediate is recovered at $k$ if it appears in the lens's top-$k$ tokens at any layer; pass@k is the fraction of intermediates recovered; the AUC integrates that curve against $\log k$.
The colorbar label, and the quantity in each cell. Normalized means the area is scaled so that a method always ranking the intermediate first scores 1.
The left panel. Per-prompt Jacobians are combined across prompts by taking the per-element arithmetic mean, which is the paper's default.
The right panel. Per-prompt Jacobians are combined by taking the per-element median instead, a more robust estimator when the per-prompt Jacobians are heavy-tailed.

Row 1. Gradients are injected at every output position with no stop-gradients. The enumerated list in the text pairs this row with a final-layer target, while an adjacent paragraph calls the penultimate target the default for Sonnet 4.5; the paper is not consistent on which layer this row uses.
Row 2. The same all-positions recipe, but backpropagating from the second-to-last layer's residual stream instead of the final one, so the last transformer block is left out of the backward pass.

Row 3. The same recipe with gradients through the query and key projections zeroed, so attention patterns are held fixed and only the value pathway contributes. It separates what gets moved from what gets attended to.
Row 4. The Jacobian is restricted to strictly later output positions, $t' > t$, isolating what the activation makes available to downstream positions rather than its effect on the current one.
Row 5. The Jacobian is restricted to $t' = t$, the effect of the activation on its own position's output with cross-position attention zeroed. This is the variant closest in spirit to the logit lens.
Column 1. Fifty two-hop factual questions where a bridging entity must be computed — for example computing Mars before answering that the fourth planet is red.

Column 2. Fifty-four prompts written entirely in a non-English language, testing whether the model routes through English-aligned representations; the intermediates include the language name, the relation, and English equivalents of the input and output words.
Column 3. Fifty-two rhyming couplets, with the lens read at the newline between the lines, looking for the second line's planned final word before any of that line has been read.
Column 4. Fifty-five arithmetic expressions such as (2 + 3) x 4, where the partial result and the pending operation must both be held as intermediates.
Column 5. Fifty short passages that depict a concept through behavioral cues without naming it; the lens is read at the closing period to see whether the implied concept has surfaced.

Column 6. Ninety-six sentences ending on a common misspelling, checking whether the correctly spelled word appears in the lens at the misspelled token — a position where that word is not the next token.
The seventh column in each panel, separated from the rest by a white gutter. It is the unweighted mean of that row's six task scores, so it ignores the differing item counts of the six benchmarks.
The vertical white stripe before the avg column, marking that the column is a summary rather than another task distribution.
The perceptually uniform colormap used for the cells and the colorbar: dark purple at the low end, blue and teal in the middle, green and yellow at the high end.
The text's term for zeroing gradients along a chosen path during the backward pass. The freeze-qk row uses stop-grads on the query and key projections.
The single-token concept each benchmark item requires the model to compute — present in neither the input nor the predicted output. Recovering it in the lens readout is what pass@k scores.

numbers.meaning: Panels. The same five recipes and six tasks are scored twice, once with mean aggregation across prompts and once with median, because heavy-tailed per-prompt Jacobians make the choice of estimator potentially consequential.
Rows, one per lens recipe: all tokens (default), all tokens penultimate, all tokens freeze-qk, future tokens only, current token only. These are the five recipes enumerated in the text.
Task columns per panel, plus the avg summary column, giving seven columns of cells in each heatmap.

The span of the viridis colorbar, set by the lowest and highest cells in the figure: 0.54 for current-token-only on multilingual under mean aggregation, and 0.89 for penultimate on order_ops under the same aggregation.
The normalization ceiling. A lens that ranked the correct intermediate first on every item at some layer would score 1, so every cell here can be read as a fraction of that ideal.

Mean panel, all tokens (default), across multihop, multilingual, poetry, order_ops, association, typo, and then the avg. This is the recipe used for the paper's main results, so the other rows are read against it.

Mean panel, all tokens penultimate. The best row in the figure. Its lead over the default comes almost entirely from multilingual (0.71 against 0.66) and typo (0.83 against 0.76); the text attributes the gain to the final block being specialized for next-token calibration and carrying less semantic content.

Mean panel, all tokens freeze-qk. Every cell sits within about 0.02 of the default row, so holding attention patterns fixed costs little readout quality. The text notes that the same variant can increase causal effect, reported in the companion figure.

Mean panel, future tokens only. Restricting to strictly later positions loses ground on most tasks but gives the highest multihop cell in the figure, 0.86 — consistent with a bridging entity being something the position makes available to later positions rather than uses itself.

Mean panel, current token only. The weakest row by a clear margin. Its two lowest cells are multilingual (0.54) and typo (0.55), both benchmarks whose readout position is one where the intermediate is not what the model is about to say.
Median panel, all tokens (default). Essentially identical to the same row under mean aggregation, so the default recipe is insensitive to the estimator.

Median panel, all tokens penultimate. Its mean-aggregation advantage disappears here: 0.76 rather than 0.79, level with the default. The text's claim of a small improvement is therefore specific to mean aggregation.
Median panel, all tokens freeze-qk. Again within about 0.02 of the default row, matching its behavior under mean aggregation.
Median panel, future tokens only. It improves on its mean-aggregation counterpart (0.75 against 0.73) and again posts the panel's best multihop cell, 0.82.
Median panel, current token only. Still last, but by a much smaller margin than under mean aggregation: 0.71 against 0.74-0.76 for the others, rather than 0.65 against 0.73-0.79.
The full range of the association column across all ten rows of the figure. No recipe separates from any other on that benchmark, so the column carries no signal about the design choices.
The range of the avg column once current-token-only is set aside. That narrow band is what the text means in saying the methods are fairly consistent across these design choices.

Item counts for multihop, multilingual, poetry, order_ops, association and typo. They matter for reading the cells because a single item moves a small benchmark more than a large one, and the avg column weights all six equally regardless.

Prompts in the corpus the Jacobian expectation is averaged over for every recipe here, each 128 tokens long, sampled from a pretraining-like distribution. It is held fixed across the figure so that only the recipe varies.

items.caption: Figure 58: Sonnet 4.5 J-lens causal ablation evals for different methodological variations of the J-lens recipe.
items.title: Causal efficacy across J-lens recipe variants
items.takeaway: Five variants of the J-lens recipe are scored on how much output change their vectors cause when ablated, under both mean and median aggregation. Restricting the gradient target to the current token alone roughly halves the causal effect, while freezing the query-key pathway slightly raises it; every other choice moves the average by less than 10%.
items.walkthrough:
This item is a pair of heatmaps that score five recipe variants of the [[jacobian-lens]] on how much the model's output moves when a lens vector is ablated. It is the causal companion to the preceding figure, which scored the same five variants on readout accuracy instead. All numbers come from [[claude-model-family|Sonnet 4.5]].

Each panel has five rows and four columns. The rows are the [[j-lens-recipe-variants|recipe variants]] under test. The columns are three of the [[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]] — [[multihop-benchmark|multihop]], [[multilingual-benchmark|multilingual]] and [[poetry-benchmark|poetry]] — followed by an avg column, set off by a white rule, holding the mean of those three.

The two panels differ in one choice only. The left aggregates per-prompt Jacobians across prompts with a per-element mean, the right with a per-element median. That is the [[jacobian-aggregation]] axis.

Each cell holds an ablation KL. The measurement takes the lens vector for the known intermediate concept, zeroes the [[residual-stream]]'s component along that vector, and records the [[kl-divergence]] between the model's output distribution before and after ([[j-lens-ablation]]). A larger number means the direction was more causally load-bearing, so on this metric high is good. The colorbar spans roughly 0.17 to 2.22, dark purple to yellow.

Multihop cells are five to ten times the poetry cells in every row. That gap belongs to the task, not to the recipe, so variants are compared down a column rather than across one.

The freeze-qk row is the strongest on avg in both panels, at 1.25 and 1.27. This is what the text reports: applying stop-grads to the query and key projections ([[frozen-qk-variant]]) can increase the causal effect.

The two restricted-target rows lose ground. Future-tokens-only falls to 0.80 and 0.96; current-token-only falls furthest, to 0.59 and 0.79. Narrowing the [[target-position-variants|target positions]] to the present token — the setting closest in spirit to the [[logit-lens]] — costs about half the causal effect under mean aggregation.

One labelling wrinkle is worth flagging. The row marked "default" here is the final-layer recipe, while the surrounding text describes the Sonnet 4.5 default used throughout the paper as taking the target at the penultimate layer.

terms.term: Sonnet 4.5 J-lens method ablations — ablation KL
terms.definition: The figure's printed title. It states the subject (variants of the J-lens construction recipe on Sonnet 4.5) and the metric (the KL divergence induced by ablating a lens direction).
The model every cell is measured on: a mid-sized member of the Claude family, and the paper's main subject for J-lens methodology work.

The paper's interpretability method. It averages the Jacobian from a layer's residual stream to a late-layer target over a corpus, giving one matrix per layer whose rows supply a direction for each vocabulary token.

Here it means an ablation of the method itself, not of the model: one ingredient of the J-lens recipe is changed at a time and the resulting lens is re-scored. It is distinct from the ablation the metric performs on activations.

The metric filling every cell. The lens vector for the item's known intermediate concept is projected out of the residual stream, and the KL divergence between the model's output distribution before and after the projection is recorded.
The colorbar label, and what a cell reports: the ablation KL averaged over the items in that benchmark. Higher means the ablated direction carried more of the computation.
The left panel's title. Per-prompt Jacobians are combined across prompts by taking the per-element arithmetic mean before the lens is built.
The right panel's title. Per-prompt Jacobians are combined across prompts by taking the per-element median, which is more resistant to the heavy tails the paper reports in per-sample Jacobians.
Row 1. Gradients are injected at all output positions at the final layer, with no stop-gradients anywhere. The label marks it as the reference recipe within this figure.

Row 2. The same all-positions recipe, but the target is the penultimate-layer residual stream, so the last transformer block is omitted from the backward pass. The paper argues that block is specialized for next-token calibration and adds noise.
Row 3. The same all-positions recipe with gradients through the query and key projections zeroed, holding attention patterns fixed so only the value pathway contributes.
Row 4. The Jacobian target is restricted to strictly later positions, $t' > t$, isolating what a position makes available to downstream positions rather than to its own output.
Row 5. The Jacobian target is restricted to the same position, $t' = t$, with cross-position attention zeroed. The paper calls this the variant closest in spirit to the logit lens.
Column 1. Fifty two-hop factual questions requiring a bridging entity, such as computing Mars before answering that the fourth planet's color is red. The ablated direction is the bridging entity's.
Column 2. Fifty-four prompts written entirely in a non-English language, testing whether the model routes through English-aligned intermediates. Ablation targets those intermediates.
Column 3. Fifty-two rhyming couplets in which the planned final word of the second line is read at the newline. For this benchmark the target position itself is excluded from the ablation.
Column 4, separated by a white rule. The unweighted mean of that row's three task cells, up to rounding; it is a summary, not a fourth benchmark.
Zeroing the gradient along a chosen path in the backward pass so that path contributes nothing to the computed Jacobian. Here it is applied to the query and key projections in the freeze-qk row.
The second-to-last transformer layer's residual stream, used as the differentiation target in row 2 instead of the final layer's.
Which output positions $t'$ the Jacobian is taken with respect to, given a perturbation at position $t$. The default mixes all $t' \geq t$; rows 4 and 5 take the two limiting cases.
The colour scale used, running dark purple through blue and teal to yellow as the value rises. It is redundant with the printed numbers and serves only to make the pattern visible at a glance.

numbers.meaning: The figure's shape: five J-lens recipe variants, three benchmarks plus an average column, evaluated once under mean aggregation and once under median aggregation. Forty cells in total.

Ablation KL on multihop, multilingual, poetry and their average for the final-layer all-positions recipe with mean aggregation. The average is (2.03 + 0.86 + 0.32) / 3 = 1.07. This row is the reference the other four are read against.
The same recipe with per-element median aggregation across prompts. Every task is flat or slightly higher than under mean aggregation, lifting the average from 1.07 to 1.14.

Moving the differentiation target back one block gains a little on multihop and multilingual and loses a little on poetry, for a net average of 1.11 against the default's 1.07 — inside the range the paper describes as fairly consistent.

The penultimate-layer recipe under median aggregation. Its average of 1.12 sits just below the default's 1.14 here, so the small advantage the paper reports for the penultimate variant on readout accuracy does not reappear as a causal advantage.

The strongest average in the left panel. The gain over the default comes mostly from multilingual, where 1.21 against 0.86 is about a 40% increase; this is the effect the text describes as stop-grads on QK increasing the causal effect.

The strongest average in the right panel, and the largest single cell in the figure at 2.22 on multihop. Freezing the attention pattern is the only variation that raises causal efficacy under both aggregations.

Restricting the target to strictly later positions costs about a quarter of the default average, 0.80 against 1.07. The drop is proportionally similar on all three tasks, so it is not driven by one benchmark.

The same restriction under median aggregation. The penalty is smaller here, 0.96 against the default's 1.14, which is consistent with the median being less sensitive to how many positions enter the average.

The weakest row in the figure. The average of 0.59 is a little over half the default's 1.07, and the multihop cell falls from 2.03 to 0.87 — the largest single loss anywhere in the figure. The poetry cell of 0.17 is the smallest value shown.

The same restriction under median aggregation. It remains the weakest row, at 0.79 against the default's 1.14, so the finding that self-only targeting sacrifices causal efficacy holds under both estimators.
The printed colorbar ticks, in units of mean KL divergence. They set the reading scale: cells near 0.2 are dark purple, cells near 1.0 blue-teal, cells above 2.0 yellow.

The full range of values in the figure, from poetry under current-token-only in the mean panel to multihop under freeze-qk in the median panel. The colour scale is shared across both panels, so cells can be compared by eye left to right.

Item counts for the multihop, multilingual and poetry benchmarks respectively, as given where those distributions are defined. Each cell is a mean over that many items, so the differences between neighbouring cells of a few hundredths carry little weight.
The causal-ablation evaluation uses three of the paper's six intermediate-concept distributions. Order-of-operations, typo and association appear in the readout comparison but not here.

The paper's separate claim, from the lens comparison, that ablating J-lens directions induces about twice the output KL of ablating logit- or tuned-lens directions on multihop. That comparison sets the scale against which the within-recipe differences in this figure are small.

items.caption: Figure 59: Sonnet 4.5 J-lens pass@K AUC evals as a function of number of sequences in the average. Error bars indicate standard errors.
items.title: How many prompts the J-lens needs
items.takeaway: Sweeping the number of prompts whose Jacobians are averaged into the lens, from 1 to 1000, shows that the J-lens overtakes both the logit-lens and tuned-lens baselines at intermediate-concept recovery with roughly ten prompts on every one of the six task distributions, and that the curve flattens after a few hundred. The paper reads this as evidence that the lens is cheap to fit: the default corpus of one thousand sequences is generous rather than necessary.
items.walkthrough:
### What is plotted

Six panels, one per prompt distribution in the [[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]]. Each panel asks the same question of one task: how good is the [[jacobian-lens]] when it is built from only $n$ prompts.

The horizontal axis, "# prompt jacobians", is $n$. Building the lens means computing one Jacobian per prompt and then averaging those matrices element by element, so $n$ is simply how many prompts entered that average. Ten values are swept, from 1 to 1000, on a log scale.

The vertical axis is the normalized [[pass-at-k-auc]] score. For each benchmark item the paper knows in advance which single-token intermediate the model ought to be computing. An item counts as recovered at $k$ if that token appears in the lens's top $k$ at any layer, pass@$k$ is the fraction of items recovered, and the AUC is the area under pass@$k$ against $\log k$, scaled so that always ranking the intermediate first would score 1.

### How to read a panel

Black circles joined by a solid line are the J-lens, one circle per corpus size, with error bars giving the standard error over items. The red dashed line is the [[logit-lens]] and the blue dotted line is the [[tuned-lens]]. Both baselines are flat, because neither is built from this corpus; they are reference levels, not curves.

The vertical range differs from panel to panel. Comparing heights across panels is not meaningful; comparing a curve to its own two lines is.

### What it shows

Every panel has the same shape. The J-lens starts below or near the red line at $n=1$, rises steeply through the single digits, crosses the red line somewhere between about 2 and 20 prompts, and then flattens.

The crossing is earliest on multihop, where two prompts already match the logit lens, and latest on association, where the curve only clears the red line at around 10 to 20. The blue tuned-lens line sits below the whole curve in all six panels, in poetry and association by a wide margin.

Beyond a few hundred prompts the points wobble inside their error bars rather than climb. The gain from 500 to 1000 prompts is at most a couple of thousandths of AUC, and on multihop and association it is slightly negative.

terms.definition: The paper's readout method: for each layer it averages the Jacobian of a late-layer residual stream with respect to that layer's activations over token positions and over a corpus of prompts, then decodes activations through that averaged linear map and the model's unembedding. The black curve here is this lens, built from varying amounts of corpus.
The x-axis label. It counts how many per-prompt Jacobian matrices were averaged together to form the lens for that point, which is the same as the number of sequences in the lens corpus.

The y-axis label and the score being compared. pass@$k$ is the fraction of benchmark items whose known intermediate token appears in the lens's top $k$ at any layer; the AUC is the area under that curve plotted against $\log k$, normalized so a method that always ranks the intermediate first scores 1.

The underlying per-item criterion: an intermediate is recovered at $k$ if it is among the top $k$ tokens of the lens readout at any layer. The figure never shows pass@$k$ directly, only its normalized area.
The series being swept. Each marker is the J-lens built from that many prompt Jacobians, evaluated on the panel's task.

The logit lens baseline: decoding an intermediate residual stream by applying the model's final normalization and unembedding directly, with no fitted map. It does not depend on the corpus, so it is drawn as a flat reference line.
The tuned lens baseline: per-layer affine maps trained to match the model's own next-token distribution. It is trained on other data and not on this corpus, so it too is a flat reference line.
Vertical whiskers on each black marker. The caption states they are standard errors, taken over the benchmark items in that panel; they are widest at one prompt and shrink as the corpus grows.

Two-hop factual questions where the answer requires a bridging entity, such as computing Mars before answering that the fourth planet's color is red. The lens is read at the position just before the answer.

Prompts written entirely in a non-English language, testing whether the model routes through English-aligned representations. Four intermediates are sought per item: the language, the relation, and the English forms of the input and output words.
Rhyming couplets where the lens is read at the newline between the two lines, before any of the second line exists, looking for the word that will end it.

The order-of-operations benchmark: arithmetic expressions such as $(2+3)\times4$, where a partial result must be computed before the remaining operation. Two intermediates are sought per item, the partial result and the pending operation.

Short passages that depict a concept through behavioral cues without naming it, with the lens read at the closing period. No single token is the trigger; the concept has to be assembled from accumulated context.

Sentences ending on a common misspelling, with the lens read at the final fragment of the misspelled token, looking for the correctly spelled word. The model is not about to emit that word, so its appearance indicates internal recognition rather than prediction.
The model all six panels are computed on, named in the caption rather than printed in the figure. It is the mid-size tier of the Claude family and the paper's default subject.
The x axis is logarithmic, labelled at the decades $10^0$ through $10^3$, so equal horizontal distance means equal ratio of corpus size rather than equal difference.

numbers.meaning: The ten corpus sizes swept along the x axis of every panel, one black marker each. They are roughly log-spaced so that a three-decade range is covered in ten runs.
The decade tick labels on the x axis, that is 1, 10, 100 and 1000 prompt Jacobians.
The default lens corpus used everywhere else in the paper, which is the rightmost point of each curve here. The sweep exists to test whether that default is more data than the lens needs.
Multihop: the J-lens score at 1 prompt and at 1000. It peaks at about 0.815 at 200 prompts and settles slightly below that, so the last half-decade of data buys nothing.
Multihop logit-lens baseline (red dashed). The J-lens matches it at 2 prompts and is clearly above it from 5 onward, which is the narrowest margin of any panel.
Multihop tuned-lens baseline (blue dotted), below every J-lens point including the single-prompt one.
Multihop y-axis range. Each panel has its own range, chosen to fit its own three series, so panel heights are not comparable to one another.
Multilingual: J-lens score at 1 prompt and at 1000. This panel keeps climbing longer than the others, gaining about 0.02 between 100 and 1000 prompts.
Multilingual logit-lens baseline. Even the single-prompt J-lens is above it, so no crossing point exists in this panel.
Multilingual tuned-lens baseline, drawn near the bottom edge of the panel's range.
Multilingual y-axis range, with labelled ticks at 0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.65 and 0.70.
Poetry: J-lens score at 1 prompt and at 1000, with most of the gain arriving by 20 prompts (≈0.764).
Poetry logit-lens baseline. The J-lens is above it from the first prompt onward.

Poetry tuned-lens baseline. The paper attributes this near-total failure to the readout position being a newline, where the next token is uninformative and a method trained to predict the next token has nothing to surface.
Poetry y-axis range, stretched down by the very low tuned-lens line.
order_ops: J-lens score at 1 prompt and at 1000. This is the highest-scoring panel in absolute terms and the only curve still visibly rising at the right edge.
order_ops logit-lens baseline, already cleared at 1 prompt.
order_ops tuned-lens baseline, sitting on the bottom gridline of the panel.
order_ops y-axis range.
Association: J-lens score at 1 prompt and at 1000. The curve is flat from about 50 prompts on, wandering between roughly 0.68 and 0.69.

Association logit-lens baseline, and the latest crossing in the figure: the J-lens only reaches it at about 10 prompts and only clears it by a visible gap at 50. This matches the main comparison, where association is one of the two tasks on which the J-lens margin over the logit lens is called modest.
Association tuned-lens baseline. As with poetry, the readout position is a period, so a next-token-matching lens recovers almost nothing.
Association y-axis range.
Typo: J-lens score at 1 prompt and at 1000, the largest total gain across the sweep, about 0.24 of AUC. The curve is also the noisiest, dipping at 200 before recovering at 500.
Typo logit-lens baseline, cleared from the first prompt.
Typo tuned-lens baseline.
Typo y-axis range. The legend is drawn inside this panel, in its upper right corner.

numbers.value: ±0.015 to ±0.04 at one prompt, shrinking to under ±0.005
numbers.meaning: Approximate half-widths of the error bars. They are largest at the left of each panel, where the lens rests on a single prompt's Jacobian, and tighten as the average takes in more sequences.

The item counts of the six benchmarks, in the order multihop, multilingual, poetry, order_ops, association, typo. These set how many items the standard errors are computed over, which is why typo's bars are not the widest despite its noisy curve.
The number of prompts the surrounding text names as the point where the J-lens beats both baselines, with only modest improvements from additional data after that.

items.caption: Figure 60: Sonnet 4.5 causal ablation evals as a function of number of sequences in the average. Error bars indicate standard errors.
items.title: Corpus size and the strength of ablation
items.takeaway: Sweeping the number of prompts averaged into the Jacobian lens matrix, from one to a thousand, shows the causal strength of the lens's directions rising with corpus size on all three benchmarks. The lens overtakes both the logit-lens and tuned-lens baselines at around two to five prompts, well below the paper's stated threshold of ten. The multilingual curve flattens by a few hundred prompts, but the multihop and poetry curves are still climbing at a thousand, so the section's description of "modest improvements" from extra data fits only one of the three panels.
items.walkthrough:
Three line charts sit side by side, sharing one x-axis label and one y-axis label. Each panel is one prompt distribution from the paper's [[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]]: [[multihop-benchmark|multihop]], [[multilingual-benchmark|multilingual]] and [[poetry-benchmark|poetry]].

The horizontal axis, "# prompt jacobians", is the size of the corpus the [[jacobian-lens]] matrix was averaged over. It runs on a log scale from $10^0$ to $10^3$, with ten sweep values: 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500 and 1000. The rightmost point is the paper's default lens for Sonnet 4.5, built from one thousand sequences of 128 tokens.

The vertical axis, "ablation mean-KL", is the [[ablation-kl-effect]]. The measurement behind one marker runs as follows. Each benchmark item has a known intermediate concept the model must compute but never writes out. The lens supplies a [[j-lens-vector]] for that concept's token. The [[residual-stream]] component along that vector is projected to zero, and the [[kl-divergence]] between the resulting output distribution and the undisturbed one is recorded. Averaging over the items of one benchmark gives the plotted value. Higher means the erased direction mattered more to the answer.

The legend appears only in the poetry panel. Black circles joined by a line are the J-lens; the red dashed line is the [[logit-lens]] baseline; the blue dotted line is the [[tuned-lens]] baseline. Both baselines are horizontal because neither method is built from this corpus, so corpus size does not move them.

All three curves rise steeply and then bend. Multihop starts at $0.83$, below both baselines, and passes them by two prompts. Multilingual starts at $0.59$, above the tuned lens but below the logit lens, and clears the logit line at two prompts. Poetry starts at $0.26$, above the logit lens only, and clears the tuned line between two and five prompts.

The error bars, described in the caption as standard errors, shrink as the corpus grows and vanish at one thousand, where only one subsample exists.

After that crossing the panels part company. Multilingual saturates near $0.90$. Multihop and poetry are still rising at the right edge, gaining roughly 48 and 32 percent between ten prompts and a thousand.

terms.definition: The model this sweep was run on, named in the caption. It is the mid-size tier of the Claude family and the model used for most of the paper's lens comparisons.

The number of prompts whose per-prompt Jacobians were averaged together to form the lens matrix $J_\ell$. This is the single quantity varied across the figure; everything else about the lens is held at the default recipe.

The Jacobian computed on one prompt: the derivative of the target-layer residual stream with respect to the residual stream at layer $\ell$, averaged over token positions within that prompt. The lens matrix is the average of these across prompts.

The plotted metric: the KL divergence induced on the model's output distribution by zeroing the residual-stream component along the lens's vector for the item's intermediate concept, averaged over the items of one benchmark.

The intervention itself: projecting out an activation's component along one chosen direction while leaving the rest of the activation untouched. It tests whether the model's computation depended on that direction.
The measure of how far the model's next-token distribution after the ablation sits from its distribution without the ablation. Zero would mean the ablation changed nothing.
The single-token concept each benchmark item requires the model to compute internally, present in neither the prompt nor the answer. The lens vector for that token is what gets ablated.
The paper's own lens, and the only curve that moves with the x-axis. Each marker is a lens built from that many prompt Jacobians and then evaluated.
The logit-lens baseline: the direction for a token is simply that token's row of the model's unembedding matrix. It requires no corpus, so its value is a constant across the panel.

The tuned-lens baseline: per-layer affine maps trained so the decoded distribution matches the model's own output. It is trained separately rather than averaged from these Jacobians, so it too is a constant here.

The per-token direction the Jacobian lens assigns in residual-stream space, obtained by pushing the token's unembedding row back through $J_\ell$. This is the object whose causal strength the y-axis measures.
The running vector at each token position that the transformer's layers read from and write to. The ablation is performed in this space.
Fifty two-hop factual questions where a bridging entity must be computed, such as computing Mars before answering that the fourth planet is red. The intermediate ablated is that bridging entity.

Fifty-four prompts written entirely in a non-English language, testing whether the model routes through English-aligned representations. The intermediates include English equivalents of the input and output words.
Fifty-two rhyming couplets, read at the newline between the lines, where the intermediate is the planned final word of the second line.

The vertical whiskers on each marker. The caption calls them standard errors. Since the same corpus and the same benchmark items are used throughout, the spread at a given corpus size plausibly reflects which subset of prompts was drawn, though the paper does not state the resampling scheme.

The horizontal axis is logarithmic, so equal horizontal distances are equal ratios of corpus size. A curve that keeps rising at a steady slope on this axis is gaining a fixed amount per tenfold increase in data.

The immediately preceding figure runs the same corpus-size sweep against the readout metric, pass@k AUC, rather than against causal effect. The section's summary claim is made about the pair together.

numbers.meaning: Panels, one per benchmark: multihop, multilingual, poetry. These are three of the six intermediate-concept distributions the paper builds; order of operations, association and typo are not swept here.
The ten corpus sizes swept along the x-axis of every panel. The text describes this as sweeping the number of prompts from 1 to 1000.
