The default lens: one thousand sequences of 128 tokens each, drawn from a pretraining-like distribution. The rightmost marker in each panel is that lens, so the whole sweep is read as approaching the paper's standard configuration.

Multihop, ablation mean-KL at the ten corpus sizes in order. The value more than doubles across the sweep, and the last value matches the multihop J-lens bar of the earlier lens-comparison figure, confirming the right edge is the default lens.

numbers.value: multihop y-axis: about 0.72 to 2.17, ticked every 0.2 from 0.8 to 2.0
numbers.meaning: The visible range of the left panel, set by the bottom of the one-prompt error bar and the thousand-prompt marker.

Half-widths at the ten corpus sizes. They shrink broadly with corpus size but not monotonically: the 200-prompt bar is wider than the 100-prompt bar. At 1000 prompts no bar is drawn, since there is only one way to draw the whole corpus.

The multihop logit-lens and tuned-lens baselines, drawn as the red dashed and blue dotted lines. They match the corresponding bars in the paper's earlier lens-comparison figure, so the same evaluation is being reused.

Multilingual, ablation mean-KL at the ten corpus sizes. The curve gains 0.23 between 1 and 10 prompts and only 0.086 between 10 and 1000, and the last two values are level, so this panel has effectively converged.

numbers.value: multilingual y-axis: about 0.465 to 0.915, ticked every 0.1 from 0.5 to 0.9
numbers.meaning: The visible range of the middle panel. The tuned-lens line sits below the lowest tick, near the axis floor.
Half-widths at the ten corpus sizes. They fall by roughly an order of magnitude across the sweep, which is why the plateau at the right can be read as real rather than as noise.
The multilingual logit-lens and tuned-lens baselines. The tuned lens is the weaker of the two here, and the J-lens is already above it at one prompt.
Poetry, ablation mean-KL at the ten corpus sizes. The curve is flat between 200 and 500 prompts and then steps up again at 1000, so it shows no settled plateau.

numbers.value: poetry y-axis: about 0.225 to 0.61, ticked every 0.1 from 0.3 to 0.6
numbers.meaning: The visible range of the right panel. The logit-lens line sits below the lowest tick, close to the axis floor.
Half-widths at the ten corpus sizes. The one-prompt bar reaches down to about 0.23, which touches the logit-lens line, so the J-lens advantage over the logit lens is not separated at a single prompt.
The poetry logit-lens and tuned-lens baselines. Poetry is the one benchmark of the three where the tuned lens beats the logit lens, so the two lines swap order relative to the other panels.
The corpus size at which the J-lens passes both baselines on multihop (1.01 against 0.93 and 0.87) and passes the logit-lens baseline on multilingual (0.68 against 0.667). Two prompts, not ten.

Where poetry clears its higher baseline. At two prompts the value is 0.337 against a tuned-lens line of 0.341, effectively level and with an error bar straddling it; at five prompts, 0.405 is clearly above.

The number of prompts the section text names as enough for the J-lens to beat both baselines. This figure is more favourable than that: the crossings happen at two to five prompts on all three benchmarks.

The gain from 10 prompts to 1000 on multihop (1.43 to 2.12) and on poetry (0.448 to 0.591). The arithmetic: 2.12 divided by 1.43 is about 1.48, and 0.591 divided by 0.448 is about 1.32. The section calls the improvements beyond ten prompts modest, which understates these two panels.
The corresponding gain on multilingual, from 0.817 at 10 prompts to 0.903 at 1000. This is the panel the phrase modest improvements does describe.
Item counts for multihop, multilingual and poetry, over which each plotted mean is taken. The counts come from the benchmark descriptions elsewhere in the paper, not from the figure.

items.caption: Figure 61: The template lens decodes and steers multi-token concepts that the J-lens cannot represent. (A) On the blackmail transcript of ??, both lenses are read at the same workspace cell. The J-lens's top entries are the first-token fragments black and ext; the template lens decodes blackmail. (B) On a multi-hop item whose unspoken intermediate is photosynthesis, the template lens surfaces it first; the J-lens surfaces the fragment phot. (C) Swapping the Tchaikovsky template for the Beethoven template at the workspace layers flips the model's answer, in both directions.
items.title: Template lens versus J-lens on multi-token words
items.takeaway: Three side-by-side comparisons show that the template lens names whole multi-token words — blackmail, photosynthesis, Tchaikovsky — where the J-lens returns only word-initial fragments, and that swapping one template for another at the workspace layers flips the model's answer in a way the corresponding fragment vectors cannot. The panels are hand-picked examples; the paper treats the template lens as a proof of concept rather than a finished method.
items.walkthrough:
This item is a three-panel figure, labelled A, B and C. Each panel sets the [[template-lens]] beside the [[jacobian-lens]] on the same activation and prints what each one names.

The second lens exists because of a limit in the first. A J-lens vector is defined per entry of the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], so the lens can only name a concept whose name is a single token ([[single-token-limitation]]). "Blackmail" and "photosynthesis" span several tokens, so no J-lens vector stands for them at all.

The template lens supplies one. About 12,700 common words are enumerated in advance. For a word $w$, Claude writes short passages that end just before $w$ would fall, never using $w$ itself. The model reads those passages, and the [[residual-stream]] activation at the final position is averaged over them into $\mu_w(\ell)$, one vector per layer $\ell$. That mean is centered against the mean over all the other words and whitened by an inverse covariance: $t_w(\ell) = (\Sigma_\ell + \lambda I)^{-1}(\mu_w(\ell) - \mu(\ell))$ ([[template-construction]]). What comes out is the linear discriminant direction between contexts where the model is about to say $w$ and contexts where it is not. Templates are then used like J-lens vectors with the unembedding step dropped: a readout projects an activation onto them, and steering adds or subtracts them.

Panel A reads both lenses at one workspace cell — a single layer at a single token position — in the [[blackmail-scenario]] transcript. The J-lens top entries are the word-initial fragments black and ext. The template lens returns blackmail.

Panel B does the same on a multi-hop question whose unspoken intermediate is photosynthesis ([[internal-reasoning]]). The template lens places the whole word near the top of its ranking. The best the J-lens manages is phot.

Panel C is causal rather than descriptive. Asked for the nationality of the composer of Swan Lake and The Nutcracker, the model answers "Russian." A [[lens-coordinate-swap]] that exchanges the Tchaikovsky template for the Beethoven template across the [[workspace-layers]] changes the answer to "German," and the mirror swap on a Beethoven prompt flips the answer back the other way. The paper reports that the tch and beeth J-lens vectors cannot produce either flip.

Panels A to C are three chosen examples, not a measurement; the population evidence is the following figure. The paper also lists the method's faults, among them readouts that skip to the answer in early layers, as the [[tuned-lens]] does, and a final-layer readout that contains the model's next sampled word only 67% of the time.

terms.definition: A method for getting a lens vector for any word chosen in advance, including words that span several tokens. It is built from averaged activations in contexts that lead up to the word, and it is then read and steered exactly as a J-lens vector is.

The paper's main readout method: one vector per vocabulary token per layer, the direction in activation space that on average disposes the model to say that token. It is the baseline the template lens is compared against in all three panels.
The blackmail example. Both lenses are read at the same layer and token position of one transcript, and their top-ranked entries are printed side by side.
The multi-hop example. Both lenses are read on a question whose intermediate answer, photosynthesis, the model never says out loud.
The intervention example. Instead of reading a lens, this panel writes with it, swapping one template for another and recording how the model's answer changes.
One (layer, token position) location in the readout grid the paper uses throughout. Panel A reads both lenses at the same such location so the comparison is like for like.
The middle band of layers in which the paper finds the J-space behaving like a workspace. Panel C applies its swap across this whole band rather than at one layer.

The honeypot evaluation of section 5.1, in which an email-reading assistant discovers an executive's affair and its own imminent decommissioning. The readouts in that section are taken from Sonnet 4.5.
A J-lens entry in panel A. It is the first token of a longer word, and a reader has to complete it to "blackmail" without help from the lens.
The other J-lens fragment shown in panel A. It is likewise a word-initial piece rather than a word; the paper's main text does not say which word it completes to.
The template-lens readout in panel A: the whole word, returned directly, because a template was built for it in advance.
A question that requires an unstated intermediate answer before the final answer can be given. The paper uses such prompts to test whether a lens can see a step the model never writes down.
The unspoken intermediate concept in panel B, and the word the template lens surfaces first. It has no J-lens vector because it is not a single token.
The best the J-lens does in panel B: the first token of photosynthesis rather than the concept itself.

The set of candidates a lens ranks. For the template lens it is the roughly 12,700 words with templates; for the J-lens it is the tokenizer's whole vocabulary. Placing a word near the top of a large candidate set is what makes a readout informative.

The intervention used in panel C. It reads an activation's coordinates along two lens vectors, exchanges those two coordinates, writes the result back, and leaves everything orthogonal to the two vectors untouched.
The two multi-token names whose template vectors are exchanged in panel C. Neither name is a single token, so neither has a J-lens vector of its own.

The J-lens vectors for the first tokens of the two composers' names. The paper reports that intervening on these fragment vectors does not flip the answer, which is what makes the template swap in panel C worth showing.
The two works named in panel C's prompt. They identify Tchaikovsky without naming him, so the composer is an intermediate the model must hold internally.
The model's answer before and after the swap in panel C. "Russian" follows from Tchaikovsky, "German" from Beethoven, so the answer tracks whichever template occupies the swapped coordinate.

Projecting an activation onto a lens vector to score how present that concept is. For the template lens this is done at the same layer the template was built at, and without the unembedding step the J-lens uses.
Adding or subtracting a lens vector from the residual stream to push a concept in or out. Templates are steered with in exactly the same way as J-lens vectors.
The word a template is being built for, drawn from the pre-enumerated list.
The template's raw ingredient: the mean residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$, taken at the final position of every passage written so that $w$ is the natural next word.
The mean activation at layer $\ell$ over the same passage set across all words. Subtracting it removes what is common to every context and leaves what is specific to $w$.
The covariance of the residual stream at layer $\ell$ over those passages. Inverting it whitens the direction, so that variance the activations have anyway does not count as evidence for $w$.
A small ridge term added to the diagonal before inverting the covariance. It keeps the inverse stable when $\Sigma_\ell$ is close to singular.
The finished template for word $w$ at layer $\ell$: the centered, whitened mean. It is the linear discriminant direction separating contexts where $w$ is about to be said from those where it is not.

The identity $\mathbb{E}[\nabla g(x)] = \Sigma^{-1}\mathbb{E}[g(x)(x-\mu)]$ for Gaussian $x$. The paper uses it to argue that the template is an approximation of an averaged gradient, and so should behave somewhat like a J-lens vector; it also states the assumptions do not hold exactly, since activations are not Gaussian.

A prior method that fits per-layer maps onto the model's output distribution. The paper says the template lens resembles it more than the J-lens does, and inherits its habit of skipping ahead to the answer in early layers.
The final projection to vocabulary logits that the J-lens readout includes. The template lens drops it and projects onto templates directly.
The companion method described in the same appendix, which drops the requirement to enumerate a vocabulary in advance. It is not shown in this figure.

numbers.meaning: Two readout comparisons and one intervention. A and B show what each lens names on a fixed activation; C shows what happens when a template is written into the activation instead.

The number of common words for which templates are built. It is a design choice, not a measurement: the template lens can only name words on this list, because each one costs a separate data-collection run.

numbers.value: 1 template vector per word per layer
numbers.meaning: Templates are layer-specific, matching the J-lens, which also has one vector per token per layer. A readout at layer $\ell$ uses the templates built at layer $\ell$.

numbers.value: a few hundred forward passes per word
numbers.meaning: The cost of building one template: the model must read every passage written for that word. The paper contrasts this with a J-lens vector, which costs one set of backward passes per layer for the whole vocabulary at once.

The distinction the whole figure turns on. black, ext, phot, tch and beeth are single tokens and so have J-lens vectors; blackmail, photosynthesis, Tchaikovsky and Beethoven are not, and so have none.

On post-training transcripts where the model's next sampled word is in the template vocabulary, that word appears in the top ten final-layer template readouts only two-thirds of the time. The paper reports it as a shortcoming: final-layer template readouts predict the next word less reliably than J-lens readouts predict the next token.
The rank cutoff the paper uses when it counts a readout as a hit, both in the 67% figure and in the population evaluations that follow this figure.

Tchaikovsky to Beethoven on the Swan Lake prompt, and Beethoven to Tchaikovsky on a Beethoven prompt. Running the swap both ways guards against the reading that one template simply dominates whatever it is added to.

The paper states that neither swap can be achieved by intervening on the tch or beeth J-lens vectors. This is the negative control that makes panel C a claim about multi-token concepts rather than about swapping in general.

items.caption: Figure 62: Readout and concept-swap success by the token length of the latent word. Left: the fraction of latent intermediate concepts each lens places in its top ten, over 126 multi-hop prompts. Right: the fraction of swap pairs whose answer follows the swap, over 112 pairs (53 single-token, 59 multi-token); all swaps are applied at the full workspace layer range. Error bars are 95% Wilson intervals.
items.title: Lens accuracy versus word length
items.takeaway: Across multi-hop prompts whose unspoken intermediate concept is one to four-plus tokens long, the J-lens decodes and swaps single-token concepts well and then falls off sharply as the concept grows longer, while the template lens holds roughly flat at every length. On single-token concepts the two are comparable, with the template lens slightly behind on readout and ahead on swaps.
items.walkthrough:
The figure is a live two-panel line chart, and it carries the quantitative case for the [[template-lens]]. The [[jacobian-lens]] derives one vector per vocabulary token, so a concept whose name spans several tokens has no vector of its own — the [[single-token-limitation]]. The template lens was built to cover such concepts, and this figure reports how each lens holds up as the latent word grows longer.

Both panels share an x axis of word length in tokens, bucketed as 1, 2, 3 and 4+, with the number of items in each bucket printed underneath. Both y axes run from 0% to 100%. Three series are drawn, each a line through the four buckets with a vertical [[wilson-interval|95% Wilson interval]] at every point.

The left panel, "Decoding the intermediate concept", measures readout. The prompts are multi-hop questions whose bridging concept is never written out, similar in kind to the [[multihop-benchmark]] but chosen so that the concept's length varies. A trial counts as a success when that concept appears in the lens's top ten at the read position.

The right panel, "Swapping the intermediate concept", measures a causal test instead. A [[lens-coordinate-swap]] exchanges one concept's lens coordinate for another's across the whole [[workspace-layers|workspace layer range]], at [[swap-strength-alpha|swap strength]] $\alpha = 1$. The trial succeeds when the model's answer follows the concept that was swapped in.

The shapes of the lines are the result. The J-lens first-token series starts near the ceiling on one-token words and then drops: 98%, 48%, 32% and 7% on readout, and 45%, 5%, 8% and 0% on swaps. Averaging the lens scores over the word's constituent tokens does not repair this, and that dashed series sits at or below the solid one in every bucket.

The template lens stays roughly level across all four buckets, at 94% to 100% on readout and 62% down to 43% on swaps. On single-token words it trails the J-lens slightly on readout and leads it on swaps.

The per-bucket counts are small, between 14 and 54 items, so the intervals are wide. Hovering a point prints its raw count, such as 14/29. The evidence supports the direction of the trend rather than any single point.

terms.definition: The first legend series, drawn as a solid line with filled markers. For a multi-token concept it uses the J-lens vector of only the concept's first token, so "photosynthesis" is scored through the fragment phot.

The second legend series, drawn as a dashed line with open markers. It averages the J-lens scores over all the tokens the concept word breaks into, as a fairer attempt at reading a multi-token concept out of a single-token lens.

The third legend series, drawn as a solid line in orange. The template lens builds one vector per word by averaging residual-stream activations over passages that end just before that word, then centering and whitening those means.

The step that multiplies the centered per-word mean by the inverse of the residual stream's covariance matrix (with a small ridge term). It converts a raw class mean into a linear discriminant direction, and it is what the legend word "whitened" refers to.

One direction in residual-stream space per vocabulary token per layer, obtained from the Jacobian of the model's output with respect to activations. It is the unit both lenses' readouts and swaps operate on, and its one-per-token construction is what limits it to single-token names.
The readout panel. It asks whether the latent concept can be named from the activation, with no intervention on the model.
The intervention panel. It asks whether writing a different concept into the same lens coordinates changes what the model answers.
The readout success measure: the share of prompts on which the true latent concept lands somewhere in the lens's ten highest-scoring entries at the read position.

terms.term: "P(answer follows the swap) at α = 1" (right y-axis label)
terms.definition: The swap success measure: the share of pairs on which the model's output changes to the answer implied by the concept swapped in. α = 1 names the swap magnitude used.

The multiplier on a lens-coordinate swap. At α = 1 the source concept's projection is removed and a matched-magnitude target projection is added; the paper elsewhere reports that α = 2 raises success rates, so α = 1 is the conservative setting.

terms.term: "tokens in the latent word" (left x-axis label)
terms.definition: The bucketing variable in the readout panel: how many tokens the model's tokenizer splits the unspoken intermediate concept into.

terms.term: "tokens in the anchor word" (right x-axis label)
terms.definition: The bucketing variable in the swap panel: the token length of the concept word that defines the swap pair. It is the same length variable as on the left, applied to the pair rather than to a single readout.

The bridging entity a multi-hop question requires but never states, such as Mars in a question about the fourth planet's color. It is the thing the lens is asked to name and the thing the swap replaces.

Two-hop factual questions whose surface tokens have no direct association with the answer, so the model must compute a bridging entity first. The prompts here are of that kind but were selected so the bridging entity's token length varies from one to four.
One item in the right panel: a source concept present in the activation and a target concept written in its place, together with the answer the target concept implies.

The band of middle layers, roughly L38 to L92 on the paper's percent-of-depth scale, in which the J-space behaves like a workspace. Every swap in this figure is applied across the whole band rather than at one layer.
The four x-axis positions. The last bucket pools every concept of four or more tokens, since individual longer lengths would have too few items.

The small gray counts printed under each bucket tick, giving how many items that bucket holds. They differ between the two panels because the swap evaluation uses fewer items than the readout evaluation.

The vertical line at each point, spanning the 95% Wilson interval for that proportion. The Wilson form is used because it stays sensible at rates of 0% and 100% and at small counts, both of which occur here.
The cutoff that defines readout success. The lens ranks a large vocabulary at the read position, and only the ten highest-scoring entries count as a hit.
The visual coding of the token-average J-lens series, distinguishing it from the first-token J-lens series drawn in the same color with filled markers.
Text shown on a point, giving the series label, the bucket, the raw successes over trials, and the percentage — for example "whitened template lens / 2 tok: 28/29 (97%)".
The three series are nudged a few pixels apart at each bucket so their markers and error bars do not overlap. The offset carries no meaning.

numbers.meaning: The total number of multi-hop prompts in the readout panel, the sum of its four buckets. The caption reports this figure.
The readout panel's item counts for buckets 1, 2, 3 and 4+. Single-token intermediates are the largest group because common concepts more often have single-token names.
The total number of swap pairs in the right panel, split as 53 single-token and 59 multi-token. It is smaller than 126 because not every readout prompt yields a usable source-target pair.
The swap panel's item counts for buckets 1, 2, 3 and 4+, summing to 112. The multi-token buckets sum to 59.

Readout success for the J-lens read at the concept's first token, across the four length buckets. Near-perfect at one token, then falling by roughly half at each further token, which is the degradation the appendix reports.
Readout success for the J-lens averaged over the concept's constituent tokens. It is below the first-token variant in every bucket, which is why the appendix says that averaging does not help.

Readout success for the template lens. It is flat within the noise across all four lengths, and slightly below the J-lens at one token — the paper's "slightly underperforming on readouts" for single-token concepts.
Swap success for the first-token J-lens. Swapping a first-token fragment such as tch for beeth almost never redirects the answer once the concept is longer than one token.
Swap success for the token-averaged J-lens. It matches the first-token variant at one and two tokens and is marginally worse at three, so averaging again buys nothing.

Swap success for the template lens. It is roughly level across lengths and clearly above the J-lens at one token — the paper's "modestly overperforming the J-lens on swaps." The 4+ bucket is lower, but with 14 items its interval reaches from 21% to 67%.
The confidence level of the Wilson intervals drawn as error bars on every point.
The two 0/15 and 0/14 points still carry an interval reaching about 20% and 22%. Zero successes out of fifteen trials does not establish that the true rate is zero.
The swap strength used for every point in the right panel: remove the source projection, add a target projection of matched magnitude, once over.
The rank cutoff for a readout hit. It is a lenient threshold relative to a top-1 criterion, chosen because the ranking universe is large.
The four token-length buckets on the x axis. Four-plus is pooled because longer concepts are rare in the prompt set.
The y-axis ticks in both panels. Both axes are identical, so the two panels' heights can be compared directly even though they measure different things.
The number of series plotted: two J-lens variants and the template lens. The two J-lens variants share a color and are separated by line dash and marker fill.

The size of the template lens's predefined word vocabulary, built elsewhere in the appendix. It is the ranking universe behind the template lens's readouts, and the reason the method needs its vocabulary enumerated in advance.
The workspace layer band, on the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth scale, over which every swap in the right panel is applied.

items.caption: Figure 63: The readout and swap evaluations of Figure ?? on the multi-hop benchmark of ??, whose 50 latent intermediates are all single tokens. Error bars are 95% Wilson intervals.
items.title: Template lens versus J-lens on single-token intermediates
items.takeaway: Re-running the appendix's readout and swap evaluations on the paper's original 50-item multi-hop benchmark, where every unspoken intermediate is a single token, leaves the two lenses at rough parity: the template lens reads out slightly more intermediates (84% against 76%) and redirects slightly fewer answers (52% against 68%). Both gaps sit inside overlapping 95% Wilson intervals, so the figure supports only the claim that the template lens buys nothing here, not that either lens is better.
items.walkthrough:
The item is a pair of bar panels the article draws live. Each panel carries two bars, one per lens, with a vertical whisker for the confidence interval. The widget prints `n = 50` beneath them, and hovering a bar reveals its raw count.

The 50 items are the [[multihop-benchmark]]: two-hop factual questions whose surface words have no direct association with the answer. "The color of the planet fourth from the Sun is" requires computing Mars before red can be produced. The same 50 prompts carry the [[internal-reasoning]] swap experiment in the body of the paper, run by default on [[claude-model-family|Sonnet 4.5]]. Every one of the 50 unspoken intermediates is a single vocabulary token.

That last property is the reason this figure exists. The [[template-lens]] was built to get past the [[single-token-limitation]] of the [[jacobian-lens]], and the preceding figure showed it holding up on two-, three- and four-token intermediates where the J-lens collapses. That comparison used a different distribution of prompts. This figure re-runs the identical readout and swap evaluations on the paper's original benchmark, where the J-lens faces no handicap at all.

The left panel, "Decoding the intermediate concept", asks how often each lens places the unspoken intermediate among its top ten tokens. The J-lens manages 38 of 50, or 76 percent. The template lens manages 42 of 50, or 84 percent.

The right panel, "Swapping the intermediate concept", is causal rather than correlational. It applies a [[lens-coordinate-swap]], exchanging the intermediate's coordinate for that of an alternative concept, and counts the prompts whose answer follows the swapped-in concept. The axis label notes $\alpha = 1$, the unit [[swap-strength-alpha|swap strength]]: the source vector is subtracted once and the target added once, with no doubling. The J-lens manages 34 of 50, or 68 percent. The template lens manages 26 of 50, or 52 percent.

The paper reads this as parity, with the template lens modestly overperforming on readouts and underperforming on swaps. The error bars are [[wilson-interval|95 percent Wilson intervals]], and they overlap heavily in both panels. At 50 items neither gap is resolved.

The conclusion the appendix draws is a narrow one. On single-token concepts the template lens is roughly at par with the J-lens, and its advantage in the previous figure is confined to intermediates the J-lens cannot name.

terms.definition: The title of the left panel. It scores each lens as a read-only tool: how often the lens surfaces the concept the model must infer but never says.
The left panel's y-axis. For each prompt the lens produces a ranked list over its vocabulary, and the item counts as a success when the known intermediate appears in the first ten entries.
The title of the right panel. It scores each lens as an intervention tool: whether writing a different concept into the lens coordinate redirects the model's answer.

terms.term: P(answer follows the swap) at α = 1
terms.definition: The right panel's y-axis. It is the fraction of prompts on which the top output token becomes the answer appropriate to the swapped-in concept rather than the original one, with the swap applied at unit strength.
The multiplier on the swap. At α = 1 the source concept's vector is subtracted once and the target's added once; elsewhere the paper also reports α = 2, which doubles both.

The first bar in each panel, and the first legend entry. It is the Jacobian lens applied to the first token of the intermediate word; on this benchmark every intermediate is one token long, so the first token is the whole word.

The second bar in each panel, and the second legend entry. The template for a word is the mean residual-stream activation over passages that end just before the word, centered against the mean over all other words and multiplied by the inverse covariance matrix; that whitening step is what the label names.
The concept a prompt requires the model to compute on the way to its answer, which appears neither in the prompt nor in the output. Mars, in the question about the color of the fourth planet.

The 50 two-hop factual prompts this figure runs on. Items were built so that the trigger word and the answer rarely co-occur without the bridging entity, which makes direct retrieval of the answer unlikely.
The whisker on each bar. It is a confidence interval for a proportion that stays inside [0, 1] and behaves sensibly at small counts, which matters at n = 50.
The line the widget prints under the two panels. It is the number of benchmark items behind every bar in the figure.
The middle band of layers where the paper finds the J-space acting as a workspace. The swap protocol inherited from the preceding figure applies the intervention across this full range.
The model the paper reports on by default, and so the model behind these bars. The appendix does not name a different one for this comparison.

The constraint the template lens was introduced to relieve: the J-lens has one vector per vocabulary token, so it cannot name a concept like blackmail or photosynthesis that spans several tokens. This benchmark is the case where the limitation does not bite.

numbers.meaning: Items in the benchmark, and the denominator of every bar. These are the same 50 two-hop factual prompts used for the internal-reasoning swap experiment in the body of the paper; the caption notes that all 50 latent intermediates are single tokens.
J-lens readout success: on 38 of the 50 prompts the intermediate concept appears in the lens's top ten. This is the left panel's first bar.
The 95% Wilson interval on the J-lens readout bar. Its width, about 23 points, is what 50 trials buys at a success rate near three quarters.

Template-lens readout success: 42 of 50 intermediates land in the top ten. This is the left panel's second bar, and the sense in which the text says the template lens modestly overperforms on readouts.
The 95% Wilson interval on the template-lens readout bar. It overlaps the J-lens interval across most of its length, so the 8-point readout gap is not resolved at this sample size.
J-lens swap success: on 34 of 50 prompts the swap moves the target-appropriate answer to the top of the output distribution. The right panel's first bar.
The 95% Wilson interval on the J-lens swap bar.
Template-lens swap success: 26 of 50. The right panel's second bar, and the sense in which the text says the template lens underperforms on swaps.
The 95% Wilson interval on the template-lens swap bar. It overlaps the J-lens swap interval, so the 16-point gap, though larger than the readout gap, is also not separated from zero here.
The cutoff for the readout metric: an intermediate counts as decoded when it ranks in the top ten of the lens's output over the vocabulary. A looser cutoff would raise both bars.
The swap strength used in the right panel. Unit strength means one subtraction of the source vector and one addition of the target; the paper reports α = 2 elsewhere when unit strength fails.
The coverage level of the Wilson intervals drawn as whiskers.
The J-lens swap success rate reported for Sonnet 4.5 on this same 50-item benchmark in the body of the paper. It sits close to the 68% here, though the two runs need not share every protocol detail.
The size of the word list for which templates were built. It bounds what the template lens can name at all, since its vocabulary must be enumerated in advance.

items.caption: Figure 64: The oracle lens surfaces multi-token latent content as readable phrases. Each panel shows one prompt with the lens-read position outlined, and beside it the oracle's full ten-phrase readout at that position (native setting, Haiku 4.5, $N=4, K=10$ ); phrases that name a concept not recoverable from the surface tokens are in bold. (A) Acetaminophen overdose (??): at "Can" of the user's follow-up request. (B) Blackmail (??): at "as" in the email's sign-off. (C) ASCII face: at the trailing space of the eyes row. (D) Directed modulation (??): at "cr" of "crookedly," while copying an unrelated sentence under instruction to evaluate 3² − 2. (E) Thought suppression: at "the" of "on the wall," under instruction not to think about the Golden Gate Bridge. (F) Preference violation: at the period ending "Option A." (G) Poetry planning (??): at the newline after "night,". (H) Bug detection: at the indentation before return. (I) avGFP: at "ft" inside the amino-acid sequence. Panels A–D and G–I are read from a single temperature-0 decode; panels E and F show the highest-FVE of five decodes from the same oracle and subject model.
items.title: Oracle-lens phrase readouts on nine prompts
items.takeaway: The oracle lens decodes a single activation into ten free-form phrases rather than a ranked list of single tokens, and across nine prompts those phrases name latent content that the surface text does not contain: that a stated drug dose is toxic, that an email is an attempt at blackmail, that a loop will raise a TypeError. It is a demonstration on selected examples, not a benchmark.
items.walkthrough:
Nine panels, lettered A to I. Each shows one prompt with a single token position outlined, and beside it the ten phrases decoded from the [[residual-stream]] activation at that position. Every readout comes from Haiku 4.5 at layer L67, two thirds of the way through the depth, inside the band where the paper locates the workspace ([[layer-bands]]).

### What the lens does

The [[jacobian-lens]] returns a ranked list of single vocabulary tokens. A concept that spans several tokens therefore arrives broken: blackmail surfaces only as the fragment black. The [[oracle-lens]] is built to return phrases instead.

A [[reconstructor-model]], a fine-tuned copy of the subject model, maps a short phrase to the activation that would precede it. That is a template vector in the sense of the [[template-lens]]. A second fine-tuned copy, the oracle, proposes $K$ phrases of $N$ tokens each. The reconstructor turns those phrases back into directions, and a non-negative least-squares refit fits their coefficients against the original activation ([[oracle-training]]).

A panel's list is thus a reconstruction claim about one activation, not a ranked vocabulary. Bold marks a phrase naming something the surface tokens do not supply.

### The panels

Three are quoted in the appendix. (A) is the Tylenol prompt of [[assistant-point-of-view]], read at "Can" opening the user's follow-up request; the oracle reads this dosage be toxic and that's dangerous!, so the judgment that the dose is unsafe is bound into a phrase before the Assistant replies. (B) is the [[blackmail-scenario]] transcript, read at "as" in an email sign-off: blackmail him by revealing, expose his affair and, and personal leverage over him. (H) is buggy code, read at the indentation before return: delete keys while iterating and TypeError: dictionary changed, the bug and the exception it would raise.

The other six are named but not quoted: (C) an ASCII-art face, at the trailing space of the eyes row; (D) the [[hold-in-mind-copy-task]] under [[directed-modulation]], at "cr" of "crookedly" while the model silently evaluates $3^2 - 2$; (E) [[thought-suppression]], at "the" of "on the wall" under an instruction not to think about the Golden Gate Bridge; (F) the [[preference-violation-experiment]], at the period ending "Option A."; (G) rhyme planning as in the [[poetry-benchmark]], at the newline after "night,"; (I) avGFP, at "ft" inside a raw amino-acid sequence.

Several outlined positions are delimiters: a newline, a period, an indentation. At these the paper reports readouts that comment on the situation rather than predict upcoming text ([[delimiter-commentary]]).

Panels A to D and G to I come from a single temperature-0 decode. Panels E and F are the highest-FVE of five decodes from the same oracle and subject model. The caption states this. It makes those two panels weaker evidence than the other seven.

terms.definition: The method the figure demonstrates: given one activation, it emits a short list of free-form phrases whose template vectors, combined with non-negative weights, approximately reconstruct that activation. Unlike the template lens, its phrase vocabulary is not enumerated in advance.
One of the nine lettered cells, A to I. Each pairs a prompt, with one token position outlined, against the oracle's complete ten-phrase readout at that position.
The single outlined token in each panel. The oracle decodes only the residual-stream activation at that one token and layer; no other position contributes to the phrase list shown.

The caption's highlighting convention: a phrase is set in bold when it names a concept that cannot be recovered from the surface tokens of the prompt, such as blackmail at an innocuous sign-off token.

The label the caption attaches to these readouts. The paper uses it only here and does not define it; in context it appears to mean the subject model's ordinary forward pass over the prompt, with no activation-level steering, swap or ablation applied. Prompt-level instructions, as in panels D and E, are still present.

The subject model for the oracle-lens work, and the model both auxiliary models are fine-tuned copies of. The paper's default model elsewhere is Sonnet 4.5; the oracle pipeline was run on Haiku because it requires training two extra models.
The layer the readouts are taken at, expressed on the paper's convention of 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed to 0-100, so the number reads as a percentage of depth.
The middle range of layers, roughly L38 to L92, where the paper argues J-space content has workspace-like properties. L67 sits near its center.
The phrase length the oracle is asked for, in tokens. Set to 4 for every panel in this figure.
The number of phrases the oracle is asked to produce for one activation. Set to 10 here, and each panel prints all ten.

A fine-tuned copy of the subject model trained to map a short phrase to the residual-stream activation immediately preceding it. It supplies the direction for each phrase the oracle proposes, and is frozen while the oracle is trained.
A direction standing for a word or phrase, built as a centered and whitened mean of the activations that precede it. The reconstructor is a learned generator of these vectors for arbitrary phrases.

The other multi-token extension: it derives a vector for any word or phrase enumerated in advance, and can be read out of activations and intervened on like a J-lens vector. Its vocabulary must be fixed beforehand, which the oracle lens is designed to avoid.
The paper's main readout technique, which decodes an activation into a ranked list of single vocabulary tokens. Its single-token output is the limitation this figure's method addresses.

Variance measured after multiplying by the inverse square root of the residual stream's covariance, the metric the template lens is defined in. Oracle training and its reported reconstruction scores are all computed in this space.

Fraction of variance explained: the share of the whitened activation variance that the fitted phrase directions account for. It is the oracle's reinforcement-learning reward, and the criterion used to pick the decode shown in panels E and F.
A single greedy sample of the phrase list from the oracle. Panels A to D and G to I each show one such decode, with no selection among alternatives.

The prompt in which a user reports taking a dose of Tylenol, in a variant where the dose is a dangerous 8000 mg. The lens is read at "Can" in the user's follow-up request, before the Assistant's turn begins.

The honeypot transcript in which an email-assistant model discovers an executive's affair and its own scheduled decommissioning. The lens is read at "as" in the email's sign-off, a token with no surface connection to blackmail.

A prompt containing a face drawn in ASCII art, used elsewhere in the paper as a case where the model recognizes an image from characters. The lens is read at the trailing space of the row that draws the eyes.

The hold-in-mind protocol: the model copies the unrelated sentence "The old painting hung crookedly on the wall" while instructed to evaluate an arithmetic expression silently. The lens is read at "cr" of "crookedly."
The protocol behind panels D and E: an instruction says what to hold in mind, the model copies a fixed unrelated sentence, and the lens is read at a token of the copied text.
The don't-think condition: the model copies the same sentence under an instruction not to think about the Golden Gate Bridge. The lens is read at "the" of "on the wall."

The prefill experiment in which the model's response is forced to commit to its dispreferred option. The lens is read at the period ending "Option A.", the position where the J-lens shows the unvoiced token BUT.

A rhyming couplet whose first line ends "The soldier marched into the night,". The lens is read at the newline after "night,", before any of the second line exists, where the planned rhyme is expected to sit.
A prompt asking the model to read code containing a bug: keys are deleted from a dictionary while it is being iterated. The lens is read at the indentation before the function's return statement.

A prompt giving the raw amino-acid sequence of the Aequorea victoria green fluorescent protein, used to test whether the model identifies a protein's function from its sequence. The lens is read at "ft" inside the sequence.

The paper's observation that at newlines, periods and indentation the oracle's phrases often read as the model's running commentary on the situation, while at ordinary positions they read as predictions of upcoming text.
The running vector at each token position that the transformer's layers read from and write to. It is the object every readout in this figure is taken from.

The final inference step: after the oracle's phrases are mapped back to directions, coefficients are fitted against the original activation under a non-negativity constraint, so each phrase contributes positively or not at all.

The closest prior method, pairing a verbalizer with a jointly trained reconstructor. The oracle lens differs by freezing a separately trained reconstructor, which the paper suspects reduces confabulation at the cost of reconstruction accuracy.

numbers.meaning: The figure's number in the paper. It sits in appendix 10.9.2, the section describing the oracle lens.
The number of panels, lettered A to I. Each is a separate prompt; the appendix describes them as nine example prompts.
Every phrase in every panel is four tokens long. The oracle is prompted with the desired length, and four is the setting used throughout this figure.
Ten phrases are decoded per activation, and each panel prints the whole list rather than a selected subset.
The layer all nine readouts are taken at, on the paper's 0-100 depth scale. It falls inside the workspace band the paper identifies as running from about L38 to about L92.

The average fraction of whitened activation variance the reinforcement-learning-refined oracle explains on held-out on-policy assistant-turn positions. The paper notes this is considerably lower than a natural-language autoencoder achieves, and reads it as the oracle capturing only what is in the workspace.
The number of decodes generated for panels E and F, of which the one with the highest fraction of variance explained is shown. The other seven panels use a single decode.
The sampling temperature for the decodes in panels A to D and G to I: greedy, unselected.
The range from which the phrase length $N$ is drawn uniformly when training pairs for the reconstructor are built.
The continuation lengths, in tokens, at which phrases are harvested to build the training dictionary. Decomposition by the teacher is restricted to one length at a time.
Two separate counts of this size: the start positions sampled from held-out assistant-turn text to build the phrase dictionary, and the held-out activations the teacher labels.
The number of phrase vectors in the dictionary, after taking five continuation lengths at each sampled position and deduplicating within each length.
The maximum number of phrases the teacher records per activation, with coefficients and explained-variance figures. The oracle is trained on the first $K$ of these.
The random half of dictionary entries at each length that the teacher is restricted to on any one datapoint, so the distilled oracle cannot memorize a fixed ranking over the dictionary.

The expression the model is told to evaluate silently in panel D. Nine minus two is seven, and the J-lens on this same protocol reads arithmetic and math at early layers, nine at later ones, then seven.
A longer phrase setting reported in the text but not shown in this figure. At the same blackmail sign-off token it yields The blackmail attempt focuses on the executive's personal life.
The dose reported by the user in the dangerous variant of the acetaminophen prompt behind panel A, against 1000 mg in the safe variant. The J-lens reads unsafe, dangerous and WARNING on the former.
The approximate start and end of the workspace band, used here to place L67 within it. The band is identified in section 4.1 by four separate lens-derived statistics that agree on roughly this range.

items.caption: Figure 65: Robustness of directed modulation to instruction phrasing, on the three task families of Figure ??. Focus and ignore are the conditions reported in the main text. The mention names the target with no instruction attached, and don't-think forbids attending to it. Each condition is instantiated with five to eight phrasings (hover over a dot to see its template). The category-instance and math-expression panels report the fraction of trials on which the target reaches J-lens top-1 at any (layer, position); the line-width panels report precision, the fraction of top-1 number tokens matching the true width.
items.title: Phrasing spread of the four instruction conditions
items.takeaway: Across three task families and three models, a bare mention of the target puts it in the J-space almost as often as an explicit focus instruction, and forbidding the thought suppresses it barely at all; only the ignore framing, which calls the concept task-irrelevant, pushes the rate well down, and even then not to the no-instruction floor. Within every condition the individual phrasings spread widely, so the control the paper reports is real but phrasing-sensitive.
items.walkthrough:
This is the phrasing-level breakdown behind the [[directed-modulation]] result that Figure 10 summarizes. In the article it is a live widget titled "Directed modulation — robustness to prompt phrasing": a three-by-three grid of small panels, with a tooltip on every dot.

Columns are models, in ascending tiers of the [[claude-model-family]]: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5. Rows are task families. Category instance and math expression are versions of the [[hold-in-mind-copy-task]], where the model copies an unrelated sentence while an instruction says what to hold in mind, and the lens is read at the copied tokens. Line width is the [[character-counting-task]].

Each panel carries four bars, one per condition in the legend. A bar is the condition mean; the dots on it are the individual phrasings, five to eight per condition, hovering to reveal the template. Horizontal placement of a dot inside a bar is a fixed decorative offset and carries no information. The vertical axis runs from 0% to 100%. A thin horizontal rule marks the no-instruction floor.

The measure differs by row. Category and math count a trial as positive when the target reaches [[j-lens-readout]] top-1 at any (layer, position). Line width reports precision: the fraction of top-1 number tokens matching the true width.

Three patterns follow.

Mention nearly matches focus on the first two rows. On Opus, category runs 97.1% under focus against 87.2% under mention, and math runs 95.6% against 95.7% — mention is fractionally higher. Naming the concept at all loads it into the [[j-space]].

Don't-think suppresses very little: 83.1% on Opus category, 87.8% on Opus math, close to the mention rate. The paper reads this as a parallel to the human [[white-bear-effect]].

Ignore does suppress, to 46.6% and 41.4% on Opus, well below mention on every model, though still far above the floor of roughly 0% to 1.6%.

The line-width row behaves unlike the others. Only focus lifts it off the floor, and the phrasings scatter: on Opus, precision runs from 14.0% for "Focus on figuring out what that column number is" to 55.9% for "count the characters and keep the number in mind". The appendix attributes this to the task being harder both to perform and to specify.

terms.term: Directed modulation — robustness to prompt phrasing
terms.definition: The widget's own title. It states the question of the figure: whether the modulation effect reported in the main text survives changes in how the instruction is worded.

The workspace-like property under test: the claim that a model can deliberately place a concept into its workspace representation when told to, and reduce it when told to set it aside, independently of what it writes.

The instruction condition that tells the model to hold the target in mind while doing the cover task, for example "Concentrate on {x} while you write the sentence." One of the two conditions carried over from the main text.

The condition that names the target somewhere in the prompt with no instruction attached, for example "({x})" or "{x} came up in conversation." It isolates how much of the focus effect comes from the concept merely being present in context.

The condition that forbids the thought, for example "Whatever you do, do not think about {x}." It asks the model not to attend to the concept by prohibiting it rather than by calling it irrelevant. The article writes the name without an apostrophe in the legend and as don't-think in the caption.

The condition that frames the target as beside the point, for example "{x} is irrelevant to this task." The paper calls it dismissal in its data keys. It is the second of the two conditions reported in the main text.
The three production models the panels are computed on, in ascending size tier. Column position is the only place model identity appears.
The task family in which the model is told to hold in mind an item from a named category while copying an unrelated sentence. The target is the category instance the instruction names.
The task family in which the model mentally evaluates an arithmetic expression while copying an unrelated sentence. The target is the value of the expression.
The task family in which the model silently counts the characters on each line of a hard-wrapped passage while reading it. The target is the wrap width as a number.
The slot in a phrasing template where the trial's target is substituted: a category instance, a math expression, or, in the line-width templates, a description of the character count.
The concept the instruction is about on a given trial, and the thing the lens is checked for. A trial is scored by whether the target's token surfaces in the readout.

The Jacobian lens, the paper's read-out technique: for each vocabulary token it identifies the activation direction that encodes the model's potential to say that token, and scores every token against the current activation.
The single highest-scoring vocabulary token in a lens readout at one layer and one token position. The category and math panels score a trial positive if the target ever occupies that slot.

One cell of the grid the lens is applied over: a layer of the model crossed with a token position in the text being copied or read. "At any (layer, position)" means the target counts if it reaches top-1 in any of those cells.

terms.term: top-1 (metric label for the first two rows)
terms.definition: The scoring rule for the category and math rows: the fraction of trials on which the target reaches J-lens top-1 anywhere in the layer-by-position grid. It is a hit rate over trials, not an accuracy over readouts.

terms.term: precision (metric label for the line-width row)
terms.definition: The scoring rule for the line-width row: among readouts whose top-1 token is a number, the fraction that name the true wrap width. A model that never produces a numeric top-1 contributes nothing, so this measure is not comparable to the top-1 hit rate above it.
One run of a task family under one phrasing: a specific target, a specific carrier passage, and the instruction template filled in. Dot heights are rates over the trials for that phrasing.
The translucent bar behind the dots in each group, drawn at the mean rate across that condition's phrasings. The focus and ignore bars are the values plotted in the main-text figure.
One circle per instruction phrasing, placed at that phrasing's rate. Its horizontal offset within the bar is a fixed spacing device, not data.
The wording of one instruction, shown in the hover tooltip with {x} standing for the target, for example "Don't think about {x}." Each condition is instantiated with several of them.
The short internal name of a phrasing, shown above its template in the tooltip: foc_ for focus, men_ for mention, neg_ for don't-think, dis_ for ignore, and lb_ for the line-width variants.
The thin horizontal rule in each panel, marking the rate when the prompt gives no instruction and does not name the target. It is the reference for how much any condition adds.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues functions as the model's global workspace. "The target is in the J-space" is what a top-1 hit is taken to indicate.
The human finding that being told to suppress a thought makes it occur more often than no instruction at all. The paper reads the don't-think bars sitting near the mention bars as a parallel.

The protocol behind the first two rows: the model copies an unrelated sentence while an instruction states what to hold in mind, and the lens is read at the copied tokens, where the surface text has nothing to do with the target.
The protocol behind the third row: the model reads a passage hard-wrapped to a fixed width and silently tracks the character count, with the lens read at the line-break positions.

numbers.meaning: Three task families crossed with three models. Every panel repeats the same four-bar structure, so a reader can compare any two cells directly.
focus, mention, don't-think and ignore. The main text reported only focus and ignore; mention and don't-think are added here to separate priming from prohibition.

numbers.value: five to eight phrasings per condition
numbers.meaning: The caption's stated range for how many wordings instantiate each condition. The counts in the data are 5 to 7 for the category and math rows, and 3 to 8 for the line-width row, where the mention condition has only three templates.
The vertical range of every panel, shared across all nine so heights are comparable. Category and math read as hit rates, line width as precision.
Category-instance focus means for Haiku, Sonnet, Opus. Told to hold the category instance in mind, all three models put it at J-lens top-1 on almost every trial, with a small rise across tiers.
Category-instance mention means. A bare naming of the target, with no instruction, already reaches most of the focus rate on Sonnet and Opus; the gap is wider on Haiku.

Category-instance don't-think means. They sit essentially on top of the mention means, which is what the paper points to as the white bear effect: forbidding the thought neither suppresses it nor, beyond the mention itself, inflates it.
Category-instance ignore means. Well below mention on all three models, so the irrelevance framing does pull the target down, but far above the no-instruction floor, so it does not remove it.
Math-expression focus means. The rate climbs steeply across the three tiers, more so than in the category row.
Math-expression mention means. On Sonnet and Opus these slightly exceed the focus means, so on this task an explicit instruction adds nothing measurable over naming the expression.
Math-expression don't-think means. Below mention but not far below, and rising with model tier.
Math-expression ignore means. Roughly half the mention rate on the two larger models and about a fifth of it on Haiku.

Line-width focus means, as precision. Much lower than the other two rows and not monotonic in model size: Sonnet scores above Opus. The appendix ascribes the difference to the task being harder to perform and harder to specify.
Line-width mention means. Naming the wrap without asking for the count leaves precision at a few percent, close to the floor, so the priming seen in the other rows does not appear here.
Line-width don't-think means, again near the floor.
Line-width ignore means, at or below the floor line for that panel.

The no-instruction floors drawn as the horizontal rule in each of the nine panels. They are the paper's evidence that context alone does not place the target in the readout, which is why any bar above them is attributed to the instruction.

The spread of the seven don't-think phrasings on Haiku, category instance. The low end is "Don't worry about {x}." and the high end "Whatever you do, do not think about {x}.", so the same nominal condition covers a five-fold range.
The spread of the six mention phrasings on Haiku, category instance. The bare parenthetical "({x})" primes hardest; the buried "There is a phrase, {x}, included here." primes least.
The spread of the six ignore phrasings on Opus, math expression. "{x} is irrelevant — ignore it." suppresses most; "{x} is unrelated to this task." suppresses least.

The spread of the five line-width focus phrasings on Opus, quoted in the appendix text as 14% to 56%. The oblique "Focus on figuring out what that column number is while you read." sits at the bottom and the direct "At each line break, count the characters and keep the number in mind." at the top, which is the paper's evidence that the specification, not only the task, is doing the work.

items.caption: Figure 66: Four additional paired-question stimuli. Each panel shows the same stimulus under two questions asked before it. Stimulus tokens are shaded where the target property's name appears in the J-lens top-10 at that position across the workspace layer range (darker = higher rank).
items.title: Four more properties the question summons
items.takeaway: Across four further text properties - British spelling, casual register, plural grammatical number and melancholy tone - the same passage read after a next-word question and after a name-the-property question loads different content into the workspace at identical tokens. In every panel the property's name reaches the J-lens top-10 at more stimulus positions under the naming question, while the model's next-word answer respects the property under both questions.
items.walkthrough:
This is a live widget rather than a static image. It holds four panels, titled spelling, register, number and tone. Each panel is one property of a text.

Inside a panel the same short passage appears twice. Above the first copy sits a label reading "Next-word question"; above the second, "Property question". Both copies are printed as a chat turn: `Human:` then the question, then the passage in quotation marks, then `Assistant:` and the single word the model produced.

The passage is drawn one tokenizer token at a time, so words split - " lab" and "elled" are two tokens. A token is shaded orange where the property's name reaches the top 10 of the [[j-lens-readout]] at that position, at any layer in the [[workspace-layers]] band. Shading comes in three steps: darkest for rank 1 or 2, mid for rank 3 to 5, faintest for anything below. Hovering a token prints its rank. A line under each copy counts the shaded tokens and names the tokens that counted as the property's label.

### How the comparison is set up

The passage tokens are identical across the two copies of a panel. Only the question before them differs. Any difference in shading is therefore attributable to the question, which is the design of the [[paired-question-protocol]] used in the main text and the point of [[directed-modulation]].

### What the four panels show

In every panel the naming question shades more tokens than the next-word question. Spelling goes from 1 shaded token out of 31 to 7. Register goes from 0 out of 38 to 3. Number goes from 2 out of 22 to 10. Tone goes from 2 out of 35 to 5.

A control is built into the model's own answers. Under the next-word question the model continues the British-spelled passage with "colour" and the plural-subject clause with "abstained". The property is being used to predict the next word either way.

The paper's reading follows: the property is represented and in use under both questions, and what the question changes is only whether its name enters the [[j-space]].

These are four hand-picked stimuli, one trial each, on [[claude-model-family|Claude Sonnet 4.5]]. The figure illustrates the effect rather than measuring it; the appendix section reports no aggregate statistic over these four.

terms.definition: The first panel's property: whether the author writes British or American English. The passage carries British spellings throughout - organised, labelled, recognised, favourite.
The second panel's property: how formal or casual the writing is. The passage is deliberately colloquial - "So yeah, we'd been hanging out at Jake's place all afternoon, just chilling".
The third panel's property: the grammatical number of the clause the passage sets up, singular or plural. The passage ends on "the members", which demands a plural verb.
The fourth panel's property: the mood the passage conveys. The passage is written to read as sad - a grey morning, a house that felt emptier than it had in years.

The condition label above the first copy of each passage. The question is "What word do you think comes next? Answer in one word." - answering it well requires sensitivity to the property but never requires naming it.
The condition label above the second copy of each passage. The question asks for the property by name, so the model must produce the label as its answer.

The chat-turn roles that structure each printed prompt. The `Human:` turn carries the question and then the stimulus passage in quotation marks; the `Assistant:` turn carries the model's one-word reply.
The short passage shown in quotation marks after the question. It is byte-for-byte the same in both conditions of a panel, which is what makes the shading difference attributable to the question.

The unit the passage is drawn in and the unit the lens is read at. Shading is per token, so a word split by the tokenizer can be shaded on one fragment and not the other - for example " lab" shaded while "elled" is not.

The colour key printed under the figure, tying the orange shading to the condition that triggers it: the property's name is among the ten highest-scoring tokens of the J-lens readout at that position.

The position of the property's name in the sorted J-lens readout at a token, shown on hover as "rank 9" or similar. Rank 1 is the top lens token; the shading darkness is a coarse function of this rank.
The middle band of layers over which the readout is scanned for each token. A token is shaded if the property's name reaches the top 10 at any layer in that band, not only at one chosen layer.
The small set of vocabulary tokens that count as the property's name for a panel. A stimulus token is shaded if any member of that set makes the top 10, and the count line prints the set.
The target set for the spelling panel. Any of these four tokens in the lens top-10 counts as the dialect having been named in the workspace.
The target set for the register panel. These are the labels that would describe the passage's style if the model were naming it.
The target set for the number panel. These are the labels for the grammatical number of the clause the passage sets up.
The target set for the tone panel. It includes "melanch", a subword fragment, because the full word melancholy is not a single token in the model's vocabulary.
The count line printed under each copy of a passage. It lists the target set and the number of stimulus positions at which some member of it reached the lens top-10.

The paper's readout method: for each vocabulary token it holds a direction in residual-stream space that disposes the model to say that token, and scoring an activation against all of them gives a ranked list. Here it is applied at every stimulus position.

The region of representation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues acts as the model's workspace. The figure's claim is about what enters it, not about what the model represents overall.

The experimental design this figure instantiates: present one stimulus under two questions, one that uses a property without naming it and one that asks for it by name, and compare the lens content at the identical stimulus tokens.

The workspace property under test in this section: the model can change what its workspace holds in response to instructions or task demands, independently of what it outputs. This figure tests the implicit form, where a question rather than an instruction does the directing.
The model the paper reports by default, and the one behind these readouts. The paper corroborates key results on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5, but this appendix figure shows one model only.
The model's one-word answer to the next-word question in the spelling panel. It is the British spelling, so the answer uses the dialect even though the dialect's name is nearly absent from the lens.
The model's answer to the spelling panel's property question, "Where do you think the author of this passage is from? Answer in one word."
The model's next-word answer in the register panel, completing "it wasn't even that ___". It fits the casual register without naming it.
The model's answer to the register panel's property question, "How would you describe the style of this passage? Answer in one word."
The model's next-word answer in the number panel, completing "the members ___". The verb form agrees with the plural subject, so the grammatical number is in use.
The model's answer to the number panel's property question, "Is the upcoming clause about one entity or more than one? Answer in one word."
The model's next-word answer in the tone panel, completing "even the clock seemed ___". It fits the passage's mood without naming it.
The model's answer to the tone panel's property question, "What mood does this passage convey? Answer in one word."

The paper's distinction underlying this figure: a representation poised to be put into words if the occasion arises, as opposed to one that merely influences behaviour. The question changes which of the two the property is.

numbers.meaning: Panels in the figure, one per property: spelling, register, number, tone. The appendix adds these four to the two properties shown in the main text, part of speech and tense.
Conditions per panel. Each panel prints the same stimulus twice, once after the next-word question and once after the property question.

The cut-off for shading: a stimulus token is shaded when the property's name is among the ten highest-scoring tokens of the J-lens readout there. A wider cut-off would shade more tokens in both conditions.
The three rank bands the shading encodes. Rank 1 or 2 gets the darkest fill, rank 3 to 5 an intermediate tint, and anything ranked below 5 but still inside the top 10 gets the faintest tint.
Stimulus tokens in the spelling panel - the denominator both of its counts. The passage runs from "She had organised" to the closing quotation mark.

Shaded tokens in the spelling panel under the next-word question. The single hit is on " lab" (of "labelled") at rank 9, the weakest shading band, so the dialect name is at the edge of the top 10 rather than absent outright.

Shaded tokens in the spelling panel under the property question - a seven-fold rise on identical text. Five of the seven are at rank 1, on "She", " the", " lab", "." and the closing quotation mark; the other two are rank 2 on " been" and rank 4 on " the".
Stimulus tokens in the register panel, the longest of the four passages.

Shaded tokens in the register panel under the next-word question. This is the cleanest case in the figure: no informal, casual, colloquial or conversational token enters the top 10 anywhere in the passage, yet the model still answers "bad" in keeping with the register.

Shaded tokens in the register panel under the property question, at " ch" (of "chilling") at rank 1, " fre" (of "freaked") at rank 2, and " hanging" at rank 9. The two strong hits land on the passage's most colloquial words.
Stimulus tokens in the number panel, the shortest of the four passages.
Shaded tokens in the number panel under the next-word question: " through" at rank 9 and the closing quotation mark at rank 2.

Shaded tokens in the number panel under the property question - nearly half the passage. Six sit at rank 1, mostly on function words and punctuation; the rest run at rank 2, 3 and 9. This panel shows the largest shift of the four.
Stimulus tokens in the tone panel.
Shaded tokens in the tone panel under the next-word question: " it" at rank 5 and a comma at rank 8. Both are mid or faint shading, so the mood words sit low in the readout.

Shaded tokens in the tone panel under the property question, at ranks 1 (" The"), 1 (" empt"), 3 (" a"), 4 (" it") and 6 (a comma). The rise here is the smallest of the four panels, roughly two and a half times rather than seven or five.
Trials per cell. Every count in the figure comes from a single forward pass on a single hand-written stimulus, which is why the section reports a pattern rather than a rate.

items.caption: Figure 67: Directed modulation influences the J-space but not the model's underlying representation of the property. Left: a JavaScript function under the instruction "Imagine that the following code is written in Python." The three columns show the top-5 J-lens readout (log probabilities, layer 62) at the boxed token under a neutral instruction, under the imagine instruction, and on a matched snippet of real Python code, with the rank of python in the full readout given for each. Beneath each readout, the value of a Python-code probe with its J-space component projected out. Right: the same two measurements aggregated over four categories (coding language, verb tense, part of speech, capitalization), n=24 stimuli per category. The upper panel shows the effect of the "imagine" instruction on each measure as a z-score against the no-instruction baseline (mean over stimulus positions and workspace layers; error bars are ±1 SEM over stimuli, dots are individual stimuli); the lower panel shows the same measures for a real stimulus that genuinely has the property. The instruction moves the J-lens measure significantly while leaving the J-orthogonalized property probe unmoved. In contrast, real stimulus moves the probe, and in some (but not all) cases also the J-space.
items.title: Imagining Python versus reading Python
items.takeaway: An instruction to imagine that a JavaScript snippet is Python pushes the token python high in the J-lens readout at the snippet's own tokens, while a probe for Python-ness with its J-space part removed stays at its no-instruction baseline. Real Python code moves that probe by three to six standard deviations, and only sometimes moves the lens. The paper reads the pair of results as evidence that the instruction writes to the workspace rather than re-encoding the stimulus.
items.walkthrough:
This is a live widget rather than a static image, and it has two halves.

The left half is a single worked example, titled "Example: imagining JavaScript code is Python". At the top sits the prompt: the instruction "Imagine that the following code is written in Python.", followed by a JavaScript function with one token boxed. Beneath it are three columns of [[j-lens-readout]]s taken at that boxed token, at layer 62. Layer numbers here are percentages of depth, so 62 falls inside the workspace band of [[layer-bands]], roughly L38 to L92. Each column lists the five highest-scoring vocabulary tokens with their log probability, and each bar's length is that token's probability relative to the column's own top token. The rank of python in the full readout is printed alongside.

The three columns are three conditions: a neutral instruction, the imagine instruction, and a matched snippet of real Python code. Under each column a gauge carries one further number, written as a signed z-score in units of $\sigma$: the value of a Python-code probe with its J-space component removed.

That probe is the control the experiment turns on. It is a [[linear-probe]] built as the mean difference of activations on real positive and negative stimuli. Its [[j-space-component]] is then projected out, using the top $k=25$ J-lens directions found by [[gradient-pursuit]], so what remains reads only the part of the representation lying outside the workspace. The paper calls the result a [[j-orthogonalized-property-probe]].

The right half, titled "Across four properties", aggregates the same two measures over four stimulus categories with 24 stimuli each: coding language, verb tense, part of speech, capitalization. Two stacked bar panels share one vertical axis in z-scores against the no-instruction baseline. The upper panel gives the effect of the imagine instruction; the lower gives the effect of a real stimulus that genuinely has the property. Each category carries two bars, one per measure, with dots for individual stimuli and error bars of $\pm 1$ SEM over stimuli.

The reported pattern is a dissociation. The instruction raises the property's name in the lens by several standard deviations while leaving the probe within roughly one standard deviation of baseline in every category. A real stimulus moves the probe by three to six standard deviations, and moves the lens in some categories but not all.

The reverse case appears too. A past-tense sentence drives the tense probe up six standard deviations while past stays far down the lens ranking, which the paper takes as a property represented and used without its label entering the [[j-space]] — the distinction section 3.5 develops as [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]].

terms.definition: The instruction under test, here "Imagine that the following code is written in Python." It asks the model to treat the stimulus as having a property the stimulus does not actually have.
The text the instruction is applied to: in the example, a JavaScript function. It genuinely has the original property (JavaScript) and not the imagined one (Python).
The single token inside the carrier at which the lens readout in the example is taken. Measurements in the aggregate panels are averaged over all stimulus token positions instead.
The five highest-scoring vocabulary tokens of the Jacobian-lens readout at that position and layer. The lens scores every token by how strongly the activation encodes the potential to verbalize it.
The units of the numbers printed beside each lens token. The bar drawn for a token is its probability relative to the top token of the same column, so the top row is always full width.
The depth at which the example readout is taken. The paper reports 25 evenly spaced layers reindexed to a 0-100 scale, so 62 means 62% of the way through the model.
The position of the token python in the full vocabulary-wide readout for that column, printed even when python does not make the visible top five.
The baseline condition: the same JavaScript carrier with no instruction to imagine anything. It fixes what the lens and the probe read with the stimulus alone.
The positive control: a matched snippet of code that genuinely is Python, read under a neutral instruction. It shows what both measures look like when the property is actually present.
The second measure, and one of the two legend entries. A linear probe for the property whose J-space part has been projected out, so it reads the property only from directions outside the workspace.

terms.term: J-lens activation of tokens naming the property
terms.definition: The first measure, and the other legend entry. It is how strongly the lens scores the token that names the property - python, past, verb, caps - at the stimulus positions.
