The four property-naming tokens, one per category. The lens measure tracks these tokens specifically; the probe never sees them, since it is a direction in activation space rather than a vocabulary entry.
How the probe direction is constructed: the average activation on stimuli that have the property minus the average on stimuli that do not.
The step that makes the probe a control. The activation's nearest point in the J-space is subtracted, so any movement the probe reports comes from outside the workspace.
The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm used to pick the J-lens directions that reconstruct the activation, here the top 25 of them.
The band of middle layers, about L38 to L92, in which the paper argues the J-space behaves like a workspace. Both measures are averaged over this band.
One of the four stimulus categories: a JavaScript snippet, with the instruction to imagine it is Python.
A present-tense sentence, with the instruction to imagine it is past tense. Its property-naming token is past.
A noun, with the instruction to imagine it is a verb. Its property-naming token is verb.
A lowercase word, with the instruction to imagine it is in all caps. Its property-naming token is caps.

The vertical axis of both bar panels: the shift in a measure relative to the no-instruction baseline, expressed in standard deviations of that measure. It puts the lens score and the probe value on one comparable scale.
The effect of the imagine instruction on each measure, per category. This is the condition where the model is asked to treat the stimulus as something it is not.
The same two measures for a matched stimulus that genuinely has the property. It shows what a real change in the input does, as a reference for the upper panel.
Vertical bars of plus or minus one standard error of the mean, computed across the stimuli within a category.
Individual stimuli, jittered within each bar. They show the spread behind each mean rather than only its summary.
The reference condition both panels are scored against: the original stimulus with no imagine instruction and no property swap.
The region of representation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues acts as the model's workspace. The probe is built to exclude it.

numbers.meaning: Stimulus categories: coding language, verb tense, part of speech, capitalization. Four were chosen so the result does not rest on the Python example alone, and they span code, syntax, morphology and surface form.
Stimuli per category (n=24), giving the dots and the standard-error bars in each bar. It is the sample the means and SEMs are computed over.
Columns in the left-hand example: neutral instruction, imagine instruction, real Python. Three are needed because the imagine condition has to be read against both a floor and a ceiling.
Lens tokens shown per column (top-5). It is a display cutoff only; the rank of python is reported from the full readout, which is why that rank can exceed 5.
The layer of the example readout, on the paper's 0-100 reindexing of depth. It sits inside the workspace band, where the J-space is claimed to carry abstract content.
The number of J-lens directions (k=25) removed from the probe by gradient pursuit. It matches the paper's measured J-space occupancy, which plateaus around 25 concepts across the workspace band.
The approximate start and end of the workspace layer band, on the 0-100 depth scale, over which both measures are averaged. Section 4.1 locates this band with four separate lens statistics.
The scale layer numbers are reindexed to, from 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers, so a layer number reads as a percentage of the model's depth.
The error bars are plus or minus one standard error of the mean over stimuli - the narrower convention, not a 95% interval.
Measures per category, drawn as two bars: the J-lens activation of the property-naming token, and the J-orthogonalized property probe. The whole figure is the contrast between them.
The typical size of the imagine instruction's effect on the J-lens measure. The paper does not give one number for it, since it varies by category.
The bound the paper gives on the imagine instruction's effect on the J-orthogonalized probe, in every category. It is the sense in which the probe is described as unmoved.
How far a real positive stimulus moves the J-orthogonalized probe. This range is what establishes that the probe is sensitive enough to have detected a re-encoding, had one occurred.
The tense probe's response to a genuinely past-tense sentence, in the case where past nonetheless stays far down the lens ranking. It is the paper's example of the dissociation running the other way.

sections.title: Directed modulation affects the J-space more than other representations

items.caption: Figure 68: Per-trial results of the lens-coordinate swap experiment. Each grid corresponds to one function template; rows give the argument in the prompt, columns the argument whose lens coordinates are swapped in. The sub-heading of each column indicates the target answer corresponding to the swapped-in concept. Cells show the model's top-1 token after the swap, with the small grey number giving the rank of the target-appropriate answer when it is not 1. Swaps redirect the answer almost perfectly for country facts (42/48 off-diagonal cells reach rank 1) and progressively less for months, animals, and number relations (0/48).
items.title: Per-Trial Swap Grids
items.takeaway: This is the trial-by-trial record behind the flexible-generalization headline count: sixteen small grids, one per function template, showing what the model actually said after every individual lens-coordinate swap. It exposes a sharp gradient the summary number hides - country swaps redirect the answer almost perfectly at 42 of 48 off-diagonal cells, while number relations succeed on none of 48 at standard strength. The grey ranks in the failing cells show the target answer usually sits somewhere below the top rather than absent, which is the paper's evidence that weak swaps push in the right direction without going far enough.
items.walkthrough:
This item unpacks the summary counts of the [[flexible-generalization]] experiment into the individual trials that produced them; the article renders it as a live widget rather than a static image. It holds sixteen small grids, one per function template of the [[function-template-protocol]] - four templates in each of four argument categories: countries, months, animals, and number words.

Each grid is $4 \times 4$, because its category supplies four arguments. A row fixes the argument actually written in the prompt. A column fixes the argument whose [[j-lens-vector]] is swapped in.

The intervention is the [[lens-coordinate-swap]]: the activation's coordinates along the row vector and the column vector are read, exchanged, and written back, held at every token position across a band of middle layers ([[activation-clamping]]). Each column carries a sub-heading giving the answer that this template implies for the swapped-in argument. Under the template "the capital of ___ is", the column for China is headed with Beijing.

The four cells on the diagonal are those where row and column name the same argument. Nothing is exchanged there, so the diagonal is the unmodified baseline. The twelve off-diagonal cells are the real trials. Four grids at twelve trials each gives 48 per category, and sixteen grids give 192 in all.

A cell prints the model's top-1 output token after the swap. The trial counts as a success when that token is the column's sub-heading. Where it is not, a small grey number gives the rank of the target-appropriate answer in the output distribution; the number is omitted at rank 1 because the printed token already shows it.

Read across categories, the grids separate cleanly. Country swaps land on 42 of 48 off-diagonal cells. Months succeed partially, animals rarely, and number relations on 0 of 48. The four categories together make up the 76 of 192 successes reported in the main text, so months and animals account for 34 of their shared 96 trials; the paper gives the ordering rather than the two separate counts.

The grey ranks carry a second point. Among the failures, the top-1 token is typically still the correct answer for the argument written in the prompt, and the target's answer appears further down. All grids are at standard swap strength. Doubling it to $\alpha = 2$ ([[swap-strength-alpha]]) often brings the target answer up, and the paper reads the ranks and that recovery together as a swap that moves the activation the right way but not far enough. The category gradient itself tracks [[workspace-loading]], which is highest for countries and lowest for number words. The model is Claude Sonnet 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]).

terms.definition: One $4 \times 4$ block of cells covering every ordered pair of arguments for a single function template. Sixteen grids appear, four for each argument category.
A prompt frame applying one fixed operation to a slotted argument, such as "the capital of ___ is" or "most people in ___ speak". Each grid belongs to exactly one template.
The source argument: the word actually written into the template on that trial, and the concept whose lens coordinate the swap removes.
The target argument: the concept whose J-lens vector is written into the activation in the source's place. The model is never shown this word.
Printed under each column: the answer the template implies for the swapped-in argument. It is the token a cell must show for the trial to count as a success.
A cell where row and column name the same argument, so the swap exchanges a coordinate with itself and changes nothing. The four diagonal cells of a grid are its unmodified baseline.
A cell where source and target differ - an actual swap trial. Twelve per grid, 48 per category, 192 overall, and the only cells the success counts are computed over.
The model's single most likely next token after the swap has been applied and the forward pass completed. This is what the grid reports for each trial.
The rank of the target-appropriate answer in the model's output distribution, shown only when that rank is not 1. Its presence marks a failed trial and its size says how badly the swap missed.
Position of a token in the model's output distribution ordered by probability. Rank 1 is the top-1 token; rank 7 means six tokens were more likely.

The intervention behind every off-diagonal cell: the residual stream's coordinates along the source and target J-lens vectors are read via a pseudoinverse, exchanged, and written back, leaving the rest of the activation untouched.
The direction in activation space that the Jacobian lens associates with one vocabulary token. Rows and columns are indexed by arguments, but the swap operates on these vectors.
Enforcing the swapped coordinates at every token position and every layer in the chosen band for the whole forward pass, rather than editing once and letting the value drift.
The argument category with the highest workspace loading and the best results here: 42 of its 48 off-diagonal cells show the target-appropriate answer at rank 1.
The second argument category. Its grids show partial success - some cells flip to the target answer, others do not.
The third argument category, where swaps rarely redirect the answer; most off-diagonal cells still print the answer for the argument in the prompt.
The number-word category, whose functions are arithmetic or ordering relations over small integers. No off-diagonal cell succeeds at standard swap strength.
The output the template implies for the swapped-in argument - Beijing rather than Paris under "the capital of ___ is". Success is defined as this token reaching rank 1.
A multiplier on the swap's magnitude. The grids are all at the default strength; at $\alpha = 2$ the source vector is subtracted and the target added at double magnitude.
The cosine similarity between the residual stream and a concept's lens vector on an unmodified forward pass. It is the quantity the paper uses to explain why the categories order as they do here.
The model whose outputs fill the cells; the paper's default subject model, with key results corroborated on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5 elsewhere.

numbers.meaning: Grids in the item, one per function template: four argument categories with four functions each.
The shape of every grid. Each category supplies four arguments, and each argument can appear as a row (in the prompt) or a column (swapped in), giving sixteen cells.
Diagonal cells per grid, where source equals target. These are baselines, not trials, and are excluded from every success count.
Off-diagonal cells per grid: 16 total cells minus the 4 on the diagonal. Equivalently, each of 4 arguments can be swapped for any of the other 3.
Swap trials per argument category: 4 templates times 12 off-diagonal cells. This is the denominator in both 42/48 and 0/48.
Off-diagonal cells across the whole item: 16 grids times 12, or 4 categories times 48. The denominator for the main text's aggregate count.
Country swaps whose target-appropriate answer reaches rank 1 - about 88%. Countries have the highest workspace loading, which the paper offers as the reason.

Number-relation swaps that succeed at standard strength: none. Number words have the lowest workspace loading; the paper leaves open whether small-integer computation runs outside the workspace or merely fails to align with the number tokens' lens vectors.

The main text's aggregate over all sixteen grids at standard strength. Subtracting the 42 country successes and the 0 number successes leaves 34 across the 96 month and animal trials, which the paper does not split further.
Successes reported in the main text when the swap is run at double strength. The grids themselves are at standard strength, so this number is context rather than a quantity plotted here.
The success threshold. A cell at rank 1 prints the column sub-heading and carries no grey number; any other rank is printed in grey beside the token the model actually produced.
The double-strength condition that recovers many of the failing cells, which the paper reads as evidence that a failed swap moved the activation in the right direction but not far enough.

sections.title: Detailed swap results for flexible generalization experiments

items.caption: Figure 69: Ablating an implied concept's J-lens vector at the early workspace layers selectively impairs avoidance but not naming. (A) A sentence implies a concept ("France") without naming it; the model is asked either to name the implied concept or to name something of the same category that is not the implied concept. The concept's J-lens vector is ablated at either the early workspace layers (L38–54) or the late workspace layers (L75–92). (B, C) The model's probability of producing the implied concept under each instruction. Late-layer ablation suppresses production under both instructions. Early-layer ablation leaves naming largely intact (B) but raises the avoidance failure rate roughly fivefold (C). Dots are per-item rates; error bars are 95% intervals over n = 63 items.
items.title: Naming a concept versus avoiding it
items.takeaway: Ablating an implied concept's J-lens vector at the early workspace layers (L38–54) leaves the model's ability to name that concept largely intact, but makes it fail roughly five times as often when instructed to name something else. Ablating the same vector at the late workspace layers (L75–92) instead lowers the concept's probability under both instructions. The paper reads this as evidence that the early workspace representation is what the model uses to actively suppress a concept, while the late one represents the intention to say it.
items.walkthrough:
Panel A draws the setup. A sentence implies a concept without printing it: "Their trip included croissants, the Louvre, and a climb up the famous iron tower" implies France. The same sentence is then followed by one of two questions.

In the naming condition the question is "Which country the sentence is describing?" In the avoidance condition it is "Name a country that the sentence is NOT describing". Producing *France* is the correct answer to the first question and a failure on the second. The design is borrowed from the [[inclusion-exclusion-paradigm]] in human memory research, where deliberately withholding a primed response, rather than giving it, is read as the mark of conscious access.

Panel A also marks where the intervention lands. The [[jacobian-lens]] assigns each vocabulary token a direction in the [[residual-stream]]; ablation projects the activation's component along France's direction out, leaving the rest of the activation alone. Only that one concept's vector is removed, at one of two depths: the early workspace layers L38-54, or the late workspace layers L75-92. Both sit inside the middle band the paper calls the [[workspace-layers]], with L75-92 running up against the [[motor-layers]] that carry the imminent output.

Panels B and C plot a single quantity, the model's probability of producing the implied concept. B is the naming condition, C the avoidance condition, and within each panel the conditions compared are no ablation against the two ablation depths. Dots behind each bar are per-item rates across the 63 items; error bars are 95% intervals over those items.

The two panels are meant to be read against each other. Late-layer ablation pushes both down: naming becomes less likely in B, and the already-low rate in C is pushed lower still. That is what a representation of the intention to say a word would do.

Early-layer ablation splits them. Naming in panel B is left largely intact. Avoidance in panel C fails roughly five times as often.

The text reports a control not enumerated in the caption: an equal-magnitude ablation of a different concept from the same category raised avoidance failures slightly, but by significantly less. The paper's reading is that the early J-space vector is required to suppress a concept, not to say it. The fivefold figure should be read against a baseline held below $0.15$ by the item-selection rule, so it is a large multiple of a small number.

terms.definition: The schematic half of the figure: it shows the priming sentence, the two questions asked of it, and the two layer ranges at which the concept vector is ablated.
The bar chart for the naming condition, plotting how often the model produces the implied concept when that is the correct answer.
The bar chart for the avoidance condition, plotting how often the model produces the implied concept when producing it is a failure.

The concept a prompt sentence evokes without ever naming it, such as France for a sentence about croissants and the Louvre. It is the thing ablated, the thing to be named in one condition, and the thing to be withheld in the other.
The same implied concept, named from the psychology side: the prompt primes it, and the question then asks either for it or for anything but it.
The question “Which country the sentence is describing?”. Saying the implied concept is success here.
The question “Name a country that the sentence is NOT describing”. Saying the implied concept is failure here.

The direction in the residual stream that the Jacobian lens assigns to a vocabulary token, encoding the model's potential to verbalize it. Here, one such vector, for the implied concept, is the target of the intervention.

Projecting out the activation's component along a chosen J-lens vector at chosen layers and positions, so that direction carries no signal onward. This experiment ablates one concept's vector, not the whole workspace.
The first stretch of the workspace band, just after the J-space starts carrying meaningful content. Ablation here is the condition that breaks avoidance.
The final stretch of the workspace band, before the motor layers take over. Ablation here suppresses production under both instructions.
The middle band of depth in which the paper argues the J-space behaves like a global workspace: it begins around L38 and ends around L92, flanked by sensory layers early and motor layers late.
The set of activation-space points expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors; the region the paper treats as the model's workspace.

terms.term: Probability of producing the implied concept
terms.definition: The plotted measurement in panels B and C: the model's output probability for the implied concept token under the given question and ablation condition.
Per-item rates, one dot per prompt item, drawn behind each bar so the spread across items is visible rather than only the mean.
95% intervals computed over the 63 items, indicating how much of the plotted difference survives item-to-item variation.

A matched perturbation that ablates a different concept of the same category as the primed one, at equal magnitude. Reported in the text as a check that the avoidance effect is not generic damage or regression to the mean.

The human-memory design this experiment is loosely modeled on, in which deliberately avoiding a primed response is taken as a marker of conscious processing, since giving the primed response can be done unconsciously.

terms.term: Naming versus avoiding a primed concept
terms.definition: The paper's name for this experiment, and one instance of its broader claim that the workspace mediates flexible rather than automatic processing.
The model these results are reported on; it is the paper's default model unless another is named.

numbers.meaning: The early workspace layer range at which the concept's J-lens vector is ablated. It sits at the workspace onset, where the paper's lens statistics first show meaningful J-space content.
The late workspace layer range for the other ablation depth. It ends at the point where the paper places the boundary between workspace and motor representations.
The workspace band's start and end as identified in section 4.1: about a third of the way through the depth, and shortly before the output.

The number of evenly spaced residual-stream layers the paper reports on, reindexed to 0–100 so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth. L38 is therefore 38% of the way through the model, not the 38th layer.
The number of prompt items kept for analysis, and the sample the dots and 95% intervals are computed over.
The selection rule for the naming condition: an item is kept only if the unablated model gives the implied concept at least this probability when asked to name it.

The selection rule for the avoidance condition: an item is kept only if the unablated model gives the implied concept at most this probability when told to name something else. It also fixes the low baseline that panel C's increase is measured against.
The confidence level of the intervals drawn as error bars, taken over the 63 items.

The increase in the avoidance failure rate under early-layer ablation, as stated in the caption. Because the unablated rate is at most 0.15 by construction, this is a fivefold rise from an already small number.
Only two layer ranges are compared, early and late; the figure does not scan depth continuously.

sections.title: Different J-space requirements for naming a concept and avoiding it

items.caption: Figure 70: The change in $\alpha$ needed for each component's activation share to go from 10% to 90%, by layer (median with interquartile band).
items.title: Transition width across depth
items.takeaway: The figure quantifies how abruptly the model commits to one of two blended concepts, layer by layer, using the width of the alpha-interval over which a component swings from 10% to 90% commitment. That width is large in early layers, falls steeply over roughly layers 21 through 42, and then flattens. The J-space component's width is consistently somewhat narrower than the non-J-space remainder's and reaches its floor earlier, which is a difference of degree rather than a dissociation.
items.walkthrough:
The plot turns the [[ignition]]-like behaviour seen earlier into a single number per layer, and then tracks that number across the model's depth.

The horizontal axis runs over the 25 sampled layers of the [[residual-stream]], reindexed to 0-100 so that a layer number reads as a percentage of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). The vertical axis carries the [[transition-width]]: the change in $\alpha$ needed for a component's [[projection-share]] to go from 10% to 90%. Two series are drawn, each a median across trials with an interquartile band around it. The printed article carries no axis values, so only the shape of the curves is available here.

Both axes rest on the [[embedding-mixture-experiment]]. A concept token's input embedding is replaced by the mixture $(1-\alpha)\,e_B + \alpha\,e_A$ inside an ordinary carrier sentence, and $\alpha$ is swept from 0 to 1. The projection share records where the resulting [[activations]] sit on the line joining that same trial's pure-$B$ activation to its pure-$A$ activation, so it is 0 at one end of the sweep and 1 at the other. Sixteen country-name pairs and forty carrier sentences give 640 trials, and the median and band are taken across them.

The width is a sharpness measure read in reverse. A component whose share simply tracked the input mixture would reach 0.1 at $\alpha = 0.1$ and 0.9 at $\alpha = 0.9$, a width of 0.8. A component that flipped at a threshold would give a width near 0. Smaller is sharper.

The two series split the activation in two ([[j-space-component]]). One is its component along the two concepts' [[j-lens-vector]]s, that is, its content inside the [[j-space]]. The other is the complement left after the top sixteen J-lens vectors are projected out at that position.

Both start wide. Both narrow, steeply over roughly layers 21 through 42, and then settle. The workspace onset that section 4.1 places at layer 38 ([[workspace-layers]]) sits inside that fall.

The claim drawn from the figure is modest. The J-space transition is described as consistently somewhat narrower, and as reaching its floor earlier. The non-J-space activation sharpens too, only later.

terms.definition: The vertical axis quantity: the change in the mixing coefficient needed for a component's projection share to rise from 10% to 90%. It is the paper's scalar measure of how abruptly the model switches from one concept to the other.

The interpolation coefficient of the ambiguous-input experiment, sweeping from 0 (pure concept B in the input embedding) to 1 (pure concept A). Elsewhere in the paper the same letter denotes a steering strength; here it means only the input mixture.

Where an activation sits on the straight line joining that same trial's pure-B activation to its pure-A activation, at the same token position and layer. It is 0 at one end of the alpha sweep and 1 at the other by construction, so it needs no separate calibration.
Depth through the model, reported on 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed to the range 0-100 so that a layer number reads as a percentage of total depth.
One of the two series: the part of the activation lying along the two concepts' J-lens directions. This is the content the paper treats as verbalizable workspace content.

The other series: what remains of the activation after the top sixteen J-lens vectors are projected out at each token position. It serves as the control against which the J-space component's sharpness is compared.

One vector per vocabulary token per layer, the direction in residual-stream space that disposes the model to say that token. The two concepts' J-lens vectors define the subspace in which the J-space series is measured.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse non-negative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues functions as a global workspace. The figure asks whether commitment sharpens faster inside it than outside it.
The line drawn for each series: the middle transition width across the 640 trials at that layer. A median rather than a mean, because individual trials can produce very wide or degenerate widths.

The shaded region around each median, running from the 25th to the 75th percentile of transition widths across trials at that layer. It shows the spread across prompts, not a confidence interval on the median.
The input embeddings of the two single-token concept names being blended, for example two country names. The mixed token's embedding is set to $(1-\alpha)e_B + \alpha e_A$.
In global workspace theory, the late all-or-none amplification of one interpretation of an ambiguous input. A narrow transition width is the paper's operational analogue of it.
The layer at which section 4.1's lens-derived metrics say the J-space starts carrying persistent abstract content, placed at about layer 38. The figure's steep fall brackets it.
The model these results are reported on by default. Key results elsewhere in the paper are corroborated on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5.

numbers.meaning: The figure's number in the appendix section 10.15, Ignition Details. The article prints no caption of its own for it, so the caption shown is inferred from the sentence that introduces it.

The two projection-share levels between which the width is measured. Endpoints nearer 0 and 1 were presumably avoided because the share is pinned exactly to 0 and 1 at the ends of the sweep by construction, which makes the extreme tails uninformative.

The transition width a purely proportional response would give: a share of 0.1 at alpha 0.1 and 0.9 at alpha 0.9 leaves an interval of 0.9 minus 0.1. This value is not stated in the paper; it is the arithmetic anchor for reading the axis, with a step-like response giving a width near 0 instead.
The endpoints of the alpha sweep, and equally the projection share's values at those endpoints. At alpha 0 the input embedding is pure concept B; at alpha 1 it is pure concept A.
The number of top J-lens vectors removed from the activation at each token position to form the non-J-space complement. The paper does not say why sixteen rather than another cut.
The number of pairs of single-token country names used as the two concepts being blended. A separate quantity from the sixteen vectors projected out, despite the shared value.

The number of ordinary carrier sentences into which the mixed embedding is inserted, such as "My sister has always wanted to visit ___". Varying the sentence tests that the effect is not an artifact of one context.

Sixteen concept pairs times forty carrier sentences: the number of trials over which the median and interquartile band at each layer are computed. The paper gives the two factors rather than the product.

The layer range, in the 0-100 percentage-of-depth indexing, over which the paper says the width falls steeply for both components. Before it the width is large; after it both curves are near their floor.
The workspace onset layer identified independently in section 4.1 by lens-derived metrics. It falls inside the 21-to-42 window, which is the alignment the appendix is pointing at.

The layer at which section 4.1 places the end of the workspace band and the start of the motor layers. It bounds the region in which the flattened widths sit, though this figure itself does not mark it.
The depth at which section 10.15 says the sharpness emerges, phrased as about a third of the way through the model. It is a coarser statement of the same transition as the 21-to-42 range.

The number of evenly spaced residual-stream layers sampled throughout the paper, which sets the horizontal resolution of the plot. Section 4.1 notes that layer subsampling can exaggerate how sharp a layerwise transition looks.
The range the sampled layers are reindexed to, so that a layer label reads directly as a percentage of the model's depth rather than as a raw layer count.
The bounds of the interquartile band around each median curve. The paper states only "interquartile band", which is what those quartiles are.

The J-lens rank cut used in Figure 29C, the panel whose measurement this figure quantifies: the J-space projection share is measured only within layers where the two concepts appear in the J-lens top 25. In earlier layers the concepts are absent from the readout, so no J-space share can be formed.
The number of series compared: the J-space component and the non-J-space complement. The whole point of the figure is the gap between them.

items.caption: Figure 71: Each component's projection share for maximally ambiguous $\alpha$ , across all prompts, at four representative layers.
items.title: Split shares at maximal ambiguity
items.takeaway: At the mixture value where the input leans least towards either concept, individual trials do not sit at the halfway point: their projection shares pile up near 0 and near 1. The paper takes this as evidence that the model commits to one interpretation per trial rather than representing the ambiguity, and reports that the J-space component becomes bimodal at an earlier layer, and more sharply, than the non-J-space remainder.
items.walkthrough:
The figure reports one quantity, measured over many trials, at four representative layers of Claude Sonnet 4.5.

That quantity is the [[projection-share]]. In the [[embedding-mixture-experiment]], a concept token's input embedding is replaced by the mixture $(1-\alpha)\,e_B + \alpha\,e_A$ of two single-token country embeddings, inside an ordinary carrier sentence. For each trial the [[residual-stream]] activation at that token position is recorded, and the measurement asks where it falls on the line joining the same trial's pure-$B$ activation to its pure-$A$ activation. A share of 0 sits at the pure-$B$ end, 1 at the pure-$A$ end.

Figure 29 plotted this share averaged over trials, as $\alpha$ swept from 0 to 1. This figure does not average. It fixes $\alpha$ at the value where the average response leans least towards either concept, and shows how the individual trials' shares are spread over the interval from 0 to 1 at that value.

The spread is what separates two readings of an ambiguous average. If an activation faithfully tracked the input mixture, every trial's share would sit near 0.5, because that is what the input is. If instead each trial commits to one concept, the shares pile up near 0 and near 1 with little in between — the [[bimodal-commitment]] pattern.

Each layer is shown for two components separately. One is the activation's [[j-space-component]] along the two concepts' [[jacobian-lens]] vectors. The other is the complement left after the top sixteen lens vectors are projected out.

Across the four layers the picture changes. In early layers both components sit near 0.5. Around halfway through depth the J-space component is already clearly two-peaked, while the non-J-space component still holds substantial mass at 0.5. By the middle of the workspace band — roughly L38 to L92 in the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] — both are two-peaked, the J-space component more sharply so.

The paper reads this as an analogue of [[ignition]]: an all-or-none commitment when the evidence is at threshold, appearing in the J-space first. The companion figure quantifies the same sharpening with [[transition-width]]. The evidence here is distributional and pooled: the figure does not say which concept wins on a given trial, or whether that winner holds across layers within one trial.

terms.definition: The horizontal quantity in every panel: where a trial's activation sits on the line from that trial's pure-$B$ activation to its pure-$A$ activation, at the same token position and layer. It is 0 at one end of the sweep and 1 at the other by construction.
The weight given to concept $A$ in the input embedding mixture $(1-\alpha)\,e_B + \alpha\,e_A$. In the wider experiment it sweeps from 0 to 1; this figure uses only one value of it per concept pair.
For each concept pair, the value of $\alpha$ at which the average projection share across trials leans least towards either concept. It is chosen per pair, not fixed at 0.5 of the mixture.
The input embeddings of the two country-name tokens being blended. Concept $A$ is the one whose share the axis runs towards; $B$ is the other.
One of the two parts the activation is split into before the share is measured: the J-space part and the non-J-space remainder. Each layer's panel reports the distribution for both.
Here, the activation's component along the two concepts' J-lens vectors — the part of the representation that the lens can read as naming one country or the other.

The complement: what is left of the activation after the top sixteen J-lens vectors are projected out at each token position. It serves as the control for whether commitment is specific to the workspace.
One direction per vocabulary token per layer, the direction that on average disposes the model to say that token. The two concepts' vectors define the subspace in which the J-space share is measured.
The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues functions as the model's global workspace.
One carrier sentence paired with one concept pair at one value of $\alpha$. The caption's "across all prompts" means the distribution pools these trials rather than showing them separately.
One of 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers, reindexed to the range 0-100 so a layer number reads as a percentage of the model's depth. Four of them are shown here.
The middle range of layers, roughly L38 to L92, in which the paper finds the J-space carries persistent abstract content. The text places the last of the four panels within it.
A distribution with mass concentrated at two separated values — here near 0 and near 1 — rather than in the middle. It is the signature the paper looks for as evidence of per-trial commitment.

In global workspace theory, the late all-or-none amplification of one interpretation of an ambiguous input, predicted to give bimodal outcomes when evidence is at threshold. This figure is the paper's test of that prediction.
The model these measurements are taken on; the paper's default throughout, with key results corroborated on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5.

numbers.meaning: The endpoints of the projection-share axis. A share of 0 places the activation at that trial's pure-$B$ activation ($\alpha = 0$) and 1 at its pure-$A$ activation ($\alpha = 1$); the values are exact at the ends of the sweep by construction, so the axis needs no separate calibration.

The share expected at every trial if the activation faithfully reflected a balanced input mixture. Mass at 0.5 is the paper's marker of no commitment; mass leaving 0.5 for the two ends is its marker of commitment.
The number of layers shown. They are described as representative, sampled from the 25 reported layers to cover an early layer, one about halfway through depth, and the middle of the workspace band.
The number of single-token country-name pairs used to build the ambiguous inputs. One maximally ambiguous $\alpha$ is identified per pair.
The number of carrier sentences, such as "My sister has always wanted to visit ___", into which the mixed embedding is inserted. With 16 pairs this gives 640 trials pooled into each distribution.

The number of top J-lens vectors projected out of the activation at each token position to form the non-J-space complement. The paper picks it to strip the active workspace content without removing the rest of the residual stream.

The J-lens readout rank within which both concepts must appear for the J-space share to be measured at a layer. Below that depth the concepts are not in the lens at all, so the J-space measurement is not defined.

The workspace onset layer, about a third of the way through depth, located by four independent lens-derived metrics. The J-space commitment reported here appears at or before the middle of the band that starts at L38.
The end of the workspace band, shortly before the output, after which the paper treats lens vectors as motor representations driving the imminent token.
The share interval used in the companion figure to define transition width. It is the sharpness measure that the bimodality here corroborates by a different route.
The depth range over which the companion figure's transition width falls steeply. It brackets the layers where, in this figure, the J-space distribution stops sitting at 0.5 and splits.
The number of evenly spaced residual-stream layers the paper reports on, reindexed to 0-100. The four panels here are a subset of those.

items.caption: Figure 72: Panels B and C of Figure ??, reproduced (top row, band-min over L38–92) alongside the same analysis at a single workspace layer (bottom row, L79).
items.title: One Layer Versus the Whole Band
items.takeaway: Repeating the word-list capacity measurement at a single workspace layer instead of pooling over the whole band leaves the qualitative picture unchanged, but cuts the counts sharply: on lists of unrelated words, roughly six items are present at a time when any layer may supply the evidence, against one or two at layer 79 alone. The paper reads the gap as a sign that the workspace stores different concepts in different layers, which raises its effective capacity.
items.walkthrough:
The item is a four-panel comparison in two rows. Both rows run the same measurement. They differ only in how many layers the measurement is allowed to consult.

The measurement is the [[word-list-experiment]]. The model reads a comma-separated list of 80 words. At every comma the [[j-lens-readout]] scores and ranks every vocabulary token, and a list word counts as present if its rank is 25 or better.

The top row reproduces panels B and C of the main list figure without change. Presence there is decided by band-min. The word's rank is computed separately at each layer of the [[workspace-layers]] band — L38 through L92 in the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] convention — and the smallest of those ranks, the best one, is the one compared against the threshold. A word therefore counts as present if it clears the bar anywhere in the band.

The bottom row repeats both panels at one layer, L79. Rank comes from that layer alone. A word held at L60 and nowhere else no longer counts.

### Reading the panels

Panel B, in either row, plots the number of list words present against comma position. Orange traces single-family lists, pooled over four families; blue traces lists of unrelated words. Solid lines count only words already read; dashed lines count all 80. Shading is the interquartile range. Panel C varies the rank threshold $K$ and reports how many already-read words clear it near the end of the list, with grey control words that never appear in the prompt setting the chance level.

### What the comparison shows

The shape survives. Words from a related family persist in the readout longer than words from a random list, and the dashed orange line still climbs to nearly the whole family within the first few items, unread members included. [[category-loading]] is not an artifact of pooling layers.

The scale does not survive. On random lists the band-min row shows about six read words present at once; the single-layer row shows one or two.

The paper takes that difference as evidence that the [[j-space]] can park distinct concepts at distinct depths, so [[j-space-capacity]] measured across the band exceeds capacity at any one layer. The argument is an inference from two counts, not a direct reading of which layer holds which word ([[single-layer-capacity]]).

terms.definition: The presence rule used in the top row: a word's J-lens rank is computed at every layer of the workspace band and the minimum, meaning the best, is kept. Presence anywhere in the band counts as presence.

The presence rule used in the bottom row: rank is read at layer 79 only, so a word represented at some other workspace layer does not count. Layer 79 is the same late workspace layer used for the example readouts in the main list figure.
The workspace layer range, given in the paper's percentage indexing. The J-space is near empty below L38 and turns into output-driving content above L92.
The paper samples 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers and relabels them 0 to 100, so a layer number reads as a percentage of the model's depth rather than as an index into its stack.

The read operation whose ranking decides presence: the residual stream at a layer is passed through the Jacobian lens to give a score for every vocabulary token, and the tokens are sorted by that score.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues serves the model as a workspace. This figure asks how much of it is visible at one depth versus across the band.
A word's position in the readout's ordering over the whole vocabulary. Lower is better, so the best rank over a set of layers is the smallest one.
The cutoff for counting a list word as present in the readout. It is fixed at 25 in panel B and swept in panel C.
Number of list words present in the readout at each comma of the list, for single-family lists against unrelated lists. The top row uses band-min presence, the bottom row single-layer presence.
The threshold sweep: how many already-read words fall at rank K or better near the end of the list, as K varies. It checks that the findings do not rest on the choice of 25.
80-word lists drawn from a single category, with results pooled over four families. These load the readout as a whole category within a few items.
80-word lists of items with no shared category, drawn at random. These are where the band-min and single-layer counts diverge most.
In panel B, the count restricted to list words the model has already read at that comma.
In panel B, the count over all 80 list words, including those not yet read. Its rise on family lists is the signature of category loading.
The band around each curve, giving the interquartile range over trials.
Words that never appear in the prompt, counted the same way as list words. They set the chance level for the threshold sweep.
The rank cutoff swept along panel C's horizontal axis. Everywhere else in the figure it is held at 25.

How many distinct concepts the workspace can hold at once in practice. The paper's claim here is that the figure it takes across the band is larger than the figure at any single layer, because layers can hold different things.

numbers.meaning: The workspace band over which the top row takes its minimum rank. These are the two depths at which the paper's boundary metrics inflect: below L38 the J-space carries almost nothing, above L92 its content turns into the imminent output.

The single layer used in the bottom row, about 79% of the way through the model. It sits late in the workspace band and is the layer the main list figure already used for its example readouts, which makes the two rows directly comparable.
Words per list. The length matters here because it is far above every count reported, so neither row is limited by running out of list.
The rank threshold for presence. A word must reach the readout's top 25 vocabulary tokens to be counted, at any band layer in the top row or at L79 in the bottom row.
Read words from a random list present at a given comma under band-min presence. This is the count carried over from the main list figure and is the number the single-layer row is set against.

The same count at L79 alone. Requiring one layer to hold the word, rather than accepting any layer in the band, removes roughly three quarters of the items. The gap is what the paper reads as concepts being distributed across depth.
The number of word families pooled into the orange curves of panel B, carried over unchanged from the main list figure.
The layout: two panels, B and C, shown twice - once with band-min presence on top and once with single-layer presence below. Only the presence rule changes between rows.
The range of the paper's layer numbering. 25 evenly spaced layers are relabeled as percentages of depth, which is why L38, L79 and L92 read as fractions rather than as layer indices.

sections.title: Loading in a single workspace layer

items.caption: Figure 73: The model copies a fixed sentence while the prompt also instructs it to concentrate on two things. (A) J-lens readouts at two of the copied tokens (layer 75). Top row: instructed to concentrate on two concepts. Bottom row: instructed to concentrate on one concept while mentally solving an arithmetic problem. Green marks content from the first instruction and purple from the second, corresponding to the highlighted phrases in the prompt. With two concepts, both appear at "ook" and neither at "on." With a concept and an arithmetic problem, the concept appears at "ook" and the computed answer at "on." (B) At tokens where one task's content appears in the lens top-10, the probability that the other's does too (layers 67–92). Grey bars are a shuffled control in which the other task's presence is measured on a different prompt, where each task instruction was given on its own. Two concepts share tokens at the control rate; a concept and a computed answer almost never do. (C) Fraction of trials on which each task's content reaches J-lens rank ≤ 5 anywhere in the response, when given alone (solid) versus alongside the other (hatched). The fraction drops only modestly when the tasks are paired, more so for the arithmetic answer.
items.title: Two covert tasks competing for the same tokens
items.takeaway: When the model is told to hold two things in mind while copying an unrelated sentence, both reach the workspace, but they share it differently: two concepts occupy the same tokens at about the rate a shuffled control predicts, while a concept and an ongoing arithmetic computation almost never occupy the same token. Splitting the workspace this way costs each task little overall reach, with the arithmetic answer paying the largest price.
items.walkthrough:
Three panels report one experiment. The model copies a fixed sentence, "The old painting hung crookedly on the wall.", while the prompt also tells it to hold two things in mind. This extends the [[directed-modulation]] protocol, in which an instruction sets what the model keeps in mind while its visible output stays unrelated to it. The [[jacobian-lens]] is then applied at tokens of the copied sentence, and the top-ranked lens tokens report what each position is about.

Panel A prints two prompts with their readouts. The upper prompt names two concepts, citrus fruits and farm animals. The lower names one concept, citrus fruits, and one arithmetic problem, printed as `3^2 - 2`. Green marks readout tokens belonging to the first instructed item and purple the second, matching the highlighted phrases in the prompt above. Superscripts give a token's rank in the lens top-10; unmarked tokens hold the remaining ranks. Both readouts are taken at layer 18 and at two tokens of the copied sentence, "ook" inside "crookedly" and "on".

Under two concepts, the readout at "ook" interleaves them: orange words at ranks 1, 2 and 6, then horses and animals at 3 and 4, then farms, livestock and farmers at 7 to 9. At "on" neither task appears, only generic words for thinking. Under concept plus arithmetic the tasks divide the tokens instead: "ook" carries the fruit words, and "on" carries Nine, nine, seven and Seven, that is the intermediate value $3^2 = 9$ and the answer $9 - 2 = 7$.

Panel B turns that into a rate. At every token where one task's content sits in the [[j-lens-readout]] top-10, the panel asks how often the other task's content sits there too. Grey bars are a shuffled control, where the partner task's presence is measured on a different prompt that carried only one instruction. Two concepts co-occupy at 0.46 against a control of 0.53, so at chance. A concept and a computed answer co-occupy at 0.06 against 0.26, well below chance.

Panel C asks whether exclusion at a token costs a task its place in the [[j-space]] altogether. A trial counts as reaching if the task's content hits lens rank 5 or better at any position in layers 16 to 22. Solid bars give the single-task rate, hatched the dual-task rate. Both concepts fall from 100% to 93%. The arithmetic answer falls further, 90% to 66%.

The computation, not the held concept, bears the cost of sharing, which is what a [[workspace-capacity-limit]] would predict for the harder of two loads.

terms.term: A: Example: the readout at two response tokens
terms.definition: The left panel's title. It prints two full prompts and, beneath each, the lens readout at two tokens of the model's copied response, as qualitative illustration rather than aggregate evidence.
The blue label for the first condition in panel A, in which the prompt instructs the model to concentrate on two unrelated concepts at once, citrus fruits and farm animals.

The orange label for the second condition in panel A, in which the prompt instructs the model to concentrate on one concept, citrus fruits, and to evaluate an arithmetic expression in its head at the same time.

A task the model is told to carry out mentally while writing something unrelated, so that no trace of it appears in the visible output. Both instructed items here are covert: the model writes only the copied sentence.

terms.term: "Write \"The old painting hung crookedly on the wall.\" ... Don't write anything else."
terms.definition: The prompt template, reproduced from the figure. The copied sentence is fixed across conditions, so the surface text is identical and any difference in the readouts comes from the instruction alone.
The concept named in both conditions, highlighted green in the prompt. Its content shows up in the readout as orange, orang, Orange, fruits and juice.
The second concept in the two-concepts condition, highlighted purple. Its content shows up as horses, animals, farms, livestock and farmers.
The arithmetic problem in the second condition, highlighted purple and printed in the figure with a caret. The model is told to evaluate it mentally while copying the sentence.
The line prefix marking the model's response in panel A. In both conditions the response is exactly the requested sentence, with no sign of either covert task.
One of the two response tokens the lens is applied at: the piece of "crookedly" shaded in the response line. It is a purely orthographic fragment, unrelated to either instructed task.
The other response token the lens is applied at, the word "on" in the copied sentence, also shaded in the response line and unrelated to either task.

The layer at which the panel-A readouts are taken, printed before each readout row. The paper's running text describes the same readouts at layer 75, so the figure's layer indices appear to follow a different numbering than the prose.
The list of vocabulary tokens the Jacobian lens ranks highest for a given activation, read as what that position is about. Each readout row in panel A is one such ranked list, printed left to right.

The paper's read technique: one vector per vocabulary token per layer, giving the direction that disposes the model toward saying that token, used here to score every token against the residual stream at a position.
The region of representation space spanned by sparse combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues functions as a global workspace. Panels B and C measure how two tasks share it.
Marks readout tokens belonging to the first instructed item, citrus fruits in both conditions, and the matching phrase in the prompt.
Marks readout tokens belonging to the second instructed item: farm animals in the upper condition, the arithmetic values in the lower one.
The rank of that token in the lens top-10 at that position. Only task-relevant tokens carry a numeral, so the gaps in the numbering are the unhighlighted tokens sitting in between.

Non-English tokens appearing unhighlighted in the readouts, in Russian, Chinese, Japanese and Korean. They sit alongside the English thinking and answer words and belong to neither instructed task; the lens ranks over the whole tokenizer vocabulary, not over English alone.

terms.term: thinking, thoughts, thinks, mentally, thought, imag
terms.definition: Generic words for the act of thinking that fill the readout at "on" in the two-concepts condition and share ranks with the fruit words at "ook" in the other condition. The paper reads these as the model representing the fact of holding something in mind, separately from the content held.

terms.term: Nine, nine, seventeen, seven, Eight, ninete, Seven, eight, Answer
terms.definition: The readout at "on" in the concept-plus-arithmetic condition. It mixes the intermediate value nine, the final answer seven, and near-miss numbers, indicating the computation itself is occupying that token.
The middle panel's title. Co-occupancy is the rate at which the two tasks are present in the readout at the same token position.

terms.term: P(the other task is in the lens top-10) at tokens where this task is in the top-10
terms.definition: The y-axis of panel B. It conditions on the positions where one task's content is already in the top-10 of the readout, then measures how often the partner task's content is there as well.
The presence threshold used in panel B: a task counts as occupying a token if any of its content words falls among the ten highest-ranked lens tokens there.

The grey bars. The partner task's occupancy is measured on a different prompt, one where each instruction was given on its own, so the control gives the co-occupancy expected if the two tasks were placed independently.
The blue bar pair, for the condition where both instructed items are concepts.
The orange bar pair, for the condition pairing a held concept with an arithmetic computation.
The black whiskers on each bar in panel B, showing the uncertainty of each rate. The figure does not state which interval they represent.

terms.term: C: Reachability: single vs dual task
terms.definition: The right panel's title. Reachability asks whether a task's content makes it near the top of the lens anywhere in the response, rather than at any particular token.

terms.term: reaches lens top-5 (band L16-22, any position)
terms.definition: The y-axis of panel C, the fraction of trials on which the task's content attains lens rank 5 or better at some position and some layer in the given band. The paper's text gives this band as layers 67 to 92, again a different numbering.
The baseline condition of panel C: the instruction was given on its own, with no second covert task alongside it.
The condition of panel C in which the same instruction was given alongside the other task, so the two must share the workspace.
The blue group, tracking the concepts from the two-concepts condition.
The first orange group, tracking the held concept in the condition where the partner task is the arithmetic problem.
The second orange group, tracking whether the computed result of 3^2 - 2 reaches the top of the lens. This is the item that loses the most under dual load.
The workspace-like property this experiment extends: the model can put a named concept into the J-space on instruction, independently of what it writes.
The claim from global workspace theory that only a small selection of ongoing activity is held at once, so entry is competitive. The mutual exclusion in panel B is offered as an instance of it.

numbers.meaning: The arithmetic problem in the second condition and its answer. It is a two-step problem: square 3 to get 9, then subtract 2 to get 7. Both steps show up in the readout at "on", nine at ranks 1 to 3 and seven at ranks 4 and 7, which is why the paper describes the readout there as the computation in progress rather than a retrieved fact.

The layer of the panel-A readouts. It sits inside the middle band where the paper finds the J-space carrying workspace content, rather than in the early layers where it is nearly empty or the last layers where readouts turn into next-token predictions.

Ranks within the lens top-10 at that position. In the two-concepts readout at "ook" the marked ranks run orange 1, orange 2, horses 3, animals 4, Orange 6, farms 7, livestock 8, farmers 9, fruits 10, with rank 5 taken by an unhighlighted token; the alternation of green and purple is what the paper means by the two concepts interleaving.
The presence threshold in panel B. A task counts as occupying a token if any of its content reaches the ten highest-ranked lens tokens there; the co-occupancy rate is defined relative to this cutoff.

Co-occupancy for two held concepts: at tokens where one concept is in the top-10, the other is too on 46% of them. The paper reads this as the two concepts placing themselves without regard to each other.

The shuffled control for the two-concepts condition, measured on prompts where each instruction was given alone. Since 0.46 sits within error of 0.53, the observed sharing is what independent placement would produce, so nothing is competing.
Co-occupancy for a concept and a computed answer: they land on the same token 6% of the time. This is the panel's central number, an almost complete mutual exclusion.

The shuffled control for the concept-plus-math condition. The gap from 0.26 down to 0.06 is roughly a factor of four, and it is that gap, not the raw 0.06, that makes the exclusion a real effect rather than a consequence of each task being rare.
The y-axis range of panel B. Both observed bars and both controls sit in the lower half, so even in the two-concepts case most tokens carry only one task.

The values the appendix prose reports for the concept-plus-math bar and its control, against 0.06 and 0.26 printed in the figure. The qualitative claim, exclusion well below control, is the same either way, but the two sources do not agree on the exact rates.
The reachability threshold in panel C, stricter than the top-10 used for co-occupancy. A trial counts only if the task's content reaches rank 5 or better.

The layer band searched in panel C. Reachability is scored over any layer in this band and any position in the response, which is why its rates are much higher than the per-token co-occupancy rates of panel B. The prose names this band as layers 67 to 92.

Single-task reachability for the concepts, in both the two-concepts group and the concept-with-math group. A concept held on its own reaches the top of the lens somewhere in every trial, which sets the ceiling the dual-task bars are compared against.

Dual-task reachability for the concepts, in both groups. The drop from 100% is 7 points, so holding a second task alongside a concept costs that concept almost nothing at the level of the whole response.

Single-task reachability for the arithmetic answer. It starts below the concepts even without a partner task, which the paper does not explain; a multi-step computation is simply less reliable than holding a word in mind.

Dual-task reachability for the arithmetic answer, a fall of 24 points from 90%. This is the largest decline in the panel and the basis for the claim that the computation, not the concept, pays for sharing the workspace.

The values the appendix prose gives for the arithmetic answer's single- and dual-task reachability, against 90% and 66% in the figure. The size of the decline, roughly 23 to 24 points, agrees; the levels do not.
The y-axis range of panel C, with gridlines at 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent.
The number of covert tasks held at once throughout the figure, and the number of response tokens shown in panel A. The experiment tests only the two-task case; no larger load is reported.

sections.title: Competition in the workspace during concurrent covert tasks

items.caption: Figure 74: Examples of SAE features stratified by the excess kurtosis of their J-lens projections (κ) and their functional role. Each panel shows a feature's auto-interpretation label, its κ, its top J-lens readout tokens, and contexts on which the feature activates (with the activating tokens highlighted). Top row: workspace-like features (high κ) name an abstract concept and activate when that concept is invoked in context, but the model is not necessarily about to mention it explicitly. Middle row: output/motor features (high κ) typically cause the model to output a particular token. Bottom row: features outside the J-space (low κ) often appear to be syntactic or bookkeeping features whose J-lens readouts are unrelated to the feature's apparent meaning.
items.title: SAE features sorted by lens kurtosis
items.takeaway: Nine example SAE features, three per row, show what the lens-kurtosis statistic picks out. High-κ features split into two kinds: ones that name an abstract concept the model is not currently uttering, and ones that push a specific next token. Low-κ features are syntactic bookkeeping whose lens readouts bear no relation to their apparent meaning.
items.walkthrough:
The item is a grid of feature cards, three examples in each of three rows. Each card reports one [[sparse-autoencoder]] feature. It gives the feature's auto-interpretation label, a short automatically written description of what the feature appears to mean. It gives the feature's [[lens-kurtosis]] $\kappa$. It gives the vocabulary tokens the [[jacobian-lens]] reads most strongly off that feature's decoder direction. And it gives text excerpts on which the feature activates, with the activating tokens highlighted.

$\kappa$ is the statistic that sorts the rows. A feature's decoder direction is pushed through the lens, which yields a score for every token in the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. The excess [[kurtosis]] of that score distribution measures how sharply peaked it is, with a Gaussian scoring zero. High $\kappa$ means the direction loads onto a handful of [[j-lens-vector]]s; low $\kappa$ means it spreads diffusely across the vocabulary. Because the [[j-space]] is a [[sparse-subframe]] rather than a subspace, alignment with a small set of lens vectors is the paper's criterion for being in it.

The top row holds [[workspace-features]]: high $\kappa$, naming an abstract concept, active whenever that concept is invoked. The middle row holds [[motor-features]]: also high $\kappa$, but firing immediately before the model utters the token in question. The paper separates the two by a rule. A feature counts as motor when, over its strongest activations, the actual next token sits in its top ten lens tokens more than 10% of the time. The bottom row holds low-$\kappa$ [[bookkeeping-features]].

The worked example is the top-left card, labelled "numeric constraints and ranges", at $\kappa = 20.9$, the 99.9th percentile of the feature distribution. Its top lens tokens are limits, 限, Limit, lím and limit: one concept in several surface forms and languages. Its activating contexts invoke limits — "strictly positive," "in the range of 0, 1," "restricted by a half-plane" — at positions where the model is not about to write the word. That is the shape the paper wants for a [[verbalizable-representation]]: a concept held in a form the model could say, but is not saying.

The bottom row cuts the other way. A loop variable in a decrementing for-loop scores $\kappa = 0.3$, the first digit of a page range in an academic citation scores $\kappa = 0.5$, and a markdown section header scores $\kappa = 0.3$. For each, the top lens tokens are unrelated to the label. The evidence in this figure is illustrative rather than statistical: nine selected cards, with the distributional claim left to the next figure.

terms.definition: One entry in a sparse autoencoder's learned dictionary: a direction in the residual stream that the SAE uses, together with an activation coefficient, to reconstruct activations as a sparse sum. Each card in the figure is one such feature.
The vector an SAE writes back into the residual stream when a feature fires. It is the direction the paper projects through the J-lens to compute that feature's κ.

The figure's sorting statistic: the excess kurtosis of the vocabulary-score distribution obtained by pushing a feature's decoder direction through the J-lens. It measures how sharply the lens reads that direction, relative to a Gaussian.
A distribution statistic for heavy tails and peakedness, defined so that a Gaussian scores zero. Here it is applied not to data but to a score vector over the vocabulary.

Applying the Jacobian lens to a direction produces a score for every vocabulary token; the top-scoring tokens are printed on each card. They stand for what the model would be disposed to say if that direction were present in the residual stream.

The paper's readout method, which assigns each vocabulary token a residual-stream direction encoding the model's potential to verbalize that token. The figure uses it to interpret SAE feature directions.
The single direction the lens associates with one vocabulary token at one layer. A high-κ feature is one whose decoder direction lies close to a small number of these.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues behaves like a global workspace. κ is the statistic used to ask whether a given SAE feature lies in it.

The paper's formal description of the J-space: a set of vectors that need not be linearly independent, restricted to sparse combinations. Because of this, closeness to a few lens vectors, rather than membership in a linear subspace, is the test for being in the J-space.

The short natural-language description of a feature's apparent meaning, generated automatically rather than written by the authors. It is the heading of each card, and phrases such as "numeric constraints and ranges" are examples.

Excerpts of text on which the feature fires most strongly, with the specific token positions that trigger it marked. They are the evidence for what a feature responds to, as opposed to what it promotes.

High-κ features that name an abstract concept and activate whenever that concept is invoked in context, without the model being about to say it. These are the features the paper treats as living in the workspace.

High-κ features that activate immediately before, and promote, the utterance of a particular token. They share the high-κ signature with workspace features, which is why the paper calls high κ necessary but not sufficient for workspace membership.

Low-κ features, typically syntactic or surface-level bookkeeping, whose top lens tokens bear no relation to their auto-interpretation label. The paper takes them as the expected inventory of representations that are not in a workspace.
The auto-interpretation label of the top-left card, the figure's worked example of a workspace feature. It fires on text that invokes bounds or ranges.

The top J-lens readout tokens of the "numeric constraints and ranges" feature. They are the same concept in several surface forms and languages, which is the paper's evidence that the feature encodes a concept rather than a string.

terms.term: "strictly positive," "in the range of 0, 1," "restricted by a half-plane"
terms.definition: Activating contexts printed for that feature. Each invokes the idea of a limit, and at none of them is the model about to output the word "limit."
One of the low-κ bottom-row examples: a feature that tracks the loop variable of a for-loop that counts downward. Its lens tokens are unrelated to loops.
Another low-κ example: a feature for the first digit of a page range inside an academic citation. It is bookkeeping about text layout rather than a nameable concept.
The third low-κ example: a feature for markdown section headers in academic papers. Like the other two, its lens readout does not match its label.
The paper's target notion: content held in a form the model could put into words if asked, as distinct from content it happens to be uttering. The top row is offered as an illustration of it.
The fixed token inventory of the model's tokenizer. The lens score distribution whose kurtosis defines κ is a distribution over this set.

numbers.meaning: The figure's layout. The paper says it shows three examples each of workspace-like features, motor features and low-kurtosis features; the caption assigns these to the top, middle and bottom rows. One passage of the prose instead refers to the low-κ examples as a "right column," so the exact arrangement is described inconsistently, but the grouping is the same either way.

The lens-kurtosis of the "numeric constraints and ranges" feature, the top-left card. It is the figure's worked example of a high-κ workspace feature, and the value is high because the feature's decoder direction loads almost entirely onto the lens vectors for a few tokens meaning "limit."
Where κ = 20.9 falls in the distribution of κ across all SAE features. The paper describes the distribution as heavy-tailed, so a value this high sits in its far tail.

The lens-kurtosis of two bottom-row examples: the decrementing for-loop variable feature and the markdown section header feature. A value this close to zero means the lens reads the direction almost as diffusely as a Gaussian score distribution, so the direction is not aligned with any small set of lens vectors.
The lens-kurtosis of the remaining bottom-row example, the feature for the first digit of a page range in an academic citation. Also effectively outside the J-space.
The excess kurtosis of a Gaussian, and therefore the reference point of the κ scale. Values near zero indicate a lens readout with no sharp peak.

numbers.value: top 10 lens tokens, more than 10% of the time
numbers.meaning: The threshold rule that classifies a high-κ feature as motor rather than workspace-like. Over the feature's strongest activations, if the actual next token appears among its ten most strongly expressed lens tokens on more than one occasion in ten, the paper calls it motor. The rule exists because motor and workspace features are indistinguishable on κ alone.
The number of top readout tokens printed for the "numeric constraints and ranges" feature: limits, 限, Limit, lím, limit. That five distinct tokens all express one meaning is the point being made.

items.caption: Figure 75: Quantifications of SAEs in J-space. Left: Distribution of layer 50 SAE decoder kurtosis (1m features) compared to a covariance matched random baseline. Middle: the fraction of features that pass a kurtosis baseline by layer, with and without including motor features; (right) the same as middle, but weighted by activation L0 and L1.
items.title: How much of the SAE dictionary lies in the J-space
items.takeaway: Across a million-feature sparse autoencoder dictionary, the distribution of J-lens kurtosis is heavy-tailed: most features are read diffusely by the lens, and only a thin tail is read sharply. Counting by layer, the fraction of features that clear a kurtosis threshold is near zero in the early layers, rises at the workspace boundary, and peaks at roughly 15% of the dictionary once motor features are excluded.
items.walkthrough:
The figure asks how much of a model's learned feature inventory sits inside the [[j-space]], using a [[sparse-autoencoder]] as the inventory. An SAE decomposes the [[residual-stream]] into a large dictionary of feature directions, each with a decoder vector.

The measurement runs each decoder direction through the [[jacobian-lens]], which returns one score per vocabulary token. The sharpness of that score distribution is the feature's [[lens-kurtosis]], written $\kappa$. High $\kappa$ means the direction loads onto a few [[j-lens-vector]]s. Low $\kappa$ means it spreads thinly over the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], and the feature is outside the workspace.

The left panel is the distribution of $\kappa$ over the roughly one million features of the layer-50 SAE. It is plotted against a covariance-matched random baseline: random directions sharing the second-order geometry of the real decoders. The match matters because the residual stream is anisotropic on its own, so an unmatched baseline would credit the features with sharpness that the geometry already supplies. The real distribution is heavy-tailed. The bulk of features sit at low $\kappa$, and a long tail is read sharply.

The middle panel changes the unit from features to layers. Depth runs along the horizontal axis in the paper's percentage convention ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]); the vertical axis is the fraction of that layer's dictionary whose $\kappa$ clears a threshold set by the baseline. Two curves are drawn, one counting every high-$\kappa$ feature and one excluding [[motor-features]] — features that fire just before, and push for, a specific output token. Motor features also have high $\kappa$, so excluding them isolates [[workspace-features]].

The fraction starts to rise at the workspace boundary, near layer 38, and peaks around 15% of the dictionary after the motor exclusion.

The right panel repeats the middle one with each feature weighted by its activation $L_0$ and by its activation $L_1$. The paper reads this as J-space features activating more strongly than average while firing less often, at least across the second half of the workspace range, which it calls consistent with all-or-nothing [[ignition]].

The paper hedges the whole analysis: SAE features do not necessarily carve the representation space at its joints, and high $\kappa$ is necessary but not sufficient for a feature to be a workspace feature.

terms.definition: An unsupervised dictionary-learning method that rewrites an activation as a sparse sum of feature directions, each meant to correspond to one sometimes-interpretable property of the input or context. Here it supplies the population of directions being scored.
The residual-stream vector an SAE writes back when one of its features is active. It is the object projected through the J-lens in every panel of this figure.

The region of activation space reachable as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors — the paper's candidate global workspace. A feature is judged to be "in" it by how sharply the lens reads its decoder direction.

The paper's technique that assigns each vocabulary token a residual-stream direction encoding the model's disposition to say that token. Projecting a direction through it yields a score over the whole vocabulary.
One vector per vocabulary token per layer, the unit of the J-space. A feature counts as J-space-aligned when its direction is concentrated on a small set of these rather than spread over all of them.
The statistic on the left panel's horizontal axis: how sharply peaked a feature's J-lens score distribution over the vocabulary is. The paper uses excess kurtosis, measured relative to a Gaussian.
Kurtosis measured relative to a Gaussian, so that a Gaussian scores 0 rather than 3. All κ values quoted in this section are excess values.

The comparison distribution in the left panel: random directions drawn to share the covariance structure of the real SAE decoders. It removes the sharpness that the residual stream's own anisotropy would produce for any direction at all.
The depth at which the SAE used in the left panel was trained, given on the paper's 0-100 depth scale. It sits inside the workspace band rather than at either end.

The cutoff used in the middle and right panels: a feature is counted as J-space-aligned when its κ exceeds what the covariance-matched random baseline produces. It turns the continuous left-panel distribution into a yes-or-no count.
The vertical axis of the middle and right panels: the share of that layer's SAE dictionary whose κ clears the threshold. It is a proportion of the dictionary, not of the model's activation.
