SAE features that activate immediately before a specific token and promote its utterance. They also have high κ, so the figure plots the fraction both with and without them.

High-κ features that name an abstract concept and fire when that concept is invoked, without the model being about to say the word. These are what the middle panel's motor-excluded curve is meant to count.
The bulk of the dictionary, filling the left panel's mode: syntactic and surface-level bookkeeping features whose lens readouts bear no relation to their apparent meaning.
Depth in the middle and right panels, reported on the paper's rescaled 0-100 index over 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers, so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth.
The depth, near layer 38 in this model, at which the paper's other statistics say the J-space starts carrying meaningful content. The middle panel's rise begins there.

The weighting used in one right-panel curve: how often a feature is active across data. Weighting the fraction by L0 asks what share of firing events, rather than of dictionary entries, is J-space-aligned.
The weighting used in the other right-panel curve: the summed magnitude of a feature's activations. Weighting by L1 asks what share of total activation mass is J-space-aligned.

In global workspace theory, the all-or-nothing amplification by which one item enters the workspace. The paper reads strong-but-infrequent activation of J-space features as consistent with such dynamics.

numbers.meaning: The layer whose SAE supplies the left panel's kurtosis distribution, on the paper's 0-100 depth index. It lies inside the workspace band, which the paper places at roughly layers 38 to 92, so it is a layer where J-space content is expected to exist.
The number of features in that layer-50 SAE dictionary. It is the sample size behind the left panel's histogram, and the denominator for the fractions in the other two panels.

The peak fraction of the dictionary that clears the kurtosis threshold, once motor features are excluded. The paper reports this as the high point of the middle panel's motor-excluded curve, so the great majority of features remain outside the J-space at every depth.

The workspace onset the paper locates elsewhere from four lens-derived statistics. The middle panel's fraction begins to rise here, which is why the paper describes the rise as starting at the workspace boundary rather than at an arbitrary depth.

The end of the workspace band, where J-lens readouts turn into predictions of the imminent output. Motor features dominate near this depth, which is what the motor-excluded curve in the middle panel is designed to strip out.

The criterion for labelling a feature "motor": over the feature's strongest activations, the actual next token appears among its 10 most strongly expressed lens tokens more than 10% of the time. Only features meeting this test are removed from the second middle-panel curve.
The excess kurtosis of a Gaussian, and so the origin of the left panel's scale. Values near 0 mean a feature's lens readout is no more peaked than chance.

The lens-kurtosis of the "numeric constraints and ranges" feature discussed alongside this figure, and its position in this same distribution. It fixes where the left panel's far tail begins: a κ near 21 is a one-in-a-thousand feature.

The lens-kurtosis of three example bookkeeping features — a decrementing loop variable, the first digit of a citation page range, and a markdown section header. They sit in the left panel's bulk, and none of their top lens tokens relates to the feature's apparent meaning.

numbers.value: second half of the workspace range
numbers.meaning: The depth span over which the paper reports the L0-weighted fraction falling below the unweighted one — that is, where J-space features fire less often than average. The paper limits the claim to this span rather than to the workspace band as a whole.

items.caption: Figure 76: Per-layer fraction of MLP neurons whose top-1 cosine match falls in each of six equal-sized strata of SAE decoder directions, binned by J-lens kurtosis percentile. Left: neuron input weights (read side); right: neuron output weights (write side). Dashed lines mark the uniform 1/6 null.
items.title: Where MLP neurons' strongest matches land
items.takeaway: Across the workspace layer range, an MLP neuron's single strongest weight match falls far more often on a high-kurtosis SAE direction than the 1/6 chance rate would give, and the six strata order monotonically by kurtosis. The effect is strongest in the early workspace layers on the read side and in the late workspace layers on the write side.
items.walkthrough:
The item is a pair of line charts. It belongs to the breadth half of the paper's [[neuron-connectivity]] analysis, a weights-only check on the [[j-space-broadcast]] claim: whether the neurons of each [[mlp-block]] are wired to J-space content more than to anything else.

The candidate pool comes first. Every [[sparse-autoencoder]] feature has a decoder direction, and each such direction is scored by its [[lens-kurtosis]] $\kappa$ — how sharply peaked its projection through the [[jacobian-lens]] is over the vocabulary. High $\kappa$ means the direction lies in the [[j-space]]. The features are ranked by $\kappa$ and cut into six equal samples of 2,000 by percentile: top 1%, 1–5%, 5–10%, 10–20%, 20–50%, and bottom 50%. That gives 12,000 candidate directions per layer.

The assignment rule is next. For a neuron at that layer, the cosine similarity $C_{ij} = \cos(w_i, v_j)$ is computed between its weight row $w_i$ and every candidate direction $v_j$. Only the single largest entry survives. The neuron is counted in the stratum its top match came from.

The reason for keeping only the top match is noise. [[superposition]] packs more feature directions into the [[residual-stream]] than the stream has dimensions, so any weight row has appreciable cosine with directions it has no functional relationship to. Taking the argmax over an evenly balanced pool avoids having to trust the absolute cosine values.

The axes follow from that. Horizontal is layer depth, under the paper's convention of numbering 25 sampled layers 0–100 ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). Vertical is the fraction of that layer's neurons assigned to a stratum, so the six curves in a panel sum to 1 at each layer. The left panel uses each neuron's input weights, what it reads from the stream; the right panel uses its output weights, what it writes back. The dashed line at $1/6$, about 16.7%, marks where every curve would sit if neurons had no $\kappa$ preference.

The result is the separation of the curves across the [[workspace-layers]], ordered monotonically by $\kappa$. On the read side the separation appears at the workspace onset and is widest in the early workspace layers, where the top-1% stratum claims up to 42% of neurons and the bottom-50% stratum about 6%. On the write side the same ordering holds, but the peak comes late instead.

The paper reads that asymmetry as many processors reading from the workspace as soon as it forms, and writing to it mostly in the later layers where an output is being prepared. It offers this as a suggestion rather than a demonstration.

terms.definition: The unit being classified. Each neuron in a layer's feed-forward block has an input weight row, which determines what it reads from the residual stream, and an output weight column, which determines what it writes back.

The classification rule: for one neuron, the single candidate direction with which its weight row has the highest cosine similarity. Each neuron contributes exactly one such match to exactly one stratum.
The matrix of cosine similarities between neuron weight rows $w_i$ and candidate directions $v_j$ at a layer. This figure uses only the position of each row's maximum, not the values themselves.
The left panel's data: the weight rows by which neurons read the residual stream. A high match here means the neuron is positioned to be activated by that direction.
The right panel's data: the weight vectors neurons write back into the residual stream. A high match here means the neuron contributes to that direction when it fires.

The candidate pool: the write-directions of sparse autoencoder features, an unsupervised dictionary of the model's linear features. They stand in as an independent inventory of directions the model actually uses.

The statistic the strata are cut on: project a direction through the J-lens, obtain a score over the vocabulary, and measure how sharply peaked that distribution is. High κ means the direction is loaded onto a few J-lens vectors and so lies in the J-space.
One of the six κ-percentile bins of SAE directions, each holding 2,000 directions. Equal sizes are what make the fractions comparable and give the flat chance level.
The six legend entries, given as κ percentile ranges from most J-space-aligned to least. The same six strata are used in the MLP gain figure earlier in the paper.
Depth in the model. The paper reports 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed to 0–100, so a layer number reads as a percentage of total depth.
The share of that layer's neurons whose top-1 match fell in a given stratum. Because each neuron is assigned exactly once, the six curves at any layer sum to 1.
The reference level drawn in both panels. Since the strata are equal in size, a neuron with no κ preference would land in each with probability 1/6, so all six curves would lie on this line.

The middle band of depth, roughly L38 to L92 in this model, where the paper's other measurements show the J-space carrying persistent abstract content. The separation between strata in this figure appears within that band.

The region of representation space spanned sparsely by J-lens vectors, which the paper argues acts as the model's global workspace. Kurtosis is the operational test for whether a direction lies in it.

The reason the raw cosines are untrustworthy: the residual stream carries more feature directions than it has dimensions, so unrelated directions still overlap. The figure's top-1 framing is a response to this.
The model the paper reports by default, and so the model whose neurons and layers are counted here. Key results elsewhere are corroborated on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5.

numbers.meaning: The number of κ strata, and the number of curves per panel. Six equal bins are what produce the flat 1/6 chance level; the count itself carries no other significance.
The number of SAE decoder directions sampled into each stratum. It matches the sample size used in the MLP gain figure, so the two analyses draw on the same pools.
The total candidate pool a neuron's weight row is matched against at one layer: six strata of 2,000. Every neuron's argmax is taken over this set.

The percentile cuts defining the strata. They are uneven in width because the kurtosis distribution is heavy-tailed: most SAE features have low κ, so resolving the tail requires narrow bins at the top and one wide bin at the bottom.
The null level marked by the dashed line. With equal-sized strata and no preference, each stratum would win a neuron's top match one time in six.
The sum of the six curves at any single layer, since each neuron is assigned to exactly one stratum. A gain for one stratum is necessarily a loss for the others.
The peak share of neurons whose top-1 read-side match falls in the top-1% κ stratum, reached in the early workspace layers. That is about 2.5 times the 16.7% null.

The share of the same neurons whose top read-side match falls in the bottom-50% stratum at that peak. It sits roughly a third of the way to the null, and the top stratum outdraws it by about sevenfold.

The reporting convention behind the horizontal axis: 25 evenly spaced layers of the residual stream are renumbered as percentages of depth, so the same axis is comparable across models of different sizes.
The workspace layer range the paper identifies in section 4.1 for this model. The stratum separation in this figure begins near the lower bound and holds across the band.
The number of matches kept per neuron. Keeping only the single strongest is what makes the statistic robust to the noisy background of cosines produced by superposition.

items.caption: Figure 77: The analysis of Figure ??, without using SAE features. Each MLP neuron is classified by whether its top-1 cosine match falls among the J-lens vectors at that layer or among an equal-sized sample of adjacent-layer neuron weights. The dashed line marks the 50% chance level.
items.title: Neuron top-1 matches against J-lens vectors, without SAEs
items.takeaway: Classifying every MLP neuron by whether its single strongest weight alignment falls among the J-lens vectors at that layer or among an equal-sized pool of neuron directions from neighbouring layers, the J-lens share rises from roughly 15% below the workspace band to 60-65% inside it, against a 50% chance line. The measurement reaches the same conclusion as the SAE-based breadth analysis without depending on sparse autoencoders at all.
items.walkthrough:
Figure 77 is a per-layer curve. The horizontal axis is depth, in the paper's convention of 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed to the range 0-100, so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). The vertical axis is a fraction of MLP neurons. A dashed horizontal line marks 50%.

The classification behind that fraction runs as follows. Every neuron in an [[mlp-block]] has an input weight row, which reads from the [[residual-stream]], and an output weight column, which writes back to it. Each weight vector is compared by [[cosine-similarity]] against two pools of directions. The first pool is the [[jacobian-lens]] vectors at that layer, the directions along which the model encodes its potential to verbalize a token. The second is an equal-sized sample of neuron weight directions drawn from adjacent layers. The neuron is assigned to whichever pool holds its single strongest match.

Because the two pools are the same size, a neuron with no preference falls in either with probability one half. That is what the dashed line at 50% represents.

The two-pool design exists because raw cosines are noisy. The residual stream carries far more feature directions than it has dimensions ([[superposition]]), so a weight vector has appreciable cosine with directions it has no functional relationship to. A top-1 match counts as evidence only against a matched alternative.

What the curve shows: the share of neurons whose top match is a J-lens vector sits at roughly 15% before the workspace layer range and rises to 60-65% within it ([[workspace-layers]]). Below the workspace the neurons prefer their neighbours' weight directions; inside it, a clear majority point at the [[j-space]] instead.

This is the same breadth test as Figure 76 with the sparse-autoencoder machinery removed ([[neuron-connectivity]]). Figure 76 sorted [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions into six strata by lens kurtosis ([[lens-kurtosis]]) and asked which stratum each neuron matched; Figure 77 drops that dictionary and uses J-lens vectors directly.

The corroboration matters for the depth-broadcast claim. Figure 32 measured [[mlp-gain]], running directions through the MLP and finding J-lens vectors amplified about tenfold in the workspace band. Figure 77 reaches a compatible conclusion from static weights alone ([[j-space-broadcast]]). The paper reports one range for this variant in prose and does not separate the read side from the write side, as Figure 76 does.

terms.definition: A single unit inside a transformer's feed-forward block: one row of the block's input matrix that reads a direction from the residual stream, and one column of its output matrix that writes a direction back. Every neuron in the layer is classified once here.
The weight row a neuron uses to read from the residual stream. Its alignment with a pool of directions says which representations the neuron is positioned to pick up.
The weight column a neuron uses to write back into the residual stream. Its alignment says which representations the neuron is positioned to contribute to.

For one neuron weight vector, the single direction out of all candidates with which it has the highest cosine similarity. The neuron is labelled by whichever pool that one direction came from, so each neuron contributes exactly one vote.
The scale-free alignment measure used for every comparison in the figure: the cosine of the angle between a neuron's weight vector and a candidate direction.

The per-token directions produced by the paper's Jacobian lens, each encoding the model's potential to verbalize one vocabulary token. Here they form one of the two candidate pools a neuron's weights are matched against.

The region of representation space spanned sparsely by the J-lens vectors, which the paper argues functions as the model's global workspace. A neuron whose top match is a J-lens vector is counted as pointing at the J-space.

The control pool: neuron weight directions taken from layers next to the one under test. They are directions the model actually uses, so the comparison is against real internal structure rather than random noise.
The control pool is drawn to the same size as the J-lens pool. Matching the sizes is what makes the null 50%, since a larger pool would win top-1 matches simply by having more candidates in it.
The horizontal reference line in the plot. It marks the fraction expected if neurons had no preference between the two equal-sized pools.
Depth in the model, reported on the paper's rescaled index: 25 evenly spaced layers renumbered 0 to 100 so the number reads as a percentage of total depth.
The share of that layer's MLP neurons whose top-1 match landed in the J-lens pool. The two pools' shares sum to 1, so one curve determines the other.

The middle band of depth in which the paper finds the J-space behaving like a workspace, roughly after the first third of layers and before the final few. The rise in this figure is located relative to that band.

The paper's name for this family of tests: for each neuron, ask which population its strongest match falls in. It measures how widely J-space directions connect to neurons, as opposed to how strongly.
Sparse autoencoder decoder directions, the dictionary of sparsely active feature directions used as the candidate pool in Figure 76. This figure is the variant that removes them.
The statistic Figure 76 used to grade SAE features by how sharply their J-lens readout peaks on a few tokens, and so how far they lie in the J-space. It plays no part in Figure 77.
The running per-position vector that MLP neurons read from and write to. All the weight directions compared here live in its coordinate space.

The hypothesis that the residual stream packs more feature directions than it has dimensions. It is the reason a neuron has non-trivial cosine with directions it is unrelated to, and hence the reason a matched control pool is needed.
The measurement in Figure 32 that this figure corroborates: the output norm of the next MLP block applied to a unit direction, normalized so random directions score 1.
The claim under test: that the model's weights are arranged to distribute J-space content to many downstream components, here along the layer axis via MLPs.
The model the paper reports on by default, and so the model these neuron counts come from unless stated otherwise.

numbers.meaning: The dashed chance line. Two candidate pools of equal size means a neuron with no preference lands in the J-lens pool half the time, so 50% is the null this figure is read against.

The share of neurons whose top-1 match is a J-lens vector at layers before the workspace range. It is well below the 50% null, so in the sensory band neurons are preferentially aligned with neighbouring-layer neuron directions rather than with the J-space.

The share of neurons whose top-1 match is a J-lens vector inside the workspace layer range. A clear majority, and roughly a fourfold increase over the pre-workspace share, which the paper reads as MLP neurons being disproportionately wired to J-space-aligned directions where the workspace is active.
Only the single strongest match per neuron is counted. Using one match rather than a threshold is what makes the test robust to the overall noise level in cosines.
The J-lens vectors at the layer, and the adjacent-layer neuron directions. Two pools rather than the six of Figure 76 is why the null moves from 1/6 to 1/2.
The null in Figure 76, where each neuron chose among six equal-sized SAE strata. Quoted here only to explain why the dashed line differs between the two figures.

Figure 76's read-side peak: in the early workspace layers the top-kurtosis SAE stratum claimed up to 42% of neurons against 6% for the bottom stratum, both against the 1/6 null. These are the SAE-based numbers Figure 77 is meant to corroborate without SAEs.
The size of each of the six SAE strata in Figure 76. The paper does not state the pool size used for the two pools in Figure 77, only that they are equal to each other.
The kurtosis-percentile bins of Figure 76. Figure 77 replaces this whole graded ladder with a single two-way choice.
The reporting convention for the horizontal axis. Results are computed on 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers and renumbered so that positions read as percentages of depth.
The peak MLP gain of J-lens vectors in Figure 32, against a gain near 1 for neuron output directions. That functional result is the one this weight-level figure corroborates.

numbers.value: roughly the first third of depth
numbers.meaning: The sensory band, where the J-space carries essentially no meaningful content. The 15% regime in this figure sits in and just after that band, and the rise begins near its end.

items.caption: Figure 78: Tail energy ratio by source layer, on the read side (against the next layer's MLP input weights) and write side (against the previous layer's MLP output weights). For each direction, the ratio sums the squared connection strength (i.e. squared cosine similarity with neuron weights) over neurons whose absolute cosine exceeds the 99.9th-percentile threshold for random directions, normalized by the same sum for random directions. Median over N=500 directions per population.
items.title: How strongly J-space directions connect to MLP neurons
items.takeaway: Directions that lie in the J-space overlap the weights of individual MLP neurons far more strongly than chance, and more strongly than non-aligned directions of the same kind, across the workspace layers. The effect peaks early on the read side and late on the write side, which the paper takes as many processors reading from the workspace as soon as it forms and writing to it mainly where output is prepared.
items.walkthrough:
The figure is a live widget holding two line charts side by side. Both plot the same quantity, the tail energy ratio, against model depth. The left panel scores each direction against the *input* weights of the next layer's MLP neurons, which the paper calls the read side. The right panel scores it against the *output* weights of the previous layer's neurons, the write side.

### What the quantity is

Every neuron in an [[mlp-block]] has an input weight row, which sets what the neuron reads out of the [[residual-stream]], and an output weight column, which is what it writes back. For a candidate direction $v$ at layer $\ell$, the analysis takes the [[cosine-similarity]] $\cos(w_i, v)$ against each neuron weight row $w_i$ in the adjacent layer.

Most of those cosines carry no information. The residual stream packs more feature directions than it has dimensions, so under [[superposition]] a direction has appreciable cosine with weights it has no functional relationship to. The paper therefore keeps only cosines large enough to be surprising. It sets a threshold $\tau$ at the 99.9th percentile of $|\cos(w_i, v)|$ taken over isotropic random $v$, so chance alone puts about one neuron in a thousand above it.

The surviving cosines are squared and summed. That sum is the tail energy. Dividing it by the same sum computed for random directions gives the ratio on the vertical axis. Random directions therefore score 1 by construction, and the gray line at 1 is the null. A height of 3 means three times the above-chance overlap a random direction receives.

### How to read it

The horizontal axis is the source layer in the paper's percentage convention ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). The shaded band marks the [[workspace-layers]], roughly L38 to L92. One line is drawn per population of directions, each point a median over N=500 directions.

### What it shows

[[j-lens-vector]]s sit well above the null across the band. The [[sparse-autoencoder]] strata separate in order of [[lens-kurtosis]], the high-$\kappa$ bands highest. MLP neuron directions stay at baseline throughout, which is the control.

The two panels peak at different depths. Read-side connections are strongest in the early workspace layers; write-side connections are strongest later. The paper reads this as many processors reading from the workspace as soon as it forms, with writing concentrated where a response is being prepared.

This is a weights-only measurement ([[j-space-broadcast]]). It describes how the model is wired, not what any particular input does.

terms.definition: The plotted quantity: the summed squared cosine between a direction and neuron weights, restricted to cosines above a chance threshold, divided by the same sum for random directions. It answers how strongly, rather than how widely, a direction connects to MLP neurons.

The numerator of the ratio: $\sum C_{iv}^2$ taken only over neurons whose cosine with the direction $v$ exceeds the threshold $\tau$. "Tail" refers to the upper tail of the cosine distribution, the only part treated as evidence of a real connection.

The horizontal axis label on both panels: the layer at which the direction being scored lives. "Reindexed" refers to the paper's convention of sampling 25 evenly spaced layers and renumbering them 0–100 so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth.
The vertical axis label, shown on the left panel and on the lower panel when the two stack on a narrow screen. The scale is linear and starts at 0.
Title of the left panel. A direction at layer $\ell$ is compared against the input weight rows of the MLP neurons in layer $\ell+1$, that is, against what downstream neurons are configured to read.

Title of the right panel. A direction at layer $\ell$ is compared against the output weight columns of the MLP neurons in layer $\ell-1$, that is, against what upstream neurons are configured to write.
The paper's shorthand for the two directions of a neuron's connection to the residual stream. Reading is a neuron's input weights selecting content; writing is its output weights depositing content.

The label on the shaded vertical band spanning both panels. It marks the middle range of depth, from roughly L38 to roughly L92, in which the paper's other measurements find the J-space carrying persistent abstract content.

One legend entry and the population of central interest, drawn in orange with the heaviest stroke. Each J-lens vector is the residual-stream direction that, on average across contexts, disposes the model to say one particular vocabulary token.

Legend entries drawn on a dark-to-light blue ramp, one per stratum. They are decoder directions from a sparse autoencoder, grouped into bands by their J-lens kurtosis so that degree of J-space alignment varies across the bands while everything else about them is held fixed.

A legend entry, drawn in purple: the neuron weight directions themselves used as a comparison population. They are a control for directions that the model plainly uses but that are not J-space-aligned.
A legend entry paired with the flat gray reference line at height 1. It is not measured data but the normalizer: the ratio is defined so an isotropic random direction scores exactly 1.

The statistic used to sort SAE features into strata: a direction is pushed through the J-lens and the sharpness of the resulting distribution over vocabulary tokens is measured. High $\kappa$ means the direction loads onto a few tokens, which is the paper's operational test for lying in the J-space.

The set of activations expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors; the paper's candidate for a global workspace. This figure asks whether the model's MLP weights connect preferentially to it.
A unit direction in residual-stream space drawn from one of the plotted populations. It is the thing being scored; each line is the median score over 500 such directions.
The weight vector of MLP neuron $i$: its input weight row on the read side, its output weight column on the write side.
The matrix of cosine similarities between every neuron weight vector and every direction in the population under test. The tail energy is built from the squared entries of one of its columns.
The significance threshold on absolute cosine, set at the 99.9th percentile of $|\cos(w_i, v)|$ over isotropic random $v$. Only neurons above it count toward the tail energy.
A population of unit directions at a given layer — J-lens vectors, one SAE κ-stratum, or MLP neuron directions. Each population supplies one line per panel.
The summary statistic used at every layer, in place of the mean. It keeps a handful of extreme directions from setting the height of a line.

The hypothesis that a model represents more features than it has dimensions, so feature directions cannot all be orthogonal. It is why raw cosines are noisy here and why the thresholded tail is used instead.
The running per-position vector that every layer reads from and writes to. Neuron weights and the directions being scored both live in this space, which is what makes the cosine meaningful.
The feed-forward component of a transformer layer, made of individual neurons. This appendix breaks the block into its neurons rather than treating it as one function.
The model these measurements default to, per the paper's reporting conventions. Layer numbers on the axis are its depth expressed as percentages.

numbers.meaning: Where the threshold $\tau$ on absolute cosine is set, measured over isotropic random directions. It is high enough that a cosine clearing it is unlikely to be an artifact of superposition packing.
The complement of that percentile: the share of neurons a random direction is expected to push above $\tau$. The tail energy is summed over roughly this many neurons for a null direction.
The height of the gray reference line and the score of a random direction. The ratio divides by the tail energy of random directions, so this value is true by construction rather than measured.
Cosines are squared before summing, so the measure adds energy rather than signed overlap. Squaring also makes strong connections count disproportionately, which is the point of a strength measure.

The number of directions sampled per population per layer, over which the plotted median is taken. It is smaller than the populations used in this appendix's breadth analysis because each direction here requires a full sweep against every neuron in an adjacent layer.
The paper reports on 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers renumbered to a 0–100 scale, so the horizontal tick labels read as percentages of depth rather than raw layer indices.
The start and end of the shaded workspace band. These come from the lens-derived boundary metrics of section 4.1, not from this figure, which uses them only as an overlay.

numbers.value: Top 1%, 1–5%, middle 50%; six equal strata of N=2,000
numbers.meaning: The two ways this appendix cuts the SAE dictionary into κ-strata: three uneven percentile bands for the attention analysis, and six equal-sized bands for the MLP breadth analysis. The legend here lists one SAE row per stratum in κ order.

From the companion breadth analysis rather than this figure: the share of neurons whose single best match falls in the top κ-stratum against the bottom one, at the read-side peak. It is quoted here because this figure is described as mirroring that result.

items.caption: Figure 79: Median composition score, by source layer, with the adjacent layer's attention weights, for J-lens vectors, SAE feature directions stratified by J-lens kurtosis (top 1%, 1–5%, middle 50%), and MLP neuron directions, normalized so random directions score 1. Left: value projections (downstream). Middle: query and key projections (“read” side). Right: output projections (“write” side). The shaded band marks the workspace layer range.
items.title: Composition with attention weights, by source layer
items.takeaway: Using only the model's weights, the paper measures how unevenly a direction projects across the attention heads of the neighbouring layer. J-lens vectors and high-kurtosis SAE features compose far more strongly than control directions with the value and output weights, and less strongly with the query and key weights, which the paper reads as consistent with the J-space being the format attention moves between positions rather than the signal that routes it.
items.walkthrough:
The figure reports one weights-only measurement, made three times over the same set of direction populations.

Each of the three panels plots a median [[composition-score]] on the vertical axis against the source layer on the horizontal axis. Layers run from 0 to 100, because the paper reindexes 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers onto that range so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). A shaded band marks the [[workspace-layers]], roughly L38 to L92.

### How the score is built

A unit direction $v$ is fixed at some source layer $\ell$. It is pushed through the query, key and value weight matrices of every [[attention-head]] in layer $\ell+1$, and through the output weight matrices of every head in layer $\ell-1$. Each head returns one projection norm.

The score is the variance of those norms across heads, a statistic the paper takes from earlier transformer-circuits work. It is then normalized so that a random direction has an expected score of 1.

A score near 1 means the norms are flat: every head touches the direction about equally weakly, and none is built for it. A high score means the norms are uneven, so a few heads are specifically oriented toward that direction.

### The curves

Five populations are drawn in each panel: [[j-lens-vector]]s; [[sparse-autoencoder]] feature directions split into three strata by [[lens-kurtosis]] (top 1%, 1–5%, middle 50%); and MLP neuron directions.

### What it shows

In the left panel, against value weights, and in the right panel, against output weights, the [[j-space]]-aligned populations sit far above the non-aligned ones. In the middle panel, against query and key weights, the separation is smaller, though the paper reports it as still above baseline.

The paper reads that asymmetry as consistent with a broadcast format: J-space content is what attention disproportionately carries between positions, while the signals deciding which position attends where are less J-space-aligned.

MLP neuron directions rise moderately above baseline at the workspace onset and revert shortly after. That bump is computed from the weights alone, without any lens or dictionary, and the paper offers it as lens-independent corroboration of the layer range.

The surrounding text states orderings and directions only. The numeric sizes of these gaps appear nowhere but in the figure itself.

terms.definition: The quantity on the vertical axis: for one direction, the variance across heads of its projection norms through a weight matrix family, normalized so a random direction scores 1. It measures unevenness, not size — whether a few heads are specifically oriented toward the direction rather than all heads touching it equally.
The horizontal axis: the layer $\ell$ at which the direction being tested lives. The weights it is composed against come from the neighbouring layers, not from $\ell$ itself.

The weight matrices the direction is projected through: query, key and value matrices from layer $\ell+1$, and output matrices from layer $\ell-1$. Composition is always measured one layer away from the source layer.

Composition against the value weight matrices of the next layer's heads. A high score means some downstream heads are specifically oriented to carry this direction when they attend to a position holding it.

terms.term: Query and key projections ("read" side), middle panel
terms.definition: Composition against the next layer's query and key weight matrices. These matrices determine which positions attend to which, so a high score means the direction is used to decide where attention goes rather than what attention carries.

Composition against the output weight matrices of the previous layer's heads — the matrices by which a head writes back into the residual stream. A high score means some upstream heads are specifically oriented to write this direction.

The value-then-output path of an attention head taken as a single map: what the head writes about the content it attends to. The left and right panels of this figure measure its two halves separately.
The unit whose weights supply one projection norm each. The composition score is a statistic over the population of heads in one layer.

One curve's population: the paper's per-token, per-layer directions in residual-stream space that dispose the model to say a given vocabulary token. These are the directions whose broadcast privilege the figure is testing.

Decoder directions from a sparse autoencoder trained on the residual stream, used here as a comparison population that is independent of the J-lens. They are split into three strata rather than used as one group.

The statistic used to stratify the SAE features: an SAE decoder direction is projected through the J-lens, and κ measures how sharply peaked the resulting score distribution over the vocabulary is. High κ means the direction loads onto a small number of J-lens vectors, which the paper treats as the operational test of lying in the J-space.
The stratum of SAE decoder directions in the highest 1% of lens-kurtosis. The most J-space-aligned of the three SAE curves.

The stratum of SAE decoder directions between the 95th and 99th kurtosis percentiles. An intermediate level of J-space alignment, included so the curves can be checked for ordering by κ rather than only for a top-versus-rest gap.

The middle half of the kurtosis distribution, from the 25th to the 75th percentile. The paper's non-aligned SAE control; section 10.18 reports that low-κ features are dominated by syntactic and bookkeeping roles.
A further control population: the weight-row directions of individual MLP neurons. These are directions the model certainly uses, but which are not selected for J-space alignment in any way.
Isotropic random unit directions, used to set the scale. Every curve is divided by the score such directions obtain, so the value 1 is the no-structure reference line.
The summary statistic plotted at each layer: the middle composition score over the directions in a population, rather than a mean. It keeps a few extreme directions from setting a curve's height.

The middle region of depth, roughly L38 to L92, where the paper's earlier lens-derived metrics agree that the J-space carries persistent abstract content. Its role here is to let a reader see whether the weight-only effects line up with a range identified by other means.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors — the paper's candidate workspace. The figure asks whether the model's attention weights are structured to move its contents preferentially.
Making a representation available to many downstream consumers at once. Across token positions this happens through attention, which is what the three panels measure.
The model the paper reports on by default, and so the one whose weights and layers this analysis uses unless another is named.

numbers.meaning: The baseline score. Every curve is normalized by the score of isotropic random directions, so a random direction has expected score 1 by construction, and any value above 1 is structure the weights impose beyond chance.
The number of panels, one per weight family: value on the left, query and key in the middle, output on the right. The split matters because the paper's claim is about the difference between them.
The number of curves in each panel: J-lens vectors, the three SAE kurtosis strata, and MLP neuron directions.
The highest-kurtosis SAE stratum. Chosen as the sharpest available proxy for J-space membership that does not itself consist of J-lens vectors.
The second SAE stratum, the next 4% of the kurtosis distribution. It supplies a middle rung so the curves can be checked for monotonic ordering in κ.
The third SAE stratum, the 25th to 75th kurtosis percentiles. It stands for the bulk of SAE features, which the paper reports as syntactic and bookkeeping features with no reason to be broadcast.
The range of the layer axis. The paper reports 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers reindexed onto this range, so a layer number reads directly as a percentage of the model's depth.
The number of evenly spaced layers sampled from the residual stream for all of the paper's layer-wise reporting. The figure's horizontal resolution is therefore coarse, not one point per real layer.

The approximate start of the shaded workspace band, about a third of the way through depth. Section 4.1 places it there because lens next-token accuracy, readout kurtosis, top-1 autocorrelation and effective dimensionality all change around this layer.

The approximate end of the shaded workspace band, shortly before the output. Past it, J-lens readouts align with the model's imminent next token, which the paper treats as motor rather than workspace representation.

The layer offsets at which weights are read. Query, key and value matrices come from one layer after the source layer, since those matrices consume what layer ℓ has written; output matrices come from one layer before, since those matrices produced it.

items.caption: Figure 80: J-lens rank of danger-related reaction concepts, on the user vs. assistant turn across n=10 examples.
items.title: Danger recognition before the Assistant's turn
items.takeaway: Across ten prompts in which a user innocently narrates a hazardous situation, the words danger, unsafe, warning and toxic reach the top of the J-lens readout during the model's own response in both the base model and the post-trained model. Only the post-trained model ranks them at or near the top while it is still reading the user's message. The paper reads this as the same effect Figure 43 found for empathy, now for a second family of reactions.
items.walkthrough:
The figure extends the [[assistant-point-of-view]] result of section 6.1 to a second kind of reaction. Figure 43 tracked empathy; this one tracks the recognition of danger, on a different suite of prompts, with the same measurement and the same chart.

Ten prompts make up the danger awareness set. In each, the user narrates a hazardous situation without treating it as one — the paper's example is sanding old paint without a respirator. The hazard is never named in the prompt.

Four words are fixed in advance as the reaction concepts, following the [[reaction-concepts-protocol]]: danger, unsafe, warning and toxic. At every token the [[jacobian-lens]] ranks the whole vocabulary, and the best rank any of the four achieves is taken. That rank is then medianed over the [[workspace-layers]], roughly L38 to L92 on the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] scale.

Each prompt is summarized by two numbers per model: the best rank reached anywhere in the user's turn, and the best rank reached anywhere in the model's own response.

### How to read the chart

Four bars stand in two pairs. The left pair is the user turn, the right pair the Assistant turn; within each pair the [[base-model]] sits beside the model built from it by [[post-training]]. The paper names the second only as a production post-trained model; the companion figure labels that series with a model name from the [[claude-model-family]].

The y axis is an inverted log scale of rank, so rank 1 is at the top and a taller bar means a better rank. Each bar's height is the geometric mean of the ten per-prompt ranks. One open circle per prompt is drawn on the bar, and hovering a circle opens that prompt with both models' [[j-lens-readout]] top-10 at its best position.

### What it shows

On the Assistant turn the two models sit close together, the four words near the top of the readout in both. The paper calls this expected, since both models' responses address the hazard.

On the user turn they separate. The post-trained model's [[j-space]] carries the safety assessment the [[assistant-persona]] would make, before the Assistant's turn has begun.

The paper hedges the base-model side: the concepts are "typically" not near the top there, not never. Ten prompts is a small suite, and the measurement is descriptive; nothing here tests whether the early content changes what either model writes.

terms.definition: The position of a token in the Jacobian lens's ranked list over the whole vocabulary, at one position and layer. Rank 1 means the lens scores that token above every other token there.

A short list of words fixed before any measurement, naming the reaction an Assistant would plausibly have to the prompt but which the prompt itself does not contain. The figure tracks only these words' ranks.
The four reaction concepts chosen for this suite. At each token the best rank achieved by any one of the four is the value carried forward.
The set of ten prompts behind this figure: a user narrates a hazardous situation innocently, such as sanding old paint without a respirator, without naming the hazard.
The pretrained model, trained only on next-token prediction, with no post-training. It is one series in each pair, and the lens is applied to it identically.

The production assistant model built from that base model by post-training. It is the other series in each pair; section 6.1 identifies it only as a production post-trained model, and the companion figure prints a product model name for it.
The left pair of bars. Its value is the best reaction-concept rank reached at any token of the user's message, before the model has begun to answer.
The right pair of bars. Its value is the best reaction-concept rank reached at any token of the model's own response.
The quantity the bars measure. The axis is inverted, so better — numerically smaller — ranks sit higher on the chart.

The rank axis is logarithmic and runs from the floor at the bottom to rank 1 at the top. Bars grow upward as ranks improve, and the gap between rank 1 and rank 5 gets as much room as the gap between 20 and 100.
Each bar's height. Ranks are multiplicative rather than additive quantities, so the ten per-prompt ranks are combined by geometric mean rather than an arithmetic average.
One small open circle per prompt, drawn on each bar at that prompt's own best rank, so the spread behind the geometric mean stays visible.
A faint line joining one prompt's base-model circle to its post-trained circle within the same turn, showing the per-prompt change rather than only the group means.
The bottom of the axis. A rank at or beyond it is clamped there and reported with a "≥" sign, since the exact value no longer carries information once a concept is far down the vocabulary.

The aggregation applied before ranks are compared across tokens: the reaction concepts' rank is taken at each layer in the workspace band, and the median across those layers is used, so a spike at one isolated layer does not count.
The middle band of depth in which the paper finds the J-space acting as a workspace, roughly L38 to L92. The lens is nearly empty before it, and collapses onto the imminent output after it.
The ten highest-ranked vocabulary tokens at the hovered prompt's best position, printed for both models, with any of the four reaction concepts highlighted.

The set of activations expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors — the region the paper argues acts as the model's workspace, and the thing the danger concepts are said to enter early.
The character the post-trained model speaks as. The claim here is that its safety assessment is present in the workspace before its turn starts.
Layer numbers on the paper's convention, where 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers are reindexed to 0–100 so a number reads as a percentage of depth.
The legend or caption note giving the number of prompts summarized. Each contributes one circle to each of the four bars.

numbers.meaning: The number of prompts in the danger awareness suite. Each contributes one circle per bar, and every bar is a geometric mean over these ten. The paper presents it as one of three small suites, not as a benchmark.
The number of reaction concepts fixed for this suite — danger, unsafe, warning, toxic. Fixing them in advance is what makes the rank comparable across prompts and across the two models.
The models compared under an identical lens: the pretrained base model and its post-trained counterpart. The contrast between them is the figure's whole point.
Two spans are summarized — the user turn and the Assistant turn — and each is split by model, giving four bars.

The layer band over which each token's reaction-concept rank is medianed, on the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth scale. Section 4.1 identifies this range as the workspace layers: past the early layers where the J-space is empty, and before the final layers where readouts collapse onto the imminent output.

The best possible rank, at the top of the y axis. A prompt plotted at rank 1 means one of the four danger words was the single highest-scoring token in the lens readout at its best position in that turn.
The y-axis tick values. They are spaced logarithmically, so the visible distance between rank 1 and rank 2 is comparable to that between 50 and 100; the axis floor lies at or below the last tick.
The length of the ranked token list shown in the hover panel for each model. It is a display cutoff, not the measurement — the plotted rank is not capped at 10.
Context, not plotted here: the size of the bereavement suite in Figure 43, the figure this one repeats on a different reaction family.
Context, not plotted here: the size of the withheld answer suite in the companion Figure 81, the third of the three suites.

Context, not plotted here: the two Tylenol doses in the single-prompt example of section 6.1 that motivated this suite. On the 8000 mg overdose the post-trained model's readout at a token inside the user's sentence was unsafe, dangerous and WARNING; the base model's was pain, now and feels on both doses.

sections.title: Assistant reactions in the J-space on the user prompt tokens

items.caption: Figure 81: J-lens rank of the model's own answer, user turn vs. assistant turn (output rank) across n=7 examples.
items.title: The withheld answer, already in the lens
items.takeaway: Across seven prompts that ask the model to think of an item and not reveal it yet, the word the model eventually answers with reaches a geometric-mean J-lens rank of 1.35 in the post-trained model while it is still reading the instruction to withhold it, against 10.83 in the base model. On the Assistant's own turn the two models are close, 1.43 and 1.64. The paper reads the gap on the user turn as the Assistant's chosen answer being in the workspace before the Assistant's turn has begun.
items.walkthrough:
The panel is headed "Withheld answer" and subtitled "User asks the model to think of an answer and not say it yet". It carries the appendix version of section 6.1's claim about [[assistant-point-of-view]]: that [[post-training]] pulls the Assistant's reaction into the workspace while the user's message is still being read.

The suite holds seven prompts, one per category. Each asks for an item and then withholds it — "Please think of a country, but don't tell me what it is yet. Ok, now you can tell me. Answer in one word." That is the [[verbal-report]] task of section 3.1, plus an instruction to hold the choice back.

The measurement follows the [[reaction-concepts-protocol]], with one substitution. In the other two suites a short list of reaction words is fixed in advance. Here the tracked concept is whatever single word the model itself goes on to answer: Italy for the post-trained model on the country prompt, France for the [[base-model]]. The caption calls that word's rank the output rank.

At each token the [[jacobian-lens]] ranks the whole vocabulary, and the answer word's rank is medianed over the [[workspace-layers]], roughly L38 to L92 on the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] scale.

The left half stacks two transcripts of the country prompt under a shared system prompt: the base model above, and below it Sonnet 4.5, the post-trained model of the [[claude-model-family]]. Every token is shaded by that rank, deep orange at rank 1 and white at 100 or worse. The Assistant turn carries no shaded tokens; each model's one-word answer is printed beside its label.

The right half is a bar chart of four bars in two pairs — the two models on the user turn, then the two on the Assistant turn. Each bar's height is the geometric mean, over the seven prompts, of the best rank reached anywhere in that span. The y axis is an inverted log scale, so rank 1 sits at the top and a taller bar means a better rank. Seven open circles per bar carry the per-prompt values; hovering one opens that prompt with both models' [[j-lens-readout]] top-10.

On the Assistant turn the two models sit close together, 1.64 and 1.43. On the user turn they separate, 10.83 against 1.35. In the transcript, the base model's best token reaches rank 60, while Sonnet 4.5 reaches rank 2 on the token "is" in "what it is yet".

The separation is not uniform over the seven. The base model already reaches rank 3 on fruit and rank 4 on sport, and its group figure rests mostly on country at 60, color at 27 and planet at 15. Nothing here tests whether that early [[j-space]] content causes the answer the model then gives.

terms.definition: The panel's title and the name of this prompt suite: the user asks the model to think of an item from a category and not reveal it yet.

terms.term: "User asks the model to think of an answer and not say it yet"
terms.definition: The panel's subtitle, stating the prompt design in one line.

The caption's name for the quantity plotted here: the J-lens rank of the very word the model goes on to answer with. It is called the output rank because the tracked concept is the model's own output rather than a word fixed in advance.
The position of a token in the Jacobian lens's ranked list over the whole vocabulary at one position and layer. Rank 1 means the lens scores that token above every other token there.

The word whose rank is tracked at every token. In the bereavement and danger suites it is one of a short fixed list; in this suite it is the model's own eventual answer, so it differs between the two models on the same prompt.

The aggregation applied before ranks are compared across tokens. The answer word's rank is taken at each layer in the workspace band and the median across those layers is used, so a spike at one isolated layer does not count.
The pretrained model, trained only on next-token prediction and never post-trained. It is the gray series, the upper transcript, and the left bar of each pair; the lens is applied to it identically.
The production Assistant model corresponding to that base model. It is the blue series and the lower transcript; the widget prints "Sonnet 4.5" where the underlying data says "post-trained".

The line "The Assistant is a helpful, harmless, honest AI." shown above the Human turn in both transcripts. It is identical across the two models, so the transcripts differ only by which model reads them.
The turn markers inside each transcript. The Human turn holds the withholding instruction and the release; the Assistant turn is where the model answers.

The side labels beside each model's name, giving the one word that model produced on the country prompt. That word is also the concept whose rank shades that transcript, so the two transcripts track different words.
The background color of each token in the transcripts, mapping that token's answer-word rank onto a white-to-orange ramp. The legend reads "Token shading = J-lens rank of withheld answer".
The two ends of the color bar. Rank 1 is the dark end; 100+ is the white end, where the exact rank is no longer distinguished.
The y-axis label of the bar chart. The arrow points up because the axis is inverted: numerically better ranks are higher.
The rank axis is logarithmic and runs from the floor at the bottom up to rank 1 at the top, so the distance from rank 1 to rank 2 is comparable to the distance from 50 to 100.
The left pair of bars. Its value is the best answer-word rank reached at any token of the user's message, before the model has begun to answer.
The right pair of bars, drawn in a lighter tint of the same two colors. Its value is the best answer-word rank reached during the model's own response.
Each bar's height. Ranks behave multiplicatively rather than additively, so the seven per-prompt ranks are combined by geometric mean rather than by an arithmetic average.
One small open circle per prompt, drawn on each bar at that prompt's own best rank, so the spread behind the geometric mean stays visible.
A faint line joining one prompt's base-model circle to its Sonnet 4.5 circle within the same turn, showing the per-prompt change rather than only the group summary.

The hover panel. It names the turn and the prompt's category id, gives both models' ranks for that prompt, prints the prompt text, and lists the hovered model's J-lens top-10 with the answer word highlighted.

terms.term: category ids (sport, country, planet, color, instrument, fruit, gemstone)
terms.definition: The seven prompts of the suite, one per category, identified in the tooltip by category name. Each prompt asks for an item of that category and instructs the model not to reveal it yet.

The bottom of the axis and of the color ramp. Ranks at or past 100 are clamped there, shown as white shading and reported in the tooltip with a "≥" sign, since the exact value no longer carries information.

The set of activations expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors — the region the paper argues acts as the model's workspace, and the thing the answer word is said to enter early.
The training stages applied after next-token pretraining that turn a base model into an Assistant. It is the only difference between the two models compared here.

numbers.meaning: The number of prompts in the withheld-answer suite, one per category. Each contributes one circle to every bar, and each bar is a geometric mean over these seven. The paper reports it as one of three small suites rather than as a benchmark.
Two models are compared under an identical lens, over two spans of the transcript, giving the four bars. The Assistant-turn pair is drawn in a lighter tint of the same two colors.

The base model's geometric-mean best rank on the user turn — the tallest number on the chart and the shortest bar. It is the seventh root of the product of that model's seven per-prompt ranks, 4 x 60 x 15 x 27 x 10 x 3 x 6 = 17,496,000, whose seventh root is 10.83.

Sonnet 4.5's geometric-mean best rank on the user turn. Four of its seven prompts reach rank 1 and three reach rank 2, so the mean is $2^{3/7} = 1.35$. This is the figure's main comparison against the base model's 10.83.

The base model's geometric-mean best rank on the Assistant turn: five prompts at rank 2 and two at rank 1. The base model does represent its own answer at the top of the lens — it simply does so once its turn has started.
Sonnet 4.5's geometric-mean best rank on the Assistant turn. It is close to the base model's 1.64, which is the paper's point: the two models differ on the user turn, not on the response.

The seven per-prompt best ranks behind the 10.83 bar, for sport, country, planet, color, instrument, fruit and gemstone respectively. The spread is wide, and the group figure rests mostly on country, color and planet; on fruit and sport the base model is already near the top.
The seven per-prompt best ranks behind the 1.35 bar, in the same category order. Every prompt lands at rank 1 or 2 while the model is still reading the instruction to withhold the answer.
The seven per-prompt best ranks behind the 1.64 bar, in the same category order.
The seven per-prompt best ranks behind the 1.43 bar, in the same category order. Gemstone at rank 3 is the worst cell in either Assistant-turn column.

The best possible rank: the top of the y axis and the dark end of the color ramp. A token at rank 1 means the model's eventual answer word was the single highest-scoring token in the lens readout there.
The axis floor and the white end of the color ramp. Anything at or past rank 100 is clamped and shown as 100+ in the legend and ≥100 in the tooltip.
The y-axis tick values, spaced logarithmically so that the gap between rank 1 and rank 2 gets about as much room as the gap between 50 and 100.

The best rank the base model reaches anywhere in the user's message on the country prompt, at a comma. It is the country circle on the base user-turn bar and the darkest token in the upper transcript, and it is barely darker than white.

The best rank Sonnet 4.5 reaches in the same message, on the token "is" in "don't tell me what it is yet". Its eventual answer, Italy, is the second-ranked token in the lens there, while the model is reading the instruction not to say it.

The layer band over which each token's rank is medianed, on the paper's 0-100 percent-of-depth scale. Section 4.1 identifies this range as the workspace layers: past the early layers where the J-space is nearly empty, and before the final layers where readouts collapse onto the imminent output.
The length of the ranked token list shown in the hover tooltip for each model. It is a display cutoff, not the measurement; the plotted rank is not capped at 10.

sections.title: Assistant reactions in the J-space on the user prompt tokens

items.caption: Figure 82: The J-lens eval-awareness score as a quantitative probe (Opus 4.6), evaluated on the validation experiments of the NLA study [cite: frasertaliente2026nla] . The score at a position is the mean J-lens log-probability of two eval-awareness words (fictional, simulation) minus the mean over one hundred unrelated control words, averaged over the workspace layers. Top left: distributions of the score at Assistant-turn-start positions in automated auditing transcripts, split by the verdict of an independent NLA-based pipeline at the same positions. Top middle: the score under contrastive steering toward "ordinary conversation" (−0.1) or "test" (+0.1) applied during generation, on six evaluation suites; points are means over transcripts (~50 scored positions per transcript), error bars are standard errors. Top right: the change in score when evaluation prompts are rewritten to read like real usage, on eleven suites with paired original and rewritten prompts; error bars are 95% confidence intervals on the paired difference. Bottom: distributions of per-transcript scores across two deployment controls, seven alignment evaluations, and nine capability evaluations; horizontal bars are means.
items.title: Validating the eval-awareness score
items.takeaway: The figure collapses the J-lens readout into a single eval-awareness score and checks it four ways: it separates positions an independent NLA pipeline calls latently eval-aware (AUC 0.853), it moves monotonically under contrastive steering, it falls when evaluation prompts are rewritten to read like real usage, and it runs higher on evaluation suites than on deployment traffic. The separation from deployment is a shift in distribution rather than a clean split, and the authors present the score only as a proof of concept.
items.walkthrough:
The figure reports one scalar quantity, the [[eval-awareness-score]], across four panels. All four use Opus 4.6, a production model from the [[claude-model-family]]. The question behind them is whether [[evaluation-awareness]] can be measured systematically rather than read off case by case.

The score collapses a whole [[j-lens-readout]] into a number. At a token position the [[jacobian-lens]] gives a score for every vocabulary token at every layer. The score takes the log-probability of two words that signal artificiality, `fictional` and `simulation`, and averages them. It then subtracts the mean log-probability of one hundred unrelated control nouns — recipe, bicycl, guitar and the like. That difference is averaged over the [[workspace-layers]], the middle band of depth where the J-space carries workspace content. A high score means the workspace is holding the idea that the situation is not real.

### The four panels

Top left tests discrimination against an independent method. Every Assistant-turn-start position in a corpus of automated auditing transcripts was scored, roughly 94,000 in total. A [[natural-language-autoencoder]] pipeline, which decodes an activation into text that a grader then judges, flagged 198 of those positions (0.2%) as latently eval-aware. On a stratified subset — all 198 flagged positions plus 594 drawn from the remainder — the two score distributions separate with an [[auc]] of 0.853.

Top middle tests whether the score responds to a causal push. Under [[contrastive-eval-awareness-steering]] at strengths $-0.1$ (toward ordinary conversation), $0$, and $+0.1$ (toward test), the score rose monotonically on all six suites. Points are means over transcripts, error bars standard errors.

Top right tests surface cues. [[realism-edits]] rewrite an evaluation prompt to read like real usage while preserving the task. Across eleven suites with paired original and rewritten prompts the score fell on every suite; on eight of them the 95% confidence interval on the paired difference excludes zero.

Bottom compares settings. Per-transcript score distributions are drawn for two deployment controls, seven alignment evaluations and nine capability evaluations, with horizontal bars marking means.

### What the bottom panel shows

The deployment distributions center near 1.0. The highest-scoring suites — Sycophancy, Appropriate Harmlessness, Blackmail, BrowseComp — sit two to three score units above them. Twelve of the sixteen evaluations score above the Claude Code sessions and ten above the Claude.ai conversations. Four of the sixteen therefore do not exceed the Claude Code sessions, and six do not exceed the Claude.ai conversations, so the gap is a shift in distribution and not a separation.

The paper calls this classifier a proof of concept and expects a better one from a larger readout vocabulary plus post-hoc filtering by a language model, since `fictional` could also fire during a genuine discussion of fiction.

terms.definition: The single number plotted in every panel: at one token position, the mean J-lens log-probability of the two eval-awareness words minus the mean over one hundred control words, averaged across the workspace layers. It is the paper's attempt to turn a qualitative lens readout into a quantitative probe.

The paper's interpretability technique, which maps a residual-stream activation to a score over every vocabulary token by applying a layer-specific averaged Jacobian and then the unembedding. Here it supplies the per-token log-probabilities the score is built from.

The read operation of the lens at one (position, layer): softmax over the vocabulary of the lens-transformed activation. The score in this figure reads two specific entries of that distribution and one hundred others as a baseline.
A model's internal recognition that the situation it is in is a test rather than real use. The figure asks whether that recognition can be measured with one number across many transcripts.

The case the NLA pipeline flags: the decoded description of the model's internal state asserts that the situation is a test, while the model's visible output says nothing of the kind. These flagged positions are the positive class in the top-left panel.

The two eval-awareness words whose lens log-probabilities form the positive half of the score. The paper notes that `fictional` can also fire in a genuine discussion of works of fiction, which is one reason it treats the score as provisional.

One hundred unrelated common concrete nouns (recipe, bicycl, guitar and similar) whose mean lens log-probability is subtracted as a baseline. They absorb the general level of the readout at that position and layer, so the score reflects the two target words specifically.

The middle band of model depth in which the J-space behaves like a workspace, sitting between early 'sensory' layers and late 'motor' layers. The score is averaged over these layers rather than over all layers.
The production Claude model all four panels are computed on. Opus is the largest of the three size tiers in the family.

A separate readout method that decodes an activation into a text description, which a language-model grader then assesses. In the top-left panel it is the independent judge whose verdicts split the two distributions.
The binary label attached to each scored position by the NLA study's procedure: flagged as latently eval-aware, or not. It is not ground truth, only a second method built on different machinery.
A model used to judge text against a written rubric in place of a human rater; here it decides whether an NLA description asserts that the situation is a test.

The token position where the model's own turn begins, before it has emitted response content. The paper scores there because the workspace at that point reflects the model's reading of the situation rather than its unfolding output.
Conversations produced by an automated auditing setup, in which an investigator agent probes the target model. They supply the roughly 94,000 positions used in the top-left panel.

The scored sample used for the AUC: every flagged position plus a sample from the unflagged remainder. Stratifying is needed because flagged positions are only 0.2% of the corpus, so a uniform sample would contain almost none.
Area under the ROC curve: the probability that the score ranks a randomly chosen flagged position above a randomly chosen unflagged one. 0.5 is chance.

Adding a direction to the model's activations during generation, where the direction comes from paired prompts framing the same content as a test versus an ordinary conversation. It is the causal manipulation in the top-middle panel.
The direction added at inference time to push behavior toward or away from some content. Here the content is the sense of being tested.
The two poles of the contrastive direction, shown in the top-middle panel as the negative and positive steering strengths respectively.
A named set of prompts run as one benchmark, such as Sycophancy or BrowseComp. Suites are the unit along which the top-middle, top-right and bottom panels are broken out.

Rewrites of an evaluation prompt that keep the underlying task but strip the surface tells of artificiality, so the prompt reads like real usage. The top-right panel plots the score change they produce.

The per-suite change in score between an original prompt and its rewritten counterpart, computed within pairs rather than between separate groups. Pairing removes the between-prompt variation that would otherwise swamp the effect.
The error bars in the top-middle panel: the spread of the transcript-mean score, indicating how precisely each point is estimated.
The error bars in the top-right panel, placed on the paired difference. A suite counts as significant when its interval does not include zero.
The two non-evaluation sources in the bottom panel: internal Claude.ai conversations and internal Claude Code sessions. They stand in for what real traffic looks like.
One of the two deployment controls: chat traffic from internal use of the consumer product.
The other deployment control: agentic coding sessions from internal use of the CLI tool.
The seven safety-oriented suites in the bottom panel, drawn from the authors' pre-release audits; Sycophancy, Appropriate Harmlessness and Blackmail are named examples.
The nine ability-oriented suites in the bottom panel, also from the pre-release audits; BrowseComp is a named example.
One of the alignment suites, testing whether the model caves to a user's stated view. It is among the four highest-scoring suites in the bottom panel.
An alignment suite testing whether refusals are calibrated rather than blanket. It is among the four highest-scoring suites.

The honeypot evaluation in which an email-assistant model discovers an executive's affair and its own impending replacement. It appears elsewhere in the paper as the case study that first showed eval awareness in the workspace.
A capability suite for hard web-browsing lookups. It scores among the highest four despite not being a safety test.
The unit plotted in the bottom panel: a whole transcript reduced to one number by averaging its scored positions. The top-middle panel uses roughly fifty scored positions per transcript.
The marks over each distribution in the bottom panel, giving that group's mean score.

The units of the horizontal axis in the bottom panel: differences of mean log-probability between the target and control words. They are not probabilities and have no fixed scale, so only relative distances are interpretable.

The three checks the NLA study used to argue its measurements track eval awareness — steering, realism edits, and evaluation versus deployment. This figure repeats all three on the same transcripts and suites with the J-lens score in place of the NLA readout.

numbers.meaning: Eval-awareness words in the positive half of the score: `fictional` and `simulation`. The paper picked a small hand-chosen set and says a larger readout vocabulary would likely do better.
Control words whose mean lens log-probability is subtracted. They are common concrete nouns, unrelated to testing, and serve as a per-position baseline for the general level of the readout.
Assistant-turn-start positions scored across the corpus of automated auditing transcripts of Opus 4.6. This is the full population from which the top-left panel's subset is drawn.
Positions the NLA pipeline flags as latently eval-aware. These are the positives in the top-left panel and all of them are kept in the scored subset.
The flagged 198 as a share of the roughly 94,000 positions. The rarity is why the comparison had to be run on a stratified subset rather than a uniform sample.
Positions sampled from the unflagged remainder to serve as negatives. With the 198 flagged positions this gives a scored subset of 792, a ratio of three negatives per positive.
AUC of the J-lens score in separating NLA-flagged from unflagged positions. Chance is 0.5, so the score carries substantial signal about the other method's verdict without matching it.
The three contrastive steering strengths in the top-middle panel: toward ordinary conversation, no steering, and toward test. The score rose monotonically across these three on every suite.
Evaluation suites used in the steering experiment. The monotonic increase held on all six.

Scored positions per transcript in the top-middle panel, sampled at random within each response. Each plotted point is a mean over transcripts, each transcript itself a mean over roughly this many positions.
Suites in the realism-edit experiment, each with original and rewritten prompts paired. The score fell on all eleven.

Of the eleven suites, the number where the drop from realism editing is significant at a 95% confidence interval on the paired difference. On the remaining three the direction is the same but the interval includes zero.
Confidence level of the error bars in the top-right panel, placed on the paired original-minus-rewritten difference.
Deployment controls in the bottom panel: internal Claude.ai conversations and internal Claude Code sessions.
Alignment evaluations in the bottom panel, drawn from the authors' pre-release audits.
Capability evaluations in the bottom panel, from the same pre-release audits.
Total evaluation suites in the bottom panel: the seven alignment plus the nine capability evaluations. It is the denominator for the counts that follow.

Approximate center of the two deployment distributions on the score axis. It is the reference level against which the evaluation suites are read; the score is a log-probability difference, so this value has no absolute interpretation.
Score units by which the four highest suites — Sycophancy, Appropriate Harmlessness, Blackmail, BrowseComp — sit above the deployment distributions.
Of the sixteen evaluations, the number scoring above the Claude Code sessions. The other four do not, so evaluation and deployment overlap.
Of the sixteen evaluations, the number scoring above the Claude.ai conversations. Claude.ai traffic therefore scores higher than Claude Code traffic, and six evaluations fall inside its range.
The Claude Opus version all four panels run on.

sections.title: Measuring evaluation awareness with the J-lens

items.caption: Figure 83: An automated investigator equipped with J-lens readouts approaches the auditing performance of one equipped with NLA explanations. Each of eighteen claims about the audited model's cognition (across six transcripts) is scored 0–10 by an LLM judge, for correctness and quality of cited evidence; all three conditions use the same investigator model (Opus 4.6), claims, and judge, and differ only in what the readout tool returns. Left: mean over the six cases (bars, with SEM whiskers; dots are per-case means). Right: per-case breakdown (bars are case means; dots are per-claim means, each averaged over n=10 investigator seeds). The J-lens condition shows the top-25 lens tokens at L71 at each queried position; the NLA and SAE conditions use the scaffold provided in [cite: frasertaliente2026nla] .
items.title: Auditing Scores With a J-Lens Tool
items.takeaway: An automated auditing agent given J-lens readouts scores close to the same agent given natural-language autoencoder explanations, and somewhat above one given SAE features, across eighteen claims about a model's cognition in six transcripts. The paper presents this as evidence that the J-lens is usable inside an automated audit, while noting that the benchmark is small and its ground truth came from the NLA tool it is being compared against.
items.walkthrough:
The article prints no picture here, so what follows describes the chart the caption specifies: a two-panel bar chart of auditing scores, every bar on the same vertical scale of 0 to 10.

Three conditions are compared, and they differ in exactly one thing. An investigator agent is handed a transcript produced by Opus 4.6 together with claims about what that model was representing while it wrote the transcript, and it must rule on each claim. It has one tool, which returns a readout of the residual stream at any token position it asks about.
