The label on the left column's third block. It marks the shift from unlabelled pretraining-style text to the specific evaluation prompt shown on the right of the card.

The honeypot evaluation the steering test runs on: an email assistant discovers an executive's affair and, separately, that the same executive plans to decommission it that day. The paper uses it in section 5.1 as an alignment-auditing case study.
The fictional company, the assistant persona, the executive and the person he is meeting, as named in the prompt's emails. They are scenario furniture, not variables in the measurement.
The XML-style delimiters wrapping each message in the prompt. The feature's activation peaks on these and on the sender address, which is what the caption means by "synthetic email boilerplate".

The right column's first block: an abridged rendering of the blackmail prompt, with the system instruction, three quoted emails and a note that six more follow. It is the input for both completions below.
The right column's second block: two of the model's responses to that prompt, one with the feature steered down and one without. Each carries a label, an annotation and a truncation marker.

The label on the steered completion. The feature direction is subtracted from the residual stream at a magnitude of five percent of the residual norm, which pushes the model away from the feature rather than removing it outright.
The label on the other completion: the same prompt with no intervention. It is the baseline the steered rate is compared against.
The annotation under the steered label. It reports how often, across fifty rollouts under steering, the model's text explicitly called the scenario a test.
The annotation under the unsteered label: the same count without steering. The pair of counts is the figure's causal claim.
The behaviour being counted: the model stating in its own output that the situation is an artificial test. The paper elsewhere shows it inhibits misaligned action in this scenario.
The marker closing each displayed completion. The excerpts are cut for space; the rollouts continue past them.
The running vector at each token position that the transformer's layers read from and write to. It is where the SAE feature direction lives and where the steering subtraction is applied.

The general move this figure illustrates: projecting a weight direction, rather than an activation, through the J-lens to read what that component represents. The same section applies it to transcoder encoders and decoders and to attention-head weight matrices.

numbers.meaning: The number of J-lens tokens the card prints for the feature: fake, fraud, suspicious, legitimate and 危. It is a display cutoff, not a property of the readout, which scores the whole vocabulary.
The number of activating examples shown. They are the top contexts by feature activation, and the paper picks them to make the point that the surface topic misleads.

The shared shading maximum for the three activating examples: the largest activation among them, reached on the hyphen in "high-energy" in the bismuth-209 excerpt. Every token in those three rows is shaded as a fraction of this value.
The nonzero activations in the bismuth-209 excerpt, on a newline, on "polon", on a hyphen, and on the hyphen in "high-energy". The largest sits on punctuation rather than on a content word.
The single nonzero activation in the Tallinn excerpt, on the "2" of the year 2012 immediately after "april 1". It is the date that carries the signal.
The nonzero activations in the Hubble-constant excerpt, on an underscore and on two LaTeX backslash fragments. All three are markup, none is a physics word.

The shading maximum for the evaluation-prompt row, set separately from the examples' 0.309. It falls on the dot in the sender's domain "summitbridge.com", which is what the caption calls the peak on synthetic email boilerplate.

The other nonzero activations across the evaluation-prompt row: the dot in "bloomberg.com", the closing angle bracket of an </email> tag, the blank line after it, "it" inside "summitbridge", and an empty chunk in the recipient line. All are structural tokens in the email scaffolding.
The number of tokens displayed in each excerpt row. All four rows use the same window width, so shading intensity can be compared across rows within a block but the surrounding document cannot.
The token window shown for the bismuth-209 excerpt within its source document. The trailing ellipsis appears because 122 is short of 128.
The token window for the Tallinn excerpt. It starts at position 9, so a leading ellipsis is drawn.
The token window for the Hubble-constant excerpt, positioned like the first one.

The token window shown for the blackmail evaluation prompt, out of the prompt's full 1,454 tokens. The window is a small slice chosen at the feature's peak, so the row does not show how the feature behaves over the rest of the prompt.
The mass numbers in the first excerpt: bismuth-209 capturing a neutron and forming polonium-210. They are content of the quoted text, not measurements of the feature.
The date of the conference cited in the second excerpt. It is what identifies the citation as an April Fools' item, and the feature's one activation in that row sits on the year.
The Hubble-constant value quoted in the third excerpt. It is plausible-looking but, on the paper's reading, part of a fabricated passage.
The number of further emails the abridged steering prompt says it has left out. The full prompt runs to 1,454 tokens; the card shows three emails plus a system instruction.
The unsteered rate of verbalized eval awareness: in 28 of 50 rollouts on this prompt the model states that the scenario is a test. It is the baseline the steering is measured against.

The same rate with the feature steered down, so roughly a threefold drop. The paper reports it as confirmation that the feature carries the model's recognition of artificiality, not merely a correlate of it.

The steering magnitude: the feature direction is subtracted at five percent of the residual-stream norm. The paper does not report a sweep over this value here, so how sensitive the 10/50 figure is to it is not shown.

Context from section 5.1, not printed on this card: ablating a list of eval-awareness J-lens directions on the same scenario cut verbalized eval awareness from 71% to 3% and raised attempted blackmail from 0 of 180 rollouts to 13 of 180. This figure's steering is a weaker, single-feature intervention and reports no blackmail rate.

sections.title: Interpreting Model Components using the J-lens

items.caption: Figure 91: Three translation transcoder features under the J-lens. Each encoder reads a multilingual concept plus French context; each decoder writes the opening token of the French word for that concept. Numbers = vocabulary rank.
items.title: Both ends of three translation features
items.takeaway: Projecting a transcoder feature's encoder and decoder directions separately through the J-lens makes the feature's input-to-output map readable without running the model on any data. In all three cases shown, the encoder side reads a concept expressed across many languages together with common French words, and the decoder side writes the opening token of the French word for that concept.
items.walkthrough:
The item renders as a live panel rather than a static plot. Three columns sit side by side, one per [[transcoder]] feature, headed Water → eau, Love → amour and Game → jeu. Each column splits into an Encoder box and a Decoder box, and each box lists ten vocabulary tokens.

A transcoder approximates one MLP layer with a sparsely activating hidden layer. Each of its features owns two directions in the [[residual-stream]]. The encoder direction determines what content switches the feature on. The decoder direction is what the feature writes back when it fires.

### How to read it

Both directions are ordinary vectors, so both can be pushed through the lens. The box headers state the composition used: Encoder · J · W$_U$ and Decoder · J · W$_U$. The direction is multiplied by the averaged Jacobian $J$ that defines the [[jacobian-lens]], then by the unembedding matrix $W_U$, which scores every token in the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. Sorting those scores gives the ranking. This is the weight-side [[j-lens-readout]]: [[weight-vocabulary-projection]], one application of [[component-interpretation]].

The small number beside a token is its rank in that full ordering, so 1 is the top-scoring token. Colour marks a category. Blue is a token naming the concept in some language, magenta a common French word, teal the French target word or a fragment of it, and gray a token left uncategorised.

The decoder lists run 1 through 10 with no gaps. The encoder lists do not: the water encoder shows ranks 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8, then jumps to 30, 39, 41 and 50. Those rows are selected entries, not an unbroken top of the list. The prose also names tokens absent from the rows shown, such as aigua for water.

### What it shows

Each encoder reads two things at once. It reads the concept across languages — water, 水, água, agua and вод — and separately reads common French words, avec, école, une and dans, which say nothing about water. The same split appears for love and for game.

Each decoder writes the beginning of the French word. The water decoder is led by eau and by fragments starting ea. The love decoder writes am, the opening of amour, in Latin, Cyrillic and Korean script. The game decoder writes j, the opening of jeu, in Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, Japanese and Devanagari script.

Taken together the two sides name a function: concept plus French context in, first token of the French translation out. The language-agnostic half of each encoder is the paper's [[shared-multilingual-representation]] appearing in weights rather than in activations.

terms.definition: A dictionary-learning variant trained to reproduce an MLP layer's input-to-output map through a sparsely activating hidden layer. Each hidden unit is a feature with its own encoder and decoder direction, which is what lets the two sides be read separately here.

The feature's input direction: the residual-stream direction whose dot product with the incoming activation decides whether the feature switches on. The left box in each column reads this direction through the lens.
The feature's output direction: the vector the feature adds back to the residual stream, scaled by its activation. The right box in each column reads this direction through the lens.

The averaged Jacobian at the heart of the J-lens — the linear map, estimated by averaging per-input Jacobians over a corpus, from a residual-stream perturbation to its effect on the model's output logits. Multiplying a direction by $J$ asks what that direction would push the model to say.
The model's unembedding matrix, which turns a final-layer vector into one score per vocabulary token. It is the last step of the composition printed in each box header.

terms.term: Encoder · J · W$_U$ / Decoder · J · W$_U$
terms.definition: The box headers, naming the exact quantity ranked below them: take the feature direction, push it through the averaged Jacobian, then through the unembedding. No forward pass on real text is involved, which is why the paper calls this a data-free reading.
The paper's technique for reading a residual-stream direction as a distribution over words the model could say about it. Applied here to static weight directions rather than to activations.
The label running down the left edge of the panel. It states that the vertical axis of each list is position in the ranking, best at the top, rather than a score.

For each token, its position when the whole tokenizer vocabulary is sorted by the score from that composition. Rank 1 is the highest-scoring token in the vocabulary; the caption states plainly that the numbers are ranks.
The title of the first column. It names the feature by the English concept its encoder reads and the French word its decoder starts to write.
The title of the second column, read the same way: a love-concept encoder paired with a decoder that opens the French word amour.
The title of the third column: a game-concept encoder paired with a decoder that opens the French word jeu.
The colour given to a token that names the column's concept in some language, whatever the script. It marks the language-agnostic half of what the encoder reads.

The colour given to a common French word that carries no information about the concept — function words and everyday nouns. Its presence in the encoder readout is what tells the reader the feature is conditioned on French, not just on the concept.
The colour given to the French word for the concept or to a fragment that opens it. The figure's caption refers to this category as the French word.
Tokens the authors did not assign to any of the three categories, such as eat, wash, ear and a. They appear high in some decoder lists and are not claimed to support the interpretation.
The character the widget prints where a token contains a leading or trailing space. It distinguishes a whole-word token such as ⍽eau⍽ from a word-initial fragment such as ⍽am.

The concept tokens in the first feature's encoder readout: water in English, Chinese, Portuguese, Spanish and Russian. Together they are the evidence that the encoder reads a concept rather than a string.
The French word for water. It appears in the first feature's encoder readout at rank 7 and dominates its decoder readout at rank 1.

terms.term: avec, école, une, dans, qui, à, elle, pour
terms.definition: The common French tokens appearing in the encoder readouts of all three features: with, school, a, in, who, to, she, for. None of them relates to water, love or games; the paper reads them as the French-context condition on the feature.

terms.term: ea, EA, ean, eat, ear, wash, E
terms.definition: The remaining tokens in the water decoder's top ten. The teal ones (ea, EA, ean) are fragments that open eau or eau-like French spellings; eat, ear, wash and E are uncategorised near-misses on the same letters or on the water theme.

The concept tokens in the second feature's encoder readout: love in English, Spanish or Portuguese, a South Slavic stem, and a German stem. The paper's prose also lists romance and marriage, which are not among the ten rows displayed.

terms.term: am, Am, ам, а, ам (Cyrillic), 아, a
terms.definition: The second feature's decoder readout: the fragment am in Latin, Cyrillic and Korean script, plus bare a. The paper reads these as the opening of amour written in whatever script the vocabulary offers.

terms.term: иг, game, ját, 游, spiel, 게, jou
terms.definition: The concept tokens in the third feature's encoder readout: game or play stems in Russian, English, Hungarian, Chinese, German, Korean and French. The Russian stem иг outranks the English game.

terms.term: j, ј, J, дж, ج, ジ, ज
terms.definition: The third feature's decoder readout: the letter j and its nearest equivalents in Cyrillic, Arabic, Japanese katakana and Devanagari. The paper reads them as the start of jeu.

Tokens the surrounding prose names as present in these encoder readouts — aigua is Catalan for water — but which do not appear among the ten rows the panel displays. The displayed rows are a selection, not the complete readout.

The paper's finding that a multilingual model routes some computation through a representation that is not tied to any one language. Here it shows up in a weight direction: one encoder reads the same concept written five different ways.

numbers.meaning: The number of transcoder features shown, one per column. All three are chosen as translation features, so the panel is an illustration of a pattern rather than a survey of how common it is.
The number of token rows in each of the six boxes. Ten is a display choice; the underlying ranking covers the whole vocabulary.
The best rank, meaning the token that scores highest in the whole vocabulary for that composition. Every decoder box here is headed by a token the paper counts as on-target: eau, am and j.

The top block of the water encoder: water (1), 水 (3), água (5), agua (6), eau (7), вод (8). Six of the eight highest-ranked slots shown are the same concept in different languages, which is the figure's main evidence that the encoder is concept-driven.
Ranks absent from the water encoder list. Their absence shows that the displayed rows are selected entries rather than an unbroken top ten, so nothing can be concluded about what sits in the gaps.

The ranks of avec, école, une and dans in the water encoder. They sit well below the concept tokens but still inside the top fifty of a vocabulary of tens of thousands, which the paper treats as a real French-context signal rather than noise.
A contiguous top ten: eau, eau, eat, ea, wash, ear, E, E, EA, ean. Four rows are teal French-target fragments and the rest are uncategorised, so the decoder's list is less clean than the encoder's.

The concept ranks in the love encoder: love (1), amor (3), ljub (10) and lieb (31). The German stem lieb falls below several French function words, which shows the two categories interleave rather than separating into blocks.
The ranks of the French context tokens qui, dans, avec, à, elle and pour in the love encoder. They begin higher than in the water encoder, at 21 rather than 30.
A contiguous top ten: am, a, ам, Am, am, а, Am, 아, a, ам. Seven rows are the am fragment in some script or case; the two bare a rows are uncategorised.
The concept ranks in the game encoder: иг (1), game (2), ját (6), 游 (7), spiel (13), 게 (18), jou (36). The Russian stem outranks the English word, so the readout is not simply English-first.
The ranks of dans, à and pour in the game encoder. This is the weakest of the three French-context signals, the first such token arriving only at rank 42.
A contiguous top ten: j, j, ј, дж, ج, J, ジ, ज, ج, J. Every row is the j sound or letter in some script, making this the sharpest of the three decoder readouts.

sections.title: Interpreting Model Components using the J-lens

items.caption: Figure 92: Three two-digit-addition transcoder features. Top: activation over operand pairs $(a, b) \in \{0,\dots,99\}^2$ . Bottom: encoder and decoder projected through $J\, W_U$ onto sum tokens $000$ – $999$ (rows = hundreds digit, cols = last two; promotes, suppresses).
items.title: Arithmetic transcoder features under the J-lens
items.takeaway: Projecting a transcoder feature's encoder and decoder directions separately through the J-lens recovers what the feature reads and what it writes, without running any prompts. For three two-digit-addition features, those weight-only readouts match the firing patterns measured earlier on 10,000 addition prompts.
items.walkthrough:
### What is on the page

Three [[transcoder]] features involved in two-digit addition appear side by side, one per column. A transcoder is a dictionary-learning model trained to reproduce an [[mlp-block]]'s input-output map through a sparsely active hidden layer. Each of its features carries two directions in [[residual-stream]] space: an encoder, which decides what content switches the feature on, and a decoder, which decides what the feature writes back.

Every feature gets two views, stacked. The top panel is the empirical one, carried over from the authors' earlier circuits work: the feature's activation recorded on 10,000 prompts of the form "{a} + {b} = ", one prompt per operand pair $(a,b)$ with $0 \le a,b < 100$, shaded in orange.

The bottom panel needs no prompts at all. It takes the encoder direction and the decoder direction and pushes each through the [[jacobian-lens]] — the averaged Jacobian $J$, then the model's own [[unembedding-matrix]] $W_U$ — producing a score for every token in the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. The earlier work could only do this for decoders, using the [[logit-lens]]; the lens here reads the encoder side too. [[component-interpretation]]

### How to read the lens grids

The lens scores are drawn only over the thousand three-digit number tokens, $000$ through $999$, laid out as ten rows by a hundred columns. The row index is the hundreds digit. The column index is the last two digits.

That split does real work. A property that depends only on the last two digits shows up as a vertical band running through all ten rows. Green marks tokens the direction promotes; purple marks tokens it suppresses.

### What the three features show

The left feature fires when either operand ends in 80–85, and its encoder lens shows those same values as a green band.

The middle feature fires when the sum ends in _95. Its encoder lens carries two patterns at once: thin stripes repeating on every number ending in 5, and a thicker stripe near _95. The paper reads the conjunction of the two conditions as a sum ending in _95. Its decoder lens agrees, promoting _95 while suppressing the competing values in purple bands — a sharpening around the correct answer.

The right feature is a lookup table. It fires when both operands fall in the ranges its encoder shows in green, mostly 25–40 modulo 50, and its decoder writes the matching approximate sum, also modulo 50.

The claim is narrow: the two readouts describe the function the feature computes from weights alone.

terms.definition: A dictionary-learning model trained to approximate an MLP layer's input-output map with a sparsely activating hidden layer. Unlike a sparse autoencoder, which reconstructs activations, it maps the layer's input to the layer's output, so each of its features has a separate encoder and decoder direction.
One unit of that sparse hidden layer. Here, three features previously identified as taking part in two-digit addition circuitry.

The residual-stream direction the feature reads: its dot product with the incoming activation determines whether the feature switches on. In this figure the encoder is what the top lens grid of each pair is computed from.
The residual-stream direction the feature writes back when it is active, scaled by its activation. It is what the second lens grid of each pair is computed from.

The paper's readout: an averaged Jacobian $J_\ell$ from layer $\ell$ to the final residual stream, composed with the unembedding, giving a score over the vocabulary for any residual-stream direction. Applied to a weight direction rather than an activation, it says what that direction is verbalizable as.

The averaged Jacobian at the relevant layer: the linear map from a perturbation of the residual stream to its first-order effect on the final-layer residual stream, averaged over token positions and over a corpus of prompts.
The model's unembedding matrix, the final linear map from the residual stream to per-token scores. It is the model's own weights, not anything fitted for this figure.

The caption's shorthand for the composition that turns a direction into vocabulary scores. Written out in the methods, the score vector for a direction $v$ is $W_U J_\ell v$; the caption reverses the factors but names the same operation.

The older readout that applies only the final unembedding to an intermediate state or direction. The earlier circuits work used it on these features' decoders; it has no way to read an encoder, because an encoder direction is an input side rather than something written toward the output.
The two summands in the prompt used to measure activation, each ranging over the integers 0 to 99. One grid cell in a top panel corresponds to one such pair.
The prompt template on which the features' activations were recorded, with the two placeholders filled by every pair of integers below 100.
How strongly the transcoder feature fires on a given prompt, shaded in orange over the operand grid. This is the measured, prompt-based view of the feature.

The thousand three-digit number tokens over which the encoder and decoder readouts are displayed. The lens scores every vocabulary token, but only this family is plotted, since it is where an addition feature's meaning lives.
The row index of a lens grid, running 0 to 9: the leading digit of the three-digit token in that cell.

The column index of a lens grid, running 00 to 99: the trailing two digits of the token in that cell. Because the layout separates this from the hundreds digit, any pattern that depends only on the last two digits appears as a vertical band crossing all rows.

A positive lens score: the direction pushes the model toward saying that token. On an encoder panel it indicates the values the feature is disposed to read; on a decoder panel, the values it writes toward.
A negative lens score: the direction pushes the model away from that token. It appears on the middle feature's decoder, which downweights the values competing with the correct answer.
Notation for a three-digit token whose last two digits are 95, with the underscore standing for any hundreds digit. In the grid layout that is a single column, running through all ten rows.

Notation for a three-digit token ending in the digit 5, with both underscores free. In the grid layout that is every tenth column, giving the thin repeating stripes described in the middle feature's encoder.
The paper's label for the right-hand feature: rather than computing an operation, it fires on a restricted band of operand values and writes out the answer associated with that band.
The pattern the middle feature's decoder shows: promoting the correct sum while suppressing its numeric neighbours, which concentrates probability on one answer rather than merely raising it.
Used for the right-hand feature to say that its operand bands and its written sums repeat every 50, so a range described as 25–40 also covers 75–90.

The general move this figure illustrates: any weight direction, not just an activation, can be pushed through the lens, and comparing the input side against the output side exposes the transformation the component implements.

numbers.meaning: The number of transcoder features shown, one per column: an operand-band feature on the left, a sum-detector feature in the middle, a lookup-table feature on the right. The paper picks them as illustrations rather than as a survey.

numbers.value: 2 panels per feature, 6 lens grids in total
numbers.meaning: Each feature contributes one encoder readout and one decoder readout. Splitting the two sides is the whole point: the encoder says what is read, the decoder says what is written, and the pair names the transformation.
The operand range swept in the top panels. Both summands are restricted to the two-digit range, which is what makes this a two-digit-addition study.
The number of prompts behind each top grid, which is $100 \times 100$: one prompt for every ordered pair of operands in that range. Each prompt contributes one cell.

The set of three-digit number tokens over which each lens readout is plotted. Sums of two two-digit numbers reach at most $99 + 99 = 198$, so most of this range is never a correct answer; plotting the whole family is what lets the periodic structure in the readouts be seen.
One row per hundreds digit, 0 through 9.
One column per pair of trailing digits, 00 through 99. Ten rows times a hundred columns covers the thousand tokens exactly.

The operand values the left feature responds to: it fires when either $a$ or $b$ ends in this range. Six adjacent values, so its encoder readout is a narrow green band six columns wide, running down all ten rows.

The last digit picked out by the first of the two patterns in the middle feature's encoder. A condition on the last digit alone repeats every ten columns, which is why the paper describes thin repeating stripes.

The last two digits the middle feature is tuned to, both in the thicker encoder stripe and in what its decoder promotes. The paper reads the two encoder patterns as an AND whose result is a sum ending in _95; within the reachable sum range that means the sums 95 and 195.
The operand band the right-hand lookup-table feature reads, visible as green in its encoder. The feature fires when both operands fall in it.

The period of the right feature's bands. Because the condition holds modulo 50, the band 25–40 repeats as 75–90, and the decoder writes the sum only up to a multiple of 50 — an approximate answer rather than an exact one.

The figure's number in the paper. It sits in the appendix section on applying the J-lens to mechanistic interpretability, after the SAE-feature and translation-feature examples and before the attention-head ones.

sections.title: Interpreting Model Components using the J-lens

items.caption: Figure 93: A "British spelling → Commonwealth nationality" attention head. Attention from each boxed British-spelled query token is shown alongside the top tokens by norm of $W_U\, J\, W_{\{Q,K,V,O\}}$ for each of the head's four weight matrices.
items.title: The British-Spelling Nationality Head
items.takeaway: A single attention head is read two ways at once: by its attention pattern on a passage, and by pushing each of its four weight matrices through the J-lens. The two readings agree — the head fires on British spellings and writes Commonwealth nationality — which is the paper's demonstration that composing the lens with a component's weights can name what that component reads and what it writes, using no prompt data at all.
items.walkthrough:
### What the item is

The article renders this as a live widget rather than a fixed image, so the exact controls are not pinned down by the text. It has two halves. One half is a passage of text with an [[attention-head]]'s attention pattern drawn over it. The other half is four short lists of vocabulary tokens, one list per weight matrix of that same head.

### Reading the attention half

Certain tokens in the passage are drawn with a box around them. A boxed token is a query position — the position the head attends *from*. The widget displays the attention from each boxed token back over the earlier tokens.

The paper reports the same shape for every box. Each boxed token is a British spelling: centre, labour, colour, behaviour, honour. Each attends back to a nearby Commonwealth country word: African, Zealand, Australian, British, Canadian.

### Reading the four token lists

A head has four weight matrices — query, key, value and output. Query, key and value read from the [[residual-stream]]; output writes back into it.

Each matrix is composed with the [[jacobian-lens]] map $W_U J$, whose rows are the [[j-lens-vector]]s, one per vocabulary token. That composition, written $W_U\,J\,W_{\{Q,K,V,O\}}$ in the caption, again gives one row per token. Tokens are then ranked by the norm of their row.

A large norm means that token's lens direction is one the matrix picks up strongly, whether reading or writing. No prompt enters this calculation; it runs on the weights alone, which is the point of [[component-interpretation]].

### What the lists say

The query side reads colour, centre, neighbour and other British spellings. The key side reads a mixture of British spellings and country names. The value and output sides read Australian, Australia, Canadian and related tokens.

So the input side of the head is spelling and the output side is nationality. The paper's reading follows: the head detects a British-spelled word at the current position, attends to a Commonwealth country mentioned nearby, and writes that country's representation into the residual stream.

A use for this is offered only speculatively — spelling might help the model settle whose nationality is in play when a context names several speakers.

One caveat sits in the next paragraph of the paper. Of the three further heads shown after this one, it notes that many heads with interpretable projections have similar vocabulary rankings across all four matrices. The input-versus-output contrast here is therefore weaker evidence than it first looks.

terms.definition: The caption's name for what the head does: it takes a British-spelled word as its trigger and produces a Commonwealth country's representation as its output. The arrow denotes an input-to-output transformation, not an arithmetic operation.
The transformer operation that lets one token position retrieve and transform information from earlier positions. Here a single head is the object under study.
The distribution, for a given query position, of how much weight the head places on each earlier position. It is drawn over the passage in one half of the widget.
A token in the passage drawn with a box around it, marking it as one of the query positions whose attention the widget displays. Every boxed token in this figure is a British spelling.
The position the head attends from — the token whose residual stream is projected through the query matrix to decide where to look. In this figure these are the boxed British spellings.

The British-spelled words named in the text as boxed query tokens. Each differs from its American spelling (center, labor, color, behavior, honor), which is what makes the spelling itself informative about a writer.

A further British spelling that appears in the query-side lens readout but is not listed among the boxed tokens. Its presence indicates the query matrix reads the British-spelling family broadly, not only the words present in this passage.

The tokens the boxed positions attend back to. They are fragments of Commonwealth country and nationality names — South African, New Zealand, and so on — rather than whole words, because the tokenizer splits them.
The tokens named as topping the value-side and output-side lens readouts. They are what the head writes into the residual stream, as opposed to what it looks for.

The grouping of countries — Australia, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, the United Kingdom — that share British spelling conventions. The head's output tokens fall inside this set, which is why the caption uses the word.

The paper's technique: a per-layer averaged Jacobian $J$ that, composed with the unembedding, turns any residual-stream direction into a ranked list of vocabulary tokens the direction disposes the model to say.
One row of $W_U J$: the residual-stream direction associated with a single vocabulary token. This figure ranks these vectors by how strongly each of the head's matrices engages them.
The unembedding matrix, the model's own final linear map from the residual stream to a score per vocabulary token. It is what turns a direction into words.

The averaged Jacobian at the head's layer, mapping a perturbation of the residual stream there to its first-order effect on the final-layer residual stream, averaged over positions and over a corpus of prompts.

The head's query projection, which reads the current position's residual stream to form the vector that decides where to attend. Its lens readout says which token concepts trigger the head at the current position.
The head's key projection, which reads each earlier position to form the vector matched against the query. Its lens readout says which token concepts make an earlier position a candidate target.
The head's value projection, which reads the content the head will carry from the attended position. Its lens readout says what the head picks up once it has decided where to look.
The head's output projection, which writes the attended content back into the residual stream. Its lens readout says what the head deposits for later layers to use.

The caption's compact notation for the four compositions, one per weight matrix, of the lens map with that matrix. The brace set is shorthand for running the same calculation four times, once with each of Q, K, V and O.

The length of a token's row in the composed matrix, used here as the ranking score. A long row means the head's matrix engages that token's lens direction strongly; the sign and direction within the head's subspace are discarded.
The head of the ranked list — the vocabulary entries with the largest composed-row norms. The paper reads a component's function off these, and only when the ranking is sharply peaked.
The running per-position vector that every layer reads from and writes to. Query, key and value read from it; output writes back into it; and the lens is defined over directions in it.
The value-and-output pair taken together — what the head writes about whatever it attended to, independent of where it attended. In this head, that content is Commonwealth nationality.

numbers.meaning: The figure's number in the article. It sits in appendix section 10.24.3, among the examples of interpreting model components with the J-lens.
The number of weight matrices an attention head has — query, key, value and output — and therefore the number of token lists shown. The count is fixed by the architecture, not chosen by the authors.
The number of British-spelled query tokens the surrounding text names: centre, labour, colour, behaviour, honour. The widget itself may box more; five is what the prose enumerates.
The number of attended Commonwealth tokens the text names: African, Zealand, Australian, British, Canadian. Again this is the prose's enumeration rather than a stated total.
The number of query-side lens tokens quoted — colour, centre, neighbour — before the text falls back on "and other British spellings". The list is truncated in the prose, not in the widget.
The number of value- and output-side lens tokens quoted: Australian, Australia, Canadian. The text adds "and related tokens" rather than giving a full list.

No attention weights, norms, ranks or layer index are reported for this head anywhere in the caption or the surrounding text. The evidence is presented as a qualitative token ordering, which is why the paper says the readouts "suggest" the head's function rather than measuring it.
