items.caption: Figure 94: Three additional attention heads, in the same format as Figure ??.
items.title: Three more heads read through their weights
items.takeaway: Three further attention heads are shown in the format of Figure 93: five attention snippets on the left, and on the right the top six vocabulary tokens for each of the head's four weight matrices projected through the J-lens. The point the section draws from them is a structural one — heads whose weights project interpretably tend to give similar token rankings across all four matrices — and no function is proposed for any individual head here.
items.walkthrough:
This is a live widget rather than a static image. It stacks three panels, one for each [[attention-head]], under the labels the authors gave them: "Async error handling", "Temperature" and "Honorific titles". Every panel repeats the layout of Figure 93. Neither the model nor the layer and head index is reported for any of the three.

### The left half: attention

Each panel carries five text snippets of eleven to fifteen tokens, clipped on the left and prefixed with an ellipsis. The last token of every snippet is outlined. That is the query position, and the header above reads "attention pattern from query token" with an arrow pointing down at it. The remaining tokens carry orange shading for the head's attention from that query. The shading runs on a scale from 0 to 1 and saturates at the top, so a fully orange token means the value reached the ramp's ceiling rather than any exact probability.

### The right half: weights read as tokens

Four columns headed $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ and $W_O$ list six vocabulary tokens each. These are not readouts of activations. Each of the head's weight matrices is composed with the [[jacobian-lens]] and the [[unembedding-matrix]] as $W_U\,J\,W_{\{Q,K,V,O\}}$, which leaves one row per entry of the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. Tokens are then ranked by the norm of their row. This is [[weight-vocabulary-projection]] applied to a model component rather than to a [[residual-stream]] activation, the use the paper calls [[component-interpretation]].

### What the three panels show

The async head's four columns are dominated by await, async, promise and try. Its attention runs from a token such as " exception", " catch" or " try" back to the nearest " await" or " async", at 1.0, 0.77, 0.615, 0.415 and 0.403 across the five snippets.

The temperature head reads thermal-quantity words on the query side — temperature, температ, hot, heat, 热 — and specific warm and cold words on the key side and on the value and output sides, which together form the head's [[ov-circuit]]. Its attention does reach " warm", " cooling" and " warming", but often lands harder on neutral neighbours such as " the", " jacket", " average" and " floor".

The honorific head lists Mr, Mrs, Dr and Ms in all four columns. Its attention mostly goes to the immediately preceding title, or stays on the query token itself, so the weight readout carries more of the story than the pattern does.

The section makes one claim about these three, and it is general: many heads with interpretable projections have similar vocabulary rankings across the different weight matrices, which the paper calls somewhat surprising. All three panels fit that description.

terms.definition: The transformer operation that lets a token position pull information from earlier positions. Each head has four weight matrices, and this figure characterises three heads by both what they attend to and what their weights project to in vocabulary space.

The paper's readout technique: a corpus-averaged Jacobian $J$ per layer, which turns a residual-stream direction into scores over the vocabulary via $W_U\,J$. Here it is applied to static weights instead of to an activation.
The label the authors give the first head. It is a name assigned from the head's behaviour, not a quantity the widget computes.
The label for the second head, whose query-side tokens are words for thermal quantity and whose key, value and output tokens are specific warm and cold words.
The label for the third head, whose four weight matrices all rank English personal titles at the top.
The header over the left half of each panel, with a downward arrow at its right end pointing at the outlined final token. It states that the shading is attention measured from that one position.
The header over the right half of each panel. It states that the four columns below are vocabulary tokens ranked by J-lens projection of the head's weight matrices.
The final token of each snippet, drawn with a thin box. The whole shading row is the attention distribution computed from this position back over the snippet.
One short passage of text, shown as a single line of tokens. Each is clipped on the left with a leading ellipsis so the query token sits flush at the right edge.
The colour ramp on each token: white at zero attention, full orange at the ceiling. Orange is reserved throughout the paper for activation or attention strength.
The head's query projection. Its column lists the tokens whose J-lens directions couple most strongly into the query subspace, that is, what content at the current position makes the head fire.
The head's key projection. Its column lists the tokens whose J-lens directions the head most strongly looks for at earlier positions.
The head's value projection: what the head picks up from the position it attends to. Together with $W_O$ it forms the head's OV circuit.
The head's output projection, which writes the attended content back into the residual stream. Its column lists the tokens that write-back most strongly promotes.
The unembedding matrix, the model's final linear map from residual-stream vectors to vocabulary scores. It is the left factor of the composition used here.
The layer's corpus-averaged Jacobian, the matrix at the centre of the J-lens. Composing $W_U\,J$ gives the linear map from a residual direction to vocabulary scores.

The composition ranked in the right half: one of the head's four weight matrices, pushed through the Jacobian and the unembedding. The result has one row per vocabulary token, and tokens are ordered by the norm of their row.
The rule that picks the six tokens in each column. A large row norm means that token's lens direction has a large component in whatever subspace that weight matrix reads from or writes to.
The running per-position vector that all four of a head's matrices read from or write to, and the space in which J-lens vectors live.
The fixed token set the ranking runs over. Because leading spaces and capitalisation make separate entries, a column can list what looks like the same word twice, for example async and " async".

A token at the top of the async head's query, key and output columns, and the token most snippets attend to. In JavaScript it marks the point where a promise is waited on and where an error can surface.
Case variants of the same word appearing across all four of the first head's columns. They are separate vocabulary entries, which is why the word repeats within a column.
A word fragment in the async head's query column: the opening piece of "await" under a different tokenization.
The sixth token in the async head's query column, and the only one there that names the failure rather than the awaiting construct.
Tokens in the async head's key, value and output columns. A promise is the JavaScript object an await suspends on, and a rejected one is what becomes an exception.
A token in the async head's value column, and the query token of one snippet. It opens the block that catches the exception.
Case variants heading the temperature head's query column, and its top output token. Most of that head's snippets end on this word as the query.
A Russian fragment, the opening of температура (temperature). It appears in the temperature head's query, key and output columns, so the head's reading is not confined to English.
Two further thermal-quantity tokens in the temperature head's query and output columns. Both also occur as query tokens in the snippets.
A Chinese character meaning hot or heat, in the temperature head's query and output columns. Another sign the head's readout spans scripts.

The top tokens of the temperature head's key and value columns. They are specific thermal values rather than the quantity word, which is what separates the key and value sides from the query side here.
Further specific thermal tokens on the temperature head's key and value sides. The same words appear as attended tokens inside the snippets.
A Russian fragment, the opening of холодный (cold), in the temperature head's value column.
The top token of every column of the honorific head, in both capitalisations. Also the query token of one snippet.
The other titles filling the honorific head's four columns. All four columns list the same small set in slightly different orders.
A title appearing only in the honorific head's key column, not in the other three.
The sixth token in the honorific head's key column. It is the abbreviation for Saint or Street, and the one entry there that is not a personal title.
The general move this figure instances: projecting a static weight direction, rather than an activation, through the lens to read what the component handles.

numbers.meaning: The figure's number in the paper. It sits in appendix section 10.24.3, on interpreting model components with the J-lens.
The figure whose format is reused here. Figure 93 shows one head, the "British spelling to Commonwealth nationality" head, with the same two-half layout.
The number of heads shown, stacked as three panels. The section calls them three more examples beyond the one worked through in Figure 93.
The weight matrices per head: query, key, value and output. Four is fixed by the transformer's attention design, not chosen by the authors.
Tokens listed per column, so 24 per head and 72 in the figure. The cut-off is a display choice; the ranking itself runs over the whole vocabulary.
Snippets per head, so 15 attention rows in total. Each snippet is a separate context in which the head was run.
The token length of a snippet. The range comes from clipping each example to a fixed display width, which lands on a whole-token boundary at a different count each time.
The range of the shading weight on each token, mapped from white to full orange. Values are clipped into this range for display, so 1 marks the ceiling rather than a probability of one.

A saturated token. It occurs on " await" in the first async snippet, on " temperature" and on both " floor" and " hot" in temperature snippets, and on " Mr" and " Mrs" in honorific snippets. Two tokens both at 1.0 in one row show the values are not a normalised distribution.
The async head's weight on the token it attends to most in each of its five snippets, in order. Four of the five peaks fall on " await"; the fourth falls on " async".

The weight on " out" in the first async snippet, the second-highest there. It is part of "the await times out", so the head spreads some weight across the failing construct rather than onto " await" alone.
The async head's weight on its own query token in each snippet. These are low, which is what makes the head read as retrieving from an earlier position rather than sitting on the current one.
The temperature head's weight on its own query token across the five snippets. Two saturate and two are low, so the head's self-weight is not consistent.

The temperature head's weight on the specific thermal word in each snippet: " warm", " cooling", " warming", " warm" and " warm". These are the tokens its key and value columns predict it should find.

Weights on non-thermal neighbours in the temperature snippets: " the", " jacket", " average" and " floor". Each exceeds the thermal word in its own snippet, so the attention pattern is looser than the weight readout suggests.
The honorific head's weight on the preceding title in each snippet: " Mr", " Dr", " Dr", " Mrs" and " Ms". The last two are small because the query token in those snippets is itself a title.

The honorific head's weight on its own query token. It is substantial in every snippet and saturates in the two where the query is a title, which is the main reason the pattern reads less cleanly than the four columns do.
The typical background weight on the scene-setting tokens at the left of each snippet. It renders as near-white and marks the part of the context the head ignores.

sections.title: Interpreting Model Components using the J-lens

items.caption: The averaged Jacobian lens matrix J_l (expectation of dh_final/dh_l over positions and prompts)
items.title: The averaged Jacobian, one matrix per layer
items.takeaway: This line defines the object the whole paper is built on: for each layer, a single fixed matrix $J_\ell$ obtained by averaging the layer-to-output Jacobian over source positions, over later positions, and over a thousand pretraining-like prompts. The averaging is what turns a per-prompt derivative into a claim about the model's general disposition to verbalize a concept rather than its use of that concept in one context.
items.walkthrough:
The equation defines the central object of the [[jacobian-lens]]: one matrix $J_\ell$ for each layer $\ell$ of the model.

The quantity inside the brackets is the piece that does the causal work. $h_{\ell,t}$ is the [[residual-stream]] vector at layer $\ell$ and token position $t$ — the running activation that every layer reads from and writes to. $h_{\text{final},t'}$ is that same stream at the model's last layer, at some position $t'$. Because attention is causal, a perturbation at position $t$ can only reach positions at or after $t$, which is why the target is restricted to $t' \geq t$.

The fraction $\partial h_{\text{final},t'} / \partial h_{\ell,t}$ is the [[jacobian-matrix]] relating those two vectors. Its entry in row $i$, column $j$ states how far final-layer coordinate $i$ moves when source coordinate $j$ is nudged. It is computed by backpropagating from the final layer down to $h_\ell$, and it describes the true effect of a perturbation only to first order, which is the paper's [[local-linearization]] assumption.

The $\mathbb{E}$ carries three subscripts, and each names one thing being averaged away. The first is the source position $t$. The second is the target position $t'$, ranging over all positions from $t$ to the end of that context. The third is the prompt, drawn from a corpus of one thousand sequences sampled from a pretraining-like distribution ([[lens-corpus]]).

The paper's stated reason for averaging is that a Jacobian from a single prompt conflates two kinds of structure. One is the model's general disposition to verbalize a given concept. The other is the particular use that concept is being put to in the context at hand. The second part changes from prompt to prompt and from position to position, so averaging over both shrinks it; what survives is the part that holds across contexts.

Both residual-stream vectors have $d_{\text{model}}$ entries, so the derivative is a $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$ matrix, and averaging leaves that shape unchanged. The output is therefore one fixed matrix per layer, mapping layer $\ell$ to the final layer $L$, not one matrix per prompt. Composing it with the [[unembedding-matrix]] $W_U$ gives the rows of $W_U J_\ell$, which the paper calls the [[j-lens-vector]]s and whose span it studies as the [[j-space]].

The appendix records that the default lens actually differentiates the penultimate-layer residual stream rather than the final one, and that the range of target positions is one of several recipe choices the authors sweep ([[target-position-variants]]).

terms.definition: The Jacobian lens matrix at layer $\ell$: the averaged derivative of the final-layer residual stream with respect to the layer-$\ell$ residual stream. It is the single object the rest of the paper reads and writes through.
The source layer index — the depth in the network at which an activation is being characterized. A separate $J_\ell$ exists for each layer.
The model's final layer, named in the sentence that follows the equation as the layer $J_\ell$ maps into.
The residual stream at layer $\ell$ and token position $t$: the vector of activations at that point in the forward pass, and the thing whose causal effect the lens measures.
The residual stream at the model's final layer and position $t'$, just before the unembedding step that produces output logits. It is the target of the derivative.
The source token position: where in the sequence the perturbed activation sits. The expectation runs over it.

A target token position at which the final-layer effect is read. It is constrained to $t' \geq t$ because a transformer's causal attention lets an activation influence only its own position and later ones.

The Jacobian matrix of the final-layer residual at $t'$ with respect to the layer-$\ell$ residual at $t$: the linear map, obtained by backpropagation, that best approximates how a small change at the source shifts the final layer.
The expectation, taken here as an empirical average over the three things listed in its subscript: source position, target position, and prompt.
The third averaging variable: a text sequence drawn from the paper's lens corpus of pretraining-like data. Averaging over prompts is what removes context-specific structure from the Jacobian.
The width of the residual stream — the number of entries in each activation vector. Both the input and output of $J_\ell$ live in this space, so $J_\ell$ is square.
The shape of $J_\ell$: a square matrix mapping residual-stream vectors at layer $\ell$ to residual-stream vectors at the final layer.

The kind of text the averaging corpus is sampled from: ordinary next-token-prediction data rather than chat transcripts or task prompts, so the average reflects broad contexts rather than one setting.
The unembedding matrix, which maps a final-layer residual vector to scores over the vocabulary. It is not in this equation, but $J_\ell$ is composed with it to produce readouts and lens vectors.
The linear part of the true effect of a perturbation, which is what a Jacobian captures. Larger perturbations, or strongly nonlinear responses, are not described by it.

numbers.meaning: The number of prompts the expectation is taken over in the default lens. The appendix reports that the J-lens already beats the logit-lens and tuned-lens baselines with as few as 10 prompts, with modest gains from more, so this size buys stability rather than a qualitative change.

The length in tokens of each sequence in the default corpus, stated in the methodological appendix rather than beside the equation. Each sequence contributes one within-prompt average over its positions before the cross-prompt average is taken.
The corpus size, in prompts, at which the appendix's sweep finds the J-lens already outperforming the logit lens and tuned lens; the sweep runs from 1 to 1000.
The order of the approximation. Only the linear term of the perturbation's effect is kept, which is what makes a single matrix per layer sufficient.
The dimensions of the resulting matrix. Source and target are both residual-stream vectors of width $d_{\text{model}}$, so the derivative is square and averaging does not change its shape.
The count of objects produced. The averaging collapses every prompt and position into a single $J_\ell$ for each layer, so the lens is fixed once and then applied to any activation.

The range of target positions in the default recipe: the source position itself plus every later position in the context. Restricting instead to $t' = t$ or $t' > t$ gives the self-only and future-only variants the appendix tests.
The reporting convention for layer $\ell$ throughout the paper: results are shown on 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers, renumbered so a layer index reads as a percentage of depth.

items.caption: The J-lens readout: lens(h_l) = softmax(W_U norm(J_l h_l))
items.title: The lens readout equation
items.takeaway: The equation defines the whole read operation of the Jacobian lens: replace every layer above $\ell$ with the single averaged matrix $J_\ell$, then run the model's own normalization and unembedding, and a softmax turns the result into a score for every vocabulary token. Sorting those scores gives the ranked word list the paper reports throughout as a readout of what an activation is disposed to make the model say.
items.walkthrough:
The item is a single display equation, the read operation of the [[jacobian-lens]]. It converts one internal activation into a ranked list of vocabulary tokens.

The input is $h_\ell$, the [[residual-stream]] vector at layer $\ell$ and some token position: one intermediate state part-way through the forward pass. The output is a score for every token in the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]].

The right-hand side is read from the inside out. $J_\ell$ is the [[averaged-jacobian]] for layer $\ell$, a fixed $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$ matrix obtained by averaging the Jacobian from layer $\ell$ to the final layer over token positions and over a corpus of a thousand prompts. Multiplying by it carries $h_\ell$ to a virtual final-layer state: where the last layer would sit, to first order and on average across contexts, given this activation. Every layer above $\ell$ is replaced by that one linear map.

The remaining two steps are the model's own output path, unchanged. $\text{norm}$ is the normalization the model applies to the final residual stream before unembedding. $W_U$, the [[unembedding-matrix]], turns the normalized vector into one logit per vocabulary token. The softmax then makes those logits a distribution.

Sorting the scores and taking the top entries gives the human-readable part: a short list of words that the activation is, on average across contexts, disposed to make the model say. The paper calls these the top lens tokens.

Two facts follow from the form of the expression. Because $W_U$ and $J_\ell$ are both linear, the pre-softmax logits are determined — approximately, up to a data-dependent normalization factor — by the inner products $\langle v_t, h_\ell \rangle$, where $v_t$ is the row of $W_U J_\ell$ belonging to token $t$. Each such row is a [[j-lens-vector]]: a direction in residual-stream space attached to a single vocabulary token. One vector can therefore be used on its own as a probe for one concept, without ranking the whole vocabulary.

The equation also places the technique against its predecessor. Setting $J_\ell = I$ recovers the [[logit-lens]], which applies $W_U$ straight to the intermediate stream. $J_\ell$ is the correction for the fact that layer-$\ell$ coordinates are not final-layer coordinates.

The readout is not uniformly informative across depth. The paper reports that in roughly the first third of the model the readouts are noisy and largely uninterpretable, and that in the last layers they flip to the imminent next token, the regime it calls the [[motor-layers]].

terms.definition: The J-lens readout of an activation: a vector of scores, one per vocabulary token, produced by the right-hand side of the equation. It is what the paper means whenever it reports the lens contents at a layer and position.
The residual-stream activation being read: the model's running vector at layer $\ell$ and some token position, taken from an ordinary forward pass. It is the only input the readout takes.
The layer index at which the activation is read. A separate lens matrix exists for each layer, so the readout is always relative to a chosen depth.

The Jacobian lens matrix for layer $\ell$: the expectation of $\partial h_{\text{final},t'} / \partial h_{\ell,t}$ over source positions, over target positions $t' \geq t$, and over a corpus of prompts. It stands in for every layer above $\ell$.

The virtual final-layer state: the first-order, context-averaged estimate of where the final-layer residual stream would be moved by the activation $h_\ell$. It lives in residual-stream coordinates, not in vocabulary coordinates.

The model's own normalization of the final residual stream, applied before unembedding in a normal forward pass. The lens reuses it unchanged, so that the vector handed to $W_U$ is scaled the way the model expects.
The unembedding matrix: the model's final linear map from a normalized residual-stream vector to one logit per vocabulary token. The lens borrows it from the model rather than fitting a new one.
The standard normalization applied to the logits, turning them into a distribution over the vocabulary. It affects the scores but not their ranking, which is what the paper mostly reads.
The composed map from a layer-$\ell$ activation to vocabulary logits, one row per token. The paper names these rows the Jacobian lens vectors at layer $\ell$.

A single J-lens vector: the row of $W_U J_\ell$ for token $t$, a direction in residual-stream space associated with the model's disposition to say that token. The pre-softmax logit for $t$ is approximately $\langle v_t, h_\ell \rangle$.
The highest-scoring tokens after sorting the readout. This short list is the human-readable description of the activation that the paper quotes in its figures and examples.
The fixed set of tokens the model's tokenizer produces. The readout assigns a score to every one of them, so the lens can only name concepts that correspond to a single token.
The width of the residual stream. $J_\ell$ is $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$, since it maps a residual-stream vector at layer $\ell$ to a residual-stream vector at the final layer.

Not in the equation itself, but the comparison the section draws: substituting the identity for $J_\ell$ turns the expression into the logit lens, which decodes an intermediate state with $W_U$ alone.

numbers.meaning: One lens matrix $J_\ell$ per layer, fixed across all prompts and positions. That sharing is what makes the readout describe a general disposition rather than the use of a concept in one context.
The shape of $J_\ell$: both its input and its output are residual-stream vectors, so both dimensions equal the model width.

The number of prompts, sampled from a pretraining-like distribution, over which the Jacobian expectation behind $J_\ell$ is taken. The appendix reports the lens already beats baselines with far fewer, so the figure is a comfortable choice rather than a threshold.

The order of the approximation. The Jacobian describes only the linear part of how a perturbation to $h_\ell$ propagates, so the readout is exact only for small perturbations and is an approximation otherwise.
The length of the output vector: $W_U$ has one row per token, so the readout is as long as the tokenizer vocabulary before any truncation to a top list.

The setting that reduces the equation to the logit lens. The paper reports the two lenses agree closely in the last several layers, where residual connections make the identity a reasonable approximation, and diverge earlier.
The target positions entering the average behind $J_\ell$: the present token and every later one, so the readout reflects effects on future output as well as immediate output.

The share of the model's depth over which the paper reports the readouts to be noisy and largely uninterpretable. It is a qualitative boundary, not a measured cutoff, and the layer-wise analysis elsewhere in the paper sharpens it.
The reporting convention for $\ell$ throughout the paper: results are read at 25 evenly spaced layers of the residual stream, renumbered so that a layer number reads as a percentage of depth.

items.caption: Lens-coordinate patching: h_patched = h + V(sigma(c) - c)
items.title: Swapping two concepts in lens coordinates
items.takeaway: These three expressions define the paper's concept-exchange surgery: read how much of a source concept and a target concept an activation carries along their two J-lens directions, exchange those two numbers, and write the difference back. Everything the activation carries outside the plane spanned by the two lens vectors is left exactly as it was, so the edit swaps one concept for another rather than replacing the activation.
items.walkthrough:
The article prints no numbered equation here. The three expressions appear inside a sentence in the methods section, and together they specify the [[lens-coordinate-swap]] used in every swap experiment in the paper.

The first expression builds the matrix. A source token $s$ and a target token $t$ are chosen — France and China, say, or spider and ant. Each has a [[j-lens-vector]] at the layer being edited: a direction in [[residual-stream]] space that, averaged over contexts, disposes the model to say that token. Those two vectors become the columns of $V$, so $V$ has $d_{\text{model}}$ rows and two columns.

The second expression reads the activation. A plain inner product $\langle v_s, h \rangle$ will not do, because the lens vectors are not orthogonal to each other: part of whatever lies along $v_t$ would show up in the source reading. The [[pseudoinverse]] $V^\dagger$ solves the least-squares problem instead. It returns the pair of weights $c$ for which $Vc$ is the closest point in $\text{span}\{v_s, v_t\}$ to $h$ — one number for how much source is present, one for how much target.

The third expression writes the edit back. $\sigma$ exchanges the two entries, sending $c = (c_1, c_2)$ to $(c_2, c_1)$. Multiplying the coordinate change by $V$ turns it back into a residual-stream vector, which is added to $h$:

$V(\sigma(c) - c) = (c_2 - c_1)\,v_s + (c_1 - c_2)\,v_t.$

The amount of source present is subtracted, and the same amount of target is added. Scaling the difference by [[swap-strength-alpha]] doubles both halves of that trade at $\alpha = 2$.

The orthogonal component follows from the algebra. Writing $h = Vc + r$ with $r$ orthogonal to the two vectors gives $h_{\text{patched}} = V\sigma(c) + r$: only the two coordinates move, and $r$ survives intact.

The swap is applied at every token position across a band of middle layers and held there, a setting the paper calls clamping. On 50 two-hop prompts it moves the target answer to top-1 on 54% of trials for Haiku 4.5 and 70% for Sonnet 4.5.

terms.definition: The activation being edited: the residual-stream vector at one layer and one token position of the forward pass, before the intervention.
The activation after the swap, written back into the forward pass in place of $h$. It differs from $h$ only within the plane spanned by the two lens vectors.
The vocabulary token naming the concept being removed — the one the model is actually representing at that position, for example France or spider.
The vocabulary token naming the concept being written in, for example China or ant. Here $t$ indexes a token in the vocabulary, not a position in the prompt.

The J-lens vectors for the source and target tokens at this layer: the rows of $W_U J_\ell$ for those tokens, each a residual-stream direction associated with the model's disposition to say that token.
The matrix whose two columns are the source and target lens vectors. Multiplying a coordinate pair by $V$ turns it into a residual-stream vector in the plane those two directions span.

The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $V$. Because $V$ is tall and its columns are not orthogonal, this is what recovers the correct coordinates rather than a plain projection onto each vector separately.
The notation for the pseudoinverse. It marks $V^\dagger$ as the least-squares generalization of a matrix inverse to a non-square matrix.
The lens coordinates: a pair of numbers giving how much of $h$ lies along $v_s$ and how much along $v_t$, in the least-squares sense of $V^\dagger h$.
The permutation that swaps the two entries of $c$, optionally with a scale factor. It is the whole content of the intervention: nothing else about $c$ changes.
The change in lens coordinates the swap requires. Multiplying it by $V$ converts that change back into a residual-stream vector to add to $h$.
An optional multiplier on the swap's magnitude, scaling how far the coordinates are pushed. The default is a plain exchange; $\alpha = 2$ subtracts the source and adds the target at double strength.
The two-dimensional plane through the origin containing all combinations of the two lens vectors. It is the only part of activation space the swap touches.
The part of $h$ perpendicular to that plane, written $r$ in the walkthrough. It carries everything else the activation represents and passes through the intervention unchanged.

Holding the swapped coordinates at their new values at every position and layer in the affected band throughout the forward pass, rather than editing once and letting later layers restore the original values.
The Jacobian lens: the per-layer matrix $J_\ell$ whose composition with the unembedding supplies the vectors $v_s$ and $v_t$ used here.
The simpler write operation the paper contrasts with the swap: adding a scaled lens vector to inject a concept, without removing anything.
The width of the residual stream. It is the number of rows of $V$ and the length of $h$, $v_s$ and $v_t$.

numbers.meaning: The number of columns of $V$, and so the number of entries in $c$. The swap is defined for exactly one source concept and one target concept, which is what makes $\sigma$ a simple exchange of two numbers.
The shape of $V$: one row per residual-stream dimension, one column per lens vector. Because it is tall, it has no ordinary inverse, which is why the pseudoinverse appears.

The plain swap, in which the source coordinate is replaced by the target coordinate and vice versa. This is what $\sigma$ does when no scale factor is named, and it is the setting reported unless the paper says otherwise.

The 'double strength' swap: the source lens vector is subtracted and the target added at twice the magnitude the plain exchange would use. The paper introduces it because the plain swap sometimes leaves the source concept still dominant.

Successful swaps at the default strength in the flexible-generalization experiment: 16 function templates times 12 source-target pairs each. Success means the target-appropriate answer reaches top-1 in the model's output.

Successful swaps in the same experiment at $\alpha = 2$. Doubling the strength converts 25 further trials, which the paper reads as evidence that many failures were partial swaps rather than absent effects.

Swap success on 50 two-hop factual prompts for Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5 respectively: the fraction of trials in which exchanging the unspoken intermediate's coordinates moves the target-appropriate answer to the top of the output distribution.
The number of two-hop factual prompts with known unspoken intermediates in that systematic evaluation, with each swap target drawn at random from the same category as the true intermediate.

sections.title: Technical details of J-lens use cases

items.caption: The J-space as a union of k-sparse cones of J-lens vectors
items.title: The J-space as a union of k-sparse cones
items.takeaway: The equation defines the J-space as $\mathcal{F}$, the union over every size-$k$ subset of J-lens vectors of the cone of their nonnegative combinations. Because the J-lens vectors are overcomplete and would otherwise span the whole residual stream, the sparsity limit $k$ is what makes the definition pick out anything at all; the price is that the resulting object is a union of cones rather than a linear subspace.
items.walkthrough:
This one line is the paper's answer to a question its earlier sections leave open: what kind of mathematical object the [[j-space]] actually is.

The ingredients come from the lens. At each layer, the [[jacobian-lens]] supplies one [[j-lens-vector]] per token in the model's [[tokenizer-vocabulary]] — here written $v_1, \dots, v_n$, with $n = n_{\text{vocab}}$. Each vector is a direction in the $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional [[residual-stream]] space, and there are more vectors than dimensions. The set is overcomplete.

Overcompleteness has a consequence the paper states plainly. The vectors typically span the entire residual stream, so any activation can be written as some linear combination of them. A set that reaches everything singles out nothing. Spanning alone therefore cannot define a workspace.

The restriction that does the work is sparsity. $k$ is the allowed number of nonzero coefficients. $S$ names one choice of which $k$ tokens may contribute, $|S| = k$ fixes its size, and $\operatorname{span}\{v_i : i \in S\}$ is the set of combinations built from those $k$ vectors alone. The coefficients are also required to be nonnegative — the sentence introducing the equation says so, though the $\operatorname{span}$ symbol does not.

Nonnegativity is what turns each piece from a subspace into a cone. Scaling a point by a positive number keeps it inside; negating a vector leaves.

$\bigcup_{|S|=k}$ then sweeps over every size-$k$ subset, so $\mathcal{F}$ collects $\binom{n}{k}$ such cones. The union is not closed under addition: two points in $\mathcal{F}$ generally sum to a point outside it, because between them they may draw on more than $k$ vectors. That is the sense in which the J-space is not a linear subspace, and the word "space" is loose.

The vectors coupled with $k$ are what the paper calls a [[sparse-subframe]] — a frame because the vectors need not be independent, sparse because of the coefficient limit, and "sub" because under that limit they no longer reach the whole space.

Two things follow. The [[j-space-component]] of an activation becomes its nearest point in $\mathcal{F}$, located by [[sparse-decomposition]]. And one candidate workspace can be compared with another through [[j-space-distance]], rather than by comparing vector sets directly.

The paper hedges on $k$. It calls the level "somewhat arbitrary", varies it across experiments, and typically keeps it at or below 25, a figure taken from the measured [[j-space-occupancy]].

terms.definition: The object being defined: the J-space itself, written as a set of points in residual-stream space. It is a union of cones, not a linear subspace.
Set union. Here it joins together one cone for every admissible choice of $k$ vectors, so a point belongs to $\mathcal{F}$ if it lies in at least one of them.
A subset of the vocabulary indices — one particular choice of which J-lens vectors are allowed nonzero coefficients. Each distinct $S$ contributes its own cone to the union.
The size constraint on the subset: exactly $k$ indices. Written under the union symbol, it says the union runs over all subsets of that size.
The allowable number of positive coefficients in a decomposition, and equally the dimension of each cone. It is a chosen parameter, not something the model supplies.
The J-lens vector for vocabulary token $i$ at the layer in question: the residual-stream direction that, averaged over contexts, disposes the model to say that token.
The full collection of vocabulary vectors at one layer, indexed by token. In the paper's use these are the J-lens vectors, but the definition is stated for any such collection.
The number of vocabulary vectors in the collection. For the J-lens it equals $n_{\text{vocab}}$, the size of the tokenizer's vocabulary.
The set of combinations of the $k$ chosen vectors. The surrounding text specifies nonnegative coefficients, so despite the notation this is the cone they generate rather than the linear span.
The set of all nonnegative linear combinations of a fixed finite set of vectors. It is closed under positive scaling and under adding two of its own members, but not under negation.
The number of tokens in the model's vocabulary, and hence the number of J-lens vectors at each layer. The paper does not print its value for the models used.
The dimension of the residual stream, and therefore of the space the J-lens vectors live in. Smaller than $n_{\text{vocab}}$, which is what makes the set overcomplete.

More vectors than dimensions, so the vectors are linearly dependent and an activation has many possible decompositions rather than one. This is why a sparsity limit is needed before the definition says anything.
A spanning set of vectors that need not be linearly independent — the generalization of a basis used when directions overlap. The J-lens vectors form one because they are overcomplete.

The paper's name for the J-lens vectors together with the sparsity level $k$. Sparse because of the coefficient limit, and 'sub' because under that limit the set no longer reaches the whole residual stream.

For a given activation, the point of $\mathcal{F}$ nearest to it: the part of the activation expressible as a sparse nonnegative sum of J-lens vectors. The leftover difference is the non-J-space component.
One row of $W_U J_\ell$: the direction in residual-stream space associated with a single vocabulary token at layer $\ell$, obtained from the corpus-averaged Jacobian.

numbers.meaning: The sparsity level the formalization section says is typically used. The appendix writes '(we typically use $k \approx 25$)' when introducing the equation.
The bound section 2.3 puts on $k$. The section calls the choice 'somewhat arbitrary' and says the value is varied throughout the paper, so 25 is a habitual ceiling rather than a fixed setting.

Where the value of $k$ comes from. Section 4.2 measures J-space occupancy — the $K$ at which sparse decomposition stops beating a same-size random control — and finds it rises to a plateau of around 25 across the workspace layers, in the median case, varying across contexts.

Each cone is spanned by exactly $k$ vectors, so the paper calls them $k$-dimensional polyhedral cones. With $k \approx 25$, each piece of $\mathcal{F}$ is a 25-dimensional cone sitting inside a much larger residual-stream space.

The number of cones in the union: one for each size-$k$ subset of the $n$ vocabulary vectors. The paper does not state this count, but it follows from the union running over all $S$ with $|S| = k$, and it is astronomically large for a full tokenizer vocabulary.

The inequality that makes the J-lens vector set overcomplete. Section 2.3 states it directly; it is why the vectors typically span the entire residual stream and why the matrix formed by concatenating them is full-rank.

The excess share of activation variance the top-$K$ J-lens vectors explain over a same-size random control, at $K$ = median occupancy. Reported in section 4.2, it indicates that most of an activation lies outside $\mathcal{F}$, so the union of cones is a thin part of what the model represents.

items.caption: Distance to the J-space d_F(x), defining the J-space component and residual
items.title: Distance from an activation to the J-space
items.takeaway: The equation defines how far an activation sits from the J-space: the smallest reconstruction error over every choice of $k$ J-lens vectors. The projection that achieves that minimum is the activation's J-space component, and what is left over is the residual the paper's ablation interventions keep.
items.walkthrough:
This equation gives a distance from a point in activation space to the J-space, and in doing so pins down two quantities the rest of the paper uses informally: the J-space component of an activation and its residual. It sits in the appendix that puts the [[j-space-formalization]] on a formal footing.

The objects come first. $v_1, \dots, v_n$ are the [[j-lens-vector]]s at one layer, one direction in [[residual-stream]] space for each token of the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. $x$ is an activation at that layer. $S$ is a subset of the vocabulary indices, and $|S| = k$ fixes its size at the allowable sparsity level. $k$ is a free parameter; the paper typically sets it near 25, the number of lens vectors it measures as meaningfully active at one time.

$\operatorname{span}\{v_i : i \in S\}$ is written as a span, but the surrounding text restricts it to nonnegative combinations of that particular choice of $k$ vectors, which makes it a $k$-dimensional cone. $\mathcal{F}$ is the union of these cones over every size-$k$ subset ([[union-of-cones]]), and that union is the [[j-space]]. It is not a subspace, because which $k$ vectors get used is part of the answer.

The second line is a search. For a given subset $S$, $\Pi_S$ projects $x$ orthogonally onto the span of those $k$ vectors, and $\| x - \Pi_S x \|$ measures how much of $x$ the projection fails to capture. The minimum of that error over all size-$k$ subsets is $d_\mathcal{F}(x)$, the Euclidean distance from $x$ to the nearest cone. The equality on the right states the same quantity directly, as the distance to the closest point $y$ anywhere in $\mathcal{F}$.

Two pieces fall out of whichever subset wins. $\Pi_S x$ is the [[j-space-component]] of $x$, the part of the activation the workspace vectors can account for. The leftover $x - \Pi_S x$ is the residual, and it is what the activation is reduced to when [[j-space-ablation]] strips the workspace contents out.

Searching every size-$k$ subset is not tractable, so the minimizing set is found in practice by [[gradient-pursuit]], a greedy algorithm that adds one vector at a time ([[sparse-decomposition]]).

A small $d_\mathcal{F}(x)$ would mean the activation lies nearly inside the workspace. The measurement runs the other way for most activations: the top-$K$ lens vectors explain under 10% of activation variance beyond a same-size random control ([[excess-variance-explained]]), so the distance stays large and the J-space accounts for a thin slice of what the model is holding.

terms.definition: The distance function from an activation $x$ to the J-space: the smallest Euclidean error left after projecting $x$ onto the span of any $k$ J-lens vectors. Small values mean the activation is close to being a sparse nonnegative sum of lens vectors.
The J-space itself, written as a set: the union, over every size-$k$ subset of the vocabulary, of the cone of nonnegative combinations of those $k$ J-lens vectors.
An activation at one layer, that is, a residual-stream vector at one token position. It is the point whose distance to the J-space is being measured.
The J-lens vectors at that layer, one per vocabulary token. Each is the direction that, on average across contexts, disposes the model to say that token later.
The number of vocabulary vectors, equal to the tokenizer's vocabulary size $n_{\text{vocab}}$. It exceeds the residual-stream width, which is what makes the set overcomplete.
The allowable sparsity level: how many J-lens vectors may carry nonzero coefficients. Without fixing $k$ the definition is empty, because the full set of lens vectors spans the whole residual stream.
A subset of the vocabulary indices, constrained to hold exactly $k$ of them. The minimization ranges over every such subset.
The set of combinations of the $k$ chosen lens vectors. The paper restricts the coefficients to be nonnegative, so this is a polyhedral cone rather than a linear subspace.
Orthogonal projection onto the span of the $k$ vectors indexed by $S$: the linear map sending $x$ to the closest point in that span.
The J-space component of $x$: the part of the activation that the winning set of $k$ lens vectors can reconstruct. This is what the paper means when it says a concept is 'in' the workspace.

The residual, or non-J-space component: everything in the activation the workspace vectors do not account for. It is the term the paper's ablation interventions leave behind after removing the J-space part.
The Euclidean norm on residual-stream vectors. The paper uses both notations for the same quantity in the two halves of the equation.
A point of $\mathcal{F}$, used in the right-hand form of the definition; the minimum over all such $y$ is the same distance as the minimum over subsets.
The minimization over all size-$k$ subsets of the vocabulary. It is combinatorial and is not computed exhaustively; gradient pursuit approximates the winning subset.
The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm the paper uses to find a nonnegative combination of $k$ lens vectors that reconstructs an activation well, standing in for the exact minimization.
The set of activation-space points expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors; the candidate global workspace this equation measures distance to.

numbers.meaning: The sparsity level, the one free parameter in the definition. The paper calls the choice somewhat arbitrary and varies it across experiments, since nothing in the model fixes a single correct value.

The value $k$ typically takes, written as $k \approx 25$. It comes from the occupancy measurement: across the workspace layers, the number of lens vectors that beat a random control in reconstructing an activation plateaus around 25 in the median case.
The dimension of each cone, one per size-$k$ subset. The J-space is a union of these cones, so it has no single dimension of its own even though every piece of it has dimension $k$.

The ceiling on the fraction of activation variance the J-space component carries, measured as variance explained by the top-$K$ lens vectors in excess of a same-size random control, with $K$ set to the median occupancy at each workspace layer. It varies by layer but never exceeds 10%, which is the paper's evidence that activations are dominated by information outside the workspace.

The overcompleteness condition: more lens vectors than residual-stream dimensions. It is why the vectors typically span the whole space, why no decomposition is unique, and therefore why the sparsity constraint $|S| = k$ is needed for the distance to be nonzero.
The subsets are of exact size $k$. Because the cones for smaller subsets are faces of the size-$k$ cones, allowing fewer vectors would not change the minimum.
